# The Corrected Treatise of Brahma

## Chapter on the Mean Motions of the Planets

<note>original: "Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta" — This title literally means 'The Corrected Astronomical Siddhānta of Brahma.' Composed in 628 CE, it is one of the most influential works in the history of mathematics and astronomy.</note>

<note>original: "Madhyamādhikāra" — This is the first chapter of the treatise. It focuses on calculating the 'mean' or average positions of celestial bodies, assuming they move in perfect circles at constant speeds before applying corrections for their actual elliptical paths.</note>

### Chapter on Mean Planetary Motions

To begin, the Master Brahmagupta—sovereign of all calculators, beholden to no other system, peerless, and expert in the methods of observing the planets—performs the auspicious invocation in the form of remembering his chosen deity, the Great God <note>Mahadeva/Shiva</note>, to ensure the completion of this book without obstacles:

> Victorious is the Great God, whose feet are streaked with the radiance of the gems in the crowns of bowing gods and demons; the creator of the world’s origin, maintenance, and dissolution. || 1 ||

-> Now the author of the commentary offers his own auspicious invocation <-

> We honor with humble compositions the Elephant-Faced Lord <note>Ganesha</note>, whose tusks possess a splendor that seems to scatter the essence of the Moon, Sun, and stars across the ten directions as they rise in constant brilliance; who is the destroyer of the mountains of obstacles, whose feet are raised in an auspicious dance, and who glows with the luster of vermilion. || 1 ||

> Having joyfully placed in his heart the planets—the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn—along with the Goddess of Speech <note>Saraswati</note>, the scholar Ramasvarupa offers this "Raft of the Scientific Commentary" as a gift for the service of the wise who desire to cross the ocean of the Brahma-treatise. || 2 ||

> Aryabhata, Brahmagupta, Varahamihira, Bhaskara, and other masters of the three branches of astronomy; the illustrious Kamalakarabhatta; the two scholars known as Srisena and Lalla; and that King named Jayasimha, who was a modern architect of astronomical instruments—these and others, such as Munishvara, are our highest objects of faith. || 3 ||

> The speech of the holy Brahma had fallen into a state of unconsciousness, as it were, due to its hidden and obscure meanings.
> To revive it, the three-branched ocean of Astral Science <note>Jyotisha, comprising mathematical astronomy, horoscopy, and samhita/omens</note> has been churned with great effort.
> Now, let the wise on earth drink this nectar of the "Science Commentary" <note>Vijnana-bhashya</note> spoken by Ramaswarupa, which is faultless and desired by the most excellent among the learned. || 4 ||

> For the swans, who discern the essence, take only the milk;
> While the restless hogs in the water, desiring only filth, take the mud. || 5 ||

**Scientific Commentary —** Mahadeva (Lord Shiva) is victorious (exists in supreme excellence). What is He like? His feet are streaked with the luster of the jewels in the crowns of the gods and demons who bow to Him (the two feet of Him are mingled with the lights and lusters of the diamonds and other gems located in the head-crowns of the gods and demons who are prostrate with bowed heads). Furthermore, what is He like? He is the agent of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe (the creator of the world's origin or manifestation, its maintenance or preservation, and its dissolution or destruction). By this, it is established that Brahmagupta accepts Mahadeva as the Supreme Lord <note>Ishvara</note>, because the power to cause the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe cannot exist in anyone other than the Supreme Lord. This subject is related to the systems of Philosophy <note>Darshana-shastra</note>, therefore there is no need for a specific investigation of it here. || 1 ||

**Hindi Commentary —** The two feet of Mahadeva are mixed with the light of the jewels (diamonds, etc.) situated on the heads of the bowing gods and demons; such a Mahadeva exists with all kinds of excellence. Furthermore, He is the doer of the world's creation, maintenance (state), and dissolution (destruction). From this statement of the teacher Brahmagupta, the divinity of Mahadeva is proved, because the power to create, maintain, and destroy the world cannot be in anyone other than God. This subject is related to the philosophy scriptures, so there is no need to consider it specially here. || 1 ||

> That planetary mathematics spoken by Brahma, which has become loose <note>inaccurate or corrupted</note> over a great length of time,

**Scientific Commentary —** The planetary mathematics spoken by Brahma (the *Brahma-siddhanta*) which exists, has become "loose" over a great length of time; meaning, after many ages had passed, it reached a state of being obstructed or decayed. For that reason, it is being stated clearly (plainly, or devoid of that "looseness") by me, named Brahmagupta, the son of Jishnu.
Among the *Brahma-siddhantas* available now: one is included within the *Shakalya-samhita*; a second is a prose version within the *Vishnudharmottara-purana*; and a third, describing a five-year Yuga cycle, is included in the *Pancha-siddhantika* composed by Varahamihira. # Chapter on Mean Motions

It is not explicitly stated what is meant by "clearly explained," yet because the values for planetary revolutions and other measurements are identical, Brahmagupta accepted the *Brahma-siddhanta* found within the *Vishnudharmottara Purana* as his authoritative source <note>original: "Agama," meaning sacred tradition or authoritative source</note>. In the chapter titled "Examination of Tantras," while describing the views of the compilers of the Samhitas—such as the idea that "a Yuga consists of five years"—it becomes clear that in Brahmagupta’s view, the *Jyotisha Vedanga* <note>The ancient astronomical auxiliary to the Vedas</note> is not the same as the Brahma tradition. Expert mathematicians should understand that this differs from the opinion of Varahamihira. This is also proven by the statement of Kamalakar in the *Siddhanta-tattva-viveka*: "Alas, even the *Vishnudharmottara* was not properly understood." It is not found anywhere in the *Brahmasphuta-siddhanta* exactly how the original *Brahma-siddhanta* became corrupted or loosened over the vast passage of time, nor how Brahmagupta specifically rectified those errors. Whether his claims are factual or otherwise is for discerning mathematicians to judge. || 2 ||

-> Now, the reason for beginning this work is stated. <-

**Hindi Commentary:** The planetary mathematics narrated by Brahma (the *Brahma-siddhanta*) became "worn out" or corrupted <note>original: "khilatva," referring to a text becoming obsolete or full of errors over time</note> due to the long passage of time. Therefore, I, Brahmagupta, the son of Jishnu, am stating it clearly. At present, three versions of the *Brahma-siddhanta* are available: first, the one within the *Shakalya Samhita*; second, the prose version within the *Vishnudharmottara Purana*; and third, the version describing a five-year Yuga found in Varahamihira’s *Pancha-siddhantika*. 

Among these three, Brahmagupta does not explicitly say which one he is clarifying. However, because the planetary revolution counts match, he accepts the *Brahma-siddhanta* from the *Vishnudharmottara Purana* as his authoritative tradition. It is clear that Brahmagupta does not consider the *Jyotisha Vedanga* to be the true Brahma tradition, as he critiques the "five-year Yuga" mentioned by the Samhita authors. This contradicts the view of the teacher Varahamihira; mathematicians should reflect on this. This is also evident from Kamalakar’s remark in the *Siddhanta-tattva-viveka*: "Alas, even the *Vishnudharmottara* was not properly understood." How the *Brahma-siddhanta* lost its precision over time and how Brahmagupta corrected it is not detailed in this text. Discerning astronomers should judge if these statements are correct. || 2 ||

-> Now he describes the motion of the celestial sphere, including the planets, which is the foundation of the science of light (astronomy). <-

> **The celestial sphere, bound to the Pole Star, was created by Brahma in the beginning, moving eastward, along with the planets situated at the junction of the constellations Revati and Ashvini.** || 3 ||

**Sanskrit Commentary:** "At the junction of Revati and Ashvini" <note>original: "Paushna" refers to the star Revati; "Ashvini" is the first nakshatra</note> means the planets (the Sun and others) were placed at the meeting point of these two constellations. "The celestial sphere bound to the Pole Star" refers to the circle of lights—the luminous stars and other celestial bodies (the Zodiac)—which is fixed to the axis or rod passing through the two poles.

Moving in a clockwise direction <note>original: "pradakṣiṇāgam"</note>, it was first created by Brahma, the creator of the world. That is to say, Brahma created the wheel or sphere of luminous objects—the stars and constellations—which rotates on the axis of the Pole Star <note>the celestial axis</note> along with the Moon and other planets situated at the beginning of the zodiac <note>starting from the constellation Ashwini</note>, as well as their apogees and nodes. Although the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> does not discuss the apogees here because they lack a physical form like the planets, their positions were nonetheless established at the very beginning of creation. || 3 ||

Here, the term "Wheel of Light" <term>Jyotish-chakra: the celestial sphere or zodiac</term> refers to the "Wheel of Stars" <term>Bha-chakra: the sidereal sphere</term>. The "Wheel of Stars" implies the spherical entity where the stars reside. For a deeper investigation into various topics—such as why the star-wheel is spherical, how its motion is understood, why planets move eastward, and why the planets (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn) are arranged in their specific vertical order—one should consult the *Vateshvara-siddhanta*. Bhaskaracharya also stated everything in accordance with Brahmagupta, saying, "Having created the wheel of stars, the Lotus-Born <note>Brahma</note> placed it with the planets in their respective revolutions," and so forth. || 3 ||

->Now the fundamental motion of the celestial sphere, including the planets, is described according to the science of astronomy.<-

**Hindi Commentary** — At the junction between the constellations Revati and Ashwini, Brahma first created the rotating celestial sphere. This sphere is bound to the polar axis <note>the line passing through both celestial poles</note> and moves in a clockwise direction along with the planets. This means Brahma created the sphere of luminous bodies—the stars and constellations—rotating on the support of the polar staff, together with the Moon and other planets located at the start of Ashwini, including their apogees. Although the Teacher does not discuss the apogees here because they do not have a physical form like the planets, he notes that their positions were marked at the beginning of creation. || 3 ||

In this context, "Wheel of Light" should be understood as the "Wheel of Stars." This term indicates that the stars and planets are all seen within a spherical structure. To consider various subjects—such as why the wheel is spherical, what its motion is and how it is known, why planets have an eastward motion, and why the planets (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) are positioned in that specific order from top to bottom—one should look at the chapter on Mean Motions in the *Vateshvara-siddhanta*. Bhaskaracharya also agrees with Brahmagupta, stating that the Lotus-Born Brahma created the wheel of stars together with the planets in their starting positions. || 3 ||

# Now he describes the commencement of time, which is without beginning or end.

> **From the sunrise of the first day of the bright half of Chaitra, the days, months, years, Eras (Yugas), and Aeons (Kalpas) began simultaneously at Lanka, on the day of the Sun.** || 4 ||

**Sanskrit Commentary** — Starting from the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Chaitra, at sunrise in the region marked by Lanka <note>the terrestrial equator</note>, the sequence of days began. This occurred on a Sunday at the beginning of creation and the beginning of the Aeon <note>Kalpa</note>. Now, if one argues that the word "bright" <note>Sita</note> is redundant because the month of Chaitra is already mentioned, that is not so. This is because there are many conflicting opinions; some desire the month to begin with the first day of the dark fortnight...

# Chapter on Mean Motions
## Page 5

The mention of the "bright half" is used to exclude the dark half. <note>The author is clarifying why the text specifies the bright fortnight (Shukla Paksha) of the month Chaitra.</note> Here, supporting evidence from Vedic and Smriti texts should also be applied:
> "That which is the New Moon of the month of Vaishakha, on that day one should establish the sacred fires; it coincides with the Rohini constellation and enters the three-fold latter half of the month. One should perform the ancestral rites (Shraddha) in the latter half, etc."

Smriti passages should be applied in this manner. Now, it is said:
> "Thus he says, the first night of the year is the Full Moon of Phalguna; that which is the latter is the last, and that which is the former [is the first]."

If it is argued that this too is a Vedic statement, then the Full Moon of the former Phalguna cannot possibly be the end of the month. This is because on the second day, the status of being in the month of Phalguna is not contradicted. The text states: "The first night of the year is the Full Moon of Phalguna, which is the latter." Therefore, its status as the beginning can be stated in this way, as both dates belong to Phalguna. This much is understood: the Phalguna Full Moon has passed, but the month of Phalguna has not yet ended. In this situation, the beginning is determined by considering the remaining statements where there is no contradiction; it cannot be imagined here by one's own will. By the mention of "in Lanka," it is indicated that while it is noon in one place, it is sunset there, midnight elsewhere, and at another place, a time exceeding one hundred and eight minutes <note>original: "eight ghatikas over a hundred"</note>. Since the progression of time and the day begins differently, the separate mention of months and years is to establish their commencement, such as the rainy season beginning in Shravana.

**Scholarly Commentary:** At the <term>Beginning of Creation</term> <note>Srishtyadi-kala</note>, starting from the bright half of Chaitra <note>Chaitra-shukla-pratipada</note>, from the time of sunrise in Lanka on the day of the Sun (Sunday), the days, months, years, Yugas, and Kalpas all commenced simultaneously. The division of all-pervading time, which is without beginning or end, into days, months, years, Yugas, and Kalpas is made for the sake of worldly transactions. The "commencement" of these divided parts of time at the <term>Beginning of Creation</term> refers to their manifestation at a single point in time. Similarly, at the end of creation (the time of dissolution), these divided parts of time come to an end. Following this logic, the introductory writing "of time which is without beginning or end" is proven to be rational. Otherwise, how could the commencement of all-pervading time be logically explained? <term>Bhaskaracharya</term> <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> also, in the <term>Siddhanta Shiromani</term> <note>Bhaskara's crown jewel of astronomical treatises</note>, says something similar to what was stated by <term>Brahmagupta</term> <note>A 7th-century astronomer</note>: "From the sunrise in the city of Lanka, on that very day, it first occurred," etc. || 4 ||

---

Now the progression of this time, which is beginningless and endless, is described.

**Hindi Commentary:** From the first day of the bright half of Chaitra, from the time of sunrise in Lanka on Sunday, at the beginning of creation, the day, month, year, Yuga, and Kalpa all began at the same time. Here, the division of all-pervading time (which has no beginning and no end) has been made for worldly use through days, months, years, Yugas, and Kalpas. The progression of these divided parts of time occurs at a single point in time at the beginning of creation, and at the end of creation (dissolution), those times end. Accordingly, writing "of time which is without beginning or end" in the introduction is logically consistent. If this were not the case, then for all-pervading time...

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

How can the commencement <note>of the planetary cycles</note> be logically consistent? Bhaskaracharya also states in the *Siddhanta-shiromani*, "From the rising of the Sun in the city of Lanka, the first day of his week began," which is in agreement with what was stated by Brahmagupta. || 4 ||

**V. Bha. <note>Commentary by Vishvanatha Jha</note>:** Now, in this science, the knowledge of all useful subjects such as the planets and stars is obtained only in relation to the Earth. Therefore, there is a deliberation to determine what its shape is and what its dimensions are. In a certain place, on level ground devoid of trees and such, someone saw at night a lit lead-pot-lamp atop a brick pillar standing at some distance. Wondering "What is this?", he approached it. Having gone near and seeing another lamp at the base of the pillar, he was astonished: "Even though there was no obstruction to my vision, why was the <insert>lower</insert> lamp not seen <insert>from a distance</insert>?" He inferred that the obstruction to his vision was the Earth itself; thus, it is proven that there is curvature on the surface of the Earth.

Furthermore, even while at the top of a tree, I observe a single ripe fruit falling in many places on the ground in all four directions; from this, it is inferred that there is an attractive force <term>akarshana-shakti<gloss>gravitational force</gloss></term> in all points residing on the Earth's surface. Likewise, by measurement, it is determined that the string <note>measuring the distance</note> from the treetop to the point of falling is shorter than the strings tied to points other than the point of falling. From seeing this natural property of a sphere—that the external segment of a line from a point outside to the surface is smaller than the external segments of other lines—the idea arose that there is a certain sphericity. Therefore, having first hypothesized that sphericity, a test is made as to whether spherical properties exist here or not.

By the power of imagination, a line is conceived passing through the center of the Earth. Since the same effect is produced by imagining the attractive force at the center of the Earth and at the surface points, it is hypothesized that this force is greatest at the very center of the Earth. A wise man certainly performs a task through many servants only if it cannot be done by one. Therefore, the wise Creator <note>Brahma</note>, for the task of attracting objects, surely passed over the surface points as "servants" and appointed the single central point of the Earth as the "servant" <note>the primary source of gravity</note>.

Having erected two equal pillars at two places on the Earth, and having sighted the top of the second pillar from both the top and the base of the first pillar, a triangle is formed. By knowing the angle of vision and the segment of the pillar within it, and by the ratio of the angles, one knows the distance between the tops of the pillars. Then: 180° — (2 $\times$ the angle at the top of the pillar) = the angle at the center of the Earth produced by the two extended pillars, because the said triangle is isosceles. Then, by the ratio of the angles:

-> (Line connecting the pillar tops $\times$ Sine of the angle at the pillar top) <-
-> ========================================================================== = Earth's Radius + Pillar Height == Known Side <-
-> Sine of the angle at the Earth's center <-

There are other subjects as well.

Now, having known the difference between two equatorial coordinates and two declinations, one calculates the maximum declination <note>obliquity of the ecliptic</note> to find the desired declination.

This calculation was performed through observation by modern scholars with extraordinary intellect via sea voyages and the like; that has been included in the *Siddhanta-Setu*. Then, from the (Known Side — Pillar Height) = Earth's Radius; having done this...

<page-num>7</page-num>
<header>Chapter on Mean Motion</header>

Everywhere, the results of observation are found to be identical; therefore, it is proven that the Earth has a spherical shape. One should not argue that this is merely a circular proof—that we are only proving what we have already assumed. By assuming sphericity, we find that in a triangle formed with a vertical pillar, the properties of an isosceles triangle are maintained <note>This likely refers to the consistency of shadow lengths and angles at equal distances from a central point</note>. Furthermore, the uniformity of results everywhere is based entirely on empirical testing; thus, all doubt is dismissed. In reality, the Earth has a slightly elongated body <note>original: "bhū-dīrgha-piṇḍa"; a reference to the Earth's non-spherical irregularities or perhaps an early intuition of its oblate nature</note>. However, because the difference between the minor diameter and the major diameter is extremely small, all the great teachers have treated them as equal.

### Here, it is explained how the Celestial Equator and the Time-Circle are defined.

Even though the celestial sphere is rotated by the *Pravaha* wind <note>The "provector wind" believed in ancient Indian astronomy to drive the daily rotation of the stars</note>, over many years, no change is observed in the distance of the stars from the fixed Pole Star (the sine of the diurnal arc). From this, it is understood that the planes of the Celestial Equator and the diurnal circles—which originate from the fixed center of the actual celestial sphere—remain stable. It is appropriate to calculate time based on these two circles rotated by the uniform *Pravaha* wind, because time is beginningless, endless, and as unchanging as the Supreme Being (*Achyuta*). This same logic is used to understand time through ancient and modern water-clocks and other instruments.

The diurnal arc of the star called *Kadamba* <note>The Pole of the Ecliptic</note> is fixed, but the stars within the *Kadamba* region are seen to move. From this, it is inferred that the zodiac has a motion other than that caused by the *Pravaha* wind. It is clear from the logic of the sphere that this motion occurs along a path that is a great circle originating from the *Kadamba*. It is inferred that the cause of this oscillating motion <note>referring to the theory of Trepidation or the precession of the equinoxes</note> is a specific "hand-strike" or impulse given to the zodiac at the moment it was released by the *Pravaha* wind. The amount of shifting of the zodiac from the Celestial Equator (the primary path of the *Pravaha*) along this great circle is defined by the teachers as the *Ayanāṃśa* <note>The precession of the equinoxes; the longitudinal difference between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</note>.

The calculation of this can be done by observing the disk of a star or a planet which has a constant position relative to the aforementioned great circle. Therefore, the knowledge of the zodiac's shift is determined specifically by observing the disk of the Sun. To determine the path of this great circle, one must understand how to find the "fixed" celestial declination from the "observed" celestial declination by knowing the difference between the planes of the observational equator and the fixed celestial equator; this is explained in this very book under the section on the "Rationalization of the Moon's Revolutions."

On the second day, in a period of sixty *ghatikas* <note>24 hours</note>, the point where the Sun is situated returns to the meridian. The time it takes for the Sun to return to the meridian, multiplied by six, gives the difference in degrees of the equator (Right Ascension), because the meridian of one's own location acts as the horizon for the equator. The declination is known by the method mentioned. By doing this over many days, placing a sphere in front of oneself, marking the great circle called the Celestial Equator, and marking the daily declinations on the meridian circles corresponding to the successive differences in Right Ascension, it is observed that a great circle connecting these points of declination is formed. By this, it is proven that the Sun's path of travel is a Great Circle. Because it passes through the points of declination (*Krānti*), the name "Circle of Declination" (*Krāntivṛtta* - the Ecliptic) is most appropriate.

<header>In the *Brahmasphuta-siddhanta* <note>The "Extensive Treatise of Brahma," a foundational 7th-century astronomical text by Brahmagupta.</note></header>

The angle formed between the celestial equator and the ecliptic <note>original: *nāḍī-krānti-vṛttayoḥ*</note> = $y$ = maximum declination <note>The obliquity of the ecliptic, approximately 23.5 degrees.</note>.
The difference in right ascension = $vi$. The middle component = $r$. Then,
by the rule that the sine of the middle arm multiplied by the radius equals the tangent of the end multiplied by the cosine of the angle:

$\sin r \times R = \cos y \times \tan(\text{declination})$, and similarly $R \times \sin(r + vi) = \cos y \times \tan(\text{declination})^1$

Therefore:
$$\frac{\sin r \times R}{\tan(\text{declination})} = \frac{\sin(r + vi) \times R}{\tan(\text{declination})^1}$$

Then:
$$\frac{\sin r \times \tan(\text{declination})^1}{\tan(\text{declination})} = \sin(r + vi)$$

Using the rule: "The sines of two desired arcs multiplied by each other's cosines and divided by the radius..." <note>This refers to the standard Sanskrit trigonometric identity for $\sin(A+B)$.</note>

$$\sin(r + vi) = \frac{\sin r \times \cos vi + \cos r \times \sin vi}{R} = \frac{\sin r \times \tan(\text{declination})^1}{\tan(\text{declination})}$$

Let the multiplier $m = \frac{\tan(\text{declination})^1}{\tan(\text{declination})}$. Thus, $\sin r \times m$.

->When both sides are multiplied by the radius:<-

$\sin r \times \cos vi + \cos r \times \sin vi = \sin r \times m \times R$. By rearranging the terms:

$\sin r \times m \times R - \sin r \times \cos vi = \cos r \times \sin vi = \sin r (m \times R - \cos vi)$

Then:
$$\frac{\sin r (m \times R - \cos vi)}{\cos r} = \sin vi$$

Therefore:
$$\frac{\sin r}{\cos r} = \frac{\sin vi}{m \times R - \cos vi} = \text{expressed value}$$

When both sides are multiplied by twelve:
$$\frac{\sin r \times 12}{\cos r} = \text{Palabhā} \text{ <note>The length of the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox.</note> at a latitude equal to } r = 12 \times \text{expressed value.}$$

The degrees of latitude of this location are the value of $r$. Alternatively, if those same two sides are multiplied by the radius:

$$\frac{\sin r \times R}{\cos r} = \text{tangent of the latitude equal to } r.$$

From the tangent, by using the inverse operation, the latitude of that place is found, which is the value of $r$. From that, the knowledge of the value of $y$ is easily obtained.

Now, the conclusion is that the motion of the celestial sphere, which is based on the ecliptic, is indeed the path of the Sun described as the ecliptic <note>original: *krāntivṛtta*</note>. By placing the pole of the ecliptic <note>original: *kadamba*</note> at the position of the celestial pole, the circle passing through the ecliptic poles at the meridian, the ecliptic at the celestial equator, and the "drkshepa" <note><term>Drkshepa</term>: The sine of the zenith distance of the highest point of the ecliptic.</note> at the position of the sine of latitude, the knowledge of the difference between the planes of the celestial equator and the ecliptic is gained. The same logic shown for calculating the declination of the planetary spheres should be applied here as well.

### Now, the determination of how the planets move eastward.

In the first quadrant, the declinations of the planets at that time are seen through observation to increase gradually; in the second quadrant, they decrease; in the third, they are like the first; and in the fourth, they are like the second. Therefore, the eastward motion of the planets is proven. Since the planets complete a <term>revolution</term><note>Sanskrit: *bhaganapurti*</note> over many days, while the <term>driving wind</term><note>Sanskrit: *pravaha* - the force believed to cause daily rotation</note> does so in a single day, the slower motion of the planets is established.

### An inquiry into whether the planetary bodies are spherical or not, and their arrangement in terms of height and depth.

If a sphere is placed anywhere and three rods are adjusted at the point of observation such that the lines of sight touch the sphere, those lines form a cone with the visible circle as its base. It is quite clear that a circle formed above the triangle created by the three lines connected at the tips of the rods, parallel to the plane of the base circle, touches the edges of the hypotenuses of said cone. The line of sight to the center of the constructed circle, when extended, passes through the center of the base circle—these are the properties of a sphere. Now, assuming sphericity in the planetary bodies, these same spherical properties are observed; therefore, the sphericity of planetary bodies is proven. How the calculation of the planetary diameters is performed through observation has been shown in this very book in the section on the <term>conjunctions</term><note>Sanskrit: *shighrochcha*</note> of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. The measurements for all planets come out unequal; for that very reason, the <term>arrangement of the orbits</term><note>Sanskrit: *kakshanivesha*</note> in vertical order (according to the principle that the orbit of a planet whose distance is greater than another's is placed above it) was established by the greatest teachers: the orbits of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the fixed stars are arranged in ascending order starting from the Moon.

->Now, how is it said that the planets move together?<-

The celestial sphere <note>original: "bhagola"</note> is indeed a sphere with a radius measured from the center of the Earth. Since the celestial equator and the celestial sphere are both threaded by the axis of the poles <note>original: "dhruva-sutra-yashti"</note>, they move together. Therefore, it is established that the spheres of the slow-moving planets <note>Saturn/Jupiter</note> and the fast-moving planets <note>Mars/Venus/Mercury</note>, which are the substrates of the planets, also move along with it.

The rotation of the celestial sphere is westward, centered on the polar axis. At the center of that axis, the Creator <note>Brahma/Nature</note> has fixed the axis of the ecliptic <note>original: "kadamba-sutra"</note> in such a way that it does not obstruct the westward rotation of the celestial sphere. When the celestial sphere rotates due to the impulse of the Creator’s hand, the ecliptic pole remains fixed at its position on the surface of the celestial sphere. Because of this, from the position of the celestial pole, the surface of the celestial sphere rubs <note>precesses/oscillates</note> up to 27 degrees in the east-west direction until the end of that velocity. Thus, it is proven that the Pole Star is not absolutely fixed; only the celestial pole itself is fixed. Therefore, the statement by Bhaskara <note>12th-century mathematician</note> that "the stars near the pole are considered the pole," and the statement by Kamalakar <note>17th-century astronomer</note> that "those who believe the Pole Star is fixed in the text are of dull intellect," are both consistent. By these proofs, the ancient teacher's statement that "the circle of the stars is bound to the Pole Star" is shown to be logically sound.

**Hindi Commentary**—In this astronomical system, the knowledge of the orbits of planets, etc., which is useful for everything, is obtained only in relation to the Earth. Therefore, we consider what its shape is and what its dimensions are to reach a conclusion. In a flat area of land free from trees, if one sees a burning lantern at the top of a brick pillar in the distance at night and walks toward it wondering "What is that?", and upon reaching the base of the pillar sees another burning lantern, a doubt arises: why was the lower lantern not visible before, even though there were no obstacles blocking the view? Upon reflection, it is understood that it is the Earth itself that blocks the sight; therefore, there is curvature on the surface of the Earth. This is proven.

Since the sky appears equal in all directions, and seeing ripe fruit falling in many places upon the Earth, it was inferred that there is a force of attraction <note>gravity</note> in every point located on the Earth's surface. And by measuring the string tied from the top of a tree to the point where the fruit falls <gloss>from the places where the fruits fall</gloss> and strings from different points to the tree-top, it was observed that the external segment of a line going to the center is smaller than the external segments of lines going from an external point to the surface. Seeing this natural property related to spheres, the idea came to mind that there is some kind of sphericity here. Therefore, one should first imagine sphericity and then see whether spherical properties exist or not. By planting two identical pillars in two places on the Earth, and placing the point of observation at the top of one pillar and then slightly away from the top, one sights the top of the second pillar. When a string is tied between the tops of both pillars, a triangle is formed. By measuring the angles at these two observation points (the top of the pillar and the other point), and knowing the distance between the two observation points by measurement, one can understand the distance between the tops of the pillars through the ratio of angles: 180 — (2 $\times$ the angle at the top of one pillar) = the angle at the center of the Earth produced by the two extended pillars. This is because the triangle formed by the two pillars and the distance between their tops is an isosceles triangle. Then the ratio of angles is calculated—

### Why the Celestial Equator is the Circle of Time.

Even when the celestial sphere is rotated by the Provector Wind <note><term>Pravaha Vayu</term>: the cosmic wind believed in ancient Indian astronomy to drive the rotation of the planets and stars</note> over many years, the distance <note>declination</note> of any star from the fixed Pole Star remains unchanged. From this, it is understood that there is stability in the planes of the Celestial Equator <note><term>Nadi-vritta</term></note> and the Diurnal Circles <note><term>Ahoratra-vritta</term></note> generated from the fixed center of the celestial sphere. It is appropriate to calculate time using these two circles rotated uniformly by the Provector Wind, because Time—which has neither beginning nor end—is always uniform according to sacred tradition. This same logic applies to the knowledge of time through ancient and modern water clocks <note><term>Ghatiyantra</term></note> and other instruments.

The declination of the Pole of the Ecliptic <note><term>Kadamba</term></note> is fixed, yet we see the stars moving around the Ecliptic Pole. This proves that besides the daily rotation <note>Provector motion</note>, the celestial sphere has another motion. This occurs along a Great Circle path originating from the Ecliptic Pole. This oscillatory motion <note>trepidation</note> can only be attributed to the initial impulse from the hand of Brahma <note>the Creator</note> at the time the celestial sphere was set in motion. The total accumulation of this movement of the celestial sphere, caused by its departure from the primary path of the Celestial Equator, is what the Teacher calls the Eastern and Western Precession of the Equinoxes <note><term>Ayanamsha</term></note>. One can determine this by observing the luminous disks of the stars or planets which remain constant relative to the aforementioned Great Circle. Thus, the movement of the celestial sphere is known through observation <note><term>Vedha</term></note>. To determine the path of this Great Circle, the method for knowing the difference between the observational equator and the fixed equator, as well as calculating celestial declination, should be sought in this very book under the explanation of the Moon’s revolutions.

On the second day, in a period of 60 *dandas* <note>24 hours</note>, the point where the Sun was on the first day returns to the Meridian <note><term>Yamyottara-vritta</term></note>. The time elapsed until the Sun itself reaches the Meridian, when multiplied by six, gives the difference in the Right Ascensions <note><term>Vishuvan-amsha</term></note> of the Sun. This is because the Meridian acts as the horizon for the equator. By the previous method, declination is also determined; by doing this over many days...

# In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta
<note>The Brahmasphutasiddhanta is a seminal 7th-century astronomical treatise by Brahmagupta.</note>

**Technical Vocabulary:** <term>Celestial Equator</term> <note>original: "Nadi-vritta"</note>, <term>Right Ascension difference</term> <note>original: "Vishuvamshantara"</note>, <term>Desired point</term>, <term>Declination</term> <note>original: "Kranti"</note>, <term>Hour circle</term> <note>original: "Dhruvaprota"</note>, <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>original: "Kranti-vritta"</note>, <term>Maximum Declination</term> <note>original: "Parama-kranti"</note>, <term>Sine</term> <note>original: "Jya"</note>, <term>Radius</term> <note>original: "Trijya"</note>, <term>Cosine-Tangent</term> <note>original: "Kospaya"</note>, <term>Tangent</term> <note>original: "Sparsharekha"</note>, <term>Equinoctial Shadow</term> <note>original: "Palabha"</note>, <term>Latitude</term> <note>original: "Akshansha"</note>, <term>Pole of the Ecliptic</term> <note>original: "Kadamba"</note>, <term>Meridian</term> <note>original: "Yamyottara Vritta"</note>.

By placing a sphere and constructing a great circle designated as the **Celestial Equator**, and by applying the difference in right ascension in the eastward direction from any desired point on it, and then applying the daily declination along the hour circles passing through that desired point and each subsequent point—it is observed that the great circle drawn through the tips of these two declinations passes through the tip of every declination. Therefore, the path of the Sun's travel is proven to be a great circle, and because that circle passes through the tip of every declination, its name is the **Ecliptic**.

Now, knowing the difference between two points of right ascension and two declinations, we calculate the **Maximum Declination** to determine the desired declination.

Here, for the derivation in Sanskrit, see (1) the diagram.
Angle produced by the Celestial Equator and the Ecliptic = Maximum Declination = *y*
Difference in Right Ascension = *vi*, Middle component = *r*,
Then, "The sine of the middle multiplied by the radius equals the product of the cosine-tangent and the end-tangent."
From this: Sine(*r*) $\times$ Radius = Cosine-Tangent $\times$ Tangent(Declination)
And: Radius $\times$ Sine(*r* + *vi*) = Cosine-Tangent $\times$ Tangent(Declination$_1$).
Here, First Declination = Declination. Second Declination = Declination$_2$.

$\therefore$ $\frac{\text{Sine}(r) \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Tangent(Declination)}}$ = Cosine-Tangent = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine}(r + vi)}{\text{Tangent(Declination}_1)}$
Then $\frac{\text{Sine}(r) \times \text{Tangent(Declination}_1)}{\text{Tangent(Declination)}}$ = Sine(*r* + *vi*),

From the rule "The sines of two desired arcs multiplied by each other's cosines," etc.:
Sine(*r* + *vi*) = $\frac{\text{Sine}(r) \times \text{Cosine}(vi) + \text{Cosine}(r) \times \text{Sine}(vi)}{\text{Radius}}$
<insert> $\frac{\text{Sine}(r) \times \text{Tangent(Declination}_1)}{\text{Tangent(Declination)}}$ = Sine(*r*) $\times$ Multiplier; here $\frac{\text{Tangent(Declination}_1)}{\text{Tangent(Declination)}}$ = Multiplier </insert>

Multiplying both sides by the Radius:

Sine(*r*) $\times$ Cosine(*vi*) + Cosine(*r*) $\times$ Sine(*vi*) = Sine(*r*) $\times$ Multiplier $\times$ Radius.
By simplifying:

Sine(*r*) $\times$ Multiplier $\times$ Radius — Sine(*r*) $\times$ Cosine(*vi*) = Sine(*r*) ( Multiplier $\times$ Radius — Cosine(*vi*) ) = Cosine(*r*) $\times$ Sine(*vi*).
Dividing by the mutual coefficients:

$\frac{\text{Sine}(r)}{\text{Cosine}(r)}$ = $\frac{\text{Sine}(vi)}{\text{Multiplier} \times \text{Radius} — \text{Cosine}(vi)}$ = Known Value.
Multiplying both sides by twelve: $\frac{\text{Sine}(r) \times 12}{\text{Cosine}(r)}$

= 12 $\times$ Known Value = **Equinoctial Shadow** of a place with latitude equal to *r*.
The value of latitude derived from this will be the value of '*r*'.
Alternatively, if those same sides are multiplied by the Radius, then $\frac{\text{Sine}(r) \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Cosine}(r)}$ = Radius $\times$ Known Value =

Tangent(*r*) = Tangent of the latitude equal to *r*. By converting the tangent segment back into an arc, the value of '*r*' becomes the latitude of that place. From this, determining the value of '*y*' <note>Maximum Declination</note> is easy.

Now, it is determined that the Ecliptic upon which the movement of the zodiac occurs is the same Ecliptic previously described as the Sun's path—the **Pole of the Ecliptic** in place of the Celestial Pole, the **Ecliptic-pole circle** in place of the Meridian, the **Ecliptic** in place of the Celestial Equator, and the Sine of Latitude...

# Chapter on Mean Motions

Taking the ecliptic zenith distance <note>original: "drkshepa"</note> at a given location, one should apply the same logic used in the demonstration of the Moon's orbit regarding the distance between the planes of the celestial equator <note>original: "nadivritta"</note>. This method is used to derive the planetary celestial declination. However, in this specific case, the difference between the vertical line and the measurement is found to be zero; thus, the proof is established.

->Now we determine why there is an absence of celestial latitude in the star Revati.<-

The lines drawn from the centers of the two spheres (the Observational Sphere and the Fixed Star Sphere) to the Ecliptic Pole <note>original: "kadamba"</note> and to the star Revati are parallel. That is to say, the pair of lines directed toward the Ecliptic Pole are parallel, and the pair of lines directed toward Revati are also parallel. Therefore, the angle formed at the Earth's center (the complement of the celestial latitude in the fixed sphere) is equal to the angle formed at the observer's station (the complement of the celestial latitude in the observational sphere). Consequently, subtracting this from ninety degrees results in a celestial latitude <note>original: "sharachapa"</note> of zero. Thus, the absence of latitude for Revati is proven.

->Now we calculate the subject at hand: the Precession of the Equinoxes.<-

When lines are drawn from the centers of the two spheres (the Earth's center and the observer's station) to the Celestial Pole <note>original: "dhruva"</note> and to Revati, the angles formed at the centers of these spheres are equal to the arc of the radius of the diurnal circle <note>original: "dyujyachapa"</note>. This is because the lines to the pole from both centers are parallel, as are the lines to Revati. Therefore, 90 minus the arc of Revati’s diurnal radius equals Revati’s declination. Then:
(Radius × Sine of Declination) / Sine of Maximum Declination = Sine of the Longitude.
By converting this sine into an arc, the longitude of Revati is found to be the Precession <note>original: "ayanamsha"</note>. This maximum value <note>original: "paramayanamsha"</note> is 27°.

The proofs for the equality of the ascendants <note>original: "lagna"</note>, the zenith distance of the nonagesimal <note>original: "vitibha-drkshepa-chapa"</note>, and the latitude arcs <note>original: "akshanshachapa"</note> of both spheres, which arise here incidentally, should be understood by the reader through similar logic.

->Now we determine why the planets have an eastward motion.<-

Through observation, we see that when a planet is in the first quadrant, its instantaneous declination increases; in the second quadrant, it decreases; the third quadrant behaves like the first, and the fourth like the second. Therefore, it is proven that planets move eastward <note>original: "purvabhimukha-gati"</note>. Furthermore, a planet's revolution <note>original: "bhaganapurti"</note> takes many days to complete, whereas the revolution of the *Pravaha* wind <note>the force believed to drive the daily rotation of the sky</note> completes in a single day. Thus, the slowness of planetary motion compared to the *Pravaha* motion is also proven.

->Now we consider whether planetary bodies are spherical and why they are arranged in a vertical order.<-

Placing a sphere at a certain point, one should position three identical rods <note>original: "yashtitraya"</note> joined at their base at the observer's station such that the lines of sight <note>original: "drishtisutra"</note> are tangent to the sphere. These lines form a pyramid <note>original: "samashuchi"</note> based on the visible circle of the sphere. The triangle formed by connecting the tips of the rods lies on a plane parallel to the base circle and passes through the edges of the aforementioned pyramid.

The <term>line of sight</term> <note>drishti-sutra</note> extending from the <term>observer's location</term> <note>drishti-sthana</note> to the <term>center of a circle</term> <note>vritta-kendra</note> passing through a triangle formed by three mutually perpendicular rods <note>samayashti-traya</note>, when extended, also passes through the center of the <term>base circle</term> <note>adhara-vritta</note>. All these are properties of a sphere, because such conditions can only exist within a spherical object. The Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note>, accepting the sphericity of the planetary bodies, observes these aforementioned spherical properties; therefore, the sphericity of the planetary bodies is proven. How the <term>knowledge of the planetary apparent diameter</term> <note>graha-bimbiya-karnajnana</note> is obtained through observation should be looked for in this very book in the section on the <term>rationale of the second inequality</term> <note>shighrochcha-upapatti</note> for **Mars**, **Jupiter**, and **Saturn**. The <term>measured values of the apparent diameters</term> of all planets were found to be unequal; therefore, the <term>arrangement of the orbits</term> <note>kaksha-nivesha</note> of the planets is in a vertical order (according to which the orbit of a planet whose measured diameter was found to be greater than another was placed above that other planet's orbit). Accordingly, the orbits of the **Moon**, **Mercury**, **Venus**, **Sun**, **Mars**, **Jupiter**, **Saturn**, and the **Constellations** have been written by all Teachers in their respective astronomical treatises in ascending order from the Moon.

### The rationale for 'With the Planets' <note>sahagrahaih</note>.

The sphere formed from the center of the Earth using a <term>desired radius</term> <note>ishta-trijya</note> or <term>semi-diameter</term> <note>vyasardha</note> is the <term>celestial sphere</term> <note>bhagola</note>. Because the <term>zodiacal belt</term> <note>bhachakra</note> and the <term>celestial sphere</term>, which are fixed to the rod of the <term>polar axis</term> <note>dhruva-sutra</note>, move together, it is proven that the <term>slow sphere</term> <note>manda-gola; related to the first inequality</note> and the <term>fast sphere</term> <note>shighra-gola; related to the second inequality</note> (which are the supporting spheres of the planets) attached to them also undergo rotation and other movements along with them.

From these proofs, everything stated by the Teachers, such as <term>'the circle of lights is bound to the Pole Star'</term> <note>original Sanskrit: "dhruvatara-pratibaddha-jyotishchakram"</note>, is proven.

The westward rotation of the <term>zodiacal belt</term> occurs on the basis of the <term>polar axis rod</term> <note>dhruva-sutra-yashti</note>. In the middle of that (polar axis), Brahma <note>the Creator</note> fixed the <term>axis of the ecliptic</term> <note>kadamba-sutra</note> in such a way that, while not obstructing the westward rotation of the zodiac, it remains fixed at the pole of the ecliptic <note>kadamba-sthana</note> on the surface of the zodiacal belt, set there by the impulse of Brahma's hand. Therefore, the <term>polar axis</term> rubs against the <term>surface of the zodiacal belt</term> <note>bhachakra-prishta</note> from the polar position up to 27° degrees towards the East and West until the completion of the stated velocity. Thus, it is proven that the Pole Star is not fixed; only the polar position <note>the celestial pole</note> is fixed. Therefore, Bhaskara’s statement, "and likewise the stars at the end [of the axis] are the poles," and Kamalakar’s statement, "Those of dull intellect consider the Pole Star to be fixed in the books," are both logically sound.

->Now, he speaks while demonstrating the identical division of time, the zodiac, and a revolution.<-

> Six breaths <note>prana</note> make one <term>vinadika</term> <note>24 seconds</note>, and sixty <term>vinadikas</term> make one <term>ghatika</term> <note>24 minutes</note>.
> Sixty <term>ghatikas</term> make a day, and from thirty days, a month is formed. || 5 ||

> Twelve months make a year. The divisions of the zodiac—ending in <term>seconds of arc</term> <note>vikala</note>, <term>minutes of arc</term> <note>lipta</note>, <term>degrees</term> <note>amsha</note>, <term>signs</term> <note>rashi</note>, and <term>revolutions</term> <note>bhagana</note>—are identical to the divisions of time starting from the <term>vinadika</term>. || 6 ||

**Vāsanā Commentary:** — A *vināḍikā* <note>approximately 24 seconds</note> is composed of six *prāṇas* <note>literally "breaths"</note> of the sidereal sphere. This refers to the relationship with the equatorial belt <note>the celestial equator</note>, because it is only on the equatorial belt that a breath of time corresponds exactly to a minute of arc. This is not the case on the ecliptic. Alternatively, for every star, there are sixty *ghaṭikās* <note>24-minute periods</note> from its rising until it returns to the same position, because the stars themselves do not move <note>referring to the fixed stars vs. moving planets</note>. However, for planets, this varies due to their own motion. Therefore, it is well said that a sidereal *vināḍikā* consists of six breaths. These breaths are measured from a healthy person, whether sleeping or awake, and not from one afflicted by disease or other ailments. Sixty of these *vināḍikās* make one *ghaṭikā*, and sixty *ghaṭikās* make one day. Thirty days make one month.

Twelve months make a year. Thus is the division of time: *vināḍikā*, *nāḍikā*, day, month, and year. The division of space <note>the celestial circle</note> is exactly the same. Just as sixty *vināḍikās* make a *ghaṭikā*, sixty *vikalās* <note>seconds of arc</note> make a *liptā* <note>minute of arc</note>. Just as sixty *ghaṭikās* make a day, sixty *liptās* make a degree. Just as thirty days make a month, thirty degrees make a *rāśi* <note>Zodiac sign</note>. Just as twelve months make a year, twelve signs make a *bhagaṇa* <note>a full revolution or circle</note>. Thus it is said that the spatial divisions ending in the revolution are equal to the time divisions ending in the year. Here, the "equality" refers to the conceptual structure of the divisions. Alternatively, in terms of arc, those *vināḍikās* correspond to six minutes of arc on the equatorial belt. This should be demonstrated on the armillary sphere.

**Vivarana Commentary:** — A sidereal *vighaṭikā* is formed by six *prāṇas* (six breaths). Sixty *vināḍikās* make one *ghaṭikā* (one *daṇḍa*). Sixty *ghaṭikās* (sixty *daṇḍas*) make a day (one solar day). A month consists of thirty days. Twelve months make a year (a solar year). The spatial divisions—seconds of arc, minutes, degrees, signs, and revolutions—should be understood as equal to the time divisions—*pala*, *daṇḍa*, day, month, and year. This means that just as a year is divided into months and days, a revolution is divided into signs and degrees. This is shown in the table below:

| | | The corresponding spatial (orbital) divisions are: | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 6 Breaths | = 1 *Pala* <note>Vināḍikā</note> | | |
| 60 *Palas* | = 1 *Ghaṭikā* | 60 Seconds of arc | = 1 Minute of arc |
| 60 *Ghaṭikās* | = 1 Day | 60 Minutes of arc | = 1 Degree |
| 30 Days | = 1 Month | 30 Degrees | = 1 Sign |
| 12 Months | = 1 Year | 12 Signs | = 1 Revolution |

In the *Siddhānta Shiromaṇi*, the teacher Bhāskarāchārya says: "In space, the divisions are equal to those of time, beginning with the year: the circle, signs, degrees, minutes, and seconds." Similarly, Śrīpati in the *Siddhānta Śekhara* states: "Thus the circle, signs, minutes, and seconds are equal in space to the time starting with the year," following the tradition of Brahmagupta. However, Śrīpati adds smaller units like the *nimeṣa* <note>a blink of an eye</note>, and Bhāskara mentions the *tatparā* <note>1/30th of a nimeṣa</note>. These measurements of the *nimeṣa* and others defined in the *Vaṭeśvara Siddhānta* differ from those stated by the aforementioned teachers. Let the discerning mathematicians examine all of these and decide for themselves. // 5-6 //

->Now the division and conception of time measurements are described.<-

Hindi Commentary—Six *asu* <note>a unit of time based on one respiration, roughly 4 seconds</note> make one sidereal *vighatika* (also called a *pala*). Sixty *palas* make one *ghati* (also called a *danda*). Sixty *ghatis* make one day, and thirty days make one month. Twelve months make one year. The divisions of space (the celestial orbit) are exactly equivalent to these units of *pala*, *danda*, day, month, and year; these are the *vikala* (arc-second), *kala* (arc-minute), *ansha* (degree), *rashi* (zodiac sign), and *bhagana* (revolution). ->The divisions of space (the orbit) are equal to these. For example:<-

| Time Units | Space Units |
|----------|----------|
| 6 *asu* = 1 *pala* | *vikala* (arc-second) |

Thus, they agree with Brahmagupta. However, Shripati adds further detail, mentioning the *nimesha* (blink of an eye) and its thirtieth part, the *tatpara*. Bhaskaracharya also goes further than Brahmagupta, defining the *tatpara* as the 1/30th part of a *nimesha* and describing even smaller units. In the *Vateshvara-siddhanta*, the teacher Vateshvara provides definitions for time measurements like *nimisha* that differ from those given by Shripati and others. Observing all these variations, discerning astronomers should reflect upon them. || 5-6 ||

# Chapter on Mean Motions
<note>original: "Madhyamādhikāra"</note>

It is stated in the Sacred Law <note>original: "Dharmaśāstra"</note> that there are four distinct ages. The *Krta*, *Treta*, *Dvapara*, and *Kali* ages are described there, and here the teacher <note>referring to Aryabhata</note> explains how they are calculated.

The word "Age" <note>original: "Yuga"</note> refers here to the **Four-Age Cycle** <note>the Mahayuga of 4,320,000 years</note>. This means: one-tenth of the Age—represented by the digits 4, 3, 2, 0, 0, 0—when multiplied respectively by four, three, two, and one, gives the individual measurements of the four ages starting with *Krta*.

Specifically: 1,728,000; 1,296,000; 864,000; and 432,000. All these are multiplied by a thousand.
- **Krta Age measure:** 1,728,000
- **Treta Age measure:** 1,296,000
- **Dvapara Age measure:** 864,000
- **Kali Age measure:** 432,000
This is the number of years for the *Krta* and other ages according to solar measurement.

**Scientific Commentary:** — A **Four-Age Cycle** <note>original: "Chaturyuga" or "Mahayuga"</note> consists of 4,320,000 solar years. Including their "twilights" <note>original: "Sandhya"</note> and "twilight-portions" <note>original: "Sandhyamsha"</note>, there are four distinct age-quarters. One-tenth of the Great Age is 432,000. When multiplied by four, the *Krta* (or *Satya*) age-quarter measure is 1,728,000. Multiplied by three, it is 1,296,000 for the *Treta* age-quarter. Multiplied by two, it is 864,000 for the *Dvapara* age-quarter. Multiplied by one, it is 432,000 for the *Kali* age-quarter.

It is further explained here that one-twelfth of an age-quarter is its **Dawn** <note>original: "Sandhya"</note>, which occurs at the beginning of the quarter. An equal amount is the **Dusk** <note>original: "Sandhyamsha"</note>, which occurs at the end of the age-quarter. The measurements of the age-quarters mentioned above include these dawns and dusks.

- Dawn years at the start of *Krta* = $\frac{1,728,000}{12}$ = 144,000. Dusk at the end of *Krta* = 144,000.
- Dawn years at the start of *Treta* = $\frac{1,296,000}{12}$ = 108,000. Dusk at the end of *Treta* = 108,000.
- Dawn years at the start of *Dvapara* = $\frac{864,000}{12}$ = 72,000. Dusk at the end of *Dvapara* = 72,000.
- Dawn years at the start of *Kali* = $\frac{432,000}{12}$ = 36,000. Dusk at the end of *Kali* = 36,000.

The sum of these four age-quarters equals the previously mentioned Great Age measure. ||6-8||

**Hindi Commentary:** — One "Age" <note>Yuga</note> consists of 4,320,000 solar years. There are four distinct age-quarters, such as *Satyayuga*, which include their respective Dawn and Dusk periods. By multiplying one-tenth of the Great Age by four, the *Krtayuga* quarter measure is 1,728,000; multiplying by three, the *Tretayuga* quarter is 1,296,000. Multiplying by two, the *Dvaparayuga* quarter is 864,000; and multiplying by one, the *Kaliyuga* quarter is 432,000.

One-twelfth of each age-quarter constitutes its own Dawn and Dusk. That is, the Dawn occurs at the beginning of the age-quarter and the Dusk occurs at the end of the same age-quarter. The previously stated age-quarter measurements include these Dawns and Dusks.

- Dawn years in *Krta* etc. $\frac{1,728,000}{12}$ = 144,000; Dusk at the end of *Krta* = 144,000.
- Dawn years in *Treta* = $\frac{1,296,000}{12}$ = 108,000; Dusk in *Treta* = 108,000.
- Dawn years in *Dvapara* = $\frac{864,000}{12}$ = 72,000; Dusk at the end of *Dvapara* = 72,000.
- Dawn at the start of the *Kali* age-quarter...

# In the Corrected Treatise of Brahma (Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta)

The Twilight period of the year == 4,320,000 / 1200 = 36,000. At the end of the Kali Yuga quarter, the Twilight portion <note>original: sandhyāṃśa</note> = 3,600. The sum of the four Yuga quarters constitutes the previously mentioned Yuga duration. Thus ends the discussion on verses 7-8.

### Now, he speaks of the flaws in the year-counts of the Kṛta and other ages as stated by Aryabhata, 
### due to their contradiction with the Sacred Tradition (Smṛti).

->**Aryabhata stated that the four quarters of the Yuga—Kṛta and the rest—are equal.**<-
->**Not a single one of those is equal to what is stated in the Sacred Tradition.**<-

**Commentary by Pṛthūdaka Svāmī <note>Vāsanā Bhāṣya</note>:** Here, "Yuga-pāda" refers to the Great Yuga <note>Mahāyuga</note>. Therefore, the "feet of the Yuga" means the four quarters of the Yuga. Aryabhata’s claim that the four ages—Kṛta and the rest—are equal quarters of a Yuga is incorrectly stated. What Aryabhata said in the *Ten Gītikā Verses*—"The quarters of the Yuga have passed from the beginning of the Manu-Yuga and the Kalpa"—is improper. This is because not even one of those Kṛta and other ages mentioned by Aryabhata is equal to the ages described in the Sacred Tradition <note>Smṛti</note>. On this matter, the Lord Manu says:

> "They say the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years. Its morning twilight is of as many hundreds, and its evening twilight is of the same amount."

By this divine measurement, the calculation is as follows: The duration of the Kṛta Yuga in divine years is 4,000; its morning twilight <note>sandhyā</note> is 400, and its evening twilight <note>sandhyāṃśa</note> is 400. Together with these twilights, the total duration of the Kṛta Yuga is 4,800. For the others, such as Tretā: Tretā is 3,000, twilight is 300, evening twilight is 300; Dvāpara is 2,000, twilight is 200, evening twilight is 200; Kali is 1,000, twilight is 100, evening twilight is 100. Thus, Tretā totals 3,600; Dvāpara 2,400; and Kali 1,200. When these are multiplied by 360 <note>the number of days in a year</note>, they become the years of the Kṛta and other ages in solar measurement, equal to the Yugas stated by Brahmagupta: 1,728,000; 1,296,000; 864,000; and 432,000. None of these are equal to Aryabhata’s figures. In the *Treatise of Pauliśa* <note>Pauliśasiddhānta</note>, the years of the Kṛta and other ages in divine measurement are:

> "Forty-eight hundred, decreasing by a quarter in sequence for the Kṛta and the rest. Those years multiplied by a hundred; their sum is the Yuga equal to the planets."

This should be seen in the *Pauliśa Siddhānta*.

**Commentary by Sudhākara Dvivedī <note>Viveka Bhāṣya</note>:** Aryabhata stated that the four ages—Kṛta and the rest—are equal quarters of the Yuga, meaning he considered the Yuga quarters to be fourth-parts of a Great Yuga. Among those Yuga quarters, not even one is equal to what is stated in the Sacred Tradition <note>Smṛti</note>. The durations of the Yuga quarters mentioned in the Smṛti are not equal. Therefore, the equal Yuga durations stated by Aryabhata contradict the Smṛti and should be disregarded. Aryabhata’s statement regarding the Yuga quarters is: "The Yuga quarters are 1,080,000 years each." Furthermore—

> "Forty-eight hundred, decreasing by a quarter in sequence for the Kṛta and the rest. Those years multiplied by a hundred; their sum is the Yuga equal to the planets."

In this way, the year-counts for the Kṛta and other Yuga quarters in divine measurement as stated in the *Pauliśa Siddhānta* are seen to be equal to those in the Smṛti. Aryabhata’s opinion is not supported by any statement from the Smṛti or the Purāṇas; therefore, his view is not sound. Among the authors of astronomical treatises, only the author of the *Vaṭeśvara Siddhānta* accepts this view of Aryabhata, but he provides no strong evidence for it. Therefore, that view is also not sound. ||9||

Now the measures of the <term>Yuga-charanas</term><note>The four quarters or stages of a Great Age: Krita, Treta, Dvapara, and Kali.</note> as stated by Aryabhata are described, and also refuted.

**Hindi Commentary:** Regarding Aryabhata’s claim that the four stages of the ages (the quarters of a <term>Mahayuga</term><note>A Great Age consisting of 4,320,000 solar years.</note>) are equal in length: none of these stages match the lengths described in the <term>Smritis</term><note>Traditional Hindu religious texts, such as the Laws of Manu.</note>. The age-lengths mentioned in the Smritis are not equal to one another <note>Traditionally, the ages decrease in length in a 4:3:2:1 ratio</note>. Therefore, Aryabhata’s view of equal age-quarters is contrary to scripture and should be disregarded. Aryabhata’s statement on this is "The quarters of the age are 1,080,000 years each." However, in the *Paulisha-Siddhanta*, the divine measures of the ages like Krita are seen to match the years stated in the Smritis. Aryabhata’s opinion is not supported by any Smriti or Purana; thus, his view is incorrect. In the *Vateshvara-Siddhanta*, the teacher Vateshvara accepted Aryabhata’s view, but he failed to provide any strong evidence to counter the established views of the lawgivers. Therefore, his opinion is also incorrect. ||6||

->Now the measures of Manu and the measures of a Kalpa are stated.<-

> A <term>Manu</term><note>A Manvantara, or the lifespan of a progenitor of humanity.</note> consists of seventy-one Great Ages. Fourteen such Manus make a <term>Kalpa</term><note>A Day of Brahma.</note>. In the junctions at the beginning, middle, and end of these Manus, there is a period equal to a <term>Krita Age</term><note>The Golden Age, lasting 1,728,000 years.</note>. From this, a Kalpa totals one thousand Great Ages. ||10||

**Sanskrit Commentary:** A Manu consists of seventy-one ages. By the word "age," a <term>Chaturyuga</term><note>A cycle of the four ages combined.</note> is meant. This means a <term>Manvantara</term> is formed by seventy-one Great Ages. A Kalpa consists of fourteen Manus. If this is so, one might doubt how a Kalpa can be called a thousand Great Ages. To answer this, he says: "In the junctions at the beginning, middle, and end of the Manus, there is a period equal to the Krita Age." There is a junction at the start, junctions between the Manus, and a junction at the very end. Thus, for fourteen Manus, there are fifteen such junctions. In each of these junctions, the time is equal to a Krita Age. For this reason, the Kalpa is described in the Smritis as consisting of one thousand Great Ages.

The calculation is as follows: A Manvantara is 71 Great Ages. Multiplied by fourteen, this equals 994. The Krita Age (1,728,000 years) multiplied by the fifteen junctions equals 25,920,000 years. Dividing this by the measure of a Great Age (4,320,000), we get 6. Adding this 6 to the previously established 994, we get exactly 1,000. Those who claim a Kalpa consists of 1,008 Great Ages are in contradiction with the Smritis. For the Lord Manu said: "A thousand cycles of the divine ages are known as a single Day of Brahma, and his Night is of the same length." Likewise, the sage Vyasa said: "Those who know that the Day of Brahma ends after a thousand ages, and the Night also ends after a thousand ages, are the true knowers of day and night." ||10||

**Scientific Commentary:** A Manu is said to be seventy-one ages. Fourteen Manus make a Kalpa. Because the time at the beginning, middle, and end junctions of the Manus is equal to a Krita Age, a Kalpa is therefore one thousand Great Ages.

### Here is the proof—demonstrating how a thousand Yugas constitute a Kalpa:—

One Manu consists of seventy-one Yugas = 71 Yugas, but there are fourteen Manus in a Kalpa; therefore 14 Manus = 71 Yugas x 14 = 994 Yugas. However, it is stated that at the beginning, middle, and end of the Manus, there are "twilight" periods <note>original: "sandhi"</note> equal to the duration of a Krita Yuga <note>The Krita Yuga is the first and longest of the four ages, often called the Golden Age.</note>.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Twilight and twilight-fractions = Krita Yuga quarters x 15 | Twilights in fourteen Manus = 15 |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 4 Yugas x 15 | Virtue-quarters in a Yuga = 10 <note>A full Great Yuga is divided into 10 parts: 4 for Krita, 3 for Treta, 2 for Dvapara, and 1 for Kali.</note> |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;= ————— = 6 Yugas | &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 4 x Yuga |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 10 | Therefore = ————— = Krita Yuga |
| | &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 10 |

Therefore: 14 Manus + Manu twilight-fractions = 994 Yugas + 6 Yugas = 1000 Yugas = 1 Kalpa = a Day of Brahma.

By this calculation, the Puranic statement that "a day of Brahma is said to be four thousand Yugas" <note>original: "chatur-yuga-sahasrena..." - this refers to 1000 cycles of the four-age system</note> and Brahmagupta's statement that a Kalpa is a thousand Yugas are both proven. In the *Surya Siddhanta*, the author says: "Thus, with a thousand Yugas, the Kalpa which causes the destruction of beings is declared a Day of Brahma." Bhaskara also says in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*: "A thousand Yugas shall be a day of the Creator; that is also a Kalpa." Thus, the same point is affirmed. || 10 ||

->The proof of why a Kalpa consists of one thousand Yugas.<-

One Manu consists of seventy-one Yugas, but there are fourteen Manus in a Kalpa; therefore 14 Manus = 71 Yugas x 14 = 994 Yugas.

But because there is a twilight <note>sandhi</note> equal to a Krita Yuga at the beginning, middle, and end of the Manus, the twilight-fractions related to the fourteen Manus = Krita Yuga x 15. Therefore, the twilights related to the fourteen Manus = 15.

# Now, he explains a specific detail regarding the Kalpa.

> Those who do not desire the transitions at the beginning, middle, and end of the Kalpa-Manus to be equal to the years of a Krita Age <note>The Krita Yuga or Satya Yuga is the first and longest of the four ages, lasting 1,728,000 years</note>, for them, a Kalpa consists of a thousand Yugas minus six (994 Yugas), totaling 4,294,080,000 years. ||11||

**Vāsanā-Bhāṣya <note>The author's own explanatory commentary</note> —** The "Kalpa-Manus" are the Manus within a Kalpa. For those who do not wish for the transition periods <term>Sandhi: a transitional period between two ages</term> at the beginning, end, and middle of these Manus to be equal to the Krita Age, their Kalpa consists of nine hundred and ninety-four Yugas. What is being said here? This was already implied by the previous explanation of the verse.

**Vijñāna-Bhāṣya <note>A scientific or technical commentary</note> —** In the opinion of those who do not accept the transition periods at the beginning, middle, and end of the fourteen Manus as being equal to a Krita Yuga, the Kalpa consists of a thousand Yugas minus six.

One Manu consists of seventy-one Yugas. Since there are fourteen Manus in a Kalpa: 14 Manus × 71 Yugas = 994 Yugas. In standard practice, the measurement of the dawn and twilight transitions <term>Sandhyā-Sandhyāṃśa</term> related to the fourteen Manus is added to this to find the true length of a Kalpa. However, for those who do not include these transition periods, the Kalpa is simply 994 Yugas. ||11||

-> Now, a specific point is made regarding the Kalpa. <-

**Hindi Commentary —** The teacher states that for those who do not consider the transitions at the beginning, middle, and end of the fourteen Manus to be equal to the years of the Krita Age (Satya Yuga), the measure of a Kalpa is one thousand Yugas minus six (994 Yugas). ||11||

### Now, he presents the opinion of Aryabhata regarding the Kalpa:

> Aryabhata desires the Manu-transition to be equal to a Yuga; because of this, his Manu consists of seventy-two Yugas. His Kalpa consists of one thousand and eight Chatur-yugas, totaling 4,354,560,000 years. ||12||

**Vāsanā-Bhāṣya —** The "Manu-Sandhi" is the transition of a Manu. Aryabhata desires this transition to be generally equal to a Yuga. Since his Manu is "Kha-Yuga" <note>A technical term here implying a specific numerical count, often interpreted as 72</note>, his Manu-interval <term>Manvantara</term> is calculated accordingly. Thus, his Kalpa consists of one thousand and eight Chatur-yugas. As it is said, "A day of Brahma consists of one thousand and eight cycles of the planets." Just as a heap of grain is measured by units like Kudava, Prastha, and Drona, time is measured in the Smritis <note>Traditional legal and religious texts</note> by Yugas, Manvantaras, and Kalpas. However, this specific calculation is not found in the Romaka Siddhanta as composed by Sri-Shena.

In the *Romaka* (the *Romaka Siddhanta* <note>An astronomical treatise influenced by Greek/Roman systems</note>), these do not exist—meaning there is no mention of their names—for that reason, the *Romaka* is outside the *Smriti* tradition, and thus the *Romaka Siddhanta* should be rejected here. In reality, only those who perform astronomical calculations can understand the importance of *Yugas*, *Manvantaras*, and *Kalpas* for the purpose of calculating the positions of the planets and other celestial bodies. Without them, the entire science of astronomy would be meaningless. Therefore, even those of dull intellect will be able to understand what kind of errors were made by the author of that system by not discussing these matters in the *Romaka Siddhanta*. || 13 ||

In the *Romaka Siddhanta*, there is no discussion of any of these; therefore, that system is "outside the *Smriti*," meaning it is excluded from the sacred traditional scriptures and is thus to be rejected. In fact, only those who calculate planetary positions can know the primacy of *Yugas* and *Manvantaras* for determining the planets. Without them, the entire science of astronomy is useless. Therefore, a very great error was made in the *Romaka Siddhanta* by not discussing them, a fact that even those with little knowledge can understand. || 13 ||

## In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
<note>The "Brahmasphuta-siddhanta" is the seminal 7th-century work by the mathematician-astronomer Brahmagupta.</note>

->[Diagram showing the celestial sphere with intersecting arcs and points labeled in Devanagari script]<note>The diagram illustrates the relationship between the observer's zenith, the ecliptic, and the planetary positions.</note><-

**Kha** = One's own zenith.
**Sam** = Intersection of the geocentric celestial sphere.
**Sam'** = Intersection of the topocentric (surface) celestial sphere.
**Stha** = The intersection point of the <term>Kadamba-vritta</term> <note>the circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic</note> and the <term>Kranti-vritta</term> <note>the ecliptic or the sun's path</note> passing over the geocentric disk.
**Stha'** = The intersection of the topocentric disk's <term>Kadamba-vritta</term> and the ecliptic circle.
**Kha-Stha'** = The topocentric zenith distance of the planet at point **Stha'**.
**Kha-Gra** = The geocentric zenith distance on the celestial sphere, equal to the zenith distance of the planet at **Stha'**.
**Gra** = The planet on the geocentric sphere's vertical circle, corresponding to the planet seen on the observational sphere.
**Vi-Kha** = The zenith distance of the geocentric disk of the planet.
**Vi** = The <term>Vitribha</term> <note>the nonagesimal, or the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note> (on the surface sphere).

In this context, in the spherical right-angled triangle **Kha-Vi-Stha'**, the value of the hypotenuse arc **Kha-Stha'** should be determined using the base and perpendicular sides **Vi-Kha** and **Stha'-Vi**. That itself becomes the value of **Kha-Gra**. This is because the vertical circle is one and the same, and the line of sight from the Earth's center to **Gra** is proven to be parallel to the line to **Stha'**. Subsequently, in the spherical triangle **Kha-Vi-Gra**, by knowing the sides **Kha-Gra** and **Kha-Vi** and the included angle (the difference in azimuth), the value of the arc **Vi-Gra** is produced. From that, the distance **Stha'-Gra** between the planets must be known. This very value is the distance between the observed (topocentric) and true (geocentric) planet—a calculation for which scholars "immerse themselves in the ocean of mathematics." What more need be said?

### Now, the Explanation of the Revolutions of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus.

Now, according to the teacher's statement that "the revolutions of the Sun are the solar years," the number of solar years in a <term>Kalpa</term> <note>an eon or vast period of time in Hindu cosmology</note> is exactly equal to the number of the Sun's revolutions. However, since the measure of a Kalpa-year is already known, the measure of the Sun's revolutions is also known. Regarding the visibility of Mercury and Venus: at the time of the Sun's rising and setting, the degrees of separation between the Sun and Mercury, and the Sun and Venus, should be determined daily using instruments. These always come to less than three signs (90 degrees). Even the teacher Varahamihira, in the *Brihat Jataka*, while refuting the characteristics of the *Vajra* and other yogas mentioned by previous teachers, states: "I have described the *Vajra* etc. according to the ancient scriptures. But how can Mercury and Venus be in the fourth house from the Sun?" By this, he means the distance between them and the Sun is very small. For that reason, because they are situated very close to the Sun, they are always seen moving like two followers, sometimes in front and sometimes behind. Therefore, the teachers have accepted that their revolutions in a Kalpa are equal to the Sun's revolutions in a Kalpa.
