### Proof of "Divine Days are Equal to the Revolutions of the Sun," etc.

The North Pole is the upper zenith for the Gods, and the South Pole is for the Demons. The circle at ninety degrees from the zenith (the Pole) is the celestial equator, which serves as their horizon circle. When the Sun is north of the celestial equator (from the start of Aries to the end of Virgo), it is a six-month day for the Gods and a night for the Demons. Similarly, when the Sun is south of the celestial equator (from the start of Libra to the end of Pisces), it is a six-month night for the Gods and a day for the Demons (following the rule that the Sun above the horizon constitutes day and below the horizon constitutes night). Therefore, the time taken to traverse the twelve signs starting from Aries (one complete revolution of the Sun) is established as one solar year, which is one full day-and-night <term>Ahoratra: a 24-hour period comprising both day and night</term> for the Gods and Demons.

In truth, in the time it takes the Sun to travel from Aries to Pisces, there is also a slight movement of the equinox. Thus, by applying a correction for the time generated by the precession of the equinoxes at the end of the Sun's revolution, the true measure of that day-and-night would be found. The movement of the equinox is called precession <term>Ayanagati: the precession of the equinoxes</term>. The Teacher <note>referring to the original author of the root text</note> did not accept the precession of the equinoxes, so there is an error here resulting from that. Even in Bhaskara's statement, "A solar year is declared as the Sun's completion of the circle," the same error exists. Brahmagupta only states that Divine days are equal to the Sun's revolutions and does not discuss the days of the Demons. Since the night of the Demons occurs when it is day for the Gods, and the day of the Demons occurs when it is night for the Gods—the two occurring simultaneously in reverse—I have shown the day of the Demons along with the day of the Gods. || 25 ||

# On the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
<note>The Brahmasphuta-siddhanta is a 7th-century astronomical treatise by Brahmagupta.</note>

It is stated in the Puranas and other texts that the Pitrs <note>Ancestors/Manes</note> reside there; based on this, we consider the following. How much of the upper surface (upper part) of the Moon should be taken? By drawing multiple tangent lines from the point of observation (the Earth's center) to the lunar orb, the region of the lunar orb generated by each point of contact is circular; what remains after subtracting this from the lunar orb is the upper part of the Moon. It is known from the words of the Puranas that the Pitrs dwell there. Where the line from the Earth's center to the Moon's center meets the radius-sphere meridian of the Pitrs, that is the Moon transformed into the Pitrs' radius-sphere, and it is also the upper zenith <term>Khasvastika: the point directly overhead</term> of the Pitrs. 

When the Sun arrives there, because the Sun and Moon are in the same location, it will be the time of the New Moon <term>Amanta-kala: the end of the lunar month</term>. Since the transformed Moon is the upper zenith of the Pitrs and the Sun is also there, the Sun's arrival at the upper zenith results in two watches of the day (midday or noon). Thus, it is proven that at the time of the New Moon, it is midday for the Pitrs. Then, when the next New Moon occurs, it will be the second midday for the Pitrs; therefore, the time from the first New Moon to the second New Moon (one lunar month) is equal to the time from the first midday to the second midday. However, the time from the first midday to the second midday is equal to the time from the first sunrise to the second sunrise (a full day and night). Therefore, it is proven that a full day and night <term>Ahoratra</term> of the Pitrs is equal to one lunar month.

But here, the consideration that the New Moon time is the midday for the Pitrs has been accepted; this is not entirely correct. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya has also accepted the New Moon time as the midday for the Pitrs with the statement: *'Since the New Moon is their midday.'* <note>original: "दर्शो यतोऽस्माद् द्युदलं तदेषाम्"</note> Midday for them occurs only when the Sun reaches the meridian of the Pitrs—that is, the secondary to the celestial equator passing through the Moon. Only if the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the Moon is the meridian of the Pitrs will there be identity between the New Moon time and the Pitrs' midday. 

But such a situation occurs only at the location where the Moon has no latitude <note>the nodes</note> and also when the Moon is at the end of Gemini <note>the summer solstice</note>. For instance, only if the Sun's center is where the line from the Earth's center to the Moon's center meets the Pitr-sphere will there be identity between midday and the New Moon time due to the Moon's lack of latitude at that New Moon point. And when the Moon is at the end of Gemini on the ecliptic, only when the Sun is at the intersection of that solstitial colure and the ecliptic does identity between the New Moon time and the Pitrs' midday occur. At places other than these two, the Pitrs' meridian is either east or west of the New Moon point—that is, the Sun's position at the intersection of the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the Moon and the ecliptic itself. The time it takes for the Sun to reach the Pitrs' meridian from the New Moon time is equal to the <term>Ayanadrikkarma: the correction for the ecliptic's obliquity</term>. If the New Moon time is corrected by that time, the Sun is then at the Pitrs' meridian; that is the true midday for the Pitrs.

See diagram (A) here. RN == minutes of the *Ayanadrikkarma*. Therefore:
**New Moon Time ± Ayanadrikkarma = True Midday of the Pitrs.**
The midnight should also be understood accordingly.

Because the Sun is at the upper zenith of the Pitrs (at the transformed lunar point), it is their midday at the New Moon. When the Sun is at the lower zenith, six signs away from the transformed Moon...

# Chapter on Mean Motions

...by remaining [there], the night-half of the ancestors is established at the end of the full moon. Now, we consider where the rising and setting times of the ancestors occur. The point where the line from the Earth's center to the Moon's center touches the Moon's surface is the "transformed Moon" <note>The point on the lunar surface directly facing Earth</note>, and that is also the upper zenith <term>Khāsvastika|The point directly overhead in the celestial sphere</term> of the ancestors. The circle formed at a radius of ninety degrees from the ancestors' zenith is the ancestors' horizon circle. When the Sun is located there, the circles passing through the transformed Moon and that Sun are called the "Circle of Illumination" <term>Sitavṛtta|The circle dividing the illuminated and dark halves of a celestial body</term>. By drawing a circle through the poles of the ecliptic <term>Kadambaprotavṛtta|A secondary circle passing through the ecliptic poles</term> passing over the transformed Moon, a spherical right-angled triangle is formed by the arcs of the Circle of Illumination, the circle through the ecliptic poles, and the ecliptic. In this, the arc of the Circle of Illumination (the zenith distance between the Sun and Moon on the illumination circle) is the hypotenuse; the arc of the ecliptic (the local zenith distance between the Sun and Moon) is the upright side; and the arc of the circle through the ecliptic poles is the latitude <note>the "arm" or base</note>. In this spherical right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse arc of the Sun-Moon zenith distance on the illumination circle = 90°. Therefore, by the logic of spherical geometry, the upright arc of the Sun-Moon zenith distance on the ecliptic will also be equal to ninety degrees. Thus, at the time of the ancestors' rising and setting, the difference between the Sun and Moon will always be equal to ninety degrees, because the intersection point of the circle through the ecliptic poles over the transformed Moon and the ecliptic is the Moon's position. Therefore, the rising of the ancestors should be understood at seven and a half days <note>the midpoint of the quarter</note> of the dark fortnight, and the setting at seven and a half days of the bright fortnight. In the *Siddhānta Shiromaṇi*, Bhāskarācārya says: "The Sun rises for the ancestors at the half-point of the dark fortnight and sets at the half-point of the bright fortnight; this is established by the very meaning." However, the rising and setting times of the ancestors stated by Bhāskara have been refuted by Mahāmahopādhyāya Paṇḍit Sudhākara Dvivedī. For example:

A triangle is formed by making a plane parallel to the lunar-core horizon from the point where the line from the Earth's center to the Moon's center touches the Moon's surface. The Moon's distance <note>hypotenuse</note> plus the Moon's radius from the Earth's center to the Moon's surface is the first side (upright). At the time of rising and setting, the Sun's center is always on the surface horizon; therefore, the Sun's distance there is the second side (hypotenuse), and the surface horizon plane is the third side. In the right-angled triangle generated by these sides, we calculate the proportion: if we get the Radius <note>Trijyā</note> in the Sun's distance, what will we get in the Moon's distance plus the Moon's radius? The sine of the angle attached to the Sun's center:

->Sine of Angle = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times (\text{Moon's Distance} + \text{Moon's Radius} \times \frac{\text{1}}{\text{2}})}{\text{Sun's Distance}}$ Its arc = Arc. By subtracting from ninety degrees, the Earth-center-<-

attached angle measurement, i.e., the Sun-Moon zenith distance on the illumination circle = 90° — Arc. Then, by the rule "The degrees of the Sun and Moon divided by twelve..." etc., the measurement of the elapsed lunar day <term>Tithi|A lunar day, 1/30th of a synodic month</term> at the time of the ancestors' rising:

->$= \frac{90 - \text{Arc}}{12} = 7 \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\text{Arc}}{12}$<-

Looking at this, it is clear that the rising time of the ancestors does not occur exactly at seven and a half days of the dark fortnight, but is established at the time resulting from subtracting $\frac{\text{Arc}}{12}$ from seven and a half. Similarly, their setting time also does not occur exactly at seven and a half days of the bright fortnight. Therefore, Bhāskara's statement "The Sun rises at the half-point of the dark fortnight" etc., is not correct. However, there is also an error in the refutation made by Mahāmahopādhyāya Paṇḍit Sudhākara Dvivedī; in the logic of the refutation mentioned above, the lunar day measurement brought from the Sun-Moon distance on the illumination circle using "The degrees of the Sun and Moon divided by twelve" is not correct. It is proper to calculate the lunar day from the Sun-Moon distance on the ecliptic; therefore, the said refutation is also flawed. Thus, now the method for its true calculation [is as follows]:

# In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta
<note>The Corrected Treatise of Brahma, a foundational 7th-century text by Brahmagupta</note>

[The calculation] is demonstrated as follows. In the triangle formed by the distance between the Sun and Moon on the white circle <note>the lunar orbit</note> as the hypotenuse, the distance between the Sun and Moon on the ecliptic as the base, and the Moon's latitude as the perpendicular side: the degrees of distance between the Sun and Moon on the white circle are known by the previously stated rule, and the Moon's latitude is also known. Then, by the rule that the product of the sine of the base and the cosine of the side is equal to the product of the radius and the cosine of the hypotenuse:

Cosine of the distance on the white circle $\times$ Radius = Cosine of the distance on the ecliptic $\times$ Cosine of the latitude.

Dividing both sides by the (Cosine of the latitude):

Cosine of the distance on the white circle $\times$ Radius
----------------------------------------------------------- = Cosine of the distance on the ecliptic.
$\quad\quad$ Cosine of the latitude

By subtracting the arc of this value from ninety degrees, the degrees of the distance between the Sun and Moon on the ecliptic are found. By means of this, one should calculate the <term>Tithi</term> <note>lunar day</note> at the time of the ancestors' <note>the Pitris, residing on the Moon</note> sunrise and sunset; that will be the true Tithi. Thus ends [this section].

---

->Now the proof is shown for why a Divine Day is equal to one revolution of the Sun<-

The zenith of the Gods is the North Pole; the zenith of the Demons <note>Asuras</note> is the South Pole. The circle formed at a ninety-degree arc from the zenith (the Pole) is their horizon circle, which is the <term>Nadivritta</term> <note>the celestial equator</note>. When the Sun is north of the celestial equator (from the beginning of Aries to the end of Virgo), it is a six-month day for the Gods and a six-month night for the Demons. Conversely, when the Sun is south of the celestial equator (from the beginning of Libra to the end of Pisces), it is a six-month night for the Gods and a six-month day for the Demons. (By the rule that the Sun being above the horizon constitutes day and below it constitutes night). Therefore, the time it takes for the Sun to traverse the twelve signs from Aries (one solar revolution) is established as one <term>Ahoratra</term> <note>a full 24-hour cycle of day and night</note> for the Gods and Demons. 

However, during one revolution of the Sun, there is also a slight movement of the equinoxes; this is called <term>Ayanagati</term> <note>precession of the equinoxes</note>. Therefore, to find the true duration of the day and night for the Gods and Demons, one must apply a correction for the time generated by this precession at the end of the Sun's revolution. Here, the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> has not included the precession, so there is that much error. Bhaskaracharya also says the same thing in "The Sun's revolution is declared a solar year," etc., and contains the same error. Here the Teacher says "Divine days are the Sun's revolutions," referring to the days of the Gods; he has not explicitly discussed the Demons. The nights and days of the Gods and Demons are inverse, but the total duration of the day-and-night cycle is equal for both. Therefore, along with the day-and-night of the Gods, the day-and-night of the Demons is also shown. If "Divine Day" is taken to include the day of the Demons as well, then no further explanation is needed. Thus ends [verse] 25.

---

Now, having raised the doubt of how the <term>Ahargana</term> <note>the heap of days; the number of elapsed days since the start of an epoch</note> and other calculations are obtained for the elapsed time from the beginning of creation up to the <term>Shaka</term> era <note>an era starting in 78 CE</note>, he states the solution with reasoning:

> **In the latter half of the Kalpa, six Manvantaras have passed, and twenty-seven Great Ages.**
> **Three ages (Krta, Treta, Dvapara) have passed; of the Kali age, 3179 years had elapsed at the end of the Shaka year.** <insert>3179</insert> **— 26.**

# Nine, seven, one, seven, four, nine, two, nine, seven, one: 1,972,947,179 years at the end of the Shaka King's era.
# Along with the elapsed Manvantaras <note>A vast period of time ruled by a Manu</note> and the junctions (Sandhis) occurring at the beginning, middle, and end. || 27 ||

**Vāsanā-bhāṣya (Commentary):** — The word *Ka* refers to Brahma. Half of the total lifespan (*Parardha*) of the Kalpas of that Brahma has passed. In the current Kalpa, six *Manus* have passed. Twenty-seven times three <note>original: "tri-ghna," meaning multiplied by three, here referring to the 27th cycle</note> of the Four-Age cycles (*Chaturyugas*) have passed. Three ages starting with the Golden Age (*Krita*, *Treta*, and *Dvapara*) have passed. From the start of the *Kali* age (the current Iron Age), the years are "cows-limbs-qualities" <note>A chronogram where cows=9, limbs=6, qualities=3, but here interpreted as 3179</note> or 3179 years; these are the years elapsed prior to the time of the Shaka King.

To illustrate: The years of a Kalpa are 4,320,000,000. When multiplied by the number of the first half of Brahma's life (an eighteen-digit number), we get the total elapsed time. From the current Kalpa, six *Manus* have passed. Having calculated the years for the three ages (Krita, etc.) and adding the elapsed years of the Kali age previously established, the years passed at the end of the Shaka era are: nine, seven, one, seven, four, nine, two, nine, seven, one... <note>The text lists a massive number representing the total solar years elapsed since the beginning of the current cosmic cycle</note> 1,972,947,179. These many years have passed for Brahma according to solar measurement (*Saura-mana*).

Others explain it differently: a *Parardha* of Kalpas is but a single day for *Ka* (the Supreme Being). Because this is taught in the "Chapter on Measurements" by the Teacher (*Acharya*). The explanation regarding the six *Manus* passing in the current Kalpa remains the same. As the author of the Puranas says: "A period of three days for the Supreme Being is said to be equal to a *Parardha* of Kalpas." || 26-27 ||

**Vivarana-bhashya (Explanatory Commentary):** — In the second half of Brahma's life, six *Manus* have passed; twenty-seven *Chaturyugas* (Great Ages) have passed; three quarters of the twenty-eighth age (Satyayuga, etc.) have passed; and 3179 years of the Kali age have passed up to the end of the Shaka King's era. Along with the junctions (*Sandhis*) located at the beginning, middle, and end of the six elapsed *Manus*, the total years at the end of the Shaka era are 1,972,947,179. In the second half of Brahma's life, six *Manus* are gone; in the current seventh *Manu*, twenty-seven cycles of ages are gone; in the twenty-eighth cycle, the first three quarters of the age are gone; and 3179 solar years of the Kali age have passed up to the Shaka era. The sum of these is calculated as follows:

->According to the verse: 6 Manus + 7 Manu-junctions + 27 Ages + 3 Age-quarters + 3179<-
->$= 6 \text{ Manus} + 7 \text{ Manu-junctions} + 27 \text{ Ages} + (\text{Age} - \text{Kali-quarter}) + 3179$<-
->$= 6 \times 71 \text{ Ages} + 7 \times 4 \times 432,000 + 27 \text{ Ages} + (\text{Age} - \text{Kali-quarter}) + 3179$<-
->$= 6 \times 71 \times 4,320,000 + 7 \times 4 \times 432,000 + 27 \times 4,320,000$<-
->$( 4,320,000 - 432,000 ) + 3179$<-
->$= 426 \times 4,320,000 + 28 \times 432,000 + 27 \times 4,320,000$<-
->$+ ( 4,320,000 - 432,000 ) + 3179$<-

<note>The calculations above use the standard Vedic astronomical units: 1 Mahayuga = 4,320,000 years. A Manu-junction (Sandhi) is equivalent to the length of a Krita Yuga (1,728,000 years or 4/10ths of a Mahayuga).</note>

# Chapter on Mean Motions
<page-num>57</page-num>

[These calculations] have been performed; without this, the calculation of the *Ahargana* <note>The number of elapsed days since a fixed epoch</note> and other factors cannot be achieved. Bhaskaracharya <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> also speaks in accordance with the teachings of Brahmagupta, stating "Six Manus have passed in the Yuga..." and so forth. || 26-27 ||

->The creation of planets and stars occurs at the beginning of Brahma's day; their dissolution occurs at the end of the day.<-
->Because the Kalpa exists, the years elapsed in the Kalpa are used in planetary mathematics.<- || 28 ||

**Vasanabhashya (Explanatory Commentary):** The creation of the planets and the stars occurs at the beginning of the day of Brahma, which is the start of the *Kalpa* <note>A vast period of time equal to 4.32 billion years</note>. At the end of the day, there is dissolution—the destruction of the planets and stars once again at the end of the Kalpa. Because this is so, only the Kalpa is utilized in planetary mathematics. This means that before or after that period, planetary mathematics does not exist [as the bodies themselves do not exist]. In the second half of the verse, <unclear>the reading of others</unclear> is: "Since the Kalpa exists, planetary mathematics exists." This means that planetary mathematics began from the very moment the Kalpa commenced. The phrase "years elapsed in the Kalpa" will be connected to what follows, as he now states those elapsed years previously mentioned.

**Vijnanabhashya (Scientific Commentary):** The "planets and stars" refers to the celestial bodies; their "origin" or creation happens at the beginning of Brahma's day, the start of the Kalpa. Likewise, at the "end of the day," meaning the conclusion of Brahma's day or the end of the Kalpa, the "dissolution" or destruction of these planets and stars occurs. This implies the following: the measure of a Kalpa is one day of Brahma. This is supported by the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit treatise on astronomy</note> which states: "A Kalpa is said to be a day of Brahma." His night is of the same duration. According to the teachings, "Having withdrawn all objects, Brahma sleeps," Brahma creates the universe at the start of his day (the Kalpa). At the end of the Kalpa, he gathers everything back into himself and sleeps. Therefore, planets and stars only exist during the "Creation-Kalpa." At the end of the Kalpa, all these planets and stars are dissolved into Him.
> "From the unmanifested, all manifestations come forth at the arrival of the day; at the arrival of the night, they dissolve into that very thing known as the unmanifested." <note>original: "अव्यक्ताद्वयक्तय: सर्वा: प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे । रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसज्ञके"</note> — This is the word of the Lord [from the Bhagavad Gita].

Now, for the reason that the Kalpa exists—here, the word "Kalpa" specifically refers to the "Day-Kalpa." It is only during this period that planets and the like exist. Only while these planets exist can their motions be understood. For this very reason, Bhaskaracharya also stated in his own *Siddhanta Shiromani*: "Since their creation is at the start of the day and their dissolution is at the end of the day, the study of their movements is only possible while they exist." Therefore, for the purpose of understanding the motion of the planets in planetary mathematics, the "years elapsed in the Kalpa" are calculated. It is noted by Mahamahopadhyaya Muralidhara Jha that this verse is not found in the edition edited by Mahamahopadhyaya Sudhakara Dvivedi. However, Munishvara has included and collected it with great respect in the commentary on the *Shiromani* titled *Marichi*. Therefore, the author's intention is that only this "Day-Kalpa" is of use [for calculations], and no other. || 28 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** One day of Brahma is equal to one Kalpa. This is the view of the *Agama* scriptures. The statement of the *Surya Siddhanta* is that "A Kalpa is said to be a day of Brahma."

> **“From the unmanifest, all manifest beings proceed at the coming of day; at the coming of night, they dissolve into that very thing known as the unmanifest.”** <note>This is a quote from the Bhagavad Gita (8.18), used here to provide scriptural authority for astronomical cycles.</note>

At the start of the day, all these things emerge in manifest form from the unmanifest Brahma, and at the start of night, they all dissolve back into that same unmanifest Brahma. Therefore, the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> states here that the reason planets exist only during the Day of Brahma (Kalpa) is due to their motion; to calculate this, one requires the measurement of years within the current Day-Kalpa, not from any other Kalpa. This is the author's intent. || 28 ||

---

->Now he describes Aryabhata’s opinion regarding the elapsed time of the Kalpa<-

> **Aryabhata’s Manu is considered greater than the Manu mentioned in the Smritis by one Chatur-yuga.**
> **The time elapsed in his Kalpa is greater by three Yugas joined with a twentieth part.** || 29 ||

**Vasanabhashya (Explanatory Commentary):** The Manu mentioned in the *Smritis* <note>Traditional legal and religious texts like Manusmriti</note> is the "Smriti-stated Manu." Aryabhata’s Manu is greater than that Smriti-stated Manu by **one Chatur-yuga** <note>A Great Age consisting of 4,320,000 years</note>. Because of this, the time elapsed in his Kalpa is greater by three Yugas plus one-twentieth of a Yuga. For example: six Manus multiplied by 72 equals 432—these are the Chatur-yugas for six Manus. Adding 27 Chatur-yugas <note>the elapsed time in the current Manu</note> equals 459. These multiplied by the years in a Chatur-yuga equal 1,972,880,000. In these quarters of the Yuga, adding three times 2,080,000 results in the number 6,240,000. Adding the Kali Yuga years... the total number of years elapsed since the start of the Kalpa according to Aryabhata’s method is 1,656,123,179. As stated in the *Dashagitika* <note>Aryabhata's famous ten-stanza astronomical work</note>: **"The elapsed Manus and Yugas..."** from the start of the Kalpa, the Yuga-quarters and the weekdays before the Bharata war. When the difference is taken between that sum and the time elapsed in Brahma’s Kalpa (1,942,947,000), the excess years are **13,176,000**. This much time is greater in Aryabhata’s system, which equals three Chatur-yugas plus one-twentieth of a Chatur-yuga. To demonstrate: a Chatur-yuga's years (4,320,000) multiplied by three is 12,960,000. One-twentieth of a Chatur-yuga is 216,000. Adding this results in 13,176,000. These years equal the excess time. Thus it is said: **the elapsed time of his Kalpa is greater by three Yugas joined with a twentieth part.**

**Vijnanabhashya (Scientific Commentary):** Aryabhata’s Manu (the Manu described by Aryabhata) is greater than the Manu of the Smritis by one **Chatur-yuga** (one Great Age). The Manu described in the *Manusmriti* and other texts is equal to 71 Yugas. Aryabhata’s Manu is equal to 72 Yugas; therefore, the difference between them is one Yuga. In Aryabhata’s system, the time elapsed since the start of the Kalpa is greater by three Yugas plus a twentieth part. The difference between the elapsed Kalpa time according to the two teachers (Brahmagupta and Aryabhata) is three Yugas and one-twentieth of a Yuga. || 29 ||

### The Proof Herein

According to the teacher's <note>referring to Aryabhata</note> view, the measure of a Yuga in the Golden Age (*Satya Yuga*) = 1/4.
The measure of the Yuga during the seven junctions (*Sandhis*) at the beginning, middle, and end of the six elapsed *Manvantaras* <note>vast periods of time presided over by a Manu</note> = 7/4 × 4 = 7.

**Hindi Commentary:** There is a difference of one Great Age (*Mahayuga*) between the Great Ages described by Aryabhata and those in the *Laws of Manu* (*Manusmriti*). According to the *Manusmriti*, there are 71 Great Ages, while according to Aryabhata's view, there are 72. The difference lies solely in the perspective of when the beginning of the *Kalpa* <note>a "Day of Brahma," lasting 4.32 billion years</note> is considered to occur. || 26 ||

### Now, two verses regarding the calculation of the elapsed Solar and Civil days of the Kalpa:

**The number of elapsed years of the Kalpa multiplied by twelve, increased by the months beginning with Chaitra, is placed below.**
**This is multiplied by the intercalary months of the Age, divided by the solar months, and the resulting intercalary months are added.** || 30 ||
**Multiplied by thirty and increased by the elapsed lunar days (*Tithis*), this is placed separately and multiplied by the omitted lunar days (*Avama*) of the Age. Divided by the lunar days of the Age, the resulting omitted days are subtracted. The result is the heap of civil days (*Ahargana*) suitable for solar calculations, beginning with Sunday.** || 31 ||

**Vasanabhashya Commentary:** In this context, the term "Age" (*Yuga*) is taken to mean the *Kalpa*. Therefore, the elapsed solar years starting from the beginning of the *Kalpa* are multiplied by twelve. That product is then increased by the lunar months elapsed since the month of *Chaitra* <note>the first month of the Hindu lunar calendar</note>.
In the current *Kalpa*, the years that have passed are 1,972,947,179 <note>original: "nava-naga-shashi-muni-krita-naya-maganda-nandendu," a numerical code where words represent digits</note> plus the elapsed years of the *Saka* era. These are multiplied by twelve. By adding the lunar months passed since the bright half of *Chaitra*, the "heap of elapsed solar months" is calculated, starting from the beginning of the *Kalpa*. Even though a solar month is defined by the sun's entry into a zodiac sign (*Sankranti*), there is no error here because the fractions of intercalary months are included. 

<margin>The calculation of the *Ahargana* (day-count) remains accurate even if the time of the intercalary month is distant.</margin>

If the sun's entry into a sign occurs exactly at the time of the new moon, there is still no error because the month is essentially a double-month. All lunar months were initiated by the Teacher to be calculated this way. To identify the intercalary month (*Adhimasa*) as the end-limit of those months, the solar month-count is calculated; because lunar months are shorter than solar months, the lunar months will be greater in number. 

Therefore, the solar month-count is placed separately below. Then, the rule of three is applied: "If in the total solar months of a *Kalpa*, a certain number of intercalary months are obtained, then how many are obtained in these elapsed solar months?" Adding these to the elapsed solar months gives the total elapsed lunar months from the start of the *Kalpa*. By stopping at the end of those months, the remainder of the intercalary months is also passed. To understand the past and future occurrences of intercalary months: if the total intercalary months of a *Kalpa* are obtained from the total solar months, then what is obtained from a single solar month? This gives the remainder of the intercalary month.

# In the Corrected Treatise of Brahma (Brahmasphuta-siddhanta)

At the beginning of the <term>Kalpa</term> <note>A vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years</note>, all months are provided as lunar months. To establish the rule of three <note>A mathematical proportion: if A yields B, what does C yield?</note> for bringing about the intercalary months <note>Extra months added to the lunar calendar to keep it in sync with the solar year</note> from the solar months, we previously performed a calculation. The result produced from that is the number of lunar months. By subtracting the remainder from the total intercalary months of a Kalpa, the remaining solar and intercalary portions are determined. This time is to be declared as the "fall" or occurrence of the intercalary month. Alternatively, one should convert the solar months into days; by that process, and by restricting the desired lunar days, the knowledge of the past and future time is obtained.

**Vasanabhashya (Commentary): —** Then, the collection of elapsed lunar months should be multiplied by thirty and added to the lunar days (<term>tithis</term>). Because a lunar day is indeed a <term>tithi</term>, the total count of elapsed <term>tithis</term> from the start of the Kalpa is calculated at the end of the desired <term>tithi</term> in mean time. That itself is the lunar day-count. That should be set aside separately. Then, multiplied by the "deficient days" of the age and divided by the lunar days of the age, the result and remainder give the solar-civil (<term>savana</term>) day-count starting from Sunday.

Here the rule of three is: if for the lunar days of a Kalpa being converted to civil days, the "omitted lunar days" (<term>avama</term>) of the Kalpa are lost, then for the elapsed lunar days, how many are lost? The result is the omitted days related to the elapsed lunar days. By subtracting these from the lunar day-count, the count of elapsed civil days from the start of the Kalpa is found. Since the difference between civil and lunar measures is the "omitted days," and the epoch is midnight at Lanka, the day-count starts from Sunday, as the Kalpa began on a Sunday.

From the remainder of the omitted days, the knowledge of the past and future time of the day-night occurrence is found. "Namely": if by the lunar days of a Kalpa, the omitted days of a Kalpa are obtained, then by one lunar day, what is obtained? ... (by the Kalpa) equal to the night... the remainder of the omitted days is obtained. The second rule of three: if this civil remainder of omitted days... of a day... what... those are the lunar days of which this desired daily remainder is civil. Here, the divisor and multiplier have equal denominators.

The measure is the lunar days of the Kalpa. In that, the desired remainder of omitted days has a multiplier of one, and the "deficient nights" of the Kalpa is the divisor. The result is the lunar days until the fall of the deficient night. By subtracting that remainder of omitted days from the lunar days of the Kalpa, and treating the remainder as the "omitted-remainder," the time is calculated as stated. At the time of the fall of an intercalary month, even if two months are given, only one month is actually counted. Even if two <term>tithis</term> are given, only one weekday is obtained.

Now, one wishes to know: after how many days does an intercalary month fall? Namely: if by the solar days of a Kalpa, the intercalary months of a Kalpa occur, then by one intercalary month, how many solar days are there? The result is the solar months: 32 <note>original: "shada-ga-nanda-randhra" (6, 3, 9, 9 reversed/coded)</note> and the fraction is 136,200,000 / 1,593,300,000.

Alternatively, if by the intercalary months of a Kalpa, the lunar days of a Kalpa are obtained, then by one intercalary month, what is the result? The lunar days are 1006 <note>original: "rasa-rudra-nanda-kha-candra" (6, 11, 9, 0, 1)</note> and the fraction is the same: 136,200,000 / 1,593,300,000.

Alternatively, if by the intercalary months of a Kalpa, the civil days of a Kalpa are obtained, then by one intercalary month, how many civil days? The result is 990 civil days and the fraction is 546,450,000 / 1,593,300,000. Within these ranges, the intercalary month remains.

Alternatively, by the remainder of omitted days: if by the deficient nights of a Kalpa, the lunar days of a Kalpa are obtained, then by one deficient night, how many lunar days? The result is 63 lunar days and the fraction 22,798,350,000 / 25,082,580,000. Here, by reducing the numerator and denominator by the common factor 2,082,181,800, the result is shown as $63 \frac{10}{11}$.

### The Proof

Now, desiring to explain the calculation of the mean planets, the Teacher first establishes the civil day-count from the beginning of the Kalpa, which is necessary for that purpose.

By the method previously described, having calculated the solar years until the desired Saka era and multiplying by twelve, the solar months at the end of the desired Saka year are found. To this, one should add the solar months equivalent to the lunar months from the end of Chaitra to the desired New Moon; this gives the solar months from the start of the Kalpa until the transit <note>Sankranti</note> of the desired month. Because of the lack of knowledge regarding the mean Aries transit, the months are taken from the end of Chaitra. This is the only way, as there is no other rule available. This becomes the count of desired solar months from the start of the Kalpa to the desired monthly transit. Then, by the Rule of Three <note>Trairashika</note>, the intercalary months associated with this, along with the remainder, are calculated.

-> Intercalary months of Kalpa $\times$ Desired solar months / Solar months of Kalpa = Desired intercalary months + Remainder/Solar months of Kalpa <-

---

-> $\therefore$ Therefore, the lunar months at the time of the desired transit, including fractions = Desired solar months + Desired intercalary months + Remainder/Solar months of Kalpa <-

---

-> Here, the fractional part of the intercalary remainder is in lunar units. It represents the interval between the New Moon and the solar transit. <-

## In the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta

> “The remainder of the intercalary month <term>Adhimāsa-śeṣa: the fractional part of an extra lunar month added to synchronize with the solar year</term> always remains prior to the time of the solar transition <term>Saṃkrānti: the moment the sun enters a new zodiac sign</term> starting from the end of the new moon.” — as stated by Bhāskara <note>original: "दर्शाग्रतः संक्रमणकालतः प्राक् सदैव तिष्ठत्यधिमासशेषः"</note>.

In this context, by subtracting the fraction of the intercalary remainder, one arrives at the time of the end of the lunar day <term>Tithi: a lunar day, roughly 1/30th of a lunar month</term>. Therefore, the desired number of lunar months elapsed since the start of the Chaitra month is: [Desired Solar Months + Intercalary Months]. This sum, when multiplied by thirty and added to the desired lunar days, results in the total lunar days elapsed at the end of that specific lunar day. Therefore, by using a proportion to find the corresponding omitted lunar days <term>Avama: 'lost' days where a lunar day ends before a sunrise</term> and subtracting them here, the result is the civil day count <term>Sāvana Ahargaṇa: the count of days from sunrise to sunrise</term> including its fractional parts at the end of the lunar day.

$\therefore \frac{\text{Total Omitted Days} \times \text{Elapsed Lunar Days}}{\text{Total Lunar Days}} = \text{Omitted Days} + \frac{\text{Omitted Remainder}}{\text{Total Lunar Days}}$

$\therefore$ The civil day count at the end of a lunar day (with fractions) = Elapsed Lunar Days $-$ Omitted Days $-$ $\frac{\text{Omitted Remainder}}{\text{Total Lunar Days}}$. Since the difference between the end of the lunar day and sunrise exists here, if the omitted remainder is added, the civil day count at sunrise becomes a whole number. The day count = Elapsed Lunar Days - Omitted Days.

By observing the equation shown here, it is understood that the solar month count at the time of the desired solar transition, when combined only with the intercalary months, becomes the lunar month count at the end of the lunar day. In this way, the lunar day count at the end of the lunar day, when deprived of the omitted days, becomes the civil day count for the sunrise immediately following the end of that lunar day. For this reason, the intercalary remainder and the omitted remainder are discarded.

->Now, this is considered for the sake of understanding:<-

 Ka     Da     Cha     Va     Am      Ti      U      Sa     U

Ka = Beginning of the Kalpa <note>The start of the current cosmic age</note>.
Cha = End of the new moon in the month of Chaitra.
Va = End of the mean solar year.
Ti = End of the lunar day of the desired month.
U = Time of sunrise.
Sa = Desired solar transition <term>Saṃkrānti</term>.
Am = End of the new moon of the desired month.

By bringing the solar year count from point **Ka** to point **Va** and multiplying by twelve, the solar month count for that interval is obtained. Here, from the end of the Chaitra new moon to the end of the desired new moon (**Am**), whatever lunar month-ends occur should be treated as solar months and added to the previously calculated solar month count. When this is done, the solar month count at the point of the desired solar transition is established. Here, to calculate the lunar months at the time of the end of the new moon (**Am**), if one grants an equal number of lunar months for every solar month starting from point **Ka**, the conclusion would have occurred earlier at some new moon point. This is because the solar month count is smaller in number <note>Solar months are longer than lunar months, so the same number of solar months covers more time</note>. Suppose this completion occurred at point **Da**. Here, the intercalary months between points **Da** and **Am** are whole numbers. The value of the intercalary remainder lies between points **Am** and **Sa**. Therefore, the solar month count contained between points **Ka** and **Da**—

It is evident that by adding the number of lunar intercalary months <note>Adhimasa: extra months added to the lunar calendar to align it with the solar year</note> contained within point *A* and *D* to the total number of lunar months, the total lunar month count at point *A* is obtained. Then, by converting this into days, the lunar day-count <note>Chandra-ahargana</note> at point *A* is established. By adding the number of elapsed lunar dates <note>Tithis</note> to this, we find the lunar day-count at point *Ti*. Here too, by assuming a civil <note>Savana</note> measure equal to the number of lunar days at point *Ti*, and by adjusting these individual civil days from point *K*, one would move somewhat forward from point *U*. This is because the number of lunar days is greater than the number of civil days. That forward point is designated as *U*. Here, it is clear by their very nature that the days between point *U* and *U* are civil in character. When these specific days are subtracted from the lunar days associated with the civil count, the civil day-count <note>Savana-ahargana</note> at point *U* is achieved. In this calculation, the remainders of the intercalary months and omitted days <note>Adhishesha and Avamashesha</note> are not taken into account. Therefore, Bhaskara has stated, "Here, the remaining ghatikas (fractions of a day) and so forth are not accepted."

Thus, in deriving lunar time from solar time, the intercalary months are lunar in nature, and likewise, the intercalary remainder is lunar. Similarly, in deriving civil time from lunar time, the omitted days <note>Avama</note> are civil in nature, and their remainder is also civil.

In this way, when determining the elapsed years of a Kalpa from the day-count, the omitted days found by proportion from the civil day-count are of the lunar class. The remainder is of the same class. This would be exactly equal to the previously calculated civil-natured omitted remainder. Similarly, in deriving solar time from lunar time, the intercalary months are of the solar class, and their remainder is the same. This is also clearly understood by those skilled in mathematics to be equal to the previously calculated lunar intercalary remainder, according to the logic demonstrated hereafter. Therefore, whether the intercalary month is considered lunar or solar, the remainder remains equivalent. However, here solar days are the divisor, whereas elsewhere lunar days are; all this has been explained in detail by the teacher Bhaskara in the spherical astronomy texts <note>Siddhanta Shiromani, Goladhyaya</note> starting with the verse "If those solar days are with the intercalary..."

### Now, the Calculation of the Total Elapsed Days (Ahargana) is Described

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the number of years elapsed since the beginning of the Kalpa <note>1,572,947,196 years</note> by twelve. Add the number of months elapsed since the start of the month of Chaitra and place this sum in two positions. In one position, multiply by the number of intercalary months <term>Adhimasa: months added to synchronize lunar and solar years</term> defined for the Yuga <note>a vast cosmic cycle of time</note> and divide by the number of solar months in a Yuga. Add the resulting intercalary months to the value in the second position. Multiply that sum by thirty and add the number of lunar dates <term>Tithi: a lunar day, roughly 0.94 of a solar day</term> elapsed since the first day of the bright fortnight <note>Shukla Pratipada</note>. Place this result in two positions. In one position, multiply it by the number of omitted days <term>Avama-dina: "lost" days where a lunar date ends before a sunrise</term> in a Yuga and divide by the lunar days in a Yuga. Subtract the resulting elapsed omitted days from the value in the second position. The result is the Solar-Civil Day Count <term>Ravi-Savana-Ahargana: the total number of civil days elapsed since the epoch</term>. The sequence of the day-count begins with Sunday; therefore, the authorities state "Beginning with the Sun" <note>original: "Arkadih"</note>. || 30-31 ||

## Proof

The calculation of the *Ahargaṇa* <note>The "heap of days" or total elapsed days since the beginning of a cosmic epoch</note> is performed using the knowledge of the Shaka year, the seven months, and the lunar date (*tithi*). From the teacher's verse beginning with "In the half of a *Kalpa*, six *Manvantaras* have passed," the number of elapsed years from the beginning of creation to the end of the previous year is known. If one marks a point representing the end of a gift <note>The author uses "gift" (dana) as a metaphor for the progression or "giving" of time units</note> equal to the lunar years since creation, that point will always fall at the end of a *Chaitra* month. Furthermore, the number of solar days from the elapsed *Mesha* <note>Aries/Solar New Year</note> to the desired date is greater than the lunar days from the end of the last *Chaitra* to the end of the desired *tithi*. This is because the starting point of the solar year (*Mesha*) occurs after the end of the lunar year (*Chaitra*). When lunar days equal to the desired *tithi* are added to the end of the lunar year, that point falls exactly at the end of the desired *tithi*, because a lunar day is shorter than a solar day <note>original: चान्द्र दिन < सौरदि.</note>.

Since the number of solar and lunar years "given" since creation are equal, the difference between the solar end-point and the lunar end-point (at the desired *tithi*) consists of the "fractional intercalary months" (*savayava-adhimāsa*). Within this, the portion from the lunar end-point to the end of the desired *tithi* is the full intercalary month, and the remainder (from the *tithi* end to the solar end) is the "intercalary residue" (*adhisheṣa*). The difference between the lunar days at the solar end and the solar-equivalent lunar days is the fractional intercalary month. While the lunar intercalary month occurs before the solar end and the solar intercalary month after, we must take the former here. Therefore, we calculate it as follows:

-> (Intercalary months in a *Kalpa* × Elapsed solar days) / Solar days in a *Kalpa* = Elapsed intercalary months + (Intercalary residue / Solar days in a *Kalpa*) <-

In this calculation, the intercalary residue is discarded because it represents the span from the end of the desired *tithi* to the solar end. By multiplying the number of elapsed intercalary months by thirty to get intercalary days and adding the elapsed solar days, we arrive at the "Lunar *Ahargaṇa*" at the end of the desired *tithi*. Then, using the proportion—if in the total lunar days of a *Kalpa* we get a certain number of omitted days (*avama*), what do we get in our calculated Lunar *Ahargaṇa*?—we find the elapsed omitted days along with the "omitted residue" (*avama-sheṣa*):

-> (Omitted days in a *Kalpa* × Elapsed lunar days) / Lunar days in a *Kalpa* = Elapsed omitted days + (Omitted residue / Lunar days in a *Kalpa*) <-

By subtracting these elapsed omitted days (including the residue) from the Lunar *Ahargaṇa*, we get the "Civil *Ahargaṇa*" (*savana-ahargaṇa*) at the end of the *tithi*. The formula is: Lunar *Ahargaṇa* – Elapsed omitted days – (Omitted residue / Lunar days in a *Kalpa*). However, since the omitted residue exists between the end of the *tithi* and sunrise, adding the omitted residue to the Civil *Ahargaṇa* at the end of the *tithi* gives us the Civil *Ahargaṇa* at the time of sunrise:

Lunar *Ahargaṇa* – Elapsed omitted days – (Omitted residue / Lunar days in a *Kalpa*) + (Omitted residue / Lunar days in a *Kalpa*) = **Lunar *Ahargaṇa* – Elapsed omitted days**

->Elapsed Omitted Lunar Days = Civil Day Count at the end of the Tithi + $\frac{\text{Remainder of Omitted Days}}{\text{Lunar Days in a Kalpa}}$ = Civil Day Count at Sunrise.<-

Since the days of the *Ahargana* <note>The total count of civil days elapsed from the start of the epoch</note> are fixed, dividing the *Ahargana* by seven and taking the remainder gives the day of the week starting from Sunday. This is because the *Kalpa* <note>A vast cosmic period of 4.32 billion years</note> began on a Sunday; therefore, the count must begin with Sunday. Thus, what has been stated by the ancient teachers is proven. The *Ahargana* derived here is the "Mean Civil Day Count" because it is calculated using proportions. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, the teacher Bhaskara II also performed the calculation in this manner, starting with the verse "The number of solar years elapsed in the Kalpa..." and so on. This concludes the explanation for verses 30-31.

### Now, the calculation of the mean positions of the planets, as well as their slow (apogee) and fast (conjunction) nodes.

> Multiply the *Ahargana* by the number of revolutions of the desired planet in a *Kalpa*, and divide by the total civil days in a *Kalpa*.
> The result, in revolutions and their fractions, is the mean position at Lanka at the time of sunrise. ||32||

**Commentary:** The term "planet" here includes the planets themselves, their *Manda* <note>slow motion/apogee</note>, *Shighra* <note>fast motion/conjunction</note>, and *Pata* <note>nodes</note>. The meaning is as follows: multiply the desired planet's total revolutions in a *Kalpa* by the current *Ahargana* and divide by the total civil days in a *Kalpa*. The result is the planet's position in revolutions, signs, degrees, etc. This is based on the Rule of Three <term>Trairashika: a mathematical proportion</term>: if in the total civil days of a *Kalpa* the planet completes its total *Kalpa*-revolutions, then in the current *Ahargana*, how many revolutions does it complete? 

In this calculation, the completed revolutions are usually discarded, and the remainder (signs, degrees, etc.) is kept. However, for specific astronomical problems or corrections, the full number of revolutions is retained. The remaining details are well-known and thus not illustrated with examples. This result is the "Mean" position, meaning it refers to the position on the celestial orbit. It is calculated for the meridian of Lanka <note>The prime meridian in ancient Indian astronomy, located on the equator</note> at the moment of sunrise. For other locations, a correction for terrestrial longitude <note>Deshantara</note> must be applied to find the local sunrise position.

The mean daily motion of a planet is found by calculating its movement for a single day. I am recording here the established daily motions for the Sun and other bodies, along with their fractional remainders in *Tatparas* <note>1/3600th of a degree</note>, as composed in verses by the scholar Balabhadra:

> The Sun's motion is 59 minutes, 8 seconds, and 10 thirds.
> The remainder is 6, 9, 9, 1, 8, 0 <note>699,180</note>.
> For Mars, the motion is 31 minutes, 26 seconds, and 28 thirds.
> The remainder is 2, 2, 0, 6, 5, 2 <note>256,022</note>.
> For the fast motion of Mercury, it is 245 minutes and 32 seconds.
> The remainder is 9, 0, 1, 2, 4 <note>90,124</note>.
> The motion of Jupiter is 4 minutes, 59 seconds, and 9 thirds.
> The remainder is 2, 7, 9, 0, 5 <note>27,905</note>.
> For the fast motion of Venus, it is 96 minutes, 7 seconds, and 44 thirds.
> The remainder is 1, 1, 6, 3, 5, 2 <note>116,352</note>.
> For the slow motion of Saturn, it is 2 minutes, 0 seconds, and 43 thirds.

### Here is the Proof

<u>Planetary revolutions in a Kalpa $\times$ Elapsed days</u> $\quad\quad$ <u>Remainder of revolutions</u>

Similarly, the mean daily motion is derived from the true daily motions. If such a planet were imagined whose civil day is a mean civil day and whose daily motion is the mean daily motion, then the ratio would be calculated by that civil day. However, this would not move along the ecliptic because even the <term>ascensions</term> <note>asu</note> of equal arcs are unequal.

<u>Now, the sum of true civil days in a year</u> $\quad$ =
$\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad$ Mean civil day $\times$ Number of true civil days in a year.

The sidereal time related to the sum of true civil days in a year = (Number of true civil days in a year + 1) sidereal days.

Therefore, Mean Civil Day = <u>(Number of true civil days in a year + 1) sidereal days</u>
$\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad$ Number of true civil days in a year

= 1 sidereal day + $\frac{\text{1 sidereal day}}{\text{Number of true civil days in a year}}$ = 1 sidereal day + <u>$\quad$ 21600 units of time <note>asu</note> $\quad$</u>
$\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad$ Number of true civil days in a year

$\quad\quad$ Number of true civil days in a year

# Chapter on Mean Motion

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;21600 Respirations <note>term: *Asu* (respiration); a unit of time equal to 4 seconds, or the time taken for one breath.</note>
= ——————————— Therefore, the Mean Solar Day = 1 Day + the respirations equal to the minutes of mean motion. Furthermore,
&nbsp;&nbsp;True Solar Day within a year

the respirations equal to the minutes [of motion] are measured on the celestial equator <note>term: *Nāḍīmaṇḍala*; the celestial equator.</note>; therefore, it is established that the motion of the planets must be calculated along this celestial equator.
Thus, from their respective revolutions and the previously mentioned proportion, because the mean Sun on the celestial equator is a mathematical fiction, this mean planet is brought to the imagined mean Sun on the ecliptic <note>term: *Krāntivṛtta*; the ecliptic or the sun's path.</note>. Regarding this, Bhāskara <note>Bhāskara II (1114–1185), a preeminent Indian mathematician and astronomer.</note> states: "When the mean Sun is near the horizon at the city of the Ten-Headed One <note>Lanka, the mythical prime meridian of Indian astronomy.</note>." When the two mean Suns of the two circles (equator and ecliptic), moving with equal velocity, are moved eastward from the vernal equinox, and when the mean Sun of the celestial equator is on the horizon of Lanka, then the mean Sun of the ecliptic—depending on the quadrant—will be above or below the horizon by the difference between the base and the hypotenuse (that is, it will be at the difference between the base and the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle formed by the equator, the ecliptic, and the declination circle). Here, the difference between the two mentioned planets is the "Equation of Time" <note>term: *Udayāntara*; the correction for the difference between mean and true solar time arising from the obliquity of the ecliptic.</note>. Even at its maximum, it is very small; therefore, Bhāskara says it is "near the horizon." However, Brahmagupta <note>Brahmagupta (c. 598–668), an earlier influential astronomer.</note>, considering that difference (the Equation of Time) to be zero, says "at sunrise at Lanka." Here, the wise should discern with an impartial mind that Bhāskara’s statement "near the horizon," which accepts the Equation of Time, is more accurate than Brahmagupta’s "at sunrise at Lanka."

### Now, in this context, the Equation of Time is briefly considered

Where the mean Sun is on the ecliptic, the hour circle (the equatorial horizon) passing through it meets the celestial equator; the respirations or right ascensions <note>term: *Viṣuvāṃśā*; right ascension or equatorial degrees.</note> produced from the minutes of the mean Sun's motion from that point to the equinox, when added to the sixty sidereal ghatikas <note>A *ghatika* is 24 minutes; 60 ghatikas make a full day.</note>, constitute the **True Solar Day**. Similarly, taking the equinox as the center, where the circle with a radius of the arc of the mean Sun's longitude on the ecliptic meets the celestial equator, the respirations equal to the minutes of the mean Sun's motion (or the arc of the mean Sun's longitude) from there to the equinox, when added to the sixty sidereal ghatikas, constitute the **Mean Solar Day**. The difference between these two, the True Solar Day and the Mean Solar Day =
(60 + respirations equal to the minutes of mean Sun's motion) ~ (60 + respirations produced by the minutes of mean Sun's motion) =
Respirations equal to the minutes of mean Sun's motion ~ Respirations produced by the minutes of mean Sun's motion = **Respirations of the Equation of Time**. The planetary motion related to this is derived as follows: If the minutes of planetary motion are obtained in the respirations of a full day and night, then what is obtained by the respirations of the Equation of Time? By this proportion, the planetary motion related to the Equation of Time is found.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Minutes of planetary motion $\times$ Respirations of Equation of Time
Its form = ———————————————————————————————————————. The planets
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Respirations in a day and night

produced from the total elapsed days <note>term: *Ahargaṇa*; the number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch.</note> (which are the planets at the time of the mean Sun's rising on the celestial equator), when subtracted or added by this motion, become the planets at the time of the mean Sun's rising on the ecliptic (situated on the equatorial horizon). By this much, Bhāskara’s statement—"The respirations passed by the mean Sun at the equator and those which are equal to the minutes of the mean Sun, etc."—is justified. However, even within the respirations of the Equation of Time, there will be some motion of the planet; Bhāskara did not account for that. Therefore, having calculated the planetary motion related to the Equation of Time by the aforementioned method, the planet at the time of the mean Sun's rising produced from the elapsed days, even when corrected, cannot be the actual planet at the time of the mean Sun's rising on the ecliptic at the equatorial horizon. Thus, Bhāskara’s calculation is not entirely accurate; therefore, the actual calculation is now being stated.

Now, let the true value of the equation of time <note>original: "udayantara," the difference between mean and apparent solar time</note> be assumed as = **y**. By this value, the planet ought to be calculated at the moment of sunrise. The motion of the planet that occurs during this interval of the equation of time, when converted into time-units <note>original: "asu," a unit of time equal to 4 seconds or the time taken for one breath</note> and applied as a correction to the equation of time stated by Bhaskara, results in the true equation of time.

For instance, if the minutes of planetary motion are obtained for the total time-units of a day and night, then what is obtained for the time-units of the true equation of time (**y**)? The resulting minutes of planetary motion related to that interval are expressed as:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Planet's motion $\times$ **y**
Form == ---------------- = (Motion of the planet per 1 time-unit) $\times$ **y**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Time-units in a day-night

Then, the proportion is: if for 1800 minutes of a zodiac sign <note>1800 minutes = 30 degrees</note>, the rising time-units of that sign are obtained, then for the minutes of planetary motion related to the true equation of time, what time-units are obtained? The related time-units are:

Rising time of sign $\times$ Planet's motion minutes related to true equation of time
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;1800

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Rising time of sign $\times$ Planet's motion $\times$ **y**
= --------------------------------- = (Motion per 1 time-unit) $\times$ **y** $\times$ (Time-units produced by 1 minute)... (1)
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;1800 $\times$ Time-units in a day-night

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Rising time of sign $\times$ 1
$\times$ ----------- = Time-units produced by 1 minute
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;1800

(1) The equation of time stated by Bhaskara, when corrected by this, becomes the true equation of time.
Therefore: Bhaskara's equation of time $\mp$ (Motion per 1 time-unit) $\times$ **y** $\times$ (Time-units produced by 1 minute) == True equation of time == **y**

== Previous equation of time $\mp$ (Motion per 1 time-unit) $\times$ **y** $\times$ (Time-units produced by 1 minute) == **y**

->By algebraic simplification<-

**y** $\pm$ (Motion per 1 time-unit) $\times$ **y** $\times$ (Time-units produced by 1 minute) == Previous equation of time
== **y** ( 1 $\pm$ Motion per 1 time-unit $\times$ Time-units produced by 1 minute ) == Previous equation of time

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Previous equation of time
Therefore: --------------------------------- == **y**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;1 $\pm$ Motion per 1 time-unit $\times$ Time-units produced by 1 minute

By this, the rule of the Great Teacher <term>Mahamahopadhyaya: a title for a great scholar</term> Pandit Sudhakara Dvivedi is proven:
"The previous equation of time divided by one, increased or decreased by the product of the motion per time-unit and the time-units produced by the sign's rising, is the corrected value; this is added or subtracted from the planet in the even and odd quadrants respectively."

### Now, it is considered where the maximum value of the equation of time occurs.

From the definition of the equation of time, it is clear that it is the difference between the degrees of the longitude <note>original: "bhujamsha"</note> and the degrees of right ascension <note>original: "vishuvanmsha"</note>.
Therefore, the Sine of the equation of time == Sine (Longitude degrees — Right Ascension degrees) for the desired arcs, and so on.

# Chapter on Mean Motion

<note>The following section uses Sanskrit abbreviations for trigonometric functions: *jya* for Sine, *kojya* for Cosine, *tri* for Radius, and *utkramajya* for Versine.</note>

(Sine of Longitude $\times$ Cosine of Right Ascension) $-$ (Sine of Right Ascension $\times$ Cosine of Longitude)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- $=$ Sine of the Equation of Time $=$ Sine(U),
                                            Radius

Since $\frac{\text{Cosine of Longitude} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Diurnal Radius}}$ $=$ Cosine of Right Ascension.

And $\frac{\text{Polar Sine} \times \text{Sine of Longitude}}{\text{Diurnal Radius}}$ $=$ Sine of Right Ascension, therefore by substituting these into the form of the Sine of the Equation of Time:

Sine(U) $=$ (Sine of Longitude $\times$ Cosine of Longitude $\times$ Radius) $-$ (Polar Sine $\times$ Sine of Longitude $\times$ Cosine of Longitude)
        -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                        Radius $\times$ Diurnal Radius

Sine of Longitude $\times$ Cosine of Longitude ( Radius $-$ Polar Sine )
$=$ ------------------------------------------------------------------
                          Radius $\times$ Diurnal Radius

Sine of Longitude $\times$ Cosine of Longitude $\times$ Versine of Obliquity
$=$ ------------------------------------------------------------------
                          Radius $\times$ Diurnal Radius

<note>Here, "Versine of Obliquity" refers to the Versine of 24 degrees, the traditional Indian value for the obliquity of the ecliptic.</note>

If the divisor and dividend are multiplied by 'Radius $+$ Polar Sine', then $\frac{(\text{Radius} + \text{Polar Sine}) (\text{Sine of Longitude} \times \text{Cosine of Longitude} \times \text{Versine of Obliquity})}{\text{Radius} \times \text{Diurnal Radius} \times (\text{Radius} + \text{Polar Sine})} =$

( Radius $\times$ Sine Long. $\times$ Cosine Long. $+$ Sine Long. $\times$ Cosine Long. $\times$ Polar Sine ) $\times$ Versine Obliq.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- $=$ Sine(U)
                       Radius $\times$ Diurnal Radius $\times$ ( Radius $+$ Polar Sine )

( Sine Long. $\times$ Cosine R.A. $+$ Sine R.A. $\times$ Cosine Long. ) $\times$ Versine Obliq.
$=$ -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                          Radius $\times$ ( Radius $+$ Polar Sine )

Sine (Longitude $+$ Right Ascension) $\times$ Versine Obliquity
$=$ ----------------------------------------------------------- $=$ Sine(U) $=$ (1)
                  Radius $+$ Polar Sine

---

> (1) By this, the formula stated by <term>Mahamahopadhyaya Sudhakara Dvivedi</term><note>A prominent 19th-century mathematician and astronomer from Varanasi.</note> is proven: "The Sine of the sum of the Right Ascension and Longitude, multiplied by the Versine of the obliquity and divided by the sum of the Radius and the minimum Diurnal Radius, yields the Sine of the Equation of Time."

(1) Here, since the 'Versine of Obliquity' and 'Radius $+$ Polar Sine' are constant as the multiplier and divisor, it is established that where the Sine of (Longitude $+$ Right Ascension) is equal to the Radius (90 degrees), the Equation of Time will be at its maximum. In other words, the maximum value of the Equation of Time occurs at that point. At the <term>Equinoxes</term><note>Intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic.</note> and the <term>Solstices</term><note>The points where the sun reaches its maximum northern or southern declination.</note>, the Equation of Time is absent (zero); this is clear from the very nature of the Equation of Time being the difference between the Longitude and Right Ascension.

### Now, the calculation of Longitude and Right Ascension at the time of maximum Equation of Time is performed:

It was previously proven that when the Sine of the sum of Longitude and Right Ascension is equal to the Radius—meaning the sum of Longitude and Right Ascension equals 90 degrees—the Equation of Time reaches its maximum. Therefore, at the maximum Equation of Time:
Longitude $+$ Right Ascension $=$ 90.
And at that time, the difference between Longitude and Right Ascension $=$ Maximum Equation of Time.

Then, by the mathematics of transition: $\frac{90 + \text{Maximum Difference}}{2} = 45 + \frac{\text{Maximum Difference}}{2} = \text{Degrees of longitude at the time of maximum difference.}$ <note>The "Maximum Difference" (Paramodayantara) refers to the greatest discrepancy between the sun's position on the ecliptic and its right ascension on the equator.</note>

And $\frac{90 - \text{Maximum Difference}}{2} = 45 - \frac{\text{Maximum Difference}}{2} = \text{Degrees of right ascension at the time of maximum difference.}$

->Alternatively<-

Let **Dhru** = the Celestial Pole; **Gra** = the mean Sun on the ecliptic; **Go** = the intersection of the circles (Equinox); **Gro-Gra** = the degrees of longitude (arc of the ecliptic); **Go-Na** = the degrees of right ascension. On the celestial equator, mark a point **Pa** such that the arc **Go-Pa** is equal to the longitude **Gro-Gra**, and draw the circle **Pa-Gra**. From point **Go**, draw a perpendicular circle **Go-Cha** onto the circle **Go-Pa**. Then the sum of the longitude and right ascension at the time of maximum difference is **Go-Pa + Go-Na = 90**. The angle **<Gra-Go-Na** = the obliquity of the ecliptic <note>original: "Jināṃśa", referring to the 24-degree inclination used in classical Indian astronomy</note>; the angle **<Gra-Go-Pa = 180 - Obliquity**; the angle **<Gra-Go-Cha** = $\frac{<\text{Gra-Go-Pa}}{2} = \frac{180 - \text{Obliquity}}{2}$
$= 90 - \frac{\text{Obliquity}}{2} =$ Half the obliquity. In the spherical right-angled triangle **Gra-Na-Pa**, the side **Pa-Na** = 90, therefore the hypotenuse **Pa-Gra** is also = 90. Since the spherical triangle **Gra-Go-Pa** is isosceles, the arcs **Gra-Cha = Cha-Pa = 45**. The angle **<Gra-Cha-Go = 90**. Then, by the ratio in the right-angled spherical triangle **Go-Cha-Pa**: $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine 45}}{\text{Cosine } \frac{\text{Obliquity}}{2}} = \text{Sine of Go-Pa} =$ the Sine of the longitude at the time of maximum difference. The arc of this value is the degrees of longitude at maximum difference. The term **Cosine $\frac{\text{Obliquity}}{2}$** is the Cosine of half the obliquity. Thus, the following formula is established:

> When the Radius is multiplied by the square root of two <note>original: "vedāṃśaguṇena", literally 'multiplied by the parts of the Vedas', a poetic way to denote mathematical constants</note> and divided by the Cosine of half the obliquity,
> the arc corresponding to that value equals the degrees of longitude; at that point, the maximum difference occurs.

This proves that the maximum difference occurs at this specific measure of longitude. If one asks what that actual value is: the Versine <note>original: "Ujjyā"</note> = $\frac{\text{Sine (Right Ascension + Longitude)} \times \text{Versine of Obliquity}}{\text{Radius + Day-radius}}$

$\therefore$ Maximum Difference = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Versine of Obliquity}}{\text{Radius + Day-radius}}$

$\therefore$ Or $\frac{\text{Radius} \cdot \text{Versine of Obliquity} \times \text{Radius}^2}{2 (\text{Radius + Day-radius}) \times \text{Radius}^2} = \frac{\text{Sine}^2 \frac{1}{2} \text{Obliquity} \cdot \text{Radius}^2}{\text{Cosine}^2 \frac{1}{2} \text{Obliquity} \cdot \text{Radius}}$ (By trigonometry)

<note>The text uses "Jina" (24) to represent the degrees of the ecliptic's tilt, a standard value in the school of Brahmagupta.</note>

## Chapter on Mean Motions

By adding [these values], the true solar day <term>Spashta-savana; the actual time between two consecutive sunrises</term> becomes clear. Taking the equinoctial point as the center and drawing a circle with a radius equal to the sine of the mean Sun's longitude on the ecliptic, the distance on the celestial equator from where it intersects to the equinoctial point is equal to the respiration-units <term>Asu; a unit of time equal to 4 seconds or the time taken for one breath</term> of the mean Sun's motion. By adding these respiration-units of the mean Sun's motion to the sixty (60) sidereal ghatis <term>Ghati; a unit of 24 minutes</term>, the mean solar day is determined. By taking the difference between these two (the true solar day and the mean solar day), we derive the "Equation of Time" in respiration-units <note>Udayantara-asu</note>. We then calculate the planetary motion corresponding to this difference. For example: if in the total respiration-units of a day and night <note>Ahoratrasu</note> we get the full daily planetary motion, then what motion corresponds to the respiration-units of the Equation of Time? Through this proportion, the planetary motion related to the Equation of Time is found.

Planetary motion (minutes) $\times$ Equation of Time (respiration-units)
___________________________________________________________________________ = Planetary motion related to the Equation of Time.
Total Day-Night respiration-units

By subtracting or adding this to the planet's position derived from the total elapsed days <note>Ahargana</note>, we find the position of the planet at the equatorial horizon (specifically, the intersection point of the celestial equator and the secondary circle passing through the mean Sun on the ecliptic). Regarding this subject, Bhaskaracharya states in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*: **"The respirations of the mean Sun's motion at the equator are equal to the minutes of the mean Sun's motion..."** <note>original Sanskrit: "Madhyarka bhukta asavo nirakshe ye ye cha madhyarkakala samana"</note> and so on. However, during the interval of the Equation of Time itself, the planet will have some motion. Bhaskaracharya did not account for that specific motion. Therefore, the planetary positions brought to the time of sunrise on the equatorial horizon using Bhaskaracharya's method are not entirely accurate. Thus, it is proven that Bhaskaracharya's calculation of the Equation of Time is slightly incomplete.

The true Equation of Time is Bhaskaracharya's Equation of Time refined by the motion the planet undergoes during that specific interval. For instance, if in the total day-night respiration-units we get the Sun's daily motion, then in the true Equation of Time ($y$), what is the Sun's motion? By this proportion, we find the Sun's motion in minutes related to the true Equation of Time:

Sun's motion (minutes) $\times$ $y$
__________________________________ = Sun's motion per respiration-unit $\times$ $y$. Then we use another proportion: if in the minutes of a zodiac sign (1800)
Total Day-Night respiration-units

Rising-units $\times$ Sun's motion $\times$ $y$

1800 $\times$ Total Day-Night respiration-units

Bhaskaracharya's Equation of Time $\mp$ (Sun's motion per respiration $\times$ Respiration-units per minute $\times$ $y$) = $y$

## In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

Here, the actual <term>Udayantara</term> <note>The Equation of Time; specifically the correction for the difference between apparent solar time and mean solar time</note> is calculated using the <term>Inagati</term> <note>original: "Inagati" = "Suryagati"</note> or **Solar Velocity**, specifically in relation to the minutes of solar motion. The calculation for other planets is performed in the same manner using their respective velocities.

(a) From this, the formula provided by the Great Preceptor Pandit <term>Sudhakara Dvivedi</term> in the Sanskrit commentary—beginning with "The velocity multiplied by one minute of arc..."—is proven.

->Now, we shall consider where the maximum value of the <term>Udayantara</term> occurs.<-

The <term>Udayantara</term> is the difference between the <term>Bhujansha</term> <note>Longitude on the ecliptic</note> and the <term>Vishuvansha</term> <note>Right Ascension on the celestial equator</note>; therefore, the **Sine of the Equation of Time** = (Sine of Longitude — Sine of Right Ascension).

Using the rule for the sine of the difference of two arcs:
(Sine Longitude × Cosine RA) — (Sine RA × Cosine Longitude)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ = Sine of Equation of Time,
                                            Radius

      (Cosine Longitude × Radius)
Since: --------------------------------------- = Cosine RA
               Day-Radius

      (Sine Longitude × Cosine Obliquity)
And: --------------------------------------------- = Sine RA, by substituting these into the expression for the **Sine of the Equation of Time**:
                  Day-Radius

(Sine Long. × Cos. Long. × Radius) — (Sine Long. × Cos. Long. × Cos. Obliquity)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                    Radius × Day-Radius

      Sine Longitude × Cosine Longitude × (Radius — Cosine Obliquity)
= ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                    Radius × Day-Radius

      Sine Longitude × Cosine Longitude × <term>Jyajiu</term>
= -------------------------------------------------------------------------- = Sine of Equation of Time,
                          Radius × Day-Radius

where <term>Jyajiu</term> = <term>Jinanshotkramajya</term> <note>The Versed Sine of the obliquity of the ecliptic, approximately 24 degrees in Indian astronomy</note>.

By multiplying both the numerator and denominator by '(Radius + Cosine Obliquity)':

  ( Radius + Cosine Obliquity ) ( Sine Long. × Cosine Long. × Versed Sine Obliquity )
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Radius × Day-Radius × ( Radius + Cosine Obliquity )

  ( Radius. Sine Long. Cosine Long. + Sine Long. Cosine Long. Cosine Obliquity ) Versed Sine Obliquity
= ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                    Radius × Day-Radius ( Radius + Cosine Obliquity )

  ( Sine Long. × Cosine RA + Sine RA × Cosine Long. ) Versed Sine Obliquity
= ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                               Radius × ( Radius + Cosine Obliquity )

  Sine ( Longitude + Right Ascension ) × Versed Sine Obliquity
= ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- = Sine of Equation of Time . . . (1)
                   Radius + Cosine Obliquity

(1) This proves the formula of the Great Preceptor Pandit Sudhakara Dvivedi in the Sanskrit commentary, "The sine of the sum of the Right Ascension and Longitude..." etc.

(1) In this equation, because the <term>Versed Sine of Obliquity</term> and the term (Radius + Cosine Obliquity) are both constants, the **Sine of the Equation of Time** will reach its maximum value where the Sine (Longitude + Right Ascension) is at its maximum. However, a <term>Sine</term> cannot exceed the <term>Radius</term> <note>In Indian trigonometry, the Sine of 90 degrees equals the Radius of the circle</note>, therefore—
