# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
<note>The Correctly Established Doctrine of Brahma, written by Brahmagupta in 628 CE</note>

-> $\frac{13}{12} \cdot \text{Sine } 3M + \dots$ <-

-> Therefore, here Mr. Gaupraum <note>Likely a reference to a Western scholar or commentator, possibly "Gaupraum" is a transcription of a name like "Goff" or "Graham"</note> has assumed $\frac{P}{R} = 2e - \frac{e^3}{4}$; since $e$ is extremely small, $\frac{e^3}{4}$ is discarded, then $\frac{P}{R} = 2e$. <-

-> $\therefore E = 2e \cdot \text{Sine } M = \frac{P}{R} \cdot \text{Sine } M$. <-

Thus, here also according to the view of Brahmagupta:

-> Sine of the Equation of Center = $\frac{\text{Sine } R \cdot \text{Sine } M}{R}$ <-

-> Or = $2e \cdot \text{Sine } M$, where Radius = 1 <-

-> $2e = \text{Sine of the maximum equation.}$ <-

-> Now, he speaks regarding the true positions of the Sun and Moon: <-

> When the corrections for the difference in longitude, the equation of center, and the equation of time are applied, the Sun and Moon are true at the celestial equator; when the correction for half the variation in daylight is applied, they are true at the local horizon. || 18 ||

<term>Vā. Bhā.</term> <note>Vāsanā Bhāṣya: The explanatory commentary by Prithudaka Svami or a similar commentator</note>—Now he states a verse to explain how the Sun and Moon appear in one's own country through corrections such as the difference in longitude. The mean Sun and Moon at the time of sunrise in <term>Lanka</term> <note>The zero-meridian in ancient Indian astronomy, located on the equator</note> become the mean positions in one's own country once the <term>Deshantara</term> <note>Correction for terrestrial longitude</note> operation is performed, because one's own country must be either east or west of the prime meridian passing through Lanka. There, the sunrise occurs earlier or later. From the sunrise on the meridian, it follows that when the <term>Bhujaphala-chapa</term> <note>The arc of the equation of center</note> and the <term>Bhujantara</term> <note>The equation of time; the difference between mean and true solar time</note> are applied, the Sun and Moon are at the <term>Unmandala</term> <note>The celestial equator or the six-o'clock circle</note>. Even when the arc of their own equation is applied, they become "true" (corrected) because the planets situated on the <term>Pratimandala</term> <note>The eccentric circle or epicycle</note>, increased or decreased by their own equations, are seen on the <term>Kaksha-mandala</term> <note>The orbital circle or deferent</note>; these are called the true positions. However, they are near the celestial equator because the <term>Savana Ahargana</term> <note>The count of civil days</note> begins at the sunrise of the mean Sun; therefore, when the equation of time is applied, they are true at the celestial equator, because the equation of time arises from the interval between the mean and true sunrises, and the celestial equator is called the <term>Niraksha-desha-kshitija</term> <note>The horizon of a place with no latitude (the equator)</note>. Thus, it is proven.

Regarding "at the horizon by half the variation in daylight": when one's own <term>Charardha</term> <note>Half the equinoctial variation; the difference between the local horizon and the celestial equator</note> is applied, the Sun and Moon become true at the local horizon. Since the interval between the local horizon and the celestial equator in one's own country is the half-variation in daylight on the <term>Svahoratrardha-vritta</term> <note>The diurnal circle of the planet</note>, this is also proven. All this should be demonstrated on the armillary sphere. Here, this half-verse is intended to characterize the planets generally, using the Sun and Moon as examples. By this, other planets also become mean in one's own country when the longitude correction is applied, and they reach the celestial equator when the two arcs of the equations of center and the <term>Shighra</term> <note>The equation of conjunction/parallax</note> and the equation of time are applied.

The positions become true. When the <term>half-equation of daylight</term> <note>Sanskrit: ravicharadala; a correction for the Sun's ascensional difference</note> is applied as appropriate, they represent the positions at the time of sunrise. If the positions are derived using the solar day count, or if other planets are derived from the current <term>day-count</term> <note>Sanskrit: ahargana; the number of elapsed days since the start of an epoch</note>, then by applying that same correction for the half-equation of daylight, they become the positions at the time of that specific planet's rising. Thus, it is said that the Sun and others, if derived by the sidereal day count, would be greater or lesser without the half-equation of daylight. Because the Sun and Moon are on the horizon when the Sun's half-equation of daylight is applied, these are merely the positions at sunrise and sunset at <term>Lanka</term> <note>The Hindu prime meridian, located on the equator</note> adjusted for <term>terrestrial longitude</term> <note>Sanskrit: desantara</note> and nothing else; therefore, he says in the half-verse: || 18 ||

**Scientific Interpretation:** In the middle of the sky (at the zenith), meaning at the time of true midday, if the true Sun and Moon are desired, then the <term>equation of the center</term> <note>Sanskrit: mandaphala; correction for elliptical orbits</note> and the <term>equation of time</term> <note>Sanskrit: bhujantara; correction for the difference between mean and true solar time</note> must be applied to the mean Sun and Moon. Once these are refined, they become true at the <term>equinoctial horizon</term> <note>Sanskrit: unmandala</note>. By further applying the Sun's half-equation of daylight, the Sun and Moon become true at the observer's own horizon. || 18 ||

### Rationale

Since one's own country is either east or west of the <term>meridian line</term> <note>Sanskrit: yamyottararekha</note> of Lanka, the mean Sun and Moon of one's own country are found by applying the longitude correction to the positions at sunrise in Lanka. Sunrise occurs either before or after the meridian sunrise. By applying the corrections for the equation of the center and the equation of time, the Sun and Moon become true at one's own equinoctial horizon; then, by applying the correction for the Sun's half-ascensional difference, they become true at one's own local horizon. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Sripati also demonstrated the clarification of the Sun and Moon in a manner following this verse, stating "by the calculation of distance, the mean positions of one's own place, the equation of the center, the Sun's equation," etc. Teachers prior to Bhaskara performed only the three previously mentioned operations—longitude and so on—to find the planets at local sunrise. Bhaskara, having first established the operation called the <term>equation of time</term> <note>Sanskrit: udayantara</note>, rejected Brahmagupta's statement that "the mean positions are at sunrise in Lanka," and provided a resolution by stating "because the difference is small and variable," etc. || 18 ||

### Now, regarding the true positions of the Sun and Moon:

**Hindi Interpretation:** If the true Sun and true Moon are required at the time of true midday, then by applying the three corrections—the equation of the center, the equation of time, and the longitude—to the mean Sun and mean Moon, they both become true at the equinoctial horizon (the observer's equatorial horizon). By applying the correction for the Sun's half-ascensional difference to those, the Sun and Moon become true at the observer's local horizon. || 18 ||

<page-num>180</page-num>
<header>In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta</header>

The true Sun and true Moon are located at one's own horizon. In the *Siddhantashekhara*, Shripati has clarified the Sun and Moon in accordance with the ancient teachers' instructions, stating "the two mean positions after the longitudinal correction is applied," and so forth. Teachers prior to Bhaskaracharya performed only the three previously mentioned operations—such as <term>Deshantara</term><note>The correction for terrestrial longitude, accounting for the distance between the observer's meridian and the prime meridian at Ujjain.</note>—to determine the planets at the time of local sunrise. Bhaskaracharya, however, introduced an unprecedented operation called <term>Udayantara</term><note>The correction for the equation of time, specifically the portion due to the obliquity of the ecliptic.</note>. While he initially seemed to disregard Brahmagupta’s statement that "the planets are mean at sunrise in Lanka," he later reconciled his view with Brahmagupta's by stating, "because the difference is variable and very small." ||18||

### Now, he explains why the method of correction taught by Aryabhata is not accurate

> Without the correction of half the ascensional difference, at the midpoints of night and day,
> the correction taught by Aryabhata is not true; therefore, this true explanation is given. ||19||

<term>Vasanabhashya</term><note>The "Vasanabhashya" is the explanatory commentary, often attributed to Bhaskara II, focusing on the underlying rationale or "flavor" of the mathematics.</note>—The two true positions at the time of sunrise in Lanka, when refined by the longitudinal correction and then further corrected by the <term>Charardha</term><note>Half the ascensional difference; the correction required to account for the difference in the length of day caused by the observer's latitude.</note>, represent the planets at the moment the Sun is on the eastern horizon of one's own location. Similarly, for sunset, when the aforementioned correction for the Sun's ascensional difference is applied, they represent the planets at the moment the Sun is on the western horizon; this applies to all planets. Without the half-ascensional difference, at the midpoints of night and day <note>midnight and noon</note>, the meridian circle does not change due to the ascensional difference, even with a great latitude; one should demonstrate all of this on the armillary sphere. Planets calculated for a desired time are true even without the ascensional difference correction, provided that time is reckoned from the local sunrise or sunset. Therefore, the correction taught by Aryabhata is not a "true statement"; this half-verse is for the purpose of clarification.

<term>Vijnanabhashya</term><note>The "Vijnanabhashya" is a technical commentary providing a scientific or analytical breakdown of the verse.</note>—Without the <term>Chara</term> correction, the Sun and Moon are true at midnight and midday. The correction stated by Aryabhata is not precise; for this reason, the author establishes the necessity of his own explanation of the true positions. ||19||

### The Mathematical Rationale

Midday and midnight occur at the exact same time at one's own location as they do on the equator <note>the "place with no latitude"</note>; therefore, the necessity for the <term>Charardha</term> correction does not arise there. ||19||

### Now he states that the correction taught by Aryabhata is not correct

<term>Hindi Commentary</term>—Without the <term>Chara</term> correction, the Sun and Moon are true at midnight and at midday. The correction stated by Aryabhata is not clear <note>accurate</note>. It is proper to state the correction; thus, the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> gives the reason for his own explanation of the true positions. ||19||

### Rationale

In one's own country and at the equator, the midday and the midnight occur at the same time.

# Page 181
## Chapter on True Positions <note>Sanskrit: Spaṣṭādhikāraḥ; the section of astronomical texts dealing with calculating the true longitudinal positions of celestial bodies.</note>

Therefore, in that case, there is an absence of the ascensional difference correction <note>Sanskrit: carārdha saṃskāra; a correction used to account for the difference in rising times of zodiac signs due to local latitude.</note>, meaning the ascensional difference correction is not required. ||19||

Now, to clarify the positions of the Sun and Moon, he states the degrees of the circumferences of the slow-moving epicycles <note>Sanskrit: manda-paridhi; the "slow" epicycle used in ancient Indian astronomy to account for the equation of center, similar to orbital eccentricity.</note>:

> For the Sun, the circumference is twice fourteen <note>original: "manu-dvitayaṃ"; Manu represents 14, so 28.</note> minus one-third at midday. When inclined to the east by fifteen ghatikas <note>A ghatika is 24 minutes; 15 ghatikas equals 6 hours, placing the body at the horizon.</note>, it is increased or decreased by one-third. ||20||
> For the Moon at midday, it is twice ten <note>original: "daśana-dvitayaṃ"; 20, but here used in a context implying 32</note> minus twenty-four minutes <note>original: "jina-lipta"; Jina represents 24.</note>. To the east, it is minus fifty-two minutes. To the west, it is added or subtracted like the Sun; these are the circumferences for the negative and positive equations. ||21||

**Commentary:** Now, wishing to explain the process of finding the true positions, he first describes the measurements of the circumferences of the Sun and Moon's slow-moving epicycles at midday, midnight, sunrise, and sunset through two verses.

The phrase "degrees of negative and positive circumferences" applies throughout. This is the meaning: For the Sun, twice fourteen minus one-third <note>28 - 1/3 = 27 degrees and 40 minutes</note> are the degrees of the negative and positive circumferences at midday, at one's own local noon. This is what is said: At midday, the circumference of the Sun’s slow epicycle is 13 degrees and 40 minutes <note>The text splits the total circumference between the negative and positive halves of the orbit</note> in both the negative and positive centers. When inclined to the east by fifteen ghatikas—meaning if the Sun is at the eastern horizon—then that which was stated as twice fourteen minus one-third is further increased or decreased by one-third to become the negative and positive circumferences respectively. For the Sun at the horizon, the negative circumference is 13 and the positive circumference is 14 degrees. "Decreased or increased to the west" refers to the Sun being at the western horizon after fifteen ghatikas from midday.

In that case, the twice fourteen minus one-third is adjusted by adding or subtracting one-third to find the negative and positive circumferences. The negative circumference is 13 degrees and the positive is 14 degrees. At midnight, the circumference is equal to the midday circumference. For the Moon at midday, it is twice ten <note>interpreted here as 32</note> minus twenty-four minutes <note>31 degrees and 36 minutes</note>. This is the circumference for the Moon's slow epicycle at both negative and positive centers. "Minus fifty-two minutes to the east" should be applied according to the rule of fifteen ghatikas; the circumferences for the Moon at the eastern horizon are 31 degrees and 36 minutes minus 52 minutes. When the Moon is inclined to the west by fifteen ghatikas—meaning at the western horizon—the same "twice ten" (32) minus twenty-four minutes is added to or subtracted from by fifty-two minutes to find the negative and positive circumferences.

Here also, the circumference at midday is the same as the circumference at midnight, as they both lie on the meridian circle...

For example, when the Sun has a negative <term>anomaly</term> <note>the angular distance of a planet from its apogee</note> at noon and midnight, the circumference is 13° 40'. At the eastern horizon <note>literally "rising prime vertical"</note>, the circumference is 14°. At that same position, if the anomaly is positive, the circumference is 13° 20'. At the western horizon, if the anomaly is negative, the circumference is 13° 20'; if positive, it is 14°. For the Moon, at its own noon and midnight, whether the anomaly is negative or positive, the circumference is 31° 36'. At the eastern horizon, for both negative and positive anomalies, the circumference is 30° 44'. At the western horizon, the negative circumference is 32° 28', and the positive is 30° 44'. The reason <note>original: "vasana"</note> for this increase or decrease in the circumference is based on observation of the maximum correction. Because the size of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>the small circle on which the planet moves</note> changes, the correction at sunrise is not the same as at noon or sunset, due to the observer's position on the terrestrial globe. This should be demonstrated using a globe. Thus, the corrected circumference of the center of the epicycle for the Sun and Moon at intervals of fifteen <term>ghatikas</term> <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 15 ghatikas equals 6 hours</note> is stated; how it is corrected in between is explained by the verse.

<term>Commentary</term>—Take twice fourteen and subtract one-third; that is, 14 degrees in two places reduced by one-third of a degree <note>20 minutes</note>. When the Sun's <term>manda-phala</term> <note>equation of center</note> is negative or positive at midday (noon), the degrees of the slow circumference are 13° 40'. For a Sun that is 15 ghatikas before noon (in the eastern hemisphere), the noon circumference value should be increased or decreased by one-third of a degree respectively if the correction is negative or positive. For a Sun 15 ghatikas after noon (in the western hemisphere), the noon circumference value should be decreased or increased by one-third of a degree respectively. These then become the degrees of the circumference for the Sun when situated on the eastern or western horizons. For the Moon, take twice sixteen and subtract the "Jina" minutes <note>24 minutes</note>; that is, 32 degrees reduced by 24 minutes in two places. This gives 31° 36' as the circumference at noon. As with the Sun, for the Moon 15 ghatikas before or after noon: if the correction is negative at noon, subtract 52 minutes; if positive, add or subtract 52 minutes respectively to find the circumference at the eastern and western horizons, as follows:

Since the epicycle of the equation of the center <note>original: "manda-paridhi"</note> is essentially the circle formed by the radius of the maximum sine of the equation of the center relative to the mean planet, the various teachers have recorded the measure of this epicycle in their respective treatises according to the maximum equation of the center observed during their own times. ||20-21||

## Proof herein

Regarding the proof, the teacher Chaturveda stated that "observation itself is the underlying rationale here," and Bhaskaracharya followed this same reasoning. ||20-21||

Now, the degrees of the epicycle of the equation of the center for the clarification of the Sun and the Moon are stated:

**Hindi Commentary—** By subtracting one-third of a degree (20 minutes) from fourteen degrees in two instances, the measure of the Sun's epicycle at midday is obtained, whether the Sun's equation of the center is negative or positive. In the case of a negative or positive equation, for a Sun inclined by fifteen *ghatis* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 15 ghatis equals 6 hours</note> before midday (in the eastern hemisphere), one should respectively add and subtract one-third of a degree (20 minutes) to the midday epicycle value. In the western hemisphere (after midday), for a negative and positive equation, one should respectively subtract and add twenty minutes to the midday value; this yields the epicycle degrees for the Sun when situated on the eastern and western equatorial horizons <note>original: "unmandala"</note>. 

When the Moon has a negative or positive equation, subtract twenty-four minutes from thirty-two in two instances; those are the epicycle degrees at midday. Just as with the Sun, for a Moon inclined by fifteen *ghatis* in the eastern and western hemispheres: for a negative equation, subtract fifty-two minutes from the midday value; for a positive equation, respectively add and subtract fifty-two minutes from the midday value for the Moon inclined by fifteen *ghatis*. This gives the epicycle degrees for the Moon on the eastern and western horizons. For example:

| In the Sun's Negative Equation | In the Positive Equation |
|----------|----------|
| Epicycle at Midday = 13°40' | Epicycle at Midday = 13°40' |
| For Sun on Eastern Horizon = 14°10' | For Sun on Eastern Horizon = 13°10' |
| For Sun on Western Horizon = 13°10' | For Sun on Western Horizon = 14°10' |

| In the Moon's Negative Equation | In the Positive Equation |
|----------|----------|
| Midday Epicycle = 31°36' | Midday Epicycle = 31°36' |
| For Moon on Eastern Horizon = 30°44' | For Moon on Eastern Horizon = 30°44' |
| For Moon on Western Horizon = 32°28' | For Moon on Western Horizon = 30°44' |

<note>The values in the final row for 'Positive Equation' (Moon) appear to repeat the subtraction result (30°44') instead of showing the expected addition result (32°28'), likely a typographical error in the original manuscript.</note>

According to Aryabhata's view, the Sun's epicycle = 13°30' and the Moon's epicycle = 31°30'. Looking at the values recorded by Brahmagupta and those by Aryabhata, there is some difference between the two. In the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>The "Sun Treatise," a primary text of Indian astronomy</note> it says:

> "The degrees of the Sun's epicycle are fourteen <note>original: "manavah"</note> and the Moon's are thirty-two <note>original: "radah"</note> at the end of even quadrants. At the end of odd quadrants, they are each reduced by twenty minutes <note>original: "nakhalis"</note>."

<note>Technical terms used: **Spashtadhikara** (Chapter on True Positions), **Manda-paridhi** (Epicycle of the equation of the center), **Rina-manda-phala** (Negative equation of the center), **Dhana-manda-phala** (Positive equation of the center), **Madhyahna** (Midday), **Unmandala** (Equatorial horizon).</note>

In this manner, by observing different portions of the circumference, it becomes evident that the <term>Mandantya-phalajya</term><note>The sine of the maximum anomaly correction in the slow/manda process.</note> of the planets is not always constant. This is because the circle formed with the <term>Mandantya-phalajya</term> as the radius, centered on the mean planet, is the circumference of the <term>Manda-nichochcha-vritta</term><note>The epicycle used to calculate the equation of center.</note>. Whichever teacher obtained a particular value for the <term>Mandantya-phalajya</term>, they recorded the measure of the <term>Manda</term> circumference in their respective treatises accordingly. ||20-21||

### Proof

Regarding this, Chaturvedacharya has stated, "In this matter, observation itself is the proof." Bhaskaracharya has also followed this same reasoning. ||20-21||

### Now he describes the calculation of the true circumference at a desired hour-angle:

> The difference between that [the horizon circumference] and the midday circumference is multiplied by the sine of the hour-angle and divided by the radius.
> If the midday circumference is less, add the result; if it is more, subtract it; the result is the true circumference. || 22 ||

**Vasanabhashya (Author's Commentary):**—The word "that" refers to the circumference at the <term>Unmandala</term><note>The equatorial horizon.</note> at the time of rising or setting. The difference between that and the midday circumference is the "midday-circumference-difference." Multiply that by the sine of the hour-angle and divide by the radius. This is what is meant: in the sky, the difference in circumference is always twenty minutes of arc. By a proportion: if for a versed sine of the hour-angle equal to the radius, this is the difference in circumference at one's own midday (either before or after) for the Sun, then what will it be for the versed sine of the hour-angle at the desired time? The result obtained from this hour-angle from one's midday is to be added to or subtracted from the midday circumference. When comparing this circumference with the midday circumference, if the midday circumference is smaller, add the result; if it is larger, subtract it. This is because the daily circumference increases or decreases every moment. By doing this, the true circumference of the planet's own <term>Manda</term> epicycle at that specific position is found. For the Moon also, using its own circumference difference of fifty-two minutes of arc, and the versed sine of the hour-angle from its midday, the true circumference is refined from its mean circumference. Having taken the sine of the hour-angle from midnight in the eastern and western hemispheres, the midnight circumference is refined to find the true circumference of the <term>Manda</term> epicycle at the desired time. Therefore, if the hour-angle is greater than fifteen <term>Ghatikas</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 15 Ghatikas equal 6 hours.</note>, it is subtracted from thirty and the remainder is taken. This is because the <term>Unmandala</term> is the limit here for maximum increase or decrease. For this reason, where the latitude is sixty-six degrees, the Sun at the end of Gemini has a daily circumference equal to the midday circumference; such phenomena should be demonstrated on the <term>Svahoratra-vritta</term><note>The diurnal circle or circle of daily motion.</note> in the armillary sphere. In all cases, the calculation of the result using the true circumference is as previously described. ||22||

**Vimalabhashya (Explanatory Commentary):**—The sine of the hour-angle (the sine of the desired elapsed time from midday) is multiplied by the difference between the midday circumference and the <term>Unmandala</term> circumference (at rising or setting). Divided by the radius, the result should be added to or subtracted from the midday circumference. If the midday circumference is less than the circumference it is being compared to, add; if more, subtract. Then the true circumference for the desired position is obtained. || 22 ||

# Here is the Rationale

The circumferences of the <term>epicycles</term> <note>original: mandanīcocca-vṛtta-paridhi; the small circles used in ancient astronomy to account for varying planetary speeds</note> previously mentioned are applicable only at the moment of midday. When the Sun or Moon is on the eastern or western horizon, the circumference changes, resulting in a positive or negative correction. To find the difference between the circumference at a specific time and the standard midday circumference, we use a proportion: "If the difference in circumference is obtained when the <term>sine of the hour angle</term> <note>the angular distance from the meridian</note> is equal to the radius, then what would it be for the desired hour angle?" 

By this calculation, the specific difference in circumference is found. This value should be added to or subtracted from the midday circumference to find the <term>true circumference</term> <note>sphuṭa paridhi</note> for that specific time. In the text *Siddhanta Shekhara*, the author Shripati stated: "Multiply the difference between the two midday circumferences by the sine of one's own hour angle and divide by the radius. If the midday circumference is smaller, add the result; if it is larger, subtract it to find the true value." This confirms that Shripati followed the same method as the earlier teachers. || 22 ||

->Now, the method for bringing forth the true circumference at a desired hour angle is described:<-

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the difference between the previously stated circumference (when the Sun or Moon is on the eastern or western horizon) and the midday circumference by the sine of the desired hour angle. Divide this by the radius. The resulting value should be added to or subtracted from the midday circumference. (If the midday circumference is less than the horizon circumference, add the result; if the midday circumference is greater, subtract the result). This gives the true circumference for the desired time. || 22 ||

## Rationale

The epicycle circumference mentioned earlier is for midday. Depending on whether the correction is positive or negative when the Sun or Moon is on the eastern or western horizon, there is a difference compared to the midday circumference. Based on the proportion: "If we get this difference in circumference for a sine of the hour angle equal to the radius, what do we get for the desired sine of the hour angle?" the specific difference is found. By adding or subtracting this from the midday circumference, the true circumference for that position is determined. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati said exactly what the ancient teachers taught in the verse beginning with "Multiply the difference between the two midday circumferences..." as written in the Sanskrit rationale. || 22 ||

When the anomaly is greater than six signs, the arc of the result is added. || 23 ||

**Vartika Commentary:** Now, the author explains the method for showing the addition or subtraction of the result obtained from the true circumference of the epicycle. The arc of the result produced by this process has already been shown for the mean Sun. That result is negative (subtracted) when the anomaly is less than six signs, because in the first quadrants of the anomaly, the result is negative...

It occurs. From that point, the subtractive correction decreases by the inverse result of the second quadrant until it reaches zero. For this reason, it is said that when the anomaly <note>the angular distance of a planet from its apogee</note> is less than six signs <note>180 degrees</note>, the correction is negative. However, it is understood even if not explicitly stated that when the anomaly is greater than half a circle, the result becomes positive. Then the result of the third quadrant is positive. Even as that decreases by the inverse result of the fourth quadrant, it remains positive until the full circle is completed. In the case of the Moon, when the anomaly is greater than six signs, it is positive, and when less, it is negative. The arc of the correction of its own sine has already been demonstrated in detail previously in the explanation of additive and subtractive corrections for the Sun. This is not meant for the Sun and Moon alone, but serves as an illustration for all planets; therefore, the same process of "Manda" <note>slow/equation of center</note> correction should be applied to the other planets as well.

**Scientific Commentary**—When the Manda-anomaly <term>Manda-kendra: the angular distance from the planet's slow apogee</term> is less than six signs, the arc of the correction <term>Manda-phala: the equation of center</term> is subtracted from the mean Sun. Similarly, when the Manda-anomaly is greater than six signs, the arc of its own correction is added to the mean Sun to obtain the true Sun. ||23||

->Here is the Mathematical Proof<-

When the mean Sun is situated between the position of the Sun's apogee <note>highest point</note> and its perigee <note>lowest point</note>, its Manda-anomaly (which is the difference between the Sun's apogee and the mean Sun) falls within the first six signs starting from Aries. Therefore, the mean Sun minus the Manda-correction (the difference between the mean and true Sun) becomes the true Sun. When the mean Sun is situated between the perigee and the apogee, its anomaly exists within the six signs starting from Libra; thus, the mean Sun plus the Manda-correction becomes the true Sun. Hence, it is proven that in an anomaly starting with Aries, the correction is negative, and in an anomaly starting with Libra, the correction is positive. In the verse, "anomaly less than six signs" refers to the Aries-half, and "anomaly greater than six signs" refers to the Libra-half. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskara says, "In the anomalies of Libra and Aries, the results are respectively positive and negative; thus should the Manda correction be known," which is stated in accordance with the Teacher's <note>Brahmagupta's</note> words. ||23||

Similarly, in a Manda-anomaly of more than six signs (meaning the Libra-based anomaly), adding the Manda-correction to the mean Sun results in the true Sun. ||23||

# Chapter on True Positions

Bhaskaracharya <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> also says, "In the quadrants starting with Libra, the correction is negative; thus should the Mandaphala <note>the correction for the equation of center</note> be understood," following the words of the ancient teachers. || 23 ||

->Now he describes the specific procedure for the true positions of the Sun and Moon<-

> The correction starting with the longitude of the place <note>Deshantara</note> should be done using the circumferences <note>epicycles</note> at midday.
> Having done this, the true positions should be calculated repeatedly <note>iteratively</note> using the true circumferences at the end of the lunar day <note>Tithyanta</note>. || 24 ||

**Vasanabhashya (Author's Commentary):** Now, to demonstrate the process of repeated calculation <term>Asakrit-karma</term><note>An iterative mathematical process used to reach a precise value where variables depend on one another</note>, he speaks this verse. Having performed the corrections starting with the longitude of the place as previously stated, the true positions of the Sun and Moon are first calculated using the midday circumferences. From those, the end of the lunar day <term>Tithi</term> is determined. At that specific end-time of the Tithi, the circumferences are themselves corrected <note>made "true"</note>, and using those, the true positions of the planets are calculated again and again. This is done until the values no longer change <note>convergence</note>. This means they are then fixed upon the ecliptic circle <term>Kaksha-mandala</term>.

The reasoning <term>Upapatti</term> here is that it is proper to calculate the correction <note>Phala</note> using the circumference of that specific moment. However, the exact end of the Tithi is not known initially; therefore, one must first find the end of the Tithi by calculating the true position using the midday circumference. Then, the true position is refined using the circumference of that moment, because the circumference of the epicycle <term>Nica-ucca-vritta</term> <note>literally "low-high-circle"</note> varies at different points in the revolution. The logic of this repeated calculation should be shown on the armillary sphere or diagrams. When the center of the epicycle is placed at the mean planet's position on the ecliptic, the sine of the epicycle's arm is one value. When it is placed at the true planet's position, it completes the epicycle differently. Therefore, to know the planet's position on the eccentric circle, one first brings the correction to the mean planets. Then, knowing the planet on the eccentric circle, one repeatedly finds the correction relative to the corresponding point on the ecliptic until the difference between the mean and true planet is finalized. This is called the "True Correction" <term>Spashta-phala</term>; thus it is proven.

**Vijnanabhashya (Scientific Commentary):** Having performed the corrections for the Sun and Moon using the midday circumferences, one should calculate the end of the Tithi for an eclipse using those true positions. Then, using the true circumferences of the Moon and Sun at that specific Tithi-end, the true Sun and Moon are to be calculated again. From those new positions, the Tithi-end is recalculated, and from that, the circumferences are refined again. By this repeated process, the true Sun and Moon suitable for eclipse calculations are obtained. This intention of the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> was made clear by Bhaskaracharya; hence it is said in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*: "The son of Jishnu <note>Brahmagupta</note> stated that for an eclipse, the positions of the Sun and Moon must be made true repeatedly." || 24 ||

### The Mathematical Proof

The "bending correction" <term>Nata-karma</term> mentioned by the Teacher can also be achieved through a non-iterative method. For example, let the time in Ghatis <note>1 Ghati = 24 minutes</note> between the mathematically calculated Tithi-end and the Tithi-end refined by the repeated bending correction be = *y*. The degrees related to this = 6*y*. At the calculated Tithi-end, the degrees of the Sun's hour angle = *n*. By correcting these, the actual degrees of the hour angle = *n* ± 6*y*. Then the proportion: if in sixty Ghatis the difference in motion between the Sun and Moon is obtained, then what is obtained in '*y*' Ghatis?

It is also understood that all celestial bodies such as planets situated in space become visible and distinct to us only when they are transformed through the sphere of the Earth's atmosphere. The specific correction applied to arrive at these visible positions—accounting for the atmospheric effect—is called <term>Nata-karma</term> <note>literally 'inclination-action' or 'zenith distance correction'; here referring to a specific parallax or refraction-related adjustment</note>. Authors prior to Brahmagupta, such as those of the *Surya-siddhanta* and Aryabhata, have written various accounts regarding this in their respective treatises. In my view, the necessity of the *Nata-karma* correction is extremely apparent; let those astronomers who are skilled in discerning the essential from the non-essential reflect deeply on this matter. ||24||

->Now, something specific is said regarding the clarification of the Sun and the Moon.<-

**Hindi Commentary—** After clarifying the Sun and the Moon using the midday circumferences through longitudinal corrections and other means, one should calculate the <term>Tithyanta</term> <note>the exact moment the lunar day or 'tithi' ends</note> for the eclipse using those distinct positions. From that *Tithyanta* time, one must again calculate the distinct Sun and Moon using their specific circumferences, and from those results, recalculate the *Tithyanta*. By repeating this process iteratively, the precise positions of the Sun and Moon suitable for eclipse calculations are obtained. Bhaskaracharya has explained this intention of the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> in great detail. Therefore, in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya says: **"The son of Jishnu <note>Brahmagupta</note> stated that the Sun and Moon at the end of an eclipse are found through repeated clarification of the tithi."** ||24||

### Mathematical Proof

The *Nata-karma* mentioned by the teachers can be performed through a single-step method or an iterative method. For instance, let the difference in time (in *ghatis* <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>) between the mathematically calculated *Tithyanta* and the *Tithyanta* produced from the Sun and Moon corrected by *Nata-karma* be represented as (y). The corresponding degrees = 6y. If the Sun's degrees of inclination at the calculated *Tithyanta* = n, then by applying these corrections, the actual degrees of inclination = n $\pm$ 6y. Then we use a proportion: if in 60 *ghatis* we find the difference in motion between the Sun and Moon, what will it be in (y) *ghatis*? From this, the difference in arc minutes between the Sun and Moon in (y) *ghatis* is derived:

y (Moon's daily motion — Sun's daily motion)
------------------------------------------------------------------ = y $\times$ g, where
                                60

Moon's daily motion — Sun's daily motion
------------------------------------------------------------------ = g. **"By the sine of the inclination at the end of the tithi..."**
                                60

**And so on.** According to the method described by Bhaskara, the Sun's *Nata-karma* = $\frac{\text{Sun's correction factor} \times \text{sine (n} \pm \text{6y)}}{4620}$ = Sun's factor$_1 \times$ sine (n $\pm$ 6y), where $\frac{\text{Sun's correction factor}}{4620}$ = Sun's factor$_1$. Similarly, the Moon's *Nata-karma* = $\frac{\text{Moon's correction factor} \times \text{sine (n} \pm \text{6y)}}{4375}$ = Moon's factor$_1 \times$ sine (n $\pm$ 6y), where $\frac{\text{Moon's correction factor}}{4375}$ = Moon's factor$_1$. The adjustment of these two must equal the previously calculated difference; otherwise, how would the difference between the mathematical Sun and Moon and the *Nata-karma* corrected Sun and Moon remain equal over the time interval (y)? Therefore, g $\times$ y = Moon's factor$_1 \times$ sine...

$(n \pm 6y) - \text{Rf} \times \text{Sine} (n \pm 6y) = (Ch\dot{m}f_1 - \text{Rf}_1) \times \text{Sine} (n \pm 6y)$ therefore $\frac{g}{Ch\dot{m}f_1 - \text{Rf}_1}$

$= \frac{\text{Sine} (n \pm 6y)}{y} = \text{Result} = P,$ then we apply the proportion: if the Sine of ten degrees $= 21$

is obtained, then what is the value for '6y' equivalent degrees? The Sine of '6y' is, $\text{Sine } 6y = \frac{21 \times 6y}{10},$

Similarly $\frac{21 \times 3y}{10} = \text{Sine } 3y = \sqrt{\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Versine } 6y}{2}} = \sqrt{60 \times \text{Versine } 6y}$
<note>The term 'Radius' (Trijya) is standardly taken as 120 or 60 in different Indian astronomical traditions; here 60 is used in the square root.</note>

By inverse operation $\frac{21^2 \times 3^2 \times y^2}{10^2 \times 60} = \text{Versine } 6y;$ From the rule "for two desired arcs" etc., $\text{Sine } (n \pm 6y)$

$= \frac{\text{Sine } n \times \text{Cosine } 6y}{\text{Radius}} \pm \frac{\text{Cosine } n \times \text{Sine } 6y}{\text{Radius}} = \text{Sine } n - \frac{\text{Sine } n \times \text{Versine } 6y}{\text{Radius}}$

$P \times H = \text{Constant} = Dhru = \frac{\text{Sine } n \times H}{y} - \frac{\text{Sine } n \times y}{2 H} \pm \text{Cosine } n$ By performing algebraic clearing

and dividing by Sine $n$, $\frac{Dhru \mp \text{Cosine } n}{\text{Sine } n} = \frac{H}{y} - \frac{y}{2 H}$ By finding a common denominator $\frac{2 H^2 - y^2}{2 H}$

$= \pm A$ Here $\frac{Dhru \mp \text{Cosine } n}{\text{Sine } n} = \text{Other} = A$ By simplifying $y^2 \pm 2A \times H \times y$

$H \times y = 2 H^2$ By completing the square $y^2 \pm 2A \times H \times y + A^2 \times H^2 = 2 H^2 + A^2 \times H^2$

$= H^2 (A^2 + 2)$ Taking the square root $y \pm A \times H = H \sqrt{A^2 + 2} \therefore y = H (\sqrt{A^2 + 2} \mp A)$

<header>In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta</header>

From the writings of the teacher <term>Bhaskaracharya</term> <note>Bhaskara II, a 12th-century mathematician</note>, it is understood that the planets and other bodies in the sky are transformed through the Earth's atmospheric sphere before they become visible (clear) to us. Therefore, the correction required to transform the calculated "clear" planets into the "perceived" planets within the atmospheric sphere is what should rightly be called <term>Nata-karma</term> <note>literally "bending-action," referring here to a correction based on the hour angle or zenith distance</note>. The authors of the ancient <term>Surya Siddhanta</term>, <term>Aryabhata</term>, and others prior to <term>Brahmagupta</term> have written nothing regarding this subject in their respective treatises. In my opinion, the <term>Nata-karma</term> correction is extremely necessary; let the learned astronomers deliberate upon this matter. || 24 ||

->Now he describes the "Nata" time (hour angle) of the Sun and Moon during an eclipse<-

> **Whether to the East or West, by however many ghatikas the Sun is inclined from midday,**
> **At the end of the lunar day (Tithi), that [same amount] is determined by the remaining thirty ghatikas.** || 25 ||
> **The opposite is true from midnight; in a lunar eclipse, the Moon [is so inclined], and in a solar eclipse,**
> **The Moon is inclined by the same ghatikas as the Sun.** || 26 ||

**Commentary:** Whether to the East or the West, by however many <term>ghatikas</term> <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> the Sun is inclined (Nata) from its own midday: at the end of the <term>Tithi</term> (the full moon), the Moon's inclination in a lunar eclipse is found by subtracting those ghatikas from thirty, and taking the remainder. The opposite occurs from midnight: if the Sun is inclined East from its own midday, then the Moon is inclined West from the Sun's corresponding midnight. The "Nata" time is equal. The meaning is that a single "Nata-sine" (zenith distance sine) should be used for the correction of the circumference in a lunar eclipse. Furthermore, in a solar eclipse, in whatever direction (East or West) and by however many ghatikas the Sun is inclined at the end of the new moon, the Moon is inclined by that very same amount; therefore, here too, the Nata time is equal. Thus, a single Nata-sine should be used for the correction of the two circumferences. 

This is demonstrated on the armillary sphere: on their respective diurnal circles, from the intersection of the meridian and the diurnal circle at midday until midnight, and again until the intersection of the diurnal and meridian circles, when the Sun is inclined, it is inclined by thirty ghatikas. At that time, the Moon is at the intersection of its own meridian and diurnal circles. There, the remainder from thirty ghatikas is zero, so there is no inclination for the Moon; and it is understood that at the Sun's midnight, there is no inclination. It is said to be inclined by thirty ghatikas relative to its own midday. However, when the Sun is to the West at midnight, the Moon is at the same distance to the East from its own midday on its diurnal circle. They have equal ghatikas. This rule applies at the end of the Tithi because the Sun and Moon are then separated by half a circle (180 degrees); at other times, the Sun's midnight and the Moon's midday differ, which is why "at the end of the Tithi" is specified. When the Sun is East of its own midnight, the Moon is West of its own midday. Because they are separated by half a circle at the end of the full moon, it is all consistent. In both lunar and solar eclipses, the results obtained for them are distinct, yet the minutes of the result for the positive corrections are calculated together. Even a fool knows that there is only one Nata time <unclear>occurring</unclear>. <unclear>Therefore, this is also consistent here</unclear>. One should demonstrate this on the respective diurnal circles.

## Chapter on the True Positions of the Planets

**Sanskrit Commentary:** In a lunar eclipse, at the moment the full moon ends <note>the exact moment of opposition</note>, the Sun's hour angle is determined by the number of hours <term>ghatikas<gloss>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</gloss></term> it is away from midday, either before or after. By subtracting these hours from thirty, the Moon’s hour angle is found relative to midnight in the opposite direction. That is, if the Sun is at an hour angle before midday, the Moon is at that calculated angle after midnight; if the Sun is after midday, the Moon is before midnight. In a solar eclipse, however, the Moon’s hour angle is exactly the same as the Sun’s and in the same hemisphere <note>east or west</note> at that moment. ||25-26||

---

### Mathematical Rationale

A lunar eclipse occurs at the moment of the full moon <term>purnanta<gloss>the end of the 15th lunar day</gloss></term>. At this moment, the Sun and Moon are separated by exactly six signs <note>180 degrees</note>. Therefore, the number of hours the Sun has moved from the upper meridian, when subtracted from thirty, gives the Moon's position relative to the lower meridian in the opposite hemisphere. In a solar eclipse, the Sun and Moon are at the same longitudinal position; thus, they share the same hour angle in the same hemisphere. This is well known to astronomers. In the treatise *Siddhanta Shekhara*, the author Shripati stated: "The Sun is at an hour angle from midday at the end of the lunar day; the Moon is at the same angle from midnight. In a lunar eclipse, subtract this from thirty <note>original: 'abhra-rama' or 30</note> and reverse the direction. In a solar eclipse, the Moon is like the Sun." This teaching by Shripati is consistent with the ancient Acharyas <note>great teachers</note> and should be understood as such by calculators. ||25-26||

### Now, the Hour Angle of the Sun and Moon during an Eclipse is explained:

**Hindi Commentary:** In a lunar eclipse, at the moment of the full moon, the Sun's hour angle is the time in hours before or after midday. By subtracting this value from 30, the remainder is the Moon's hour angle, but measured from midnight in the opposite sense. If the Sun has an eastern hour angle, the Moon has a western hour angle from midnight; if the Sun is western, the Moon is eastern. In a solar eclipse, the Moon's hour angle is identical to the Sun's at that same time. ||25-26||

### Rationale

A lunar eclipse happens at the full moon. At that time, the Moon is six signs away from the Sun. Therefore, the hours the Sun is away from the upper meridian, subtracted from thirty, show the Moon's distance from the meridian in the opposite hemisphere. In a solar eclipse, the Sun and Moon are in the same degree and sign, so their hour angles in the hemisphere are equal. Shripati said the same in the *Siddhanta Shekhara* in accordance with the teacher's words. See his verse in the Sanskrit rationale above. ||25-26||

-> Now, he describes the calculation for the meridian offset (Nata-karma) by another method <-

> The product of the corrected circumference at midday, the corrected date, and the sine of the meridian offset is the multiplier for the Sun and Moon.
> Multiply by 161 and 499 respectively, then divide by the square of the radius (10,692,600). **[27]**
> The resulting seconds of arc are subtracted from the Sun if it is before the meridian, and added if after.
> For the Moon, if the equation of center was subtractive, it is the opposite: add before the meridian. Thus they are made corrected. **[28]**

**Vasanabhashya (Commentary):** The corrected circumferences of the Sun and Moon are stated for midday; from these, the corrected <term>Tithi</term> <note>a lunar day, or the longitudinal separation of the Sun and Moon</note> is found at its end. The "meridian offset" (<term>Nata</term>) is the time elapsed from the meridian to the end of that Tithi. The versine of that offset, the corrected circumference at midday, and the sine of the anomaly (<term>Kendra-jya</term>) at that moment are multiplied together. This product is related to the specific center of each body. One should multiply by 161 for the Sun and 499 for the Moon, then divide both by the square of the radius. This is the explanation:

First, calculate the corrected positions of the Sun and Moon from their mean positions using their own circumferences. Then, determine the end of the Tithi from them. At the end of the Tithi, find the number of minutes (<term>Ghatikas</term>) the body is away from its own midday. These should be converted into units of breath (<term>Prana</term>) and their versine taken. If the offset is 15 Ghatikas, subtract from 30 and calculate the sine from the remainder relative to midnight; that becomes the <term>Nata-jya</term> (sine of the offset).

Then, at the end of the Tithi, take the mean Sun and Moon with their highest points (<term>Apogees</term>) and correct them using the midday circumferences. The sines of the anomalies (<term>Kendra</term>) resulting from this correction should be taken. Multiply the Sun’s sine of anomaly by the sine of the offset, then by 161, and divide by the square of the radius. The result is in seconds of arc (<term>Vikala</term>). Similarly, multiply the Moon’s sine of anomaly by the sine of the offset and by 499, then divide by the square of the radius. The result is in seconds.

Then, using the multiplier derived from the difference in sines used for the sine of anomaly, multiply by the daily motion (<term>Bhukti</term>) and divide by 225. The result is the motion of the anomaly. <note>This refers to adjusting the rate of change in the planet's position.</note>

Regarding the application of these seconds: for the Sun, if it is in the eastern hemisphere (before the meridian), the result is subtracted; if in the western hemisphere (after the meridian), it is added. The word "or" in the verse refers to the method of correcting the Moon and Sun. This means: when the Sun is in the east, the result is a decrease; in the west, an increase. For the Moon, however, if the equation of center was originally subtractive, then it is the opposite: add in the eastern hemisphere and subtract in the western. If the Moon's equation of center was additive, the result is subtracted. By performing this calculation regardless of the hemisphere, the two bodies become "corrected" (<term>Sphuta</term>).

This process must be performed repeatedly (<term>Asakrit</term>). After performing it once, the end of the Tithi must be recalculated using the new corrected values, and the process repeated until the values stabilize.

**The mathematical proof (Upapatti):** The maximum difference in circumference is 20 minutes. When multiplied by the maximum sine (the radius), it equals 65,400. Dividing this by the degrees in a circle gives 161 seconds. This is the maximum difference in the equation for the Sun. For the Moon, the difference in circumference is 52 minutes; multiplied by the radius, it becomes 1,700,040. Dividing by the degrees...

Dividing by the divisor, the result is 472 seconds <note>original: *vikala*</note>. For the Moon, this value is 499. This is the maximum difference in the Moon's correction. This occurs when both the Sun and Moon are on the equatorial horizon <note>original: *unmandala*</note>, at which point the sine of their center and the radius <note>original: *trijya*</note> are equal, and the sine of the zenith distance <note>original: *nata-jya*</note> is also equal to the radius. Therefore, the Teacher <note>referring to the author Bhaskara or the authority being cited</note> has applied the Rule of Three <note>a mathematical proportion: if A gives B, what does C give?</note> here. If the sine of the center and the sine of the zenith distance are equal to the radius, the difference is equal to the seconds of the Sun's motion. But when the sine of the zenith distance and the sine of the center at a desired time have specific values, what is the difference? The result is the seconds of arc. For the Moon, when the product of the sines of the zenith distance and the center is divided by the square of the radius, the result is 499 seconds. If we multiply by the product of the desired zenith distance and center sines, what is the result? The result is the seconds of arc. The same applies to the sines of the arc of the center. Thus, it is proven.

One should subtract these seconds from the Sun when it is in the eastern hemisphere <note>original: *prak-kapala*</note>. Because the instantaneous circumference <note>the planetary orbit adjusted for the specific moment</note> differs from the midday circumference—why is the result subtracted here? Because when the multiplier is small, the result is reduced, which makes the Sun "true" <note>corrected</note> by the instantaneous circumference. Like the center of decrease, for the Moon also, if it is less than or greater than the midday circumference, that circumference is less, so it remains as an additive quantity. Later, it is subtracted in the western hemisphere by reversal. Since for the Sun it is made additive, for the Moon it is made subtractive; otherwise, in the eastern time, the instantaneous circumference is less than the midday circumference, so a greater subtraction remains. Again, it is given in the western hemisphere by reversal, being reduced when additive. Since in the eastern hemisphere the instantaneous circumference is less than the midday circumference, a greater additive amount remains, which is then subtracted. Thus, all is proven. As stated previously, when the difference of the arms is applied to the arc of the result of the arm, the planet becomes "true" (corrected) on the equatorial horizon. **[Verses 27-28]**

**Scientific Exposition:** From the midday circumferences, two "true" (corrected) positions for the Sun and Moon are found. From these, the lunar day <note>original: *tithi*</note> is determined. The product of the sines of the zenith distance <note>time from noon</note> and the center should be calculated. If for the Sun, multiply by 161; if for the Moon, multiply by 499. Divide by the square of the radius (10,692,000). The result is in seconds of arc. This result should be subtracted from the Sun in the east and added in the west. For the Moon, the previously obtained seconds should be added to the anomaly correction <note>original: *manda-phala*</note> if it is negative in the eastern hemisphere; otherwise, in the east or west, it should be subtracted. By doing this repeatedly, the Sun and Moon become "true." Previously, the zenith distance was brought in by the phrase "multiplied by the difference of the midday circumference," and now it is calculated again, hence the word "or" <note>original: *va*</note> is used. **[Verses 27-28]**

The difference in the Sun's circumference = $\frac{\text{sine of zenith distance}}{3 \times \text{radius}}$.

->Now, the Zenith Distance Correction (Nata-karma) is explained in another way<-

**Hindi Commentary—** From the midday circumferences, the true Sun and true Moon are calculated. At the end of the lunar day, multiply the Sine of the zenith distance at that moment by the Sine of the anomaly. If it is for the Sun (meaning the product of the Sun's Sine of zenith distance and Sine of anomaly), then multiply it by 191 and divide by the square of the Radius (10,692,900). If the product is for the Moon (meaning the product of the Moon's Sine of zenith distance and Sine of anomaly), then multiply it by 496 and divide by the square of the Radius (10,692,900). The resulting correction in seconds of arc should be subtracted from the Sun in the east and added to the Sun in the west. For the Moon, if the equation of center is negative in the eastern hemisphere, then add that previously obtained correction; otherwise, in both the eastern and western hemispheres, it should be subtracted. By performing this operation repeatedly, the true Sun and true Moon are found. Previously, the zenith distance correction was calculated using "the difference in midday circumferences," etc.; here it is calculated again, which is why the word "or" is used. — 27-28

### Now, the correction for the equation of time and the true motion are described:

->Multiply the daily motion of the planet by the Sun's correction and divide by the minutes in a circle; the result is the <term>Equation of Time</term> <note>original: "Bhujantara"; literally 'the interval of the arm,' used here for the correction to convert mean solar time to true solar time</note>, applied like the Sun's.<-
->The true motion is the difference between the positions of the planet on the previous and subsequent days at the present time.<- || 29 ||

**Vasanabhasya (Author's Commentary):** One should multiply the mean motion of the desired planet by the correction of the Sun's center and divide by the minutes in a revolution (21,600). The result is the correction called *Bhujantara*. It should be added or subtracted from that planet just as it is done for the Sun. If the calculation is based on true motion, it is applied to the true planet; if based on mean motion, it is applied to the mean planet. This is because the true planets are initially calculated for the time of mean sunrise. By applying this correction, they are adjusted for the time of true sunrise. Since the difference between the mean and true Sun at that moment arises from the Sun's correction, the rule of three is applied. It is as follows: if a planet moves by its daily motion in the time it takes for the 21,600 minutes of the circle to rise, then how much will it move during the rising of the minutes of the Sun's correction? This gives the *Bhujantara*.

The second half of the verse describes <term>True Motion</term> <note>original: "Sphuta-bhukti"</note>. The difference between the positions of the planet—calculated as true planets as described—on the previous day and the current day is the true daily motion for the current day.

Alternatively, having calculated the true planet for the following day, the difference between that and the true planet at the same time on the current day is the true motion; this is stated for practical usage. Otherwise, true motion cannot be stated with absolute precision because it changes every moment. This is because the difference between the eccentric circle and the equinoctial circle varies even in a very small area of the field. This should be demonstrated using the actual positions of the equinoctial circles and others. ||29||

**V. Bha.** <note>Commentary by Vishnukanta Jha</note> — From the product of the Sun’s correction for anomaly <term>Manda-phala; the correction applied to a planet's mean position to find its true position relative to its elliptical orbit</term> and the motion of the planet, divided by the minutes in a circle <note>21,600 minutes</note>, the resulting value is the **Bhuja-antara** <note>the correction for the difference between mean and true solar time</note>. This should be applied to the planets in the same manner as the Sun. That is, the resulting value is subtracted or added because the true sunrise occurs before the mean sunrise when the correction is negative. Since the difference between the planets of the past and future <note>the difference between positions on two consecutive days</note> constitutes the true motion on the current day, the difference between today’s and tomorrow’s true planetary positions is the true motion for that interval. || 26 ||

---

->**The Mathematical Rationale**<-

The planets calculated for the time of mean sunrise are converted to the time of true sunrise through the process called **Bhuja-antara**. Planets calculated via the "heap of days" <term>Ahargana; the total number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</term> according to the teacher’s method are mean positions at sunrise in Lanka <note>the hypothetical observatory on the equator</note>; in other words, they correspond to the time of mean sunrise. However, what is required are the positions at the time of **true sunrise**. The difference between the mean Sun and the true Sun is the Sun’s correction for anomaly in minutes. The teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> has accepted the time-measures <term>Asu; a unit of time equal to four seconds or the time taken for one minute of arc of the celestial equator to rise</term> generated by this solar correction to be equal to the minutes of the correction itself.

Therefore, the proportion is: if the planetary motion in minutes is obtained in the total time-measures of a day and night <note>21,600 Asus</note>, then what will be the motion corresponding to the time-measures of the Sun’s correction?
**Planetary Motion = (Planet's Daily Motion × Sun's Correction in Time) / Total Time in a Day.**

When the correction is negative, the true sunrise occurs before the mean sunrise; therefore, the mean planet, decreased by the motion corresponding to those solar correction time-measures, becomes the planet at true sunrise. Similarly, when the solar correction is positive, true sunrise occurs after mean sunrise; thus, the mean planet, increased by that displacement value, becomes the planet at true sunrise.

There is an obvious approximation here, as the teacher assumes the minutes of the Sun’s correction are exactly equal to the time-measures <note>Asus</note> of that correction. Furthermore, a planet corrected this way is not *perfectly* accurate for the true sunrise (because the planet also moves during the interval of the solar correction itself, which is not accounted for here, leading to a slight discrepancy). To find the true **Bhuja-antara**, one should follow the same method previously shown for finding the true "difference in rising" <term>Udayantara</term>, substituting the ancient Bhuja-antara in place of the ancient Udayantara. In the teacher’s version, the term "minutes in a circle" should be understood as the time-measures of a day and night. The method for Bhuja-antara provided by any [other] teacher is not entirely accurate; it is only clarified by the logic previously demonstrated. || 26 ||

# Chapter on True Motion <note>Sanskrit: Spaṣṭādhikāra</note>

By subtracting the <term>Equation of Time correction</term> <note>Sanskrit: Bhujāntara-phala; literally 'the result of the difference in longitude'</note> from the planet calculated for the time of mean sunrise, one obtains the planet for the time of true sunrise. When the <term>Solar Equation of Center</term> <note>Sanskrit: Ravi-mandaphala</note> is positive, the true sunrise occurs after the mean sunrise; therefore, by adding the Equation of Time correction to the planet at mean sunrise, the planet at true sunrise is obtained. The difference between the planet's position on the previous day and the following day (the daily difference in true planetary position) constitutes the true motion for the current day. That is, the difference between today's true planet and tomorrow's true planet is the true motion. Here, the term "revolutions in minutes" should be understood as the <term>sidereal breaths of a day and night</term> <note>Sanskrit: Ahorātrāsu; 21,600 breaths make one day</note>. || 26 ||

### Mathematical Rationale <note>Sanskrit: Upapatti</note>

The process of applying the necessary correction to a planet at mean sunrise to find its position at true sunrise is called the <term>Bhujāntara</term> operation. According to the Teacher's <note>Likely referring to Bhāskara or the author of the primary text</note> doctrine, planets calculated from the <term>Ahargaṇa</term> <note>The count of elapsed days since the start of the epoch</note> are mean positions for the time of sunrise at <term>Lankā</term> <note>The hypothetical city on the equator used as the prime meridian in Indian astronomy</note>; however, positions for the time of true sunrise are required. The difference between the mean sun and the true sun is the Solar Equation of Center in minutes. The Teacher has accepted that the time-breaths produced by this solar equation are equal to those minutes. 

Now, a proportion is made: if the planetary motion in minutes is obtained in the total breaths of a day and night, then what motion is obtained in the breaths corresponding to the Solar Equation of Center? From this proportion, the planetary motion related to the solar equation breaths is derived. When the Equation of Center is negative, the true sunrise occurs before the mean sunrise; therefore, by subtracting the motion derived from the proportion from the mean sun, one gets the true sun at the time of true sunrise. Similarly, by subtracting that motion from a planet, one gets the planet at true sunrise. 

When the Solar Equation of Center is positive, the true sunrise occurs after the mean sunrise; therefore, by adding the previously calculated <term>motion-correction</term> <note>Sanskrit: Cālana-phala</note> to the mean sun, one gets the true sun at true sunrise. By adding the motion-correction to the planet, one gets the planet at true sunrise. 

The imprecision here is evident, as the Teacher has assumed the breaths of the solar equation to be exactly equal to the minutes of the solar equation. Another error is that the planet at true sunrise cannot be perfectly obtained by simply applying the motion related to those breaths to the mean sunrise planet, because the Teacher has not accounted for the planet's own motion during those specific breaths. For a true understanding of the <term>Bhujāntara</term>, one should follow the same method previously shown for the true <term>Equation of Time</term> <note>Sanskrit: Udayāntara</note>. In calculating the true Equation of Time, the ancient <term>Bhujāntara</term> should be used in place of the ancient <term>Udayāntara</term>, and all other factors remain the same. The <term>Bhujāntara</term> methods of the authors of the *Sūrya Siddhānta* and others are not entirely correct, as is clear from the reasoning provided above. || 26 ||

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

<page-num>200</page-num>

To explain the application of the correction, the author states the verse. From the product of the velocity of the equation of the center and the sine of the hour angle, divided by 18,000 for the Sun and 4,499 for the Moon <note>original: "indudhṛti" (18) and "navanavaveda" (449) multiplied by 1000 and 10 respectively; these are technical mnemonic numbers</note> by the square of the radius, a result is obtained. It is often not known when this result should be added to or subtracted from one's own velocity; this verse is for that purpose. 

Namely: In the first quadrant of the anomaly, it is a decrease (subtraction); in the second, an increase (addition); in the third, a loss (subtraction); and in the fourth, an increase (addition) to the **true velocity of the Sun**. Because the result was calculated using the circumference at midday, and the instantaneous circumference here is greater than the midday circumference, too little was subtracted; therefore, the difference in results is now subtracted. In the second quadrant, however, an addition was made to the velocity, also using the midday circumference; since the instantaneous circumference is greater, too little was added, [so the difference is added]. In the third quadrant, the circumference is always less than the midday circumference, so too much addition remains; that is subtracted. In the fourth quadrant, a subtraction was made from the velocity using the midday circumference; since the instantaneous circumference is smaller (due to the anomaly exceeding six signs), too much was subtracted previously; that difference is now given back (added). 

This applies to the Sun in the eastern hemisphere. Just as the addition/subtraction is determined for the Sun in the eastern hemisphere, if it were for the Moon in the western hemisphere—what is the Moon's negative circumference? Since it is possible to perform even a greater subtraction, the <term>True Velocity</term> <note>Sanskrit: sphuṭa-bhukti; the actual daily motion of a planet corrected for its elliptical orbit</note> is refined by the instantaneous circumference. 

In the second quadrant, it is an addition, because an addition was made to the velocity in the second quadrant; it is proper to make it greater because the instantaneous circumference is greater. In the third quadrant, an addition was made to the velocity using the midday circumference; since the instantaneous circumference is less, too much addition was made, so that difference is subtracted. In the fourth quadrant, a subtraction was made from the Moon's velocity using the midday circumference; since too much was subtracted compared to the instantaneous circumference, that difference is given back. Thus, according to the quadrant of its own anomaly. 

In the eastern hemisphere, however, for the Moon's <term>True Velocity</term>, the corrections are addition, subtraction, subtraction, and addition in the respective quadrants. Since the Moon's negative circumference is less than the midday circumference, the result brought by the midday circumference was subtracted from the velocity; that is now given back. Thus, it is established: in the first quadrant it is an addition; in the second quadrant also, an addition was made with the midday circumference, but since the instantaneous circumference is less, the excess is [adjusted]. || 30 ||

---

**Vāsanā Bhāṣya (Explanatory Commentary):**
The result in seconds (arc-seconds) brought by the rule "midday circumference, true lunar day, and the sine of the anomaly," etc.—it is now told when that is an addition or subtraction to the motion. In the eastern hemisphere, for the Sun, according to the anomaly, those results are subtraction, addition, loss (subtraction), and addition to its own motion (the previously calculated slow-corrected velocity of the Sun). This means: in the first quadrant of anomaly, subtraction; in the second, addition; in the third, loss; in the fourth, addition to the true velocity. In the western hemisphere, it is the opposite: addition, subtraction, addition, subtraction. For the Moon, in the western hemisphere, it is as before (like the Sun in the east): subtraction, addition, loss, addition. In the eastern hemisphere, they are addition, subtraction, subtraction, and addition to the Moon's slow-corrected true motion. || 30 ||

### Here is the Derivation:

In the first and third quadrants, the sine of the anomaly increases; in the second and fourth quadrants, it decreases. In the Sun's eastern hemisphere, the hour-angle correction is negative, and in the western hemisphere, it is positive. Therefore, in the first and third quadrants, due to the increase of the negative result, the difference of the hour-angle correction is negative; in the second and fourth quadrants, due to the decrease of the negative result...

The difference in the correction becomes additive; in the western hemisphere, because the zenith distance correction <note>Nata-karma</note> is additive, it becomes the reverse. In the case of the Moon in the western hemisphere, whether the equation of center <note>Manda-phala</note> is subtractive or additive, the zenith distance correction is always subtractive; therefore, based on the quadrant of the anomaly <note>Kendra-pada</note>, the resulting corrections become subtractive, additive, subtractive, and additive. In the eastern hemisphere, in the first quadrant where the equation of center is subtractive, because the sine of the anomaly <note>Kendra-jya</note> is increasing <note>Upachaya</note> and the zenith distance correction is additive, the difference in the zenith distance correction is additive. In the second quadrant, because the sine of the anomaly is decreasing <note>Apachaya</note>, the difference is subtractive. In the third quadrant, the equation of center is additive, the zenith distance correction is subtractive, and the sine of the anomaly is increasing, therefore the difference is subtractive. In the fourth quadrant, because the sine of the anomaly is decreasing and the zenith distance correction is diminishing, the difference is additive. According to the rule that the difference between the true positions of the planets on successive days is the true motion, the zenith distance time of the previous day is taken as the zenith distance time for the second day as well; thus, it is entirely appropriate that the second motion-correction, in the form of the difference in zenith distance correction, becomes additive or subtractive based solely on the increase or decrease of the sine of the anomaly. || 30 ||

->Now the author describes the motion-correction for the Sun and Moon resulting from the zenith distance correction<-

**Hindi Commentary:**—In the calculation involving the circumference of the epicycle at midday and the sine of the anomaly at the zenith distance of the true lunar day, the difference (in seconds of arc) between today's and tomorrow's correction results in the following for the Sun's true motion in the eastern hemisphere, based on the quadrant of the Sun's anomaly: subtractive, additive, subtractive, additive. ### Mathematical Rationale

In the first and third quadrants, the sine of the anomaly is <term>increasing</term> <note>Upachiyamana: growing in value</note>, and in the second and fourth quadrants, it is <term>decreasing</term> <note>Apachiyamana: diminishing in value</note>. In the eastern hemisphere for the Sun, the zenith distance correction is subtractive, and in the western hemisphere it is additive. Therefore, in the first and third quadrants, due to the increase of the subtractive result, the difference in zenith distance correction is subtractive. In the second and fourth quadrants, due to the decrease of the subtractive result, the difference is additive. In the western hemisphere, it is the reverse due to the additive nature of the zenith distance correction. For the Moon in the western hemisphere, whether the equation of center is subtractive or additive, the zenith distance correction remains subtractive. Therefore, based on the quadrant of the anomaly, the results are subtractive, additive, subtractive, additive. In the second quadrant, due to the decrease of the sine of the anomaly, the difference is subtractive. In the third quadrant, the equation of center is additive, the zenith distance correction is subtractive, and the sine of the anomaly is increasing <note>The text here notes "decreasing," likely a scribal variation or specific geometric context</note>; therefore the difference is subtractive. In the fourth quadrant, due to the decrease of the sine of the anomaly and the diminishing of the zenith distance correction, the difference is additive. The difference between <term>today's</term> <note>Adyatana</note> and <term>tomorrow's</term> <note>Shvastana</note> true planetary positions is the true motion. By this rule, the zenith distance time of the elapsed day is the same for the second day; thus, it is proper that the second motion-correction, representing the difference in zenith distance, is additive or subtractive based on the increase and decrease of the sine of the anomaly. || 30 ||
