# Chapter on True Planetary Positions

The calculation method suitable for all astronomical operations has been accepted due to its precision. Regarding the statement by Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, a 12th-century mathematician</note> that "the true positions of the Sun and Moon are repeatedly refined during an eclipse," the learned should understand that what he describes as the "Teacher's view" <note>referring to the author's or Aryabhata's school</note> is not actually their intended meaning. ||32||

->Now the practical method for clarifying the positions of the Sun and Moon is described<-

**Hindi Commentary:** Using the circumference at midday as previously described, one should calculate the "Equation of the Center" <term>Mandaphala: the correction needed due to a planet's elliptical orbit</term>. By applying this correction to the mean Sun and mean Moon, and performing other longitudinal corrections as before, the positions are clarified for practical use. The Teacher describes this simplified clarification for general practice without the complex "zenith distance" <term>Natakarma</term> correction. Bhaskaracharya accepted this simplified clarification of the Sun and Moon as sufficiently precise for all operations. However, in his text beginning with "the true positions of the Sun and Moon are repeatedly refined during an eclipse," Bhaskaracharya has interpreted the Teacher's view differently. ||32||

->Now the reason for clarifying the positions of Mars and other planets is stated<-

> Because of Aryabhata's lack of knowledge regarding the mean, slow-apogee, and fast-circumferences,
> Mars and the others are not accurate; they become true using the mean apogees stated by Brahma. ||33||

**Vasanabhashya <note>The author's own prose commentary</note>:** There is no explanatory commentary for this verse.

**Sanskrit Commentary:** Due to Aryabhata's lack of knowledge regarding the mean, slow-apogee <term>Mandocca: the point of highest altitude/apogee</term>, and fast-circumferences <term>Shighra-paridhi: the epicycle used to account for retrograde motion</term>, Mars and the other planets do not reach their true positions. Therefore, Mars and the others should be made "true" using the mean apogees stated by Brahma <note>referring to Brahmagupta, the 7th-century astronomer</note>. The Teacher's intention is that since Aryabhata did not know the actual mean apogees, clarifying Mars and the others according to his system is not appropriate; they should be clarified using the actual apogees stated by me. ||33||

->Now the reason for the clarification of Mars and other planets is stated<-

**Hindi Commentary:** Aryabhata did not have knowledge of the actual mean apogees and fast-circumferences; therefore, Mars and the other planets are not accurately calculated according to his doctrine. They become accurate through the apogees stated by Brahma (Brahmagupta). The Teacher's point is that because Aryabhata lacked this knowledge, the planets like Mars <note>original: "Kujadi" - Mars and the rest</note> are correctly clarified only by using our apogee values. ||33||

->Now the degrees of the slow and fast circumferences for Mars and other planets and their clarification are stated<-

> The degrees of the circumference of the slow-apogee circle for Venus at the end of the odd quadrants
> are nine; at the end of the even quadrants, they are eleven 11. At the end of the fast-odd quadrants, they are two hundred sixty-three 263. ||34||

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

At the end of the even quadrants, the <term>Shighra-phala</term><note>The "fast" correction or equation of center relating to the planet's orbital position relative to the Sun.</note> is 258. From the <term>Manda-phala</term><note>The "slow" correction or equation of center relating to the planet's apsis.</note>, the mean planet becomes the "mean-true" planet. From the <term>Shighra-phala</term>, it becomes the true planet. This process is repeated iteratively for Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn using their respective corrections. || 35 ||

The degrees of the <term>Manda</term> circumference for Mercury are 38; for Jupiter, they are 33. For Saturn, they are 30. The <term>Shighra</term> circumference degrees for Mercury are 132. || 36 ||

For Jupiter, they are 68; for Saturn, they are 35. These are the "true" values. To find the motion of the <term>Shighra-kendra</term><note>The anomaly of the fast correction.</note> for Mars, the smaller sine is multiplied by 6 degrees and 40 minutes <note>original: "seven parts diminished by one-third"</note>. || 37 ||

When multiplied by the sine of the sign and increased by half, the <term>Manda</term> correction for Mars becomes true at the beginning of Capricorn and Cancer. || 38 ||

Its true <term>Manda</term> circumference is 70. The true <term>Shighra</term> circumference is 243 degrees and 40 minutes <note>original: "244 diminished by one-third"</note>. Such is the correction process for Mars. || 39 ||

Apply half of the <term>Manda-phala</term> to the mean planet; then apply half of the <term>Shighra-phala</term> to that mean. Then apply the full <term>Manda-phala</term> to the mean, and finally the full <term>Shighra-phala</term>. Thus, Mars is made true repeatedly. Its velocity is also made true like the planet. || 40 ||

**Explanatory Commentary:**
The degrees of the <term>Manda</term> epicycle <note>original: "Manda-ucca-nica-vrtta"</note> and the <term>Shighra</term> epicycle, which are demonstrated in the *Chapter on the Sphere*, are obtained based on their maximum equations within the assumed 360 degrees of their own orbits. These are called the circumference degrees of the epicycle. For all planets, as will be said for Venus, at the end of the odd quadrants—meaning the end of the first and third quadrants—the <term>Manda</term> epicycle circumference is 11 <note>original: "Rudra"</note>, and at the end of the even quadrants—the second and fourth—it is 11. <margin>The rule of three for the intervals was already stated by the Teacher.</margin> For the <term>Shighra</term> epicycle, at the end of the odd quadrants, it is 26 <note>original: "Rasa-yamala"</note>, and at the end of the even quadrants, it is 258. The rule of three applies to the intervals between them.

As before, the "mean-true" planet comes from the <term>Manda-phala</term>. This is the mean planet at the time of local sunrise, corrected by the terrestrial longitude, the equation of time, and the ascensional difference. It becomes "mean-true" by its own <term>Manda-phala</term>. Because the center of the <term>Shighra</term> epicycle is the "mean-true" planet, the true planet is derived from the <term>Shighra-phala</term>. Since the true planet is seen on the circumference of the circle <note>the ecliptic</note>, this operation is performed to find it.

For Venus: place Venus at the desired time in its own position, subtract its <term>Manda-ucca</term> <note>apogee</note> to get the <term>Kendra</term> <note>anomaly</note>. Then find the <term>Bhuja-jya</term> <note>sine of the anomaly</note>. Calculate the true <term>Manda</term> circumference using the radius and sine. Multiply the sine by this and divide by 360. The arc of the result is the <term>Manda-phala</term>. If the anomaly is less than six signs, subtract it from the mean; if more than six signs, add it. This result we call the <term>Manda-sphuta</term> <note>mean-true longitude</note>.

Then, subtract that from its own <term>Shighra-ucca</term> to get the <term>Shighra-kendra</term>. From that, calculate the sine and cosine <note>Bhuja and Koti jya</note>. Calculate the true <term>Shighra</term> circumference, multiply the sine and cosine by it, and divide by the degrees of the circle. The results are the <term>Bhuja-phala</term> and <term>Koti-phala</term>. Add the <term>Koti-phala</term> to the radius in the first and fourth quadrants, and subtract in the second and third to get the "true cosine." Then, the square root of the sum of the squares of the <term>Bhuja-phala</term> and the true cosine is the <term>Sphuta-karna</term> <note>true distance/hypotenuse</note>. From the radius multiplied by that and divided by the distance, the arc is the <term>Shighra-phala</term>. Apply this to the <term>Manda-sphuta</term> of Venus...

# Chapter on True Motion

If the <term>conjunction anomaly</term> <note>original: śīghrakendra; the angular distance between the planet and its point of fastest motion</note> is greater than 180 degrees, the correction should be added; if less, it should be subtracted. By applying these two corrections—the <term>apsis correction</term> <note>original: mandaphala; correction for the elliptical shape of the orbit</note> and the <term>conjunction correction</term> <note>original: śīghraphala; correction for the observer's position relative to the planet</note>—Venus becomes "true" or corrected. Then, treating that as the mean position, subtract its own <term>higher apsis</term> <note>original: mandocca; apogee</note> and calculate the apsis correction. By adding or subtracting this to the mean position obtained from the calculation, the "mean-true" position is established. Then, subtracting the <term>conjunction point</term> <note>original: śīghra</note>, calculate the conjunction correction as stated before. After adding or subtracting that to the mean-true position, Venus becomes fully "true." This process is repeated until the difference is negligible and the position is fixed. However, in this process, the correction of the <term>epicycle circumference</term> <note>original: paridhi</note> must be performed.

**Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn** are corrected in the same way. In this very manner, Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn are to be made "true" repeatedly. However, the method for correcting their specific apsis and conjunction circumferences has been shown previously.

The degrees of the circumference for **Mercury’s** <term>apsis epicycle</term> are 38 <note>original: vasu-rāmā; "Vasus" (8) and "Ramas" (3)</note>. For **Jupiter** <note>original: suraguru; teacher of the gods</note>, the apsis circumference degrees are 33. For **Saturn** <note>original: ravijya; son of the Sun</note>, the apsis circumference degrees are 30. The calculation of the apsis correction for these is the same as for Venus. The degrees of the circumference for **Mercury’s** conjunction epicycle are 132 <note>original: dviguṇa-candrāḥ; "twice-moons" (2) and "moons" (1), read as 132</note>.

For **Jupiter**, the conjunction circumference is 68. For **Saturn** <note>original: bhāskaraputra; son of the Sun</note>, it is 35. The calculation of the conjunction correction using these is the same as for Venus. These results are considered "true" because they do not have a <term>solar correction</term> <note>original: bhāskara; likely referring to a specific solar equation applied to outer planets</note>. The underlying logic <note>original: vāsanā</note> for these values is based on observation of the maximum correction.

Now, the author provides three and a half verses for the correction of **Mars** <note>original: kuja</note>. Half of the apsis correction is applied to the mean; then half of the conjunction correction is applied to that mean; then the full apsis correction is applied to the mean; and finally, the full conjunction correction is applied. Thus, the motion is made true, just like the planet itself.

First, take the position of Mars for the desired day and time. Subtract it from the current conjunction point to find the <term>conjunction anomaly</term>. Depending on which quadrant it occupies, take the sine <note>original: jyā</note> of the degrees traversed or remaining (whichever is less). That sine of the Mars-anomaly quadrant is multiplied by 6 degrees and 40 minutes <note>original: tribhāgonaiḥ saptabhiraṃśaiḥ; seven degrees minus one-third</note>. This is then multiplied by the sine of the "half-sign-added" arc <note>original: dalāḍhya-rāśi-jyā</note>, which is 2312. The resulting degrees are added or subtracted to the Mars apsis depending on whether the anomaly is in the signs beginning with Capricorn or Cancer. When this is done, it becomes "true."

Its "true circumference" is said to be "mountains-sky" (70). This refers to the apsis circumference; its value is not always constant. The "true conjunction circumference" is reduced by the calculated parts. The base value is 243 degrees and 40 minutes <note>original: veda-jinās-tryaṃśonāḥ; 243 and 1/3</note>. The sine of the Mars conjunction anomaly is multiplied by 6 degrees and 40 minutes and divided by the sine of the "half-sign-added" arc. The resulting degrees are subtracted from the 243 degrees and 40 minutes to find the true conjunction circumference of Mars. This is how the correction of Mars is performed. Using these tools, the correction should be carried out as follows:

How is it done? The author explains:
First, the apsis correction is calculated using its own tools. **Half of this correction** is added to or subtracted from the mean planet. Then, from that "half-apsis-corrected" mean, the conjunction correction is calculated; **half of that** is added to or subtracted from the mean. Then, from this second corrected Mars, the **full apsis correction** is calculated as described and applied to the original mean. Finally, the **full conjunction correction** is calculated and applied to that result.

By performing this process repeatedly, the position of the Son of the Earth <note>Mars; original: "Kshitisuta"</note> becomes accurate. The <term>motion</term> <note>original: "bhukti"; refers to the daily angular velocity</note> of Mars and the other planets must also be calculated accurately, just like the planets themselves. A clearer method is demonstrated as follows: Having subtracted the position of Mars from its <term>apex of quick motion</term> <note>the Shighra-uchcha or "fast anomaly," roughly corresponding to the Earth's orbital motion in modern heliocentric terms</note> at the desired time in one's own location, and having refined the <term>circumference of the fast epicycle</term> <note>original: "Shighra-paridhi"</note> using the rules for the quadrants of Mars's fast anomaly, one should first <term>calculate the correction for slow motion</term> <note>original: "manda-phala"; the equation of center</note>. 

Using its own slow epicycle circumference, if Mars is less than six signs from the <term>slow anomaly</term> <note>manda-kendra</note>, the correction is subtracted; if more, it is added. Then, having subtracted that from its fast anomaly, one should calculate the <term>fast correction</term> <note>shighra-phala</note>. Half of that correction is applied to the planet—added if the fast anomaly is less than six signs, and subtracted if more. From that twice-corrected Mars, subtract its <term>slow apex</term> <note>manda-uchcha; aphelion</note> to find the slow correction. By applying this full correction to the mean Mars as previously described (adding or subtracting), it becomes the <term>slow-corrected</term> <note>manda-sphuta</note> mean planet. Then, subtracting that from its fast anomaly and calculating the fast correction with its own parameters, that full correction should also be added or subtracted as was done for the slow-corrected position. By doing this, Mars becomes "clear" <note>accurate/true position</note>. 

Then, treating that as the mean, one should subtract it from its fast anomaly and refine the slow correction and the fast epicycle circumference using the sines of the quadrants of Mars's fast anomaly. Then, subtracting the slow apex from the refined Mars, calculate the slow correction. Apply half of that to the mean, then subtract from the fast anomaly to find the fast correction as before. Apply half of that as well. Finally, by applying the full slow and fast corrections to the mean Mars, the true position is established. This should be repeated until the values stabilize. In every re-calculation, the refinement of the slow and fast epicycle circumferences must be performed. For whichever planet the calculation is done only by the slow process, its daily motion is also calculated by that single process.

Where two processes are required, the daily motion is also found by two; where four are required, the daily motion must be made accurate by four. The <term>rationale</term> <note>original: "vasana"; the underlying logic or geometric proof</note> for the fourfold process for Mars is this: When Mars is at the apex of the fast circle, its slow apex remains as it was. Then it gradually increases until the middle of the quadrant, and decreases until the end of the quadrant; similarly in the fourth quadrant, and inversely in the second and third quadrants at the junctions of the quadrants. In all four, a <term>rule of three</term> <note>trairashika; a mathematical proportion</note> is calculated for the intervals derived from the calculation. For the sake of the slow correction, the fast epicycle circumferences are read as seven degrees minus one-third <note>6° 40'</note> at the junctions of the four quadrants. <insert>Or the matter is small in all cases</insert>. The first operation, using half of the two corrections (slow and fast), is also for the sake of refining the slow correction. The rationale here is not easily grasped; if there is a reason, it is found through the excellence of yoga <note>disciplined observation/application</note>, or perhaps the Tradition <note>Agama</note> itself is the authority. This specific method for Mars, regarding the slow and fast circumferences, is given because of its unique behavior compared to the remaining planets.

**Commentary:** For Venus <gloss>original: "Sita"</gloss>, at the end of the odd quadrants <gloss>at the end of the 1st and 3rd quadrants</gloss>, the degrees of the <term>circumference of the slow epicycle</term> <note>manda-niccha-vritta</note> are 9. At the end of the even quadrants <gloss>2nd and 4th</gloss>, the slow epicycle degrees are 11 <gloss>original: "rudra"</gloss>. At the end of the odd quadrants, the fast epicycle degrees are 263; at the end of the even quadrants, 258. A mean planet corrected by the slow correction becomes the "slow-clear" <gloss>manda-spashta</gloss> planet. When the slow-clear planet is corrected by the fast correction, it becomes "clear" <note>true</note> through repetition. This means: calculate the slow correction from the mean planet, apply it to get the slow-clear position; from that <gloss>slow-clear position</gloss>, calculate the fast correction and apply it to the slow-clear planet to get the true planet...

# Chapter on True Longitudes

From this true planet, the <term>Manda</term> <note>slow/equation of center</note> and <term>Shighra</term> <note>fast/anomaly</note> corrections should be calculated repeatedly as before until the values stabilize. In this manner, Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn <gloss>Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn</gloss> become true through their respective corrections <gloss>the corrections for the equation of center and the anomaly</gloss> as previously described. The degrees of the <term>Manda</term> circumference for Mercury = 38; for Jupiter <gloss>Jupiter</gloss> = 33; for Saturn <gloss>Saturn</gloss> = 30 at the end of the odd quadrants. At the end of the even quadrants, there is no adjustment to the <term>Manda</term> circumferences of Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn. The <term>Shighra</term> <note>anomaly</note> circumferences are: Mercury = 132; Jupiter = 72; and for the son of the Sun <gloss>Saturn</gloss> = 35. For these three—Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn—there is no further adjustment to the <term>Shighra</term> circumferences as they remain constant. 

For the movement of the <term>Shighra</term> anomaly of Mars, take the smaller sine <gloss>whichever is smaller between the elapsed or remaining degrees of the quadrant where the Mars anomaly is located</gloss>. Multiply that by 6 degrees and 40 minutes <note>original: 6:40</note> (which is 7 degrees minus one-third of a degree and minus 20 minutes). Divide this by the sine of 45 degrees <gloss>the sine of the middle of the quadrant</gloss>. With the resulting degrees, the <term>Manda-uchcha</term> <gloss>apogee</gloss> of Mars should be increased or decreased respectively starting from the signs of Capricorn or Cancer. Thus, the corrected apogee of Mars suitable for the calculation becomes clear. Its corrected circumference <gloss>the Manda circumference of Mars</gloss> is 70 <note>original: "Khanaga" using the Katapayadi system where Kha=0, Naga=7</note>. This is 243 degrees and 40 minutes <note>original: "Vedajina" where Veda=4, Jina=24</note> minus one-third, further reduced by the quotient obtained earlier for the apogee correction—when subtracted <gloss>decreased</gloss>, it becomes the corrected <term>Shighra</term> circumference of Mars. 

The procedure for the true position of Mars is as follows: To the mean position <gloss>the mathematically calculated mean Mars</gloss>, apply half of the <term>Manda</term> correction (positive or negative as calculated). From that, calculate the <term>Shighra</term> correction and apply half of it <gloss>half of the Shighra correction derived from the mean Mars already adjusted by half the Manda correction</gloss> to the mean <gloss>the mean Mars already adjusted by half the Manda correction</gloss>. Then, apply the full <term>Manda</term> correction derived from that twice-adjusted mean, and finally the full <term>Shighra</term> correction. These full <gloss>complete</gloss> corrections are applied to the mean <gloss>mathematically calculated</gloss> Mars. This process should be repeated, as with Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn, until the value is consistent. Then the son of the Earth <gloss>Mars</gloss> is considered "true" (accurate). The true velocity <gloss>true daily motion</gloss> should be calculated like the planet itself; the difference between the true positions on two consecutive days is the true motion of the planet for that interval. ->### Here is the Rationale<-

The <term>Shighra</term> circumference of Saturn stated by Brahmagupta = 35°; the <term>Shighra</term> circumference of Saturn stated by the author of the *Surya Siddhanta* = 40°; the degrees of that same circumference stated by Bhaskara = 40°. Furthermore, the <term>Manda</term> circumference of Saturn stated by the Teacher <note>likely referring to Aryabhata or Lalla</note> = 30°, while Bhaskara states it as 50°. Only they can truly know why Bhaskara created such a discrepancy in Saturn's circumferences. The author of the *Surya Siddhanta*, keeping in mind that the sine of the maximum <term>Shighra</term> correction is not fixed, taught different circumferences based on the distinction between the ends of even and odd quadrants, as it is said:

> For Mars and the others, the <term>Shighra</term> [circumferences] at the end of even quadrants are: 235, 133, 70, 262, and 39. 
> At the end of odd quadrants, they are stated for the <term>Shighra</term> process as: 232, 132, 72, 260, and 40.
<note>These verses list the circumferences for Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn respectively in the Surya Siddhanta tradition.</note>

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

The method for correcting the circumference <note>the epicycle</note> as described by Brahmagupta was followed exactly by Bhaskara. For Mars, at the end of all four quadrants of the anomaly of the apex <note>shighra-kendra</note>, the calculated slow-moving apogee <note>mandoccha</note> remains uniform. However, in the middle of a quadrant, it is always less by seven degrees minus one-third <note>6 degrees and 40 minutes</note>. Therefore, an interpolation is used: if the sine of the anomaly at 45 degrees yields a difference of six and two-thirds degrees in the apogee, then what would the difference be for the desired sine of the anomaly? The resulting value should be added to or subtracted from the calculated apogee of Mars—depending on whether the center is in the signs beginning with Capricorn or Cancer—to arrive at the corrected <term>Mandoccha</term> <note>the slow-moving apogee used to calculate planetary orbits</note>.

Similarly, the circumference of the fast-moving epicycle <note>shighra-paridhi</note> for Mars is uniform at the ends of the quadrants, but in the middle, it is always less by six and two-thirds degrees. The result obtained from the previous interpolation should be applied as a positive or negative correction to that circumference to find the corrected fast-moving epicycle. Bhaskara’s statement is identical to the Teacher’s <note>Brahmagupta's</note> instruction. In the process of clarifying planetary positions, Brahmagupta observed this specific difference only in Mars and Venus, and the irregularity in the apogee of Mars. No specific logic was provided for this; it is known from Bhaskara’s writings that observation <note>vedha</note> alone is the authority here, and no other cause can be stated.

In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, Sripati stated: "For the son of the Earth <note>Mars</note>, when the Sun has set, take the sine of the anomaly, multiply it by the constant, and divide by 1446. The resulting degrees should be added to or subtracted from the apogee of Mars to make it corrected in the signs of Capricorn, Cancer, etc." This follows the Teacher’s method for correcting the apogee of Mars. In place of the multiplier for the six and two-thirds degrees, the multiplier is $\frac{20}{3}$. Instead of the divisor being the sine of the 45-degree arc, he used the 12th sine (2145). By reducing these by a factor of $\frac{5}{3}$, the multiplier becomes 4 and the divisor becomes 1446.

Similarly, Sripati says: "They say the slow epicycle of the Earth-born one <note>Mars</note> is 70 degrees. The fast epicycle is always less than 243 degrees and 40 minutes by the degrees obtained." This statement by Sripati regarding the "corrected circumference starting with 70" matches the Teacher’s. Furthermore: "First apply half the slow correction to the mean Mars, then apply half the fast correction. Then apply the full slow and fast corrections repeatedly; thus the experts say the son of the Earth is corrected." This instruction by Sripati—to apply half the slow correction to the mean, then the fast, and so on—is rooted in the Teacher’s original rule. The method mentioned by Bhaskara, "first with the two halved corrections," should also be considered by the learned. || 34-40 ||

---

### Now the degrees of the slow and fast epicycles of Mars and other planets, and their correction, are described.

For Venus, at the end of an odd quadrant, the degrees of the slow epicycle <note>manda-nicocca-vritta</note> are 9, and in an even quadrant, they are 11. In an odd quadrant, the fast epicycle degrees are 263, and in an even quadrant, they are 258. By applying the slow correction <note>manda-phala</note> to the mean planet, the "slow-corrected" planet is found. By applying the fast correction <note>shighra-phala</note> to the slow-corrected planet through an iterative process <note>asakrit</note>, the true planet is found. That is, from the mean planet, calculate the slow correction and apply it to get the slow-corrected planet. From that, calculate the fast correction and apply it to the slow-corrected planet to get the true planet. Again, from this true planet, calculate the slow and fast corrections as before until the values are perfectly consistent.

# Chapter on True Planets

<note>The text describes the iterative process (Asakrit-karma) used in Indian astronomy to find the true position of a planet.</note> This process should be repeated until the values stabilize. Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn are made true (refined) through the repeated application of the Equation of Center <term>Mandaphala: the correction for the planet's elliptical orbit</term> and the Equation of Anomaly <term>Shighraphala: the correction for the observer's position on Earth</term> as previously described. The degrees of the epicycle of the center <note>Mandaparidhyansha</note> for Mercury are 38°, for Jupiter 32°, and for Saturn 30°. At the end of odd and even quadrants—that is, at these specific degrees of the planets' epicycles—there is an absence of further correction <note>Samskarabhava</note>. The degrees for the epicycle of anomaly <note>Shighra-paridhyansha</note> for Mercury are 132°, for Jupiter 58°, and for Saturn 35°; at these points, the correction is also absent, meaning the epicycle remains constant (uniform).

For Mars, whichever is less between the elapsed degrees of the anomaly <note>Gata-kendransha</note> and the remaining degrees <note>Gamya-kendransha</note> in its current quadrant, take its sine <note>Jya</note>. Multiply this by 6° 40' <note>seven degrees minus one-third</note> and divide by the sine of 45°. The resulting degrees should be added to the calculated apogee <note>Mandochcha</note> of Mars if the anomaly is in the signs beginning with Capricorn <note>Makaradi</note>, and subtracted if in the signs beginning with Cancer <note>Karkyadi</note>. This yields the corrected apogee suitable for the calculation. To find the true epicycle of anomaly for Mars, subtract the degrees previously obtained for the apogee correction from the base values of 70° and 243° 40'.

[The clarification of Mars follows this rule: To the mathematically derived position of Mars, add or subtract half of the Equation of Center. Use this adjusted mean position to calculate the Equation of Anomaly. Apply half of that result to the previously adjusted mean Mars. Then, calculate the full Equation of Center from this doubly-adjusted position and apply it to the original mean Mars. Finally, calculate the full Equation of Anomaly. Like Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn, this iterative process <note>Asakrit-karma</note> must be performed until the results are perfectly consistent; only then is Mars considered "True" <note>Sphuta</note>. The true motion <note>Sphuta-gati</note> is found by taking the difference between the planet's position today and its position tomorrow.] — Verses 34-40.

### Rationale

The epicycle of anomaly for Saturn according to Brahmagupta is 35°; according to the *Surya Siddhanta* it is 40°; and according to Bhaskara it is 40°. The epicycle of the center for Saturn according to our Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> is 30°, while Bhaskara states it is 50°. Only they can know why Bhaskara's values differ from the Teacher's. The author of the *Surya Siddhanta*, keeping in mind that the sine of the maximum anomaly is not always constant, provided different epicycle degrees for the ends of even and odd quadrants, as noted in the Sanskrit commentary: "For Mars and others, at the end of even quadrants..." etc. The way the Teacher (Brahmagupta) has clarified the epicycle is the same way Bhaskara has described it in his *Siddhanta Shiromani*. At the ends of the four quadrants of Mars's anomaly, the calculated apogee remains uniform. However, in the middle of a quadrant, it decreases by 6° 40'. Therefore, we use a proportion: if for the sine of a 45° anomaly we get a difference of 6° 40' in the apogee, then what difference do we get for the sine of the lesser of the elapsed or remaining anomaly in the current quadrant? The result of this proportion is applied to the mathematically derived value in the Capricorn-based or Cancer-based quadrants...

By adding or subtracting from the <term>Mandocca</term><note>Apogee or the point of slowest motion</note> of Mars, the <term>Sphuta-mandocca</term><note>True or corrected apogee</note> is determined. Furthermore, at the ends of the quadrants (<term>Pada</term>) for Mars, the <term>Shighra-paridhi</term><note>The circumference of the epicycle of fast motion</note> remains uniform. However, in the middle of a quadrant, it is always less by seven degrees minus one-third ($6^\circ 40'$). By adding or subtracting the result obtained from previous proportions to their <term>Shighra</term> circumference measurements, the <term>Sphuta-shighra-paridhi</term><note>True circumference of the fast epicycle</note> is calculated. Bhaskaracharya states this exactly as the earlier Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> did. The Teacher observed a discrepancy in the correction of planets specifically regarding Mars and Venus, as well as an irregularity in the apogee of Mars; no specific mathematical logic was given for this, and it appears from Bhaskaracharya’s statements that observation (<term>Vedha</term>) alone is the authority here. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, Shripati has also described the correction of the apogee of Mars according to the Teacher’s instructions in the Sanskrit commentary verse beginning with "When Mars is subtracted from the Sun..." etc. In a quadrant, whichever is less between the elapsed center-degrees (<term>Kendra</term>) and the remaining center-degrees, its sine (<term>Jya</term>) is multiplied by a factor of $7/3$ in the multiplier place, and in the divisor place, the sine of 45 degrees ($2145$) is used. By reducing these, the multiplier becomes 4 and the divisor becomes $914 \frac{6}{7}$ <note>Visual reading suggests 914 followed by a small 6/7 or decimal notation.</note>. Furthermore, Shripati’s statement in the Sanskrit commentary "The epicycle of the Earth-born (Mars)..." is consistent with the Teacher’s words "Its true circumference is..." etc. Similarly, Shripati’s method "Half of the slow-correction at the beginning..." and Bhaskara’s method "From the two halved initial results..." are rooted in the Teacher’s original method: "The slow-correction is in the middle, half of that is in the middle of the fast-correction," etc. || 34-35-36-37-38-39-40 ||

### Now he describes the corrected slow-motion and the true motion of the planets:

> The motion of the planet's slow-center, multiplied by the difference of sines and divided by the first sine (214).
> The result, multiplied by the true circumference and divided by the degrees of a circle (360), gives the minutes of arc. || 41 ||
> In the signs beginning with Capricorn and Cancer, this is added to or subtracted from the mean motion for the true Sun and Moon. For Mars and others, take the fast-motion minus the corrected slow-motion. || 42 ||

> If the result is less than the fast-motion, the difference is the true motion. If the result is greater than the fast-motion, subtract the fast-motion from the result to find the retrograde motion (<term>Vakra-gati</term>). || 44 ||

Just as the center is found by subtracting the apogee from the mean planet, the "center-motion" (<term>Kendra-bhukti</term>) is found by subtracting the motion of the apogee from the motion of both. This should be multiplied by the "difference of sines" (<term>Jyantara</term>). This means one should use the sine-difference applicable to the arc being calculated. Then, multiply the result by the true slow-circumference and divide by the degrees of the circle. The resulting minutes of arc, when the planet is situated in the signs beginning with Capricorn or Cancer...

# Chapter on True Motion
<note>original: "Spashtadhikara"</note>

When the mean motion is increased or decreased accordingly by its own **anomaly of the apsis**, it becomes the **slow-corrected motion**. For Mars and the other planets, this is called the slow-corrected motion <note>manda-sphuta</note>. However, for the Sun and the Moon, this is the true motion in the highest sense, because they wander within the epicycle of the apsis; this is the underlying rationale.

In whatever region of the **deferent circle** <note>kaksha-mandala</note> the Moon or the mean epicycle of the apsis and conjunction of Mars and others revolves, the difference in sines <note>jyantara</note> found there is used in a **rule of three** <note>trairashika; a mathematical proportion</note>. If for 225 minutes of arc <note>the standard sine table interval</note> one obtains a certain sine difference, then what is obtained for the minutes of the motion of the anomaly? Then a second rule of three is applied: if in a circle of 360 degrees the result is in the form of a sine, how much would it be in its own epicycle? Then a third rule of three: if for a sine result equal to 225, the arc minutes are 225, then what is produced for this? Thus, in the first rule of three, the divisor is 225. The result is the increase or decrease in its own motion. Wherever the epicycle is above the deferent circle, there is an increase in motion; where it is half-way, there is an increase <note>or specific variation</note>. Therefore, it is said that in the signs beginning with Capricorn and Cancer, the mean motion is increased or decreased; all this should be shown in those deferent circles and others.

This is established: if the motion of the Moon's anomaly spans many sine-differences, some teachers desire the correction of motion starting from the sine-difference occupied by the Moon, using past sine-differences. Others perform the operation using future sine-differences. Thus, with the motion corrected by the past and the motion corrected by the future, they take the average of the two. Others, however, for calculating the time elapsed, use the past sine-differences, and for calculating the time to come, use the future sine-differences to perform the operation on the Moon's motion. In that case, the true motion can be stated for a single moment. Because of the different positions of the deferent circle and the epicycle, there would be the risk of infinite regress; therefore, the Teacher <note>likely referring to Aryabhata</note> calculated the motion-sine using only the occupied sine-difference. Because the difference is very small, these methods are also possible for the Sun and others, since their motion is small. The reason why the arc in this verse is fixed by the first sine is that other sine-differences are not possible; therefore, the minutes of the motion-sine result are not equal to 225. Thus, everything stated is established.

Now, he speaks two and a half verses for the purpose of calculating the motion of Mars and the others. The **fast motion** <note>shighra-gati; motion related to the planet's conjunction</note> of the star-planets like Mars—of what kind? Being multiplied by the "tabular difference of the sine to be crossed" <note>bhogya-jiva</note> of the fast-correction, the slow-corrected motions should be divided. By what? By the **first sine** <note>225</note>. This is what is said: for a planet like Mars, one subtracts the slow-corrected motion (found by the previously shown operation) from its own fast motion; this becomes the "fast motion of the slow-corrected motions." Then one should multiply that. The sine-difference that occurs while calculating the sine of the fast-anomaly of the planet being corrected is called the "tabular difference of the sine to be crossed." Having multiplied the fast motion (diminished by the slow motion) by that, one should divide by the first sine—meaning by 225.

Then, the **radius** <note>vyasardha</note> multiplied by that result should be divided by the **fast hypotenuse** <note>shighra-karna</note>. The fast motion should always be diminished by whatever is obtained from that. That diminished value becomes the true motion of the planet situated in that region. If the result is greater than the fast motion, then from the radius multiplied by the result...

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
## Page 212

The value obtained by dividing [the product] by the <term>shighra-karna</term> <note>the hypotenuse or distance from the earth to the planet in the second epicycle</note> may be greater than the <term>shighra-gati</term> <note>the fast motion or velocity of the anomaly</note>. In that case, by subtracting the velocity from the result, the <term>vakra-gati</term> <note>retrograde motion</note> is found. If the subtraction is performed in reverse, the result is the non-retrograde <note>direct</note> motion. This is how it occurs.

There is a specific rule for Mars <note>Sanskrit: *Bhauma*</note>: first, one should take the motion corrected by the <term>manda-phala</term> <note>the correction for the first epicycle/equation of center</note> and add or subtract half of it from the mean motion. Then, take the <term>shighra-bhukti</term> <note>velocity of the anomaly</note> diminished by that, multiply it by the tabular difference of the sines <note>Sanskrit: *bhogya-jiva*</note> at the arc of the <term>shighra-phala</term>, and divide by the first sine <note>the radius or the first element of the sine table</note>.

With the result obtained as described, the true velocity is calculated. If the difference between that and half of the true velocity derived from the <term>manda-phala</term> is found, it should be added or subtracted from the motion calculated in a single operation. If the true velocity is greater than the <term>manda-sphuta-bhukti</term> <note>velocity corrected by the first equation</note>, it is added; otherwise, it is subtracted. By doing this, the true motion of Mars is determined through two operations. One should demonstrate all of this by arranging the <term>kaksha-mandala</term> <note>the orbit or deferent circle</note> and other diagrams, just as with the remaining planets.

The underlying logic <note>Sanskrit: *vasana*</note> is as follows: the planet, corrected by the <term>manda-phala</term>, is located at a certain point on the orbit. When the center of the <term>shighra</term> epicycle is placed there, the planet is at the intersection of that circumference and the circumference of the <term>shighra</term> eccentric circle. Its distance from the line of the <term>shighra-ucca</term> <note>the apex of fast motion</note> increases daily by the difference between its own <term>shighra</term> velocity and the velocity corrected by the <term>manda-phala</term>. Since the <term>shighra</term> velocity is reduced by the <term>manda-phala</term> velocity, the difference between them becomes the <term>shighra-kendra-bhukti</term> <note>the velocity of the anomaly</note>. 

That velocity of the anomaly is then rectified. In the calculation of the arc of the result, the rod passing through the center of the <term>shighra</term> epicycle is considered the limit. The planet's result depends on its distance from that limit; therefore, the sines <note>Sanskrit: *kramajya*</note> are calculated from that point. As stated previously regarding the <term>shighra-phala</term>, a <term>trairashika</term> <note>Rule of Three</note> is applied: if for 225 minutes <note>the standard sine interval</note> the difference in sines is obtained, what will it be for the minutes of the velocity of the anomaly? In this calculation, the number 225 is the divisor and also the multiplier in the second step; thus they cancel out. The difference in sines of the velocity of the anomaly becomes the multiplier, and the first sine is the divisor. The result is the true <term>shighra</term> velocity at the planet's position on the eccentric circle. 

This is then converted to the scale of the orbit. It is said that one should divide the result multiplied by the radius by the <term>shighra-karna</term>. This is another Rule of Three. The result is the true velocity of the anomaly on the orbit. This represents the difference between the planet's motion and its true <term>shighra</term> motion. Therefore, by subtracting it from the <term>shighra</term> velocity, the true velocity of the planet is found. 

If the result is greater than the <term>shighra</term> velocity, then by reverse subtraction, retrograde motion occurs because the <term>shighra-karna</term> is small. Because the planet is positioned above the orbit, when the result multiplied by the radius is divided by the <term>shighra-karna</term>, the true velocity of the anomaly becomes greater than the <term>shighra</term> velocity itself. Due to the increase in parallax <note>Sanskrit: *drig-bheda*</note> caused by the positions of the orbit and the eccentric circle, the planet—though moving with its own mean velocity—is perceived to be behind the position it occupied on the previous day.

Thus, the difference in the true velocity of the anomaly is calculated. It is rightly said that by subtracting the result from the <term>shighra</term> velocity, one obtains the retrograde motion. To praise the method of rectification in his own treatise by pointing out the errors of other teachers, the author speaks three verses (41-44).

# Chapter on True Motion

**Commentary by Vishvanatha Daivajna:** The difference in the sine of the anomaly <note>manda-kendra-gati-jya-antara; the difference between two consecutive sines</note> is multiplied by the "tabular difference" <note>bhogya-khanda</note> and divided by the first sine <note>3° 45' or 225'</note>. The result is then multiplied by the corrected circumference <note>sphuta-paridhi</note> and divided by the 360 degrees of the circle. The resulting minutes of arc are either subtracted from or added to the mean motion depending on whether the anomaly is in the quadrant starting with Capricorn or Cancer <note>the first and second halves of the anomaly cycle</note>. This gives the true motion of the Sun and Moon. For the planets starting with Mars <note>the five star-planets: Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note>, the teachers say that the mean motion minus the correction for the anomaly is the "slow-corrected motion" <note>manda-spashta-gati</note>.

The velocity of the "apex of quick motion" <note>shighrocca-gati; the motion of the planet's conjunction with the Sun</note> minus the planet's own slow-corrected motion is the velocity of the "anomaly of quick motion" <note>shighra-kendra-gati</note>. When calculating the sine of this quick anomaly, take the "tabular difference" <note>bhogya-jya</note>, multiply it by that velocity, and divide by the first sine. Multiply this result by the radius <note>trijya</note> and divide by the "quick hypotenuse" <note>shighra-karna</note>. The quick motion <note>shighrocca-gati</note> minus this result is the true motion <note>sphuta-gati</note>. If the result is greater than the quick motion, then subtract the quick motion from the result; the remainder is the retrograde motion <note>vakra-gati</note> of Mars and the other planets. || 41-42-43-44 ||

### Here is the Proof:

Motion is of two types based on the distinction between mean and true: that motion which differs from moment to moment is "true" <note>spashta</note>, and the other is "mean" <note>madhya</note>. True motion is also of two types: daily and instantaneous. Thus, there is daily slow-corrected motion and instantaneous slow-corrected motion; daily true motion and instantaneous true motion. The Teacher here derives both the daily slow-corrected motion and the daily true motion.

### Now the Mandasphuta (slow-corrected) and True Velocities of the planets are described:

**Hindi Commentary** — Multiply the velocity of the slow anomaly by the sine-difference (tabular segment) and divide by the first sine. Multiply the resulting quotient by the corrected circumference and divide by the degrees in a circle (360). The resulting minutes of arc should be subtracted from the mean velocity when the anomaly is in the half-circle beginning with Capricorn, and added when in the half-circle beginning with Cancer; this gives the true velocity of the Sun and Moon. By applying the slow-motion correction to their mean velocities, the slow-corrected (Mandasphuta) velocity of Mars and the other planets is obtained.

By subtracting one's slow-corrected velocity from the velocity of the fast apex (Shighra-uchcha), the fast-anomaly velocity of Mars and the others is found. Multiply the fast-anomaly velocity by the tabular sine-segment and divide by the first sine. Multiply that quotient by the radius and divide by the fast-hypotenuse (Shighrakarna). Subtracting this final result from the velocity of the fast apex gives the true velocity. If the result is greater than the velocity of the fast apex, then subtract the apex velocity from the result; the remainder is the **retrograde motion** of Mars and the other planets. Thus ends the explanation. || 41-42-43-44 ||

# Chapter on True Motion

## Mathematical Proof

->Motion is of two types: Mean and True. The motion that varies at every moment is True Motion <note>Sanskrit: *Spashta-gati*</note>, while the motion that does not vary at every moment is Mean Motion <note>Sanskrit: *Madhya-gati*</note>. Slow motion <note>Sanskrit: *Manda-gati*; referring to the motion affected by the first inequality or equation of center</note> is also of two types: daily and instantaneous. These are further divided into Daily Slow-True Motion, Instantaneous Slow-True Motion, Daily True Motion, and Instantaneous True Motion. The Teacher <note>referring to the author of the primary text being commented upon</note> now establishes the means for calculating Daily Slow-True Motion and True Motion. Refer to diagram (A) in the Sanskrit commentary.<-

Earth = Center of the Earth, Earth-L = Sine of the maximum slow-correction <note>Sanskrit: *Mandantya-phala-jya*</note>, L = Center of the planet's slow-epicycle, Planet = The calculated mean planet on the slow-epicycle. U = Apex of slow motion <note>Apogee</note>, Planet-U = Slow anomaly <note>Sanskrit: *Manda-kendra*</note>, Planet-N = Sine of the slow anomaly <note>Sanskrit: *Manda-bhuja-phala*</note> = Sine of the slow correction <note>Sanskrit: *Manda-phala-jya*</note> (with slight difference), Planet-N = Earth-R = Sine of the slow anomaly, P-D-N = Maximum slow correction sine. ->By taking the difference between the two:<-

# In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta

By this reasoning, the result for the rapid motion <note>original: "shighragati-phala"; the correction for a planet's anomaly related to its orbit around the Sun</note> as stated in the *Surya Siddhanta*—"Subtract the velocity corrected by the slow anomaly from the velocity of the rapid apex; multiply the remainder by the difference between the radius and the last hypotenuse"—is proven logical.

On this very point, Ranganatha, in his commentary *Gudharthaprakashika*, calculates the rapid motion result using the instantaneous velocity <gloss>(1)</gloss> through an equation. He supports the *Surya Siddhanta* view by interpreting the word "radius" <note>original: "Trijya"</note> in the solar text as the "cosine of the rapid correction" <note>original: "shighraphala-kotijya"</note>. In the *Sauravasana* commentary on this same topic, Kamalakara has provided extensive arguments in defense of Lalla’s view, accepting the standard radius. My supreme teacher <note>a title of respect for the author's primary instructor</note>, the author of the *Madhuvarshini* commentary, states that Kamalakara's view is not to be respected. He supports Ranganatha’s interpretation by establishing that the "radius" here refers to the sine at three signs <note>90 degrees</note> after the correction of the result. Otherwise, according to Lalla’s statement—"At the intersection of the two circles, the mean motion of the planet is the true motion"—the mean motion would equal the true motion at the intersection of the circles even according to the *Surya Siddhanta*. That is not correct. The equality of motion is only established where the "mean velocity in the orbit occurs at the intersection of the eccentric circle."

**Now he explains to whom this calculation of true positions should not be given:**

->This should not be given to one who is not a son, even under oath, for it destroys the merit of the giver.<-
->Because the accuracy of results for journeys, marriages, and horoscopes depends on true planetary positions. ||45||<-

**Vasanabhashya—** There is no commentary by Bhaskara on this verse.

**Vijnanabhashya—** Because (for the reason that) the accuracy of the results for journeys <term>Yatra: astrological timing for travels or military expeditions</term>, marriages <term>Vivaha</term>, and horoscopes <term>Jataka</term> arises only from true planetary positions <note>Spashta-grahas</note>, therefore, even if pressured by oaths, this method of true calculation <note>Spashtikarana</note> should not be given to one who is not a son <note>meaning an unworthy or unlineal student</note>. Otherwise, it leads to the destruction of the giver's accumulated spiritual merit. It should only be given to a devoted disciple who has resided with the teacher for a long time. ||45||

**Now he explains why the calculation should not be given to others in Hindi:**

**Hindi Commentary—** Since the accuracy of the fruits of journeys, marriages, and horoscopes comes only from the true planets, one should not give this calculation to a non-son even upon swearing an oath. That is, it should be given to a devotee or students who have stayed with the teacher for many days; giving it to a non-son destroys one's beautiful deeds <note>Sukrita/merit</note>. ||45||

**Now he describes the faults of Aryabhata and others:**

->At the beginning of the Age <note>Yuga</note>, Aryabhata’s true planets did not begin from the first point of Aries.<-
->The planets of Shrishena, starting with Mars, and all those of Vishnuchandra,<-
->Are not seen to be accurate in the works of Shrishena, Aryabhata, and Vishnuchandra.<-
->Because of this, learned men have no respect for their calculations of Mars and the other planets. ||46-47||<-

**Vasanabhashya—** There is no commentary by Bhaskara on this verse.

For Mars and the others, the values are respectively: for Mars 163, for Mercury 145, for Jupiter 125, for Venus 165, and for Saturn 113. Convert that difference into minutes <note>kalā</note>. These minutes are then divided by the difference between the fast motion and the true motion (corrected by the first equation). The result is the time in days until the start of retrograde or direct motion...

**The underlying rationale <note>original: "vasana"</note> is as follows:**
From the center of the Earth to the center of the epicycle <note>original: "shighrocca-vritta"</note> is the vertical side <note>upright side of a right triangle</note>. The radius of the epicycle, which is equal to the sine of the maximum correction <note>maximum equation</note>, is the horizontal side <note>base</note>, whether to the east or west. **Scientific Exposition:** — By the degrees of the anomaly of conjunction mentioned as "by the fires and sticks" <note>numerical code for 163</note> and "by the arrows and Manus" <note>numerical code for 145</note> etc., the retrograde motion of Mars and other planets occurs. At these specific degrees of anomaly, their retrograde motion begins. By subtracting these from the 360 degrees of the circle, the commencement of the "re-retrograde" <note>resumption of direct motion</note> path occurs. 

The motion corrected by the equation of center <note>manda-spashta-gati</note> minus the motion of the apex of conjunction <note>shighrocca-gati</note> results in the motion of the anomaly of conjunction. By dividing the degrees and minutes by that, the elapsed or remaining days are found. This is done using the final degrees of the anomaly of conjunction, stabilized through the repeated process of successive approximation <note>asakt-vidhina</note>. || 48-51 ||

### Here is the Mathematical Proof <note>Upapatti</note>

Now, [Motion of the Apex] – [True Motion of the Anomaly] = [True Motion]. When the Motion of the Apex is less than the True Motion of the Anomaly, then by reverse subtraction, the motion must be retrograde. But where exactly does this state occur? This is considered here. 

| According to the method stated by Bhaskara, "The sine of the difference between the degrees of the result and the sky..." | $\frac{\text{Cosine of Correction Sine} \times \text{Motion of Anomaly}}{\text{Hypotenuse of Conjunction}} = \text{True Motion of Anomaly}$ |
| :--- | :--- |

From the appearance of this formula, it is established that where the cosine of the correction sine is at its maximum and the hypotenuse of conjunction is at its minimum, the True Motion of the Anomaly can reach its maximum. At the perigee <note>lowest point</note>, due to the absence of the equation <note>correction</note>, the cosine of the correction sine is at its maximum. The hypotenuse is also at its minimum there. Therefore, only at the perigee can the True Motion of the Anomaly reach its maximum. Thus, the possibility of [Motion of Apex] < [True Motion of Anomaly] occurs only at the perigee, where planets become retrograde. However, the commencement of retrograde motion must occur prior to reaching the perigee. Therefore, we investigate at what degree of the anomaly of conjunction the retrograde motion begins.

->Let the value of the cosine of the anomaly at the time of the start of retrogradation = $y$<-

$\frac{\text{Cosine of Correction Sine} \times \text{Motion of Anomaly}}{\text{Hypotenuse}} = \text{True Motion of Anomaly}$. Since the perigee exists in the center of the orbit, the hypotenuse relative to the orbital center is $= \sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 + \text{Max Sine Correction}^2 - 2 \times \text{Max Sine Correction} \times y}$. # Chapter on True Motion

According to the statement in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A foundational 12th-century astronomical treatise by Bhaskara II</note> regarding the sine of the correction, the <unclear>cosine of the distance</unclear> is the standard measure.
$= \frac{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \times \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}}{\text{Hypotenuse}},$ therefore $\frac{\text{Cosine of Correction} \cdot \text{Velocity of Anomaly}}{\text{Hypotenuse}^2} = \text{Mean Velocity of Anomaly} = \frac{(\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \cdot \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}) \text{Velocity of Anomaly}}{\text{Hypotenuse}^2}$

By substituting the square of the hypotenuse: $\frac{(\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \times \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}) \text{Velocity of Anomaly}}{\text{Radius}^2 + \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}^2 - 2 \text{Sine of Maximum Equation} \cdot \text{Cosine of Anomaly}} = \text{Mean Velocity of Anomaly}$. Here, Velocity of Anomaly = the speed of the fast-moving center <term>Shighra-Kendra-Gati</term>, Hypotenuse = the fast-moving hypotenuse <term>Shighra-Karna</term>. However, at the start of retrograde motion, the planet's true velocity $= 0$; therefore, the velocity of the apex <term>Shighra-Uchcha-Gati</term> equals the true velocity of the center. Let Velocity of Apex = $VA$.

Then, $\frac{(\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \cdot \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}) \text{Velocity of Anomaly}}{\text{Radius}^2 + \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}^2 - 2 \text{Sine of Maximum Equation} \cdot \text{Cosine of Anomaly}} = VA,$ by cross-multiplication:

$\text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Velocity of Anomaly} - \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \cdot \text{Sine of Maximum Equation} \cdot \text{Velocity of Anomaly} = \text{Radius}^2 \cdot VA + \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}^2 \cdot VA - 2 \text{Sine of Maximum Equation} \cdot \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \cdot VA$
By rearranging the terms: $\text{Radius}^2 \cdot VA - \text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Velocity of Anomaly} + \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}^2 \cdot VA = 2 \text{Sine of Maximum Equation} \cdot \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \cdot VA - \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \cdot \text{Sine of Maximum Equation} \cdot$
Velocity of Anomaly. By factoring out common terms $= \text{Radius}^2 (VA - \text{Velocity of Anomaly}) + \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}^2 \cdot VA = \text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Slow-corrected True Velocity}$
$+ \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}^2 \cdot VA = \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \cdot \text{Sine of Maximum Equation} (2 VA - \text{Velocity of Anomaly})$
$= \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \cdot \text{Sine of Maximum Equation} (VA + VA - \text{Velocity of Anomaly})$
$= \text{Cosine of Anomaly} \cdot \text{Sine of Maximum Equation} (VA + \text{Slow-corrected True Velocity})$

Therefore, $\frac{\text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Slow-corrected True Velocity} + \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}^2 \cdot VA}{\text{Sine of Maximum Equation} (VA + \text{Slow-corrected True Velocity})} = \text{Cosine of Anomaly}$. Here, the Mean Velocity is accepted as the Slow-corrected True Velocity.
$= \frac{\text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Mean Velocity} + \text{Sine of Maximum Equation}^2 \cdot VA}{\text{Sine of Maximum Equation} (VA + \text{Mean Velocity})} = \text{Cosine of Anomaly} = \text{Cosine of the Center's Anomaly};$ when ninety is added to the resulting arc,

the degrees of the fast-moving center at the time of the start of retrograde motion are found. Thus, the researcher's statement is proven:
> "The square of the Radius multiplied by the planet's mean motion, 
> added to the square of the maximum equation multiplied by the motion of the apex. 
> Divide this sum by the sine of the maximum equation, 
> and again by the sum of the motion of the apex and the planet's velocity. 
> The degrees of the arc obtained, when increased by ninety, 
> are the true degrees of the fast-moving center at the start of retrograde motion." 
This is established. It should be noted that this method is not entirely precise because it assumes the slow-corrected velocity and mean velocity are equal.

$\text{Radius}^2 = (120)^2 = 14400,$ $\text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Mean Velocity} = 14400 \times 31$
$= 446400,$ and $\text{Sine of Maximum Equation}^2 = 78^2 = 6084, \text{Motion of Apex} = 56$

This is because the degrees of Mars' retrograde center previously calculated using the cosine of the result are 164$^\circ$. The difference between this and the textually recorded center is only 1$^\circ$. Discerning scholars should observe that Kamalakara refuted Ranganatha's view without cause.

Retrograde motion begins at a certain distance from the <term>perigee</term><note>The point in the orbit closest to Earth.</note>; it ends at the same distance in the opposite direction. Therefore, the degrees of the circle (360$^\circ$) minus the degrees of the center at the start of retrograde motion equal the degrees of the center at the start of direct motion (the end of retrogradation). To determine if a planet has entered or will enter retrograde or direct motion, one should subtract the recorded degrees for retrograde/direct motion from the desired <term>Shighra-Kendra</term> degrees. If the daily motion of the center yields one day, then by proportion, the remaining degrees will show how many days ago the planet became retrograde/direct or in how many days it will do so. ||48-46||

---

->Now the degrees of the fast anomaly (Shighra-Kendra) at the start of retrograde and direct motion for Mars and other planets are stated:<-

**Hindi Commentary:** — Mars and the other planets become retrograde at the following recorded degrees of the fast anomaly: 163$^\circ$, 145$^\circ$, 155$^\circ$, 165$^\circ$, and 113$^\circ$ respectively. By subtracting these from the total degrees of the circle (360$^\circ$), the remaining degrees indicate when they become <term>Anuvakra</term><note>Direct or "following the retrograde" motion.</note>. The daily motion of the fast anomaly is found by subtracting the <term>Manda-Spashta</term><note>The mean motion corrected by the first equation.</note> velocity from the velocity of the <term>Shighrocha</term> (apex of fast motion). By taking the difference between the desired anomaly and the recorded anomaly and dividing by the daily motion, one finds the "past days" or "future days"—meaning how many days before or after the current day the planet began its retrograde or direct path. ||48-56||

### Mathematical Proof

<term>Mean Motion of the Quick One</term> <note>Sanskrit: Shi-u-ga (Shighra-ucca-gati); the angular velocity of the planet's apex of quick motion</note> — <term>True Mean Velocity</term> <note>Sanskrit: Spa-ke-ga (Spashta-kendra-gati)</note> $=$ True Velocity. When the Mean Motion of the Quick One is less than the True Mean Velocity, retrograde motion <note>Sanskrit: Vakragati; the apparent backward movement of a planet</note> occurs due to inverse subtraction. We shall now consider where exactly this condition arises. Based on the difference between the arc of the result—

| Cosine of the Result $\times$ Mean Velocity of the Center | = True Mean Velocity |
| :--- | :--- |
| Quick Hypotenuse | |

By observing this according to the method stated by Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note> starting with "multiplied by the sine," it is proved that the True Mean Velocity reaches its maximum where the Cosine of the Result <note>Sanskrit: Phala-koti-jya</note> is at its maximum and the Quick Hypotenuse <note>Sanskrit: Shighra-karna</note> is at its minimum. Because there is an absence of "result" <note>equation of center/anomaly</note> at the perigee <note>Sanskrit: Nichasthana; the point in orbit closest to Earth</note>, the Cosine of the Result is at its maximum and the Quick Hypotenuse is at its minimum. Therefore, the condition where Mean Motion of the Quick One $<$ True Mean Velocity can only occur at the perigee. However, the commencement of retrogradation begins slightly before reaching the perigee; we shall now calculate the degrees of the "Quick Center" <note>anomaly</note> at which retrogradation begins.

->Let us assume the Cosine of the Center at the start of retrogradation $=$ $y$<-

According to the method of Bhaskara, "multiplied by the sine of the difference of the result's degrees," etc.: $\frac{\text{Cosine of Result} \cdot \text{Mean Velocity}}{\text{Hypotenuse}}$

$=$ True Mean Velocity. The perigee is at the beginning of the orbit's center; retrogradation begins near the perigee.

Therefore, $\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 + \text{Sine of Max. Result}^2 - 2 \text{ Sine of Max. Result} \times y} = \text{Hypotenuse};$ and the Cosine of the Quick Center multiplied by the Sine of Maximum Result:

| $\text{Radius}^2 - y \cdot \text{Sine of Max. Result}$ | = Cosine of the Result |
| :--- | :--- |
| Hypotenuse | |

By substituting the Cosine of the Result and the Hypotenuse into the formula for True Mean Velocity, as per the "multipliers" etc. described by the revisers of the *Siddhanta Shiromani*:

| $(\text{Radius}^2 - y \cdot \text{Sine of Max. Result}) \cdot \text{Mean Velocity}$ | $(\text{Radius}^2 - y \cdot \text{Sine of Max. Result}) \cdot \text{Mean Velocity}$ | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\text{Hypotenuse}^2$ | $\text{Radius}^2 + \text{Sine of Max. Result}^2 - 2 \text{ Sine of Max. Result} \cdot y$ | = True Mean Velocity |

Where Mean Velocity $=$ Mean Velocity of the Quick Center. Hypotenuse $=$ Quick Hypotenuse. However, at the start of retrogradation, the True Velocity $= 0$, therefore the Velocity of the Apex of the Quick One $=$ True Mean Velocity. Velocity of the Apex $=$ $u-g$.

| $(\text{Radius}^2 - y \cdot \text{Sine of Max. Result}) \cdot \text{Mean Velocity}$ | = $u-g$, by cross-multiplication: |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\text{Radius}^2 + \text{Sine of Max. Result}^2 - 2 \text{ Sine of Max. Result} \cdot y$ | |

$\text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Mean Velocity} - y \cdot \text{Sine of Max. Result} \cdot \text{Mean Velocity} = \text{Radius}^2 \cdot u-g + \text{Sine of Max. Result}^2 \cdot u-g - 2 \text{ Sine of Max. Result} \cdot y \cdot u-g$

By rearranging the terms:

$\text{Radius}^2 \cdot u-g - \text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Mean Velocity} + \text{Sine of Max. Result}^2 \cdot u-g = 2 \text{ Sine of Max. Result} \cdot y \cdot u-g - y \cdot \text{Sine of Max. Result} \cdot \text{Mean Velocity}$

## In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

By squaring, we get:
$KG^2 \cdot R^2 = UG^2 \cdot K^2 = UG^2 (R^2 + AFJ^2 - 2 \cdot Keko \cdot AFJ) = R^2 (UG^2 - 2 \cdot UG \cdot MG + MG^2)$
<note>The abbreviations used in these equations refer to: KG (Kendra-gati/Anomaly velocity), R (Trijya/Radius), UG (Uchcha-gati/Apogee velocity), AFJ (Antya-phala-jya/Sine of maximum correction), Keko (Kendra-kotijya/Cosine of the anomaly), and MG (Madhya-gati/Mean velocity).</note>

-> $= UG^2 \cdot R^2 + UG^2 \cdot AFJ^2 - UG^2 \cdot 2 \cdot Keko \cdot AFJ$ <-
-> $= R^2 \cdot UG^2 - 2 \cdot UG \cdot MG \cdot R^2 + R^2 \cdot MG^2$ <-

By simplification: $UG^2 \cdot AFJ^2 - UG^2 \cdot 2 \cdot Keko \cdot AFJ = R^2 \cdot MG^2 - 2 \cdot UG \cdot MG \cdot R^2$. By further simplification:
$UG^2 \cdot 2 \cdot Keko \cdot AFJ = UG^2 \cdot AFJ^2 + 2 \cdot UG \cdot MG \cdot R^2 - R^2 \cdot MG^2$
-> $= UG^2 \cdot AFJ^2 + R^2 \cdot MG (2 \cdot UG - MG)$ <-

<margin>Therefore</margin>
-> $UG^2 \cdot AFJ^2 + R^2 \cdot MG (2 \cdot UG - MG)$ <-
---
-> $2 \cdot UG^2 \cdot AFJ$ <-

-> $UG^2 \cdot AFJ^2 + R^2 (UG^2 - KG^2)$ <-
$= \text{---------------------------------------------} = Keko$,
-> $2 \cdot UG^2 \cdot AFJ$ <-

By adding ninety degrees to the arc <note>the inverse cosine</note> of this value, we obtain the <term>Shighra-Kendramsha</term> <note>degrees of the anomaly of speed</note> at the time of the commencement of retrograde motion, according to the opinion of Kamalakara.

-> We now demonstrate the mathematics for verification <-

For example, for Mars: <term>Antya-phala-jya</term> <note>Sine of maximum correction</note> $= 78$, <term>Madhya-gati</term> <note>Mean daily motion</note> $= 31' 26"$,
-> <term>Uchcha-gati</term> <note>Velocity of the apogee</note> $= 56' 18"$, <term>Trijya</term> <note>Standard Radius</note> $= 120$, <term>Shighra-kendra-gati</term> <note>Velocity of the anomaly</note> $= 28'$ <-
$AFJ^2 = (78)^2 = 6084$, $UG^2 = 3481$, $UG^2 \cdot AFJ^2$
-> $= 6084 \times 3481 = 211784041$ <-
$KG^2 = 28^2 = 784$, $UG^2 - KG^2 = 3481 - 784 = 2697$,
-> $R^2 = (120)^2 = 14400$ <-
$R^2 (UG^2 - KG^2) = 2697 \times 14400 = 38836800$
$UG^2 \cdot AFJ^2 + R^2 (UG^2 - KG^2) = 211784041 + 38836800$
-> $= 60015204$, $2 \cdot UG^2 = 6962$ <-
$2 \cdot UG^2 \cdot AFJ = 6962 \times 78 = 543036$

$\therefore \frac{UG^2 \cdot AFJ^2 + R^2 (UG^2 - KG^2)}{2 \cdot UG^2 \cdot AFJ} = \frac{60015204}{543036} = 111$

The arc of this value $= 68^\circ$. Adding ninety degrees: $68^\circ + 90^\circ = 158^\circ$. This is the <term>Shighra-Kendramsha</term> of Mars at the start of retrograde motion according to Kamalakara's opinion. This differs greatly from the $163^\circ$ stated by the ancient teachers <note>the Acharyas</note>.

This statement by Shripati is consistent with what was said by Brahmagupta and Lalla; the calculation for days passed and future is easily understood. //50-51//

# In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta

The rule of the celestial bodies is established through observation and the superior application of instruments. Therefore, it is proven that when the orbits and other circles are laid out, these specific degrees of rising and setting are seen—whether the planet is at its node <note>undeviating from the ecliptic</note> or deflected <note>deviated in latitude</note>—according to the position on the circle. For that purpose, this chapter on Risings and Settings is provided. || 52 ||

Now, he speaks an *Arya* verse to explain the knowledge of the rising and setting of Mercury and Venus. Following the previous rule regarding the degrees of the terminal anomaly <term>shighra-kendra: the anomaly of the planet's fast motion, used to calculate its position relative to the Sun</term>:

With **50** <note>original: "kha-sharaih," literally "sky-arrows"</note> degrees of its own terminal anomaly, the **rising of Mercury** occurs in the **west**.
With **24** <note>original: "jinaih," referring to the 24 Jinas</note> degrees, the **rising of Venus** occurs in the **west**.
With **155** <note>original: "ishu-tithibhih," arrows (5) and lunar days (15)</note> degrees of the terminal anomaly, the **setting of Mercury** occurs in the **west**.
With **177** <note>original: "muni-naga-indubhih," sages (7), mountains (7), and moon (1)</note> degrees, the **setting of Venus** occurs in the **west**.

The rising and setting are reversed by the degrees of the circle <note>360 degrees</note>. Thus, for the western half-rising degrees of Mercury (50), subtracting them from the circle degrees leaves **310**; at these degrees, the **setting of Mercury** <insert>in the east</insert> occurs. For the western rising degrees of Venus, subtracting them from the circle degrees leaves **336** <note>original: "rasa-agni-gunah," flavors (6), fires (3), and qualities (3)</note>; at these degrees, the **eastern setting of Venus** occurs.

Furthermore, for the western half-setting degrees of Mercury (155), subtracting them from the circle degrees leaves **205** <note>original: "shara-kha-yamah," arrows (5), sky (0), and twins (2)</note>; at these degrees, the **eastern rising of Mercury** occurs. Likewise, for the western half-setting degrees of Venus (177), subtracting them from the circle degrees leaves **183** <note>original: "tri-vasu-chandrah," threes (3), Vasus (8), and moon (1)</note>; at these degrees, the **eastern rising** occurs.

Thus, the anomalies for the western rising in signs and degrees are:
Mercury: 1s 20° | Venus: 0s 24°
And for the western setting:
Mercury: 5s 15° | Venus: 5s 27°
For the eastern rising:
Mercury: 6s 25° | Venus: 6s 3°
And for the eastern setting:
Mercury: 10s 10° | Venus: 11s 16°

The calculation of the days past or remaining is done as before, by dividing the difference in anomaly by the corrected motion <note>the difference between the planet's speed and the Sun's speed</note>, similar to the calculation for retrograde motion. The logic here is: because of the rapid motion of Mercury and Venus, they linger in the west. Therefore, when the Sun has set, they are observed in the western direction like the Moon. When they become retrograde, the Sun moves faster than them. Being in eastward motion, they linger in the west; their eastern rising is like the setting of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, due to the reversal. The rest should be demonstrated by laying out the orbits on a globe or a diagram, specifically for when they possess latitude. || 53 ||

# Chapter on True Planetary Motion

### The Mathematical Rationale Here

For Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, the Sun itself acts as their "Apex of Swift Motion" <note>Sighrocca: the point that governs the planet's second inequality, similar to the center of the epicycle in Ptolemaic astronomy</note>. At the position of this Apex, these planets reach their maximum combustion <note>disappearance due to proximity to the Sun</note>. Because the Sun moves faster than these planets, it passes ahead of them. When the distance between them equals the "Degrees of Time" <note>Kalāṃśa: the specific arc of separation required for a planet to become visible to the naked eye</note>, the planet is seen rising in the east at the end of the night due to its distance from the Sun. Therefore, when the arc of the result <note>equation</note> generated by the true anomaly is added to the Degrees of Time, the result is the anomaly of the planet's rising. For example:

If the Sine of the Degrees of Time is obtained by the Radius, then what is obtained by the Sine of the Maximum Equation?

The resulting Sine of the Equation produced by the Degrees of Time = (Sine of Max Equation $\times$ Sine of Degrees of Time) / Radius.

The arc of this value added to the Degrees of Time gives the anomaly for the rising of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. Thus, the specific rule is derived:

> "The Sine of the Degrees of Time multiplied by the Sine of the Maximum Equation and divided by the Radius; the arc of the result added to the Degrees of Time gives the anomaly parts for the rising of slow-moving Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn."

->The calculation is shown here for demonstration<-

For Mars: Sine of Max Equation = 81; its Degrees of Time = 17°; Sine of Degrees of Time = 35;
Radius = 120. Then (Sine of Degrees of Time $\times$ Sine of Max Equation / Radius) = (35 $\times$ 81 / 120) = Sine of the result = 23. The arc of this 
= 11°. When added to the Degrees of Time (17°), then 11° + 17° = 28°. This is the anomaly for the rising of Mars. The rising anomalies for Jupiter and Saturn should be calculated in the same way.

For Mercury and Venus, the Mean Sun is considered equal to their motion. Taking the slow-corrected <note>Mandaspaṣṭa</note> Mercury or Venus as equal to this, their rising is seen in the west when the distance from the true Mercury or Venus equals the Degrees of Time. Therefore:

(Sine of Degrees of Time $\times$ Radius) / Sine of Max Equation = Sine of the True Anomaly. The arc of this added to the Degrees of Time gives the anomaly for the western rising in the first quadrant. In the second quadrant, having reached retrograde motion and because the Sun moves slower <note>relative to the planet's apparent speed</note>, they reach their setting there. In the third quadrant, they rise again; because they reach maximum combustion at their perigee, that rising is seen in the east at the end of the night. In the fourth quadrant, because they are at the distance of the Degrees of Time, they set there. Therefore, the anomaly for the eastern rising = Arc — Degrees of Time + 180 = Arc + (180 — Degrees of Time). By this, the rule is derived: "For Mercury and Venus, the Sine of the Degrees of Time multiplied by the Radius and divided by the Sine of the Maximum Equation; the arc [is used]. That arc, subtracted from or added to the Degrees of Time and 180, gives the anomaly for the western and eastern risings."

->The calculation is shown here for demonstration. For Mercury: Sine of Max Equation = 44, Radius = 120<-

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

For the western rising, the degrees of time <note>original: "kalāṃśa," the time-degrees required for a planet to become visible from the sun's glare</note> are $13$, and the sine of these time-degrees is $27$. Then, $\frac{\text{Sine of time-degrees} \cdot \text{Radius}}{\text{Sine of Latitude}} = \frac{27 \times 120}{44} = 73$. The arc of this value is $37^\circ$. Adding the $13$ time-degrees, $37 + 13 = 50$; these are the degrees of the center <note>original: "kendrāṃśa," the anomaly or angular distance from the sun</note> for the western rising. For the eastern rising, the time-degrees are $12$. Thus, the degrees of the center for the eastern rising are $(180 - \text{time-degrees}) + \text{arc} = 37 + 168 = 205$. In this same manner, the degrees of the center for Venus should also be calculated. As stated in the *Siddhanta-shekhara*:

> "With 28, 14, and 17 degrees, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn respectively rise in the East. By these same degrees of the fast-center <note>the anomaly</note> subtracted from the degrees of a full circle <note>360 degrees</note>, their setting in the ->West<- is again determined.
> With 50 and 24 degrees, Mercury and Venus rise in the direction of the Noose-Handed One <note>the West, ruled by the deity Varuna</note> while moving North. Their setting in that same direction is declared by planetary experts to be at 155 and 177 degrees."

These were stated by Sripati; and in the *Siddhanta-shiromani*:

> "Mars rises in the East at 28 degrees, Venus <note>Note: likely a scribal error for Jupiter in this context</note> at 14, and Saturn at 17. With their respective rising degrees subtracted from the degrees of the circle, these three go to their setting in the ->West<-.
> Mercury and Venus rise in the West at 50 and 24 degrees, and set at 155 and 177 degrees. Their rising in the East occurs at 205 and 183 degrees, and their setting there occurs at 310 and 336 degrees.
> The difference between the current degrees and those stated for the setting and rising of direct and retrograde planets, divided by the daily motion of the fast-center, gives the days passed or remaining until the setting or rising."

Everything stated by Bhaskara follows exactly what was said by the ancient Teacher. || 52-53 ||
