## Mathematical Rationale

For Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, the Sun itself acts as the <term>Apex of Quick Motion</term> <note>original: "Sheeghrochcha"; the point that determines the planet's second inequality, similar to an epicycle's center</note>. At the position of this Apex, their maximum combustion <note>disappearance due to proximity to the Sun</note> occurs. Because the Sun moves faster than these planets, the Sun moves ahead. When the distance between them equals the <term>Degrees of Time</term> <note>original: "Kalansha"; the specific arc of separation required for a planet to become visible from the Sun's rays</note>, they rise in the last part of the night due to their proximity to the Sun. Therefore, by adding the arc of the result—derived from the true degrees of anomaly equivalent to the Degrees of Time—to the Degrees of Time, their degrees of anomaly at rising are determined.

For example: if for the <term>Radius</term> <note>original: "Trijya"</note> we find the sine of the true anomaly equal to the Degrees of Time, then what would it be for the <term>Sine of Maximum Correction</term> <note>original: "Antyaphalajya"</note>? By this proportion, the sine of the result generated by the sine of the anomaly equal to the Degrees of Time is:
$$\frac{\text{Maximum Sine} \cdot \text{Sine of Degrees of Time}}{\text{Radius}}$$
By adding the Degrees of Time to the arc of this value, the degrees of anomaly at rising for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are found. Thus, the formula of the Great Scholar <note>original: "M. M. (Mahamahopadhyaya)"</note> Pandit Sudhakara Dvivedi is proven. See the formula written in the Sanskrit rationale: "The sine of the Degrees of Time multiplied by the Sine of Maximum Correction and divided by the Radius," etc.

Observe the practical calculation: For example, the Sine of Maximum Correction for Mars = 81, the Degrees of Time = 17, the Sine of the Degrees of Time = 35, and the Radius = 120. Then, according to the aforementioned formula:
$$\frac{\text{Sine of Degrees of Time} \cdot \text{Maximum Sine}}{\text{Radius}}$$
$= \frac{35 \times 21}{120} = \text{Sine of the result}$. Its arc = 11°. Adding the Degrees of Time: $11^\circ + 17^\circ = 28^\circ =$ the degrees of anomaly for the rising of Mars. In this same manner, one should calculate the rising anomaly for Jupiter and Saturn.

The mean Sun is roughly equal to Mercury and Venus. Considering the <term>Slow-Corrected</term> <note>original: "Mandaspashta"; corrected for the first inequality/apsis</note> Mercury or Venus to be equal to the Sun, their rising is observed in the west at an interval equal to the Degrees of Time from the true Mercury or true Venus. Then:
$$\frac{\text{Sine of Degrees of Time} \cdot \text{Radius}}{\text{Maximum Sine}} = \text{Sine of the True Anomaly}$$
By adding the Degrees of Time to the arc of this value, the western rising anomaly occurs in the first quadrant. In the second quadrant, having attained retrograde motion and due to their slower speed relative to the Sun, they both (Mercury and Venus) set at that same point. In the third quadrant, they both rise again. Because their maximum combustion occurs at the <term>Perigee</term> <note>original: "Neecha-sthana"</note>, that rising is seen in the eastern direction during the remainder of the night. In the fourth quadrant, because they remain at the interval of the Degrees of Time, they set at that same point. Therefore, the previously mentioned anomaly = Arc — Degrees of Time + 180 = Arc.

Header: In the *Corrected Treatise of Brahma* <note>original: "Brahmasphuta-siddhanta"</note>

By using (180 — degrees of time), the formula provided by the Great Scholar Sudhakara Dvivedi in the Sanskrit commentary, "For Mercury and Venus, multiplied by the sine of three signs, etc.," is proven. Now, for the sake of understanding, the calculation is shown:

The sine of the maximum equation <term>Antyaphalajya: the sine of the maximum distance a planet deviates from its mean position</term> for Mercury = 44. The degrees of time for its setting in the west = 13. The sine of the degrees of time = 27. The radius = 120. Then, according to the previously written formula:

(Sine of degrees of time × Radius) / Maximum Equation Sine = (27 × 120) / 44 = 73.

The arc of this is 37°. Adding the degrees of time: 37° + 13° = 50°, which is the anomaly for the western setting. The degrees of time for the eastern rising = 12. Then the anomaly for the eastern rising = (180 — degrees of time) + arc = 27 + 178 = 205. In this same manner, the anomaly for Venus should also be calculated. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati, using the formula "By the 8, 8, 27, etc.," and in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya, using the formula "It rises in the east by 8 and 2..." have said everything in accordance with the teachings of the ancient masters. ||52-53||

->Now he explains how these planets become "true" or "corrected" at one's own location<-

**The planets become "true" at the midpoints of day and night, and at rising and setting, by means of the Sun's half-equinoctial shadow. If the current position is greater than the previous day's, the planet is direct; if less, it is retrograde.** ||54||

**Commentary:** These planets, which have been corrected by the methods just mentioned, would be "true" (accurate) if they were calculated for midday. However, if they are for the time of rising or setting, they must be adjusted by the Sun's half-ascensional difference <term>Charardha: the difference between the time of rising at the equator and at a specific latitude</term> at one's own location. He will explain the operation of the ascensional difference further on. If the true planet on the coming day is greater than the true planet of the past day, then there is no retrogradation; the planet is then in "direct motion." If it is less, the planet is to be known as "retrograde."

The reasoning here is: a planet at rising at the equator has its declination reaching the prime vertical of that location. The rising at one's own location occurs at one's own horizon. The difference between these two is the ascensional difference <note>original: "charadala"</note>. By moving the planet forward or backward by that amount, the planets are adjusted to the time they reach one's own horizon. The same applies to the setting. Therefore, at rising and setting, they become "true" through the operation of the ascensional difference. However, at the midpoints of day and night, because the meridian circle is the same for both one's own location and the equator, there is no difference in the operation and no ascensional difference exists.

If the mean positions are brought by solar time, they are adjusted to the time of sunrise by the Sun's ascensional difference. Otherwise, the planets are adjusted to their rising time by this ascensional difference. This applies to the Sun and other planets. When a planet is retrograde, it is observed to be further back every moment; therefore, it must be less than the true position of the previous day. If it is not retrograde, it is greater than the previous day's position. This is why the definition of non-retrograde (direct) motion was given in the latter half of the verse. Now, he introduces a verse to calculate the sine of declination for all planets.

**Sanskrit Commentary:** The planets such as Mars and others that were previously calculated are considered "true" at the time of local noon or at the midpoint of their motion. **Hindi Commentary:** The planets like Mars, etc., calculated earlier are true at the time of midday or at the half-motion point. Because the <term>Chara</term> <note>ascensional difference</note> correction has not yet been applied to them, if the planets are calculated at the time of the Sun's rising or setting, then by performing the <term>Ravichara-phala</term> correction, they become true for the local sunrise or sunset. If the planet's value for the next day is higher than the current day, the planet is moving forward (direct); if it is lower, it is moving backward (retrograde). The proof of this is self-evident. ||54||

### Now, the calculation of the Five Sines (Panchajya) is described:

> The Sine of the Sun <note>the sine of the planet's longitude</note> multiplied by the Sine of 24 degrees <note>the maximum declination</note> and divided by the radius results in the Sine of the desired declination of the Sun, which is North or South of the Equator. ||55||
> 
> Subtract the square of the desired Sine of declination from the square of the radius; the square root of the remainder is the radius of the diurnal circle, North or South of the Equator. ||56||
> 
> The Sine of declination multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by twelve is the <term>Kshitija</term> <note>earth-sine</note>. This <term>Kshitija</term>, kept separately, is multiplied by the radius and divided by the radius of the diurnal circle. ||57||
>

These divided by six are <term>Vinadis</term> <note>seconds of time</note>, and sixty <term>Vinadis</term> make one <term>Nadi</term> <note>24 minutes</note>. ||58||

**Sanskrit Commentary:** Here, the mention of "the Sun" is illustrative of all planets. Therefore, the meaning is: "Jina-degrees" refers to twenty-four degrees. Their sine (which is 1326) is multiplied by the "Sine of the Sun," which here means the sine of the true longitude of the planet at the desired time. That product is then divided by the radius. The result is the Sine of Declination for the desired time, whether for the Sun or another planet. This declination is North or South of the Equator. For signs starting with Aries or Libra respectively, this becomes the true declination. For the Moon and others, this is further adjusted by adding or subtracting their specific latitude...

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

<page-num>238</page-num>

When the directions are the same, the result is the **true declination** <note>original: *sphuta-kranti*</note>. The sine of that is the sine of its own declination. Here is the **underlying theory** <note>original: *vasana*; the geometric rationale or demonstration</note>: Where the sine of the circle is equal to the radius, the distance between the **equator** <note>original: *vishuvat-mandala*</note> and the **ecliptic** <note>original: *apamandala*</note> is the declination. This declination is North when the Sun is in the half of the ecliptic starting with Aries, and South when starting with Libra. The **versed sine** <note>original: *utkramanti-jya*</note> of the Sun is itself the "true" declination because the Sun moves exactly on the ecliptic. However, for the Moon and other planets, they deviate from the path of the ecliptic. Even when planets are at the same longitude as Aries, they may be South of the equator due to their **celestial latitude** <note>original: *vikshepa*</note>, as the Moon and others move along their own inclined orbits. Therefore, the sine of the arc of the declination, when added to or subtracted from its own latitude (depending on direction), becomes the planet's **true sine of declination**. This was already explained by us previously in the Section on the Sphere <note>the *Gola-adhyaya*</note>. All of this should be demonstrated on a physical globe.

Now, he <note>the author, Brahmagupta</note> presents two verses regarding the two semi-diameter chords of the **diurnal circle** <note>original: *svahoratra-ardha-sutra*</note>. By mentioning "declination," the sine of one's own declination is intended. The meaning is this: For any desired body—the Sun, or stars like Ashvini, Canopus <note>original: *Agastya*</note>, or Sirius <note>original: *Mrigavyadha*</note>—one should subtract the square of its own **sine of declination** from the square of the **radius** <note>original: *vyasardha*</note>. The square root of the remainder is the radius of that body's own diurnal circle. This circle exists to the North of the equator if the declination is North, and to the South if the declination is South. With that radius, the planet, wandering westward, completes a full circle in a day and night <note>24 hours</note>. For the fixed stars, these diurnal circles are permanent. 

The **geometric demonstration** <note>original: *vasana*</note> is as follows: Placing this on the globe, one should tie one end of a string at a distance equal to the degrees of the declination arc North or South of the equator on the horizon, and tie the other end at the same distance on the **unmandala** <note>the equatorial horizon</note>. This string stands like a chord extending North-South. Half of that is the sine of declination. Tying one end of a string to the tip of that declination and the other to a rod at the center of the Earth, a rectangular area is formed extending East-West. In a place with no latitude <note>the equator</note>, this is level; in a place with latitude, the North is raised. Gradually, as it reaches Aries, it enters the **prime vertical** <note>original: *samamandala*</note>. In that figure, the sine of declination is the **vertical side** <note>original: *koti*</note>, the radius of the diurnal circle is the **horizontal side** <note>original: *bhuja*</note>, and the distance from the intersection to the center of the Earth is the **hypotenuse** <note>original: *karna*</note>, which is the radius. By subtracting the square of the vertical side from the square of the hypotenuse, the square root gives the horizontal side. Thus, by subtracting the square of the sine of declination from the square of the radius, the root is taken. This produces the side, which is the **radius of the diurnal circle** <note>original: *svahoratra-ardha*</note>. Thus, it is proven.

Now, he presents two verses for calculating the **ascensional difference** <note>original: *charadala*</note>. Take the sine of declination of the desired planet or star, multiply it by the **equinoctial shadow** <note>original: *vishuvat-chaya*</note> of one's own location, and divide by twelve. The result is the **earth-sine** <note>original: *kshitijya*</note>. This is produced within the diurnal circle; set it aside for calculating the shadow. Then, multiply the earth-sine by the radius and divide by the radius of the diurnal circle. The result is the **sine of the increase/decrease** <note>original: *kshaya-vriddhi-jya*</note>. The arc of that sine represents the **ascensional difference in breaths** <note>original: *charadala-prana*</note>. Six breaths make a *vinadi*, and sixty *vinadis* make a *nadi* <note>standard Indian units of time</note>. What is being said here? The demonstration is as follows: Having calculated the **amplitude** <note>original: *agra*</note> by the method to be described, one should create a circle with that radius. Place that circle in the eastern part of the globe such that its center is the string reaching the center of the Earth from the intersection of the four circles: the equator, the equatorial horizon, the local horizon, and the prime vertical. It rises in the **meridian** <note>original: *yamyottara-mandala*</note>. Just as in the meridian the **sine of colatitude** <note>original: *avalambaka*</note> is the vertical side, here the sine of declination is the vertical side. Just as the **sine of latitude** <note>original: *akshajya*</note> is the horizontal side in the meridian, so in this circle...

<page-num>236</page-num>

# Chapter on True Positions
<note>original: Spashtadhikara</note>

The distance between the horizon and the equatorial circle <note>unmandala</note> is the "earth-sine" <note>kshitijā</note>. Therefore, the Teacher has proposed a rule of three <note>trairāśika; a mathematical proportion</note>: if for the "cosine of latitude" <note>lambaka</note> as the base, the "sine of latitude" <note>akshajyā</note> is the side, then for the "versed sine of declination" as the base, what is the side? In this calculation, the number twelve <note>representing the standard gnomon height</note> is used in place of the cosine of latitude, and the equinoctial shadow <note>vishuvacchāyā</note> is used in place of the sine of latitude.

The result is the "earth-sine" <note>kshitijā</note>. From this, another rule of three is applied: if this is the side in the diurnal circle <note>svāhorātravṛtta</note>, what would it be in the radius-circle <note>the standard celestial sphere</note>? The result is the "sine of increase/decrease" <note>kshayavṛddhijyā, commonly known as the sine of ascensional difference or charajyā</note>. On the day when the diurnal circle is equal to the radius-circle—due to the rotation of the celestial sphere on the equatorial circle—sixty ghatikas <note>a unit of time; 1 ghatika = 24 minutes</note> are projected there. The minutes of the circle <note>arc-minutes</note> are the same in number. Therefore, the earth-sine, which is the distance between the equatorial horizon and the local horizon, is transformed into the form of the sine of ascensional difference. The arc-minutes of that sine become "breaths" <note>prāṇas; a unit of time equal to 4 seconds</note>. As previously explained in the Chapter on the Sphere <note>Golādhyāya</note>, the earth rotates one arc-minute in one breath. From breaths, the "vighatikas" <note>24 seconds</note> and "ghatikas" are calculated as stated; what more need be said here?

Thus, the "half-ascensional difference" <note>charadala</note> is the time difference, representing a segment of the diurnal circle between the local and equatorial horizons. These values, brought forth by the solar day calculation <note>ravisāvana</note>, are relative to the time of sunrise at Lanka <note>the theoretical observatory on the equator</note>. Therefore, the Teacher explains the calculation of the Sun's half-ascensional difference in the following verses (55-58).

**Mathematical Commentary:**
The sine of the Sun's longitude <note>ravibhujajyā</note> multiplied by the sine of maximum declination <note>jinabhāgajyā; 24 degrees in ancient Indian astronomy</note> and divided by the radius <note>trijyā</note> gives the Sun's desired sine of declination <note>krāntijyā</note>. This is north when the Sun is in the northern half of the celestial equator and south when in the southern half. Subtracting the square of the sine of declination from the square of the radius and taking the square root gives the "radius of the diurnal circle" <note>dyujyā</note>.

The sine of declination multiplied by the equinoctial shadow <note>palabhā</note> and divided by twelve gives the "earth-sine" <note>kujyā/kshitijā</note> in the diurnal circle. This value should be kept separately. That earth-sine multiplied by the radius and divided by the radius of the diurnal circle gives the "sine of ascensional difference" <note>charajyā</note>. The arc of this sine gives the "ascensional breaths" <note>charāsu</note>. These divided by six become "vighatikas" <note>palas</note>, and those divided by sixty become "ghatikas." ||55-56-57-58||

### The Geometric Proof
<note>original: Atropapatti</note>

One should construct a "declination-prolonged circle" <note>dhruvaprotavṛtta; a secondary circle passing through the poles</note> passing over the Sun's position on the ecliptic. Then, from the intersection of the equator and the ecliptic <note>the equinox or golasandhi</note>, a circle should be drawn at ninety degrees <note>the solstitial colure</note>. This creates a spherical right-angled triangle. From the equinox to the intersection of the solstitial colure and the ecliptic, there are ninety degrees on the ecliptic—this is one part. From the same equinox to the intersection of the solstitial colure and the equator, there are ninety degrees on the equator—this is the second part. On the solstitial colure, the distance between the equator and the ecliptic is the maximum declination—this is the third part. These three parts form one triangle.

Similarly, from the equinox to the Sun's position, the Sun's longitude on the ecliptic is the hypotenuse <note>one part</note>. From the Sun to the intersection of the equator and the declination-prolonged circle, the Sun's desired declination is the side <note>the second part</note>...

It provides both the algebraic rules (Rule of Three) and the beginning of a geometric proof using spherical trigonometry.</summary>

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
## Page 240

...component. The <term>right ascension</term> <note>original: "vishuvamsha"; the degrees along the celestial equator</note> on the celestial equator, measured from the intersection of the spheres <note>the equinox</note> to the intersection of the equator and the secondary circle passing through the poles, is the "base" <note>side</note> and the third component. Thus, a second triangle is formed by these three components. The sine-figures <note>geometric representations of sines</note> of these two triangles are of the same type <note>similar triangles</note>; therefore, the sine-figure of the smaller triangle (the second triangle) is constructed.

From the center of the sphere (the center of the Earth), a line should be drawn to the intersection of the spheres. A perpendicular dropped from the planet's position onto this line is the <term>sine of the longitude</term> <note>original: "bhujajya"</note>. Similarly, a line should be drawn from the center of the Earth to the intersection of the equator and the polar circle; the perpendicular dropped from the planet's position to this line is the <term>sine of declination</term> <note>original: "krantijya"</note>. The line connecting the bases of these two (the sine of longitude and sine of declination) is not the actual sine of the right ascension arc. The triangle formed by the sine of longitude, the sine of declination, and the line connecting their bases is the sine-figure of the aforementioned spherical right-angled triangle.

Because the sine of declination is perpendicular to the plane of the celestial equator, and the line connecting the bases lies within the plane of the celestial equator, the sine of declination is also perpendicular to that base line. Therefore, the triangle "formed by the sine of longitude, the sine of declination, and the line connecting their bases" is right-angled in nature.

The perpendicular from the intersection of the polar circle and the equator onto the line passing through the equinox is the <term>sine of right ascension</term>. If the connecting line is perpendicular to the line through the equinox, then the line from the center of the sphere to the intersection of the equator and the polar circle is the <term>radius</term> <note>original: "trijya"</note>, acting as the hypotenuse. The sine of right ascension is the "arm" <note>opposite side</note>, and the distance from the base of that sine to the center of the sphere is the <term>cosine of right ascension</term> <note>original: "kotijya"</note>; these three sides form one triangle.

In the second triangle, the <term>day-radius</term> <note>original: "dyujya"; the radius of the diurnal circle, calculated as the radius minus the versed sine of declination</note> is the hypotenuse from the center of the sphere to the base of the sine of declination. The line connecting the bases is the "arm," and the distance from the center of the sphere to the base of the sine of longitude is the "base" <note>adjacent side</note>. Because these two triangles are similar, a proportion is formed: if the radius yields the sine of right ascension, then what does the day-radius yield? Through this proportion, the line connecting the bases is established. By this much, it is proved that for any spherical right-angled triangle, the sine of the hypotenuse-arc is real.

Between the arcs of the "arm" and the "base," the sine of one is real, while the sine of the other is not <note>meaning it does not lie on the great circle of the same radius</note>. That is to say, the sine which is "real" is transformed into the radius-circle of its base. As in the sine-figure of the spherical right-angled triangle described above, the sines of the longitude and declination (the hypotenuse and arm arcs) are real. The sine of the right ascension (the base arc) is not real, but when transformed into the radius of the declination-base (the radius of the diurnal circle), it becomes the line connecting the bases <note>referred to by the astronomer Kamalākara as the "sine of the rising-point parts"</note>.

The sine-figure of the triangle formed by 90 degrees, 90 degrees, and the <term>obliquity</term> <note>original: "jinamsha"; 24 degrees</note> (the triangle formed by the radius, the maximum sine of declination, and its cosine/minimum day-radius) is similar to the previously mentioned triangle (produced by the sine of longitude, sine of declination, and the rising-point sine). Therefore, by proportion: if the radius yields the maximum sine of declination (sine of 24°), then what does the sine of longitude yield?

The form of the **Sine of Declination** is:
-> $\text{Declination Sine} = \frac{\text{Sine of 24°} \times \text{Sine of Longitude}}{\text{Radius}}$ <-

Where the Radius is the hypotenuse, the Sine of Declination is the "arm," and its cosine (Day-radius) is the "base." In the triangle produced by these three sides:
-> $\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Declination Sine}^2} = \text{Day-radius}$ <-

Then, there is one triangle produced by three sides where the <term>equinoctial shadow hypotenuse</term> <note>original: "aksha"</note> is the hypotenuse, the sine of declination is the "base," and the <term>earth-sine</term> <note>original: "kujya"</note> is the "arm."
A second triangle is produced where the <term>gnomon</term> (12 digits) is the "base," the <term>equinoctial shadow</term> <note>original: "palabha"</note> is the "arm," and the <term>hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow</term> <note>original: "palakarna"</note> is the hypotenuse.

Due to the similarity of these two "latitude-fields" <note>triangles related to local latitude</note>, by proportion:
-> $\frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \times \text{Sine of Declination}}{12} = \text{Earth-sine (Kujya)}$ <-

It explains how sines on different circles (great circles vs. diurnal circles) relate to one another through proportions involving the radius and day-radius.</summary>

On the <term>declination circle</term><note>original: "dhruvaprota-vṛtta"; a circle passing through the celestial poles</note> passing through the intersection of the circles, there are ninety degrees from the pole to the <term>celestial equator</term><note>original: "nāḍī-vṛtta"</note>. From the pole to the East point on the <term>six-o'clock circle</term><note>original: "unmaṇḍala"; the equatorial horizon</note>, there are ninety degrees. On the celestial equator, from the East point to the intersection of the declination circle and the equator, is the <term>ascensional difference</term><note>original: "cara"</note>. From these three sides, a spherical triangle is formed. On the declination circle, from the pole to the intersection of the horizon and the <term>diurnal circle</term><note>original: "ahorātra-vṛtta"</note>, is the arc of the <term>day-radius</term><note>original: "dyujyā-cāpa"</note>. From the pole to the intersection of the six-o'clock circle and the diurnal circle is also the arc of the day-radius. On the diurnal circle, the interval between the horizon and the six-o'clock circle is the <term>earth-sine</term><note>original: "kujyā-aṃśa"</note>. A second triangle is formed by these three sides. By the similarity of the chord-figures of these two triangles, the following proportion arises: if the day-radius yields the earth-sine, then what does the <term>radius</term><note>original: "trijyā"</note> yield? The result is the <term>sine of ascensional difference</term><note>original: "carajyā"</note>. Its formula is:
  
  (Earth-sine × Radius) / Day-radius = Sine of ascensional difference
  
The arc of this is the <term>ascensional difference in respirations</term><note>original: "carasavaḥ"</note>. The sine of the Sun's longitude, the sine of declination, the day-radius, the earth-sine, and the sine of ascensional difference—these are the "Five Sines" whose calculation was performed previously. Even when the absence of degrees is mentioned according to the teacher's view, the Sun's position is calculated by the best of astronomers. It should be understood that according to Bhāskara's view, the sine of the Sun's longitude is calculated using the <term>tropical Sun</term><note>original: "sāyana-ravi"</note>. || 55-56-57-58 ||

---

### Now, the Calculation of the Five Sines is Explained

Hindi Commentary—Multiply the sine of the Sun's longitude by the sine of maximum declination and divide by the radius; the result is the Sun's desired <term>sine of declination</term><note>original: "krāntijyā"</note>. If the Sun is North of the celestial equator, the direction of the declination is North; if South of the equator, the direction is South. Subtract the square of the desired sine of declination from the square of the radius; the square root of the remainder is the radius of the diurnal circle (<term>day-radius</term>). Its direction is the same as the declination. Multiply the sine of declination by the <term>equinoctial shadow</term><note>original: "palabhā"</note> and divide by twelve (12); the result is the <term>earth-sine</term><note>original: "kujyā"</note>. Set this aside. Multiply that earth-sine by the radius and divide by the day-radius; the result is the <term>sine of ascensional difference</term><note>original: "carajyā"</note>. Its arc is the ascensional difference in respirations (<term>carāsu</term>). Dividing the respirations by 6 gives the <term>vināḍī</term> (minutes of time). Dividing the <term>nāḍī</term> (ghatika) by 60 gives the <term>vināḍikā</term>. || 55-56-57-58 ||

---

### Proof

Place the declination circle over the position of the Sun in the ecliptic. From the intersection of the equator and the ecliptic (the equinox), draw a circle with a radius of ninety degrees (the <term>solstitial colure</term>). Then two right-angled spherical triangles are formed. In the first, one side is ninety degrees on the ecliptic from the equinox to the solstitial colure; the second side is ninety degrees on the equator from the equinox to the solstitial colure; the third side is the arc of the solstitial colure between the equator and the ecliptic (the <term>maximum declination</term>). A triangle is formed by these three sides. Similarly, a second triangle is formed where the hypotenuse is the arc of the Sun's longitude on the ecliptic from the equinox to the Sun; the second side is from the Sun to the intersection of the declination circle and the equator...

# On the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
<note>The Brahmasphuta-siddhanta is the seminal 7th-century work by Brahmagupta; this text appears to be a later commentary or pedagogical explanation of its trigonometric principles.</note>

<page-num>242</page-num>

Up to the <term>Pole-prota circle</term><note>The circle passing through the celestial poles; a meridian</note>, the desired declination is the second side. From the intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic <note>the equinox</note> to the intersection of the Pole-prota circle and the <term>Nadi-vritta</term><note>The celestial equator</note>, the right ascension <note>Vishuvamsha</note> is the third side. From these three sides, a second triangle is formed. The sine-areas <note>geometric representations of sines</note> of these two spherical right-angled triangles are of the same type <note>similar</note>. Therefore, we first calculate the sine-area of the smaller triangle (the second triangle).

Drawing a line from the center of the sphere <note>the Earth's center</note> to the equinox, and then a perpendicular line from the center of the Sun to that line, gives the <term>Bhujajya</term><note>Sine of the longitude</note>. Drawing a line from the Earth's center to the intersection of the celestial equator and the Pole-prota circle, and then a perpendicular line from the center of the Sun to that, gives the <term>Kranti-jya</term><note>Sine of the declination</note>. Connecting the bases of these two (the Sine of longitude and Sine of declination) creates a line; however, this is not the Sine of the right ascension. The triangle formed by the Sine of longitude, the Sine of declination, and the line connecting their bases is the sine-area of the aforementioned spherical right-angled triangle. 

The Sine of declination is perpendicular to the plane of the celestial equator, and since the base-line lies within the plane of the celestial equator, the Sine of declination is also perpendicular to the base-line (by the definition of a line perpendicular to a plane). Therefore, the said triangle is a right-angled triangle. 

From the intersection of the celestial equator and the Pole-prota circle, a perpendicular line to the equinoctial line is the Sine of the right ascension. The base-line is perpendicular to the equinoctial line. A triangle is formed by these three sides: the Radius <note>Trijya</note> as the hypotenuse from the center of the sphere to the intersection of the equator and the Pole-prota circle, the Sine of right ascension as the side <note>Bhuj</note>, and the Cosine of right ascension as the vertical <note>Koti</note> from the base of the Sine of right ascension to the center of the sphere. 

Additionally, a second triangle is formed where the hypotenuse is the <term>Dyujya</term><note>The radius of the diurnal circle; literally 'day-radius'</note> (which is the Radius minus the versed sine of declination), the base-line is the side, and the distance from the center of the sphere to the base of the Sine of longitude is the vertical. These two triangles are similar. Therefore, we use the following proportion: if we obtain the Sine of right ascension within the Radius, what would we obtain within the Day-radius? This calculation yields the base-line. 

This proves that in the sine-area of any spherical right-angled triangle, the sine of the hypotenuse-arc is real. Between the sine of the base-arc and the vertical-arc, only one is real; the other is not "real" in the same sense, meaning the sine that is real is transformed into the radius of its corresponding cosine-circle. For example, in the sine-area of the spherical right-angled triangle described above, the sines of the hypotenuse and the declination-side are real, but the sine of the right ascension-side is not real; rather, it is transformed into the base-line (which Kamalakar calls the "inverted rising perpendicular sine") within the radius of the declination-cosine circle (the Day-radius circle).

The sine-area of the triangle produced by the sides of 90 degrees, 90 degrees, and the <term>Jinansha</term><note>The obliquity of the ecliptic, approximately 24 degrees in ancient Indian astronomy</note> (a triangle produced from the Radius as hypotenuse, the Sine of obliquity as the side, and the Cosine of obliquity as the vertical—the minimum Day-radius) is similar to the previously mentioned triangle (produced from the Sine of longitude, Sine of declination, and the base-line). Therefore, we calculate the proportion: if we obtain the <term>Jina-jya</term><note>Sine of maximum declination/obliquity</note> within the Radius, what do we obtain within the Sine of the Sun's longitude? From this proportion, the desired Sine of declination is derived:

-> (Sine of Obliquity × Sine of Longitude) / Radius = Sine of Declination <-

In the triangle produced by these sides—Radius as hypotenuse, Sine of declination as the side, and Cosine of declination (<term>Dyujya</term>) as the vertical:
$\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Sine of Declination}^2} = \text{Day-radius}$

Another triangle is formed by the <term>Agra</term><note>Amplitude at rising</note> as hypotenuse, Sine of declination as vertical, and Day-radius as the side; and another from the vertical of twelve <note>the Gnomon</note>, the <term>Palabha</term><note>Equinoctial shadow</note> as the side, and the <term>Palakarna</term><note>Hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow</note>.

### Now he describes the correction for ascensional difference:

> **The half-ascensional difference in ghatikas, multiplied by the daily motion and divided by sixty, gives the result in minutes of arc.**
> **Subtract it at sunrise and add it at sunset when the Sun is in the northern hemisphere; do the opposite in the southern.** ॥ ५६ ॥

**Vasanabhashya (Author's Commentary):—** One should multiply the <term>desired planet's daily motion</term> by the <term>ghatikas of the half-ascensional difference</term> and divide by <term>sixty</term>. The result is in <term>minutes of arc</term> <note>liptadi</note>. When the Sun is in the northern hemisphere, for a planet at <term>sunrise</term>, it is <term>subtracted</term>; at <term>sunset</term>, it is added. When the Sun is in the southern hemisphere, for a planet at <term>sunrise</term>, it is added; at <term>sunset</term>, it is <term>subtracted</term>. Thus the planet is determined for the time of sunrise or sunset at one's own location. The <term>sunset</term> position is calculated by half the daily motion, and at that time, the elapsed time is equal to the <term>half-ascensional difference</term>. Therefore, the planet at <term>sunrise</term> is corrected by the result of the half-ascensional difference. The result is found by the <term>rule of three</term> <note>trairashika</note>: if in sixty ghatikas the <term>minutes of arc equal to the planet's daily motion</term> are obtained, then what is obtained by the ghatikas of the half-ascensional difference? This <term>result in minutes</term> is also for the time of the six-o'clock circle, and at that time, the <term>remaining ghatikas of the day are equal to the half-ascensional difference</term>. Thus, the planet corrected by the result of the half-ascensional difference becomes the planet at <term>sunrise</term>. In the southern hemisphere, it is the opposite because the six-o'clock circle is situated <term>below the horizon</term>; one should demonstrate all this on the globe as it exists. One should place the <term>latitude of one's own country</term> on the globe.

### The Mathematical Proof

The planets calculated by the <term>Ahargana</term><note>The count of elapsed days since the beginning of the Epoch</note> are those at the time of sunrise on the horizon of Lanka. When these are corrected by the <term>Deshantara</term><note>The correction for terrestrial longitude</note> result, they represent the planets at the time of the <term>Unmandala</term><note>The equatorial horizon or the six-o'clock circle</note>. However, what is required are the planets at the time of sunrise on one's own local horizon. The interval between the equatorial horizon and one's own horizon is the <term>Charardha</term><note>Half the variation of the day-length; the ascensional difference</note>. Therefore, a proportion is made: if the minutes of planetary motion are obtained in sixty <term>Ghatis</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 Ghatis make a full day</note>, then what is obtained in the Ghatis of the ascensional difference? The result is the minutes of planetary motion within the duration of the ascensional difference. 

In the Northern Hemisphere, because the local horizon is below the equatorial horizon, the planet at the time of the equatorial horizon must be decreased by these minutes to become the planet at the time of local sunrise. In the Southern Hemisphere, because the local horizon is above the equatorial horizon, the planet (at the equatorial horizon) must be increased by those minutes to become the planet at the time of local sunrise. However, this can only be truly accurate if the planetary motion within the duration of the ascensional difference is accounted for. Since such inclusion is necessary, the <term>Chara-phala</term><note>The correction for ascensional difference</note> correction mentioned by the Teacher <insert>Brahmagupta</insert> is not entirely refined. Through the process of iteration <note>repeated calculation to find a precise value</note>, the planet at sunrise can be correctly determined here. Even with a single calculation, if the ancient ascensional difference is taken in the place of the dividend—as in the previous proof regarding the calculation of the true difference in rising—then the true ascensional difference result would be obtained. || 59 ||

### Now, the Correction for Ascensional Difference is described.

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the planetary motion by the <term>Charakhanda</term><note>The segments of ascensional difference</note> in Ghatis and divide by sixty. The resulting minutes and seconds should be subtracted from the planet at the time of rising in the Northern Hemisphere, and added in the Southern Hemisphere. At the time of setting, the opposite (reverse) should be done: that is, add to the planet in the Northern Hemisphere and subtract in the Southern Hemisphere. || 59 ||

### Proof

The planets calculated from the <term>Ahargana</term> are at the time of sunrise on the Lanka horizon. By applying the <term>Deshantara</term> correction to them, they are at the time of the equatorial horizon. But the planet at the time of one's own local sunrise is what is desired. The difference between the equatorial horizon and one's own horizon is the <term>Charardha</term>. Therefore, we calculate the proportion: if we get the minutes of planetary motion in 60 Ghatis, then what do we get in the <term>Charardha</term> Ghati? From this, the minutes of planetary motion relating to the <term>Charardha</term> Ghati are found. 

In the Northern Hemisphere, because one's own horizon stays lower than the equatorial horizon, subtracting these from the planet at the equatorial horizon gives the planet at the time of local sunrise. In the Southern Hemisphere, because one's own horizon stays above the equatorial horizon, adding the previously obtained minutes of planetary motion relating to the <term>Charardha</term> Ghati to the planet at the equatorial horizon gives the planet at the time of local sunrise. However, the Teacher has not included whatever planetary motion occurs within the <term>Charardha</term> Ghati; but its inclusion is necessary. Therefore, the <term>Chara-phala</term> correction stated by the Teacher is not perfect. Through iteration, here...

# Chapter on the True Positions of Planets

Planetary positions can be calculated for sunrise. Even in the previous method for determining the interval between observations, the reasoning in the commentary—such as "the motion of the cycle multiplied by one minute of arc," etc.—shows that using the <term>Caraphala</term><note>The correction for local variation or the difference between the local horizon and the celestial equator</note> mentioned by the ancients yields the true <term>Caraphala</term>. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, the method used by Shripati, "from the product of the planet's motion and the respiration-units of the ascensional difference," follows the teacher's instructions. Bhaskaracharya also addresses this subject with "the minutes of the ascensional difference multiplied by the motion," etc. It is clear from the above reasoning that the <term>Caraphala</term> correction used by some ancient teachers is not entirely accurate. || 59 ||

->Now he describes the measure of the duration of day and night<-

**In the Northern Hemisphere, fifteen ghatikas increased and decreased by the ghatikas of the half-ascensional difference, and in the Southern Hemisphere, decreased and increased, then doubled, result in the measures of day and night.** || 60 ||

**Vasanabhashya (Explanatory Commentary):** The explanation here is clear. Having marked the <term>Svahoratravritta</term><note>The diurnal circle or the daily path of a planet</note> with <term>ghatikas</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 ghatikas make a full day</note> on a given day, there are fifteen <term>ghatikas</term> in one quadrant of that circle. The intersections of the diurnal circle with the <term>Unmandala</term><note>The equatorial horizon or six-o'clock circle</note> occur on both the east and west sides of the meridian. Because the local horizon is different, the sunrise and sunset on the local horizon are separated from the <term>Unmandala</term> by the <term>Caradala</term><note>Half the ascensional difference</note>. In the Northern Hemisphere, an observer on earth sees the sun rising above the horizon; therefore, fifteen <term>ghatikas</term> increased by the previously shown <term>Caradala-ghatikas</term> constitute half the day. Similarly, at sunset, the sun sets at the western horizon; thus, fifteen <term>ghatikas</term> increased by that same segment called <term>Caradala</term> complete the half-day. Therefore, twice the half-day is the total duration of the day. The remaining <term>ghatikas</term> of the diurnal circle are the measure of the night. This is found by subtracting twice the <term>Caradala</term> from thirty <term>ghatikas</term> <insert>to get the half-night, then doubling</insert>. In the Southern Hemisphere, everything should be applied in reverse. At the equator, however, because the horizon and the <term>Unmandala</term> are the same, there is no <term>Caradala</term>. In the Northern Hemisphere, the half-day increases until the <term>Carardha</term><note>Half-ascensional difference</note> becomes fifteen <term>ghatikas</term>, at which point there is no night, only day. This occurs where the latitude is 66 degrees; beyond that, it increases until the North Pole. At the Pole, the day lasts six months and the night lasts six months. The same logic applies to the south of the equator. The Teacher will explain this further in the "Chapter on the Three Problems," and we shall describe it in detail there as well.

**Vijnanabhashya (Scientific Commentary):** In the Northern Hemisphere, fifteen <term>nadikas</term><note>Synonym for ghatika</note> plus and minus the <term>Carardha-ghatikas</term>, doubled, and in the Southern Hemisphere, fifteen <term>ghatikas</term> minus and plus the <term>Carardha-ghatikas</term>, doubled, give the measures of the duration of the day and the duration of the night respectively. || 60 ||

### Rationale (Upapatti)

There are fifteen <term>ghatikas</term> between the <term>Unmandala</term> and the meridian. The <term>Carardha</term> is the interval between one's own horizon and the <term>Unmandala</term>. In the Northern Hemisphere, because the <term>Unmandala</term> stays above the local horizon, the <term>ghatikas</term> of the <term>Cara</term> are added...

Fifteen <term>ghatis</term><note>A ghadi or ghati is a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 ghatis make a full day of 24 hours.</note> constitute the measure of half a day <insert>at the equator</insert>. ### Mathematical Proof

There are fifteen ghatis between the <term>unmandala</term> and the meridian circle, and the <term>chara</term> ghati lies between one's own horizon and the unmandala. In the Northern Hemisphere, the unmandala is above the local horizon; therefore, adding the charaghati to fifteen ghatis results in the half-day measure. In the Southern Hemisphere, the unmandala is lower than the local horizon; therefore, subtracting the charaghati from fifteen ghatis results in the half-day measure. Subtracting the half-day measure of both hemispheres from thirty gives the half-night measure of both hemispheres (Northern and Southern). Doubling these gives the full day and night durations. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskara Acharya says the same: "with the charaghati added or subtracted, etc." || 60

### Now, the calculation of the Nakshatras (Lunar Mansions) for the planets is stated:

> **The Nakshatras begin with Ashvini. Divide the arc-minutes of the planet by 800 <note>original: "khakha-vasu" where kha=0, kha=0, vasu=8. Using the Katapayadi system, this represents 800.</note>. The quotient is the number of elapsed Nakshatras. Divide the past and remaining portions by the daily motion to find the days; multiply the remainder by sixty for the ghatis. || 61 ||**

**Sanskrit Commentary:** Now, the verse for calculating the Nakshatras for all planets is given. One should divide the desired true arc-minutes of the planet by 800. The resulting quotient gives the elapsed Nakshatras starting from Ashvini. The remaining arc-minutes are termed "past" (elapsed), and subtracting these from 800 gives the "future" (remaining) arc-minutes. Then, divide both the past and future portions by the daily motion (<term>bhukti</term>) of that same planet. The result is days; from the remainder multiplied by sixty, one gets ghatis and vighatis. Thus, the time elapsed or remaining is found. Just as the end of a Nakshatra is calculated for the true Moon in common practice, here it is applied to all planets. Because this practice—calculating without the <term>charadala</term><note>Half-ascensional difference</note>—is well known, no specific example is provided. The logic here is that the counting of signs starting from Aries in a true planet is based on the fact that Aries and the other signs are composed of nine quarters of Nakshatras each, and a Nakshatra quarter consists of 200 arc-minutes, making a full Nakshatra 800 arc-minutes...

# Chapter on True Longitude

A ninth part of a zodiac sign: four of these make eight [hundred]. This means the twenty-seventh part of the total minutes in a circle <note>original: "chakraliptānām"; a full circle contains 21,600 minutes of arc. 21,600 divided by 27 equals 800</note>.

Therefore, one day is formed by the planet's daily motion in minutes. With the remaining minutes, how many days [have passed or remain]? This calculation of time should be done from the elapsed or remaining portions. The increase or decrease of the duration of a lunar mansion <note>Nakshatra</note> occurs because of the eccentric circle <note>pratimandala</note>; the planet is always at the point closest to its true motion. Therefore, it is proven that everything should be demonstrated within the previously established orbital circles.

**Scientific Commentary** — The planetary minutes <note>arc minutes of longitude</note> divided by eight hundred (800) always yield the elapsed lunar mansions starting from Ashvini <note>the first of the 27 Nakshatras</note>. When the elapsed or remaining minutes are divided by the daily motion <note>bhukti</note>, the result is the elapsed or remaining days. When the remainder of that is multiplied by sixty and divided by the daily motion, the result is the ghatikas <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. || 61 ||

->Rationale<-

If twenty-seven lunar mansions are obtained in a full circle of minutes, then what is obtained in the desired planetary minutes? The form of the elapsed lunar mansions is: $\frac{27 \times \text{Planetary Minutes}}{21600} = \frac{\text{Planetary Minutes}}{800} =$ Elapsed Nakshatra + $\frac{\text{Remainder}}{800}$. Here, the remainder is the portion of the current lunar mansion already traversed. When subtracted from the divisor <note>800</note>, it becomes the portion yet to be traversed. Then the proportion is: if one day is obtained for the total daily motion, then what is obtained for the elapsed or remaining minutes? The results are the elapsed and remaining days. When the remainder is multiplied by sixty and divided by the motion, the result is the ghatikas. || 61 ||

->Now he describes the calculation of the lunar day (tithi)<-

**The minutes of the Moon minus the Sun, divided by 720, give the elapsed lunar days.**
**The elapsed or remaining portions multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference in daily motions give the time in ghatis. || 62 ||**

*Vasanabhashya* <note>The author's own explanatory commentary</note>—Now he provides a verse for the purpose of calculating the lunar day. This verse is self-explanatory. At the end of the New Moon (*Amavasya*), the Sun and Moon are equal and aligned on the same longitudinal line. From that point, the Moon moves ahead daily. Therefore, subtract the Sun's motion from the Moon's; the difference in their daily motions is established. Since both started from the end of the New Moon, one lunar day occurs for every twelve degrees of difference between them. This is because twelve degrees is the thirtieth part of the 360 degrees of the circle. In minutes of arc, twelve degrees is equal to 720 <note>original: "khayama-svara," a numerical code where kha=0, yama=2, svara=7. Read right-to-left as 720</note>. Therefore, it is said that the minutes of the Moon minus the Sun divided by 720 equals the lunar day. With the remainder, a rule of three <note>A mathematical proportion</note> is applied: if sixty ghatis are obtained from the full difference in daily motion, how much is obtained from the remaining minutes? The remainder is treated as before. Furthermore, I have already explained this in detail in the *Goladhyaya* <note>The section on the celestial sphere</note> while discussing the three-day calculation. He now speaks to show the distance between the Sun and Moon.

*Vigyanabhashya* <note>A modern or clarifying commentary</note>—The minutes of the Moon minus the Sun (the arc minutes of the interval between Sun and Moon) divided by 720 (divided by these) results in the elapsed lunar days. When the elapsed portion is subtracted from the divisor, the remaining portion is found. The elapsed and remaining minutes multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference in daily motions (divided by the minutes of the difference between the Sun's and Moon's daily motion) result in the elapsed ghatis and the remaining ghatis of the lunar day. || 62 ||

->Here is the mathematical proof:<-

At the end of the New Moon (*Amanta*), the Sun and Moon are at the same place (as it is said, "The New Moon is the meeting of the Sun and Moon"). After that, the Moon, having a faster velocity, moves ahead. Moving in this way, when the Moon meets the Sun again, the second New Moon occurs and the lunar month is completed. In that interval, the degrees of the difference in motion between the Sun and Moon are 360. Therefore, the proportion: if 30 lunar days are obtained by a 360-degree difference in motion (since a lunar month consists of thirty lunar days), then what is obtained by the desired difference between the Sun and Moon?

The result is the elapsed lunar days, the form of which is:
= (30 × Difference in degrees) / 360
= (30 × Difference in degrees × 2) / (360 × 2)

= (60 × Difference in degrees) / 720
= (Difference in minutes) / 720
= Elapsed Tithi + (Remainder / 720)

Here, the remainder represents the elapsed fraction of the current lunar day. When that is subtracted from the divisor, the remaining fraction of the current lunar day is found...

-> = (Difference in degrees between Sun and Moon) / 12 <-

That remainder, subtracted from the divisor, is the 'to-be-passed.' Those [remainders] in minutes, divided by the difference in daily motions, are the elapsed and remaining ghatikas." ### Now the calculation of the Tithi is described.

**Hindi Commentary —** Dividing the difference in minutes between the Sun and the Moon by seven hundred and twenty (720) gives the elapsed tithi as the quotient. ### Mathematical Proof (Upapatti)

At the time of the New Moon (<term>Amanta</term><note>The moment the Sun and Moon are at the same longitude.</note>), the Sun and Moon are at the same position. After that, because the Moon has a faster velocity, it moves ahead of the Sun. Moving in this manner day by day, it meets the Sun again; then the second New Moon occurs, and a lunar month is completed. At that point, the difference in degrees of motion between the Sun and Moon = 360°. 

Then we use a proportion: if thirty (30) tithis (one lunar month consists of thirty tithis) are obtained in a motion difference equal to three hundred and sixty (360) degrees of the Sun and Moon, then what is obtained in the desired difference of degrees between the Sun and Moon? This gives the measure of the elapsed tithi:
-> (30 $\times$ Difference in degrees) / 360 = (30 $\times$ Difference in degrees $\times$ 2) / (360 $\times$ 2) = (60 $\times$ Difference in degrees) / 720 <-
-> = (Difference in minutes) / 720 = Elapsed Tithi + $\frac{Remainder}{720}$ <-
<margin>Note: 720 minutes equals 12 degrees, the length of one tithi.</margin>
Here the remainder is the elapsed portion of the current tithi. By subtracting it from the divisor, the portion of the current tithi yet to be experienced is found. Then the proportion is applied: if sixty ghatikas are obtained in the difference of daily motion, then what is obtained in the elapsed minutes and remaining minutes? From this, the elapsed ghatikas [are found].

The Yogas are produced by the combined motion of the Sun and Moon. By this, everything stated is exactly in accordance with the Teacher's <note>Brahmagupta's</note> words. || 63 ||

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
<note>The Corrected Treatise of Brahma, a foundational 7th-century text by Brahmagupta</note>

There are thirty lunar days <term>tithis|a lunar day, defined as the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the Sun and Moon to increase by 12 degrees</term> in this context. Therefore, the degrees of difference between the Sun and the Moon are: 30 $\times$ 12 = 360°, or equal to zero. Thus, the Sun and Moon become equal in their components, starting from their zodiac signs. At the end of a fortnight <note>the half-month or Paksha</note>, there are fifteen lunar days; therefore, the degrees of difference between the Sun and Moon are: 15 $\times$ 12 = 180° = 6 signs. Consequently, at that time, the Sun and Moon are equal in their components starting from degrees. How else could it be, since only the signs remain as the difference between them? At the end of any lunar day, the degrees of difference between the Sun and Moon must be divisible by twelve; because of this, at the end of a lunar day, since minutes and seconds of arc are absent <note>meaning they are identical for both bodies</note>, only the degrees are produced as a difference.

In the *Siddhanta-Shekhara*, Shripati says: "At the end of the month, there is equality of the Sun and the Moon <note>original: "arka-shitamahasoḥ"</note> in terms of the field, starting with the zodiac signs. At the end of the fortnight, their similarity arises again starting from the degrees. At the end of any other lunar day, there is equality in minutes and so on." By this, he says exactly what corresponds to the Teacher's <note>Brahmagupta's</note> statement. The teacher Lalla also says: "At the end of the month, the Sun and Moon should be equal; at the end of the fortnight, they are equal in degrees, minutes, and seconds. At the end of any other lunar day, they are indeed always equal in minutes and seconds." This is precisely what is being stated here. || 64 ||

-> Now, the difference between the Sun and the Moon is described. <-

**Hindi Commentary:** At the end of the true lunar month, the zodiac signs, degrees, minutes, and seconds of the Sun and Moon are equal; that is, both are equal in all components starting from the sign. At the end of a lunar day, their minutes and seconds are equal; that is, they are equal in components starting from the minutes. || 64 ||

### Proof

When the degrees of difference between the Sun and Moon are twelve degrees, it constitutes one lunar day. At the end of the true lunar month, there are thirty lunar days; therefore, the Sun-Moon difference = 30 $\times$ 12 = 360, or equal to zero. Thus, the Sun and Moon are equal there in components starting from the zodiac signs. At the end of the fortnight, there are 15 lunar days; therefore, the Sun-Moon difference = 15 $\times$ 12 = 180 = 6 signs. Thus, the Sun and Moon are equal there in components starting from degrees, because by subtracting one from the other, only the signs remain. At the end of any lunar day, the difference between the Sun and Moon remains divisible by twelve; therefore, at the end of a lunar day, the Sun and Moon are equal in components starting from the minutes. In the *Siddhanta-Shekhara*, Shripati says "At the end of the month, equality of the Sun and Moon..." etc. From the verse written in the Sanskrit proof, he speaks in accordance with the Teacher's words. Lalla also says "At the end of the month, the Sun and Moon should be equal..." etc., stating the same thing through the verse written in the Sanskrit proof. || 64 ||

### Chapter on True Motions

**Bala Bhashya (Commentary for Beginners):**—This verse is clear in its meaning. Now, he provides a verse for the calculation of the fixed *Karanas* <note>A Karana is half of a Tithi or lunar day. There are 11 types of Karanas.</note>.

**Vistara Bhashya (Detailed Commentary):**—In the latter half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight <note>Krishna Paksha</note>, the *Shakuni* Karana occurs. In the first half of the New Moon day <note>Amavasya</note>, the *Chatushpada* Karana occurs. In the latter half of the New Moon day, the *Naga* Karana occurs, and in the first half of the first day of the bright fortnight <note>Shukla Paksha Pratipada</note>, the *Kinstughna* Karana occurs. || 65 ||

### Here is the Rationale

By Lallacharya:
> "When the moon's body is diminished, on the fourteenth day, *Shakuni* certainly arises in the latter part. Following that, in the two halves of the New Moon day are *Chatushpada* and *Naga*, and that which is in the first half of the first day of the bright fortnight, they call *Kinstughna*."

And by Shripati:
> "In the final half of the fourteenth day of the waning moon, *Shakuni* occurs. In the first segment of the New Moon, the Karana called *Chatushpada* is declared. In the final half of that same day, the wise say *Naga* occurs. On the first day of the bright fortnight, it is always *Kinstughna* in the first half."

And by Bhaskara, through the original statement "Following the half of the dark fourteenth from *Shakuni*":
> "Those three which remain after the half of the dark fourteenth day, and the fourth which is in the first half of the first day of the bright fortnight—these four are the fixed ones: *Shakuni*, *Chatushpada*, *Naga*, and *Kinstughna*."

In this explanation, the *Chatushpada* and *Naga* Karanas are stated for the first and second halves of the New Moon day. However, in the *Surya Siddhanta*:
> "The fixed ones are *Shakuni*, *Naga*, the third is *Chatushpada*, and *Kinstughna* starting from the latter half of the dark fourteenth."

By this, the *Naga* and *Chatushpada* Karanas are stated for the first and second halves of the New Moon day. Regarding the difference in the sequence of these two Karanas, in the *Sudhavarshini* commentary on the *Surya Siddhanta*:
> "In the opinion of almost everyone, the order of Brahma is appropriate; therefore, first is *Shakuni*, second is *Chatushpada*, and the third is *Naga*—this is to be understood."

Thus wrote the Great Scholar Sudhakara Dwivedi. || 65 ||

---

Now the fixed Karanas are described.

**Hindi Commentary:**—In the latter half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight is the *Shakuni* Karana; in the first half of the New Moon day is the *Chatushpada* Karana and in the latter half is the *Naga* Karana; and in the first half of the first day of the bright fortnight is the *Kinstughna* Karana. || 65 ||

### Rationale

In the *Surya Siddhanta*, through the verse "The fixed ones are *Shakuni*, *Naga*, the third is *Chatushpada*...", the *Naga* Karana is said to be in the first half of the New Moon and the *Chatushpada* in the latter half. ### Now he describes the Mobile Karanas

-> The minutes of the longitude of the Moon minus the Sun, divided by three hundred and sixty, and the quotient diminished by one; <-
-> are the mobile Karanas starting with *Bava*. For the remainder after dividing by seven, the rest is like the calculation for a lunar day. <- || 66 ||

**Vasanabhashya (Commentary on the Meaning):** — The meaning is clear. The logic for the *Karana*, which consists of half the duration of a *Tithi* <term>Tithi: a lunar day, or 12 degrees of separation between the Sun and Moon</term>, should be applied just like the *Tithi*. The result of the division by 360 <note>original: "kharasagunaih" (6 x 60)</note> is diminished by one because the sequence of mobile *Karanas* starting with *Bava* begins after the first half of the first lunar day of the bright fortnight. This is because the first half is always the fixed *Karana* <note>Kimstughna</note>. Because there are so many things that ought to be said in the chapter on Clear Motion, I shall describe them in the supplementary chapter on Clear Motion.

**Vivarana-bhashya (Explanatory Commentary):** — The minutes of the distance between the Sun and Moon <note>original: "vyarkendu-kala"</note> divided by 360, the quotient diminished by one, and the remainder after dividing by seven <note>original: "agahata-shesha"</note> gives the mobile *Karanas* starting with *Bava*. The rest of the operation is to be done like the calculation of a lunar day. || 66 ||

### Here is the Proof

For the purpose of calculating the lunar day (*Tithi*), if 30 lunar days are obtained by a 360° separation of the Sun and Moon, then for a desired separation, the elapsed lunar days are:

     30 × (Distance between Sun and Moon in degrees)
--------------------------------------------------------- =
                        360

      (Distance between Sun and Moon in degrees)
---------------------------------------------------------
                          12

Since there are two *Karanas* per lunar day, the *Karanas* are:

   2 × (Distance between Sun and Moon in degrees)
---------------------------------------------------------
                          12

      (Distance between Sun and Moon in degrees)
= -----------------------------------------------
                          6

      (Distance in degrees) × 60
= -----------------------------------------------
                        6 × 60

      (Distance between Sun and Moon in minutes)
= -----------------------------------------------
                        360

There are four fixed *Karanas* whose positions are clear from the previous verse. However, because the fixed *Karana* named *Kimstughna* occupies the first half of the first lunar day, and the *Bava* sequence begins from the second half of the first lunar day of the bright fortnight, one is subtracted from the quotient obtained by:
(Distance in minutes) / 360.
Then, the remainder after dividing by seven gives the *Bava* etc. *Karanas*. Here too, the elapsed or remaining time of the current *Karana* in *Ghatis* <term>Ghati: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> is found by multiplying the elapsed or remaining distance by 60 and dividing by the difference in daily motion.

In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, Shripati calculated the *Karanas* based on the degrees of separation between the Sun and Moon, saying: "From the sum of degrees of the Moon minus the Sun, the *Bava* etc. *Karanas* are found by dividing by six. Subtract one and divide by seven..." Bhaskara also did the same. The Teacher (Brahmagupta) performs this knowledge using the minutes of the separation between the Sun and Moon. || 66 ||

# Chapter on True Motion
Page 255

->Now, the variable *Karanas* are described.<-

**Hindi Commentary** — Divide the difference in minutes of arc between the Sun and the Moon by 360. Subtract one from the resulting quotient and then divide by seven; the remainder indicates the *Karanas* starting from *Bava*. Other operations (calculating the elapsed and remaining time in *ghatis* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>) should be performed similarly to the calculation of a *tithi* <note>A lunar day</note>. || 66 ||

->Mathematical Rationale<-

For the calculation of a *tithi*, if thirty *tithis* are contained within the 360 degrees of the difference between the Sun and Moon's motion, then what is the elapsed *tithi* for the desired difference?
30 $\times$ (Sun-Moon difference in degrees) / 360 = (Sun-Moon difference in degrees) / 12 = Elapsed *tithi*.
According to the rule that doubling the *tithi* gives the *Karana*:
2 $\times$ (Sun-Moon difference in degrees) / 12 = (Sun-Moon difference in degrees) / 6 = (Sun-Moon difference in degrees $\times$ 60) / (6 $\times$ 60) = (Sun-Moon difference in minutes) / 360 = *Karana*.
There are four fixed *Karanas* whose positions were mentioned in the previous verse. Because the *Kinstughna* <note>The first of the four fixed Karanas</note> *Karana* occupies the first half of the first lunar day of the bright fortnight, and the variable *Karanas* (starting with *Bava*) begin from the second half of that first lunar day, one must subtract one from the quotient obtained (Sun-Moon difference in minutes / 360). Then, dividing by seven, the remainder indicates the specific variable *Karana*. Here too, by multiplying the elapsed and remaining minutes of arc by sixty and dividing by the difference in daily motion, one finds the elapsed and remaining *ghatis* of the current *Karana*. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, the verse beginning with "From the group of degrees of the Moon minus the Sun..." provides the Sanskrit rationale. Sripati, as well as Bhaskaracharya in the verse "The degrees of the Sun and Moon multiplied by..." etc., calculated the *Karanas* using the degree-difference of the Sun and Moon. The Teacher <note>Referring to the author of the primary text</note> has calculated them based on the difference in minutes of arc; there is no fundamental difference in the result. || 66 ||

# The Corrected Treatise of Brahma
<note>original: "Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta"</note>

## Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>original: "Tripraśnādhikāra"</note>

The chapter in which the answers to the three problems regarding direction, place, and time are declared is the "Chapter on the Three Problems." Within this, he first describes the knowledge of directions.

->The two points of equal shadow in the east and west indicate the west and east directions.<-
->The eastern point is adjusted by the declination; from the center of those two, the base of the gnomon gives the other directions. || 1 ||<-

**Vāsanā-bhāṣya <note>Explanatory Commentary</note>:** Two points should be marked at the tips of shadows of equal length <term>digit-measure|angula</term> in the eastern and western halves of the sky. This is what is meant: On ground leveled with water, one should place a gnomon <term>vertical pillar used for measuring shadows|śanku</term> of twelve digits, or of any desired measure. Then, at a desired time when some part of the day has passed, a point should be marked at the tip of the shadow; this is called the first point. Then, when the same amount of time remains in the day as had passed when the first point was marked, a second point should be marked at the tip of the shadow. Furthermore, it is said: when the sun is in the eastern half of the sky and the first point is marked, that becomes the western direction. When the sun is in the western half and the other point is marked, that is the eastern direction.

If, indeed, a difference in direction arises due to the sun's declination: one must calculate the sine of declination <note>original: "krāntijyā"</note> for the sun at the time the first point was marked, and also for the sun at the time of the second point. The difference between them is the sine of declination for the interval between the points. The radius is converted into a circle equal to the circumference of the sun's shadow-digits. Therefore, one should multiply by the shadow-digits and divide by the radius. The result is in digits on the shadow-circle; the point should be moved by that amount.

In determining directions for a place on the equator, or if at a place with latitude, one should multiply that [result] by the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "viṣuvatkarṇa"</note> and divide by twelve. The resulting calculation should be used to move the first point. Thus, for one who knows the directions without [error from] high latitudes, the second point on the shadow-circle is moved northward during the sun's northern course <note>original: "uttarāyaṇa"</note> and southward during the southern course <note>original: "dakṣiṇāyana"</note> by the resulting digits; thus, that becomes the true eastern direction.

Then, stretching a cord over the tops of the eastern and western points, one should draw a line. That is the East-West line. "From the center of those, the base of the gnomon is the other" means the midpoint of those two points. Stretching a cord from that [midpoint] to the base of the gnomon, one should draw a line; that is the North-South line. In this way, following those lines, both North and South are established.

Furthermore, placing one point in the center, a circle is drawn with the measure of the cord reaching the second point. In this way, from the mutual intersection of two circles, "fishes" <note>the vesica piscis shape formed by intersecting circles</note> are produced. A cord passing through its mouth and tail is the North-South line from the middle of the East-West line. The logic here is: in the forenoon, the shadow-tip is in the western direction for a gnomon situated at a desired location; therefore, the first point is the western direction. In the afternoon, the shadow-tip falls in the eastern direction, so that is the eastern direction. Because the time is equal, the line between them is established as East-West. Because the sun's path follows the celestial equator, the half-motion is in the ecliptic itself...

<summary>This page explains the geometric method for determining the cardinal directions (East, West, North, South) using a gnomon's shadow and intersecting circles. It accounts for solar declination and the sun's seasonal path to ensure accuracy in orientation.</summary>

--- Page 277 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of gnomonics and the determination of the cardinal directions from the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta, specifically focusing on the correction for the Sun's changing declination between morning and afternoon observations.</meta>

<page-num>260</page-num>
<header>In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta</header>

The difference in directions arises due to the <term>true declination</term><note>The angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator.</note>. During the <term>Northern Progress</term><note>Uttarayana: the period between the winter and summer solstices.</note>, because the Sun moves further north every moment, the tip of the gnomon's shadow moves toward the south. That line, however much it has moved, is shifted back toward the north so that it becomes truly aligned with the east. It is to the south of the first point. Similarly, during the <term>Southern Progress</term><note>Dakshinayana: the period between the summer and winter solstices.</note>, it is adjusted by the <term>sine of declination</term> or the <term>amplitude</term><note>Agra: the distance on the horizon between the east point and the point where the Sun rises.</note> derived from the shadow circle. Since the <term>radius</term> is constant in its own circle, the <term>Rule of Three</term><note>A mathematical proportion: if A gives B, what does C give?</note> is applied there to calculate the change in the sine of declination between the two points. This is clearly used for shifting the points. At the equator, because the horizon and the <term>unmandala</term><note>The equatorial horizon or six-o'clock circle.</note> are the same, and elsewhere because they differ, the correction is made using the amplitude. The method for calculating this amplitude is explained through the underlying theory. Regarding the "Book of Three Shadows," he provides the answer for one who wishes to know the directions without using declination or latitude. ||1||

**Scientific Commentary:** The two points formed at the tips of equal shadows in the eastern and western <term>hemispheres</term><note>Kapala: literally 'bowls', referring to the morning and afternoon halves of the sky.</note> are as follows: the first (the initial point) is the western direction; the other (the second point) is the eastern direction. Due to the declination (it should be understood that a discrepancy arises because of the declinations at the times of the two equal shadows), the <term>base of the gnomon</term><note>Shankutala: the distance from the center to the line connecting the shadow tips.</note> and the other directions (North and South) are derived from the midpoint of those two shadow tips.

The meaning is this: On ground leveled with water, draw a circle with a radius equal to the shadow at a desired time on that day. A <term>twelve-digit gnomon</term><note>The standard Indian astronomical gnomon of 12 units.</note> should be placed at its center. When the Sun is in the eastern hemisphere, the point where the tip of the gnomon's shadow touches the circumference of that circle is the "rough" West. When the Sun is in the western hemisphere, the point where the shadow tip exits the circumference in the eastern part is the "rough" East. The line passing through these rough East and West points is the "rough" East-West line. The line drawn from the midpoint of those two shadow tips to the base of the gnomon becomes the North-South line. ||1||

### The Proof Here

Now, because the declinations at the time of the shadow's entry into and exit from the circle are unequal:
$\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sin(Declination)}}{\text{Sin(Co-latitude)}}$ = Amplitude,

$\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sin(Declination)}<gloss>1</gloss>}{\text{Sin(Co-latitude)}}$ = Amplitude<gloss>1</gloss>, where "Declination" is the declination at the time the shadow enters the circle, and "Declination<gloss>1</gloss>" is the declination at the time it exits. By the difference between the two amplitudes:
$\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sin(Declination)}<gloss>1</gloss>}{\text{Sin(Co-latitude)}}$ - $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sin(Declination)}}{\text{Sin(Co-latitude)}}$ = $\frac{\text{Radius}}{\text{Sin(Co-latitude)}}$ (Sin(Declination<gloss>1</gloss>) ~ Sin(Declination))

= Amplitude<gloss>1</gloss> ~ Amplitude = Difference in Amplitudes. This is brought into the sphere of the <term>shadow-hypotenuse</term><note>Chhayakarna: the distance from the top of the gnomon to the tip of the shadow.</note>. If this difference in amplitude is obtained for the Radius, what is obtained for the radius of the shadow-hypotenuse?

Difference in Amplitudes for the shadow-hypotenuse = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Shadow-Hypotenuse}}{\text{Sin(Co-latitude)} \times \text{Radius}}$ (Sin(Declination<gloss>1</gloss>) ~ Sin(Declination)), which equals $\frac{\text{Shadow-Hypotenuse}}{\text{Sin(Co-latitude)}}$ (Sin(Declination<gloss>1</gloss>) ~ Sin(Declination)).

By shifting according to this difference in amplitude, knowledge of a line parallel to the true East-West line is gained. Then, a line drawn from the center point parallel to that becomes the true East-West line. "The difference between the sines of the Sun's declination at the times of the shadow's exit and entry, multiplied by its own hypotenuse and divided by the <term>Lambaka</term><note>The sine of the co-latitude.</note>, results in the correction in digits..."

It provides the geometric proof for calculating the "Difference in Amplitudes" to refine rough directional measurements.</summary>
