<header>Chapter on the Three Problems</header>

result. "Afterward, one should shift the western point according to the Sun's declination in reverse, or shift the eastern point according to the declination to find the true east-west line." Observing this very method of Sripati, Bhaskara stated, "The distance between the sine of the amplitude at that time and the equinoctial sine is multiplied by the hypotenuse of the shadow..." and "The point is moved in the direction of the declination by the required digits." However, because it is inappropriate to apply the difference of the amplitudes directly to the circle of the shadow's hypotenuse, the method described by Sripati and others does not yield the true knowledge of the east-west direction. Therefore, the actual method for determining it is now demonstrated.

->[Diagram Description: A circle used for directional calculations. Point 'Pu-Na' represents the gross East. Point 'Pa' represents the gross West. A line is drawn to find the true orientation.]<-

Pu-Na = Gross East direction. Pa = Gross West direction. From the midpoint of the line Pu-Pa, a circle for calculating the semi-chord <note>The 'ardhajya' or semi-chord is a fundamental trigonometric function in Indian astronomy, similar to the modern sine</note> should be made. The line Pu-Pa is parallel to the true east-west line. From point Pu, a line equal to the difference of the amplitudes <term>Agrantara: the difference between the solar amplitude at two different times</term> or the difference of the sides should be drawn as the full chord (Na). The line Pa-Na should be drawn. Angle <Pa-Na-Pu = 90 degrees. In this way, the line becomes parallel to the true east-west line, and from that, the knowledge of the true east-west line will certainly be obtained. ||1||

### Now begins the Chapter on the Three Problems

The "Chapter on the Three Problems" <term>Triprasnadhi-kara: a standard section in Sanskrit astronomical texts dealing with the three problems of direction, place, and time</term> is that in which the answers to three questions (Direction, Place, and Time) are given. Within that, the knowledge of direction is explained first.

**Hindi Commentary—** In the eastern hemisphere and the western hemisphere, there are two points at the tips of two equal shadows. Of these, the first point is the West direction and the second point is the East direction. There is a difference caused by the declination <term>Kranti: the celestial declination of the sun</term> of the two equal shadow-tips in the eastern and western hemispheres. The line that goes from the midpoint of the two shadow-tips to the base of the gnomon <term>Shanku: a vertical pillar or 12-digit staff used to measure shadows</term> is the North-South line. On that line lie the South and North directions. On ground leveled with water, on the desired day, one should draw a circle with a radius equal to the midday shadow and place a 12-digit gnomon at its center. When the Sun is in the eastern hemisphere, the point where the shadow-tip of that gnomon enters the circumference of the circle is the "gross" <note>meaning approximate or uncorrected</note> West direction. When the Sun is in the western hemisphere, the point where the shadow-tip exits the circumference in the eastern part is the "gross" East direction. The line passing through both points (gross East and West) is the gross East-West line. The line from the midpoint of those two shadow-tips to the base of the gnomon is the North-South line. ||1||

### Proof (Upapatti)

Due to the inequality of the declination at the time the shadow enters and exits the circle, the two hypotenuses and amplitudes are also unequal. Kranti-1 = Declination at the time of shadow entry. Kranti-2 = Declination at the time of shadow exit.

# Page 262
## In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

Declination, $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine Declination}_1}{\text{Sine Co-latitude}} = \text{Amplitude}_1$, $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine Declination}_2}{\text{Sine Co-latitude}} = \text{Amplitude}_2$. By taking the difference of both: $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine Declination}_1 \sim}{\text{Sine Co-latitude}}$

$\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine Declination}_1}{\text{Sine Co-latitude}} = \frac{\text{Radius}}{\text{Sine Co-latitude}} (\text{Sine Declination}_1 \sim \text{Sine Declination}_2) = \text{Amplitude}_1 \sim \text{Amplitude}_2 = \text{Difference of Amplitudes} = \text{Difference of Base-sides}$.

This is brought into the sphere of the shadow-hypotenuse <note>The hypotenuse formed by the gnomon and its shadow</note>. We use a proportion: if we find this difference of amplitudes in a circle with the standard Radius, then what would it be in a circle with the shadow-hypotenuse as the radius? From this, the difference of amplitudes in the shadow-hypotenuse sphere is derived as: $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Shadow Hypotenuse}}{\text{Sine Co-latitude} \times \text{Radius}}$

$(\text{Sine Declination}_1 \sim \text{Sine Declination}_2) = \frac{\text{Shadow Hypotenuse}}{\text{Sine Co-latitude}} (\text{Sine Declination}_1 \sim \text{Sine Declination}_2) = \text{Difference of Amplitudes in the shadow-hypotenuse sphere}$. By shifting the East point by this amount, a line parallel to the true East-West line is known. A line parallel to that passing through the center point is the true East-West line. A perpendicular line drawn from the midpoint of the line parallel to the East-West line, or from the center point of the East-West line, is the North-South line. 

In the *Siddhanta-shekhara* <note>A major astronomical work by Sripati, c. 1039 CE</note>, the verse beginning with "The difference of the sine of declination at the times of exit and entry of the shadow..." etc., is written in the Sanskrit commentary. Having seen Sripati's method, Bhaskaracharya stated in the *Siddhanta-shiromani* <note>The 12th-century masterpiece by Bhaskara II</note>: "From the difference of the sines of declination at those times..." and so on. However, it is improper to apply the difference of amplitudes or the difference of base-sides directly to the circumference of the shadow-hypotenuse circle; therefore, the knowledge of the corrected East-West direction cannot be accurately obtained by the method described by Sripati and others. Thus, a logical method for true knowledge is provided here.

Look at figure (A) written in the Sanskrit commentary. E' = approximate East direction, W' = approximate West direction. The line E'W' is a line not parallel to the true East-West line. From point E', draw a chord-line equal to the difference of amplitudes or difference of base-sides (using the logic from Chapter 4, Verse 4). Draw the line W'N <note>N represents the corrected point</note>, such that $\angle \text{E'NW'} = 90^\circ$. Then, this line W'N is parallel to the true East-West line. A line parallel to this passing through the center point will be the true East-West line. In this way, the true East and West directions are known. A line perpendicular to the East-West line from the center point is the North-South line. Thus, the North-South directions are also known. ||1||

### A Special Deliberation Here:

> The two points of East and West, where the shadow-ends are equal, result in a directional error.
> The East-chords <note>The correction for the East point</note> arise due to declination; between their centers is the gnomonic base. ||1||

Regarding the two points of East and West with equal shadow-ends: of the two points occurring in the Eastern and Western hemispheres, the first point (from the Eastern hemisphere) becomes the West direction. The other point (from the Western hemisphere) becomes the East direction. This is what is being said. On level ground, at a distance greater than the midday shadow—

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>The "Three Problems" in Indian astronomy refer to the determination of direction, place, and time.</note>

One should draw a circle using a compass with a radius equal to the <term>radius of the sine-circle</term> <note>Sanskrit: Trijya; the standard radius used in trigonometric calculations, often 3438 minutes</note>. In the center of that circle, one should place a <term>gnomon</term> <note>Sanskrit: Shanku; a vertical pillar used for measuring shadows</note> marked with twelve digits. When the sun is in the eastern hemisphere, mark the point where the tip of its shadow enters the circle in the western hemisphere. This is designated as the first or "western point." As the sun moves and reaches the western hemisphere, another point should be made with chalk where the tip of the gnomon's shadow exits the circle. This is the "eastern point." This too should be marked.

The portion to the east of the <term>meridian</term> <note>Sanskrit: Yamyottara-vritta; the north-south line</note> is the eastern hemisphere. The half-sphere to the west of the meridian circle is known as the western hemisphere. Thus, when the sun is in the eastern hemisphere, the tip of the twelve-digit gnomon's shadow touches the circumference of the circle in the western hemisphere. Similarly, when the sun is in the western hemisphere, the shadow tip intersects the circumference in the eastern hemisphere. The first point is the West direction, and the second point is the East direction. The line connecting these two points is the East-West line. By the "production of a fish" <note>A geometric method of drawing an intersecting arc to find a perpendicular</note>, the midpoint of that line should be found. From that, the other line passing through the base of the gnomon becomes the North-South line.

This would be the case if the sun's <term>declination</term> <note>Sanskrit: Kranti; the angular distance of the sun north or south of the celestial equator</note> remained constant throughout a single day, but it does not. Therefore, the East-West direction must be examined in light of the change in declination. By the phrase **"due to declination,"** it is implied that the aforementioned calculation only holds true if the sun moves along the same diurnal circle from the time the shadow enters until it exits. Otherwise, if the motion of declination changes, the line connecting the entry and exit points of the shadow tip will not be the true East-West line. Since the two "arms" <note>Sanskrit: Bhuja; the north-south distance of the shadow tip from the east-west line</note> of the shadow would be unequal, the intention of the Teacher <note>Likely referring to Brahmagupta or a similar authority</note> is clearly understood to be that a "correction for the difference in the arms" must be performed.

On this point, the commentator Chaturveda Acharya, having calculated the difference in the <term>amplitude</term> <note>Sanskrit: Agra; the distance of the sun at rising/setting from the east/west point</note> relative to the hypotenuse-circle based on the difference in declination, has refined the determination of direction mentioned by the Teacher. Keeping this very calculation in mind, Bhaskaracharya also spoke of a unique method for determining direction, stating: **"The East point is shifted in the direction of the sun's course by digits calculated from half the difference of the sines of declination at the two times, multiplied by the hypotenuse and divided by the cosine of latitude."** Similarly, Sripati also clarified the method of determining direction with the rule beginning: **"The difference between the sines of the sun's declination at the times of the shadow's exit and entry..."**

The mathematical proof here is easy, yet it is stated for the understanding of students. Let it be assumed that at the time of the shadow's entry, the sun's declination = **D**, and at the time of the shadow's exit, its declination = **D'**.

->Then, by proportion<-

<center>
Amplitude = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine of D}}{\text{Cosine of Latitude}}$, Amplitude' = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine of D'}}{\text{Cosine of Latitude}}$
</center>

Then, having determined the amplitude relative to the hypotenuse-circle, the "arm" of the shadow is calculated.
$\therefore$ The arm of the first shadow tip = Amplitude relative to the hypotenuse $\sim$ <note>The symbol $\sim$ denotes the difference between two values</note> Equinoctial shadow.
<center>
= $\frac{\text{Sine of D} \times \text{Hypotenuse}}{\text{Cosine of Latitude}}$ $\sim$ Equinoctial shadow.
</center>

### Now he describes the knowledge of directions by means of the shadow-path line

->Where the two "fish" <note>The 'fish' is a geometric shape formed by the intersection of two circles, used to find perpendiculars.</note> produced from the tips of three shadows meet in the middle.<-
->In the northern hemisphere, the south is from the base of the gnomon; in the southern hemisphere, the north. ||2||<-
->The intersection of the shadow-tip path line and the thread touches the circumference of the circle.<-
->The distance between the middle shadow and the other is the difference between the gnomon and the circles. ||3||<-

**Vasanabhashya (Explanatory Commentary):**—From the three shadows, two "fish" are produced from their tips; the meaning of <term>the two fish produced from the tips of three shadows</term> is explained more clearly here. On ground leveled with water, one should place a <term>gnomon</term> <note>A vertical pillar or rod used to cast a shadow for astronomical measurements.</note> of desired measure. Then, while the sun is in a single half-day (morning or afternoon), three points should be marked at the desired tips of the shadows. Then, making one point the center, one should draw a circle with a compass of desired size. With that same compass, draw a second circle centered on the second point. Draw a third circle centered on the third point. The circles should be of such a size and drawn in such a way that the appearance of <term>two fish</term> <note>Sanskrit: Matsyadvaya; the vesica piscis shape.</note> is produced. In the direction where there is a great distance between them, those are the "mouths," and where they are close, those are the "tails." Then, placing fine pegs at the two mouths and tying a thread between them, one should produce a single curve from the middle of the tails by the movement of the threads. The intersection of those two threads, following the path of their mouths and tails, is the South direction. This is when the sun is in the <term>Northern Hemisphere</term> <note>Uttaragola; the half of the year when the sun is north of the celestial equator.</note> relative to the base of the gnomon. But in the <term>Southern Hemisphere</term> <note>Dakshinagola</note>, such as when the sun is at the beginning of Libra, then the intersection point of the two middle threads is the North direction from the base of the gnomon. Thus, extending a thread passing through the base of the gnomon and the intersection point, one should draw a line; that is the North-South line. Then, making each point a center, one should produce two fish with two circles. The thread passing through its mouth and tail is the East-West direction. Now, if there are three points produced from different half-days (morning and afternoon), one should draw circles centered on each point such that each circle encompasses the three points; the rest is as before. Thus is the determination of directions in a place with latitude. In a place with no latitude (the equator), the <term>line of falling points</term> <note>Bindupatapankti; the straight line formed by shadow tips at the equator.</note> is itself the East-West line, and the North-South line is to be achieved as before. This is the <term>rationale</term> <note>Vasana; the underlying geometric or physical logic.</note>. Having drawn a new circle with a desired radius and marking the directions, it is shown according to one's own location—

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<page-num>265</page-num>

At the same distance north of the east-west line where the sun rises in the eastern direction, the tip of the shadow will be at that same distance south in the western direction. From the <term>gnomon</term> <note>Shanku: a vertical pillar used as a sundial</note> situated at the center of the circle, as the sun moves south due to the motion of its own diurnal circle—governed by the <term>latitude</term> <note>Aksha: the terrestrial latitude of the observer</note>—the shadow circle moves north by inverse relation. Therefore, when the sun is on the <term>prime vertical</term> <note>Samamandala: the east-west vertical circle</note> in the east, the shadow tip is on the prime vertical in the west. When the sun reaches the <term>meridian</term> <note>Yamyottara-rekha: the north-south line</note> in the south, the shadow tip is also on the meridian <insert>in the north</insert>. In this sequence, as the sun sets in the west at a certain distance north, the shadow tip sets at that same distance south in the east. 

Thus, when the sun is south of the prime vertical and does not re-enter it, and when the sun is north on the meridian line, the shadow is south on that same line. This occurs in locations where the latitude is less than twenty-four degrees <note>referring to the tropics/obliquity of the ecliptic</note>. In the northern hemisphere, a segment of the shadow’s path necessarily faces south. In the southern hemisphere, it always faces north due to the inversion of the underlying logic. 

Therefore, the surfaces of the shadow’s path are formed according to the movement of the shadow tip. From these, two <term>fish-figures</term> <note>Matsya: a geometric construction formed by the intersection of two circles, resembling a fish</note> are produced. These form the surfaces of the shadow-rotation circle. The intersection of the two lines drawn through the "mouth" and "tail" of these fish-figures—which lie inside the circle—is the point of union. Because this intersection moves south when the shadow segment faces south, it is said that "in the northern hemisphere, it is south of the gnomon's base." Since the shadow faces north when the sun is in the north, it is said "south or north." 

To the one who knows the three shadow tips, the author provides the answer to these two questions: <term>how to find the rotation of the shadow tip without knowing declination or latitude</term> and how to find the midday shadow.

The intersection of the lines from the circumference of the circles formed by the shadow tips is indeed the line of the shadow's rotation. This is what is meant: the intersection of the two lines passing through the middle of the two "fish" generated by the three shadow tips (as shown in the previous verse) is made the center. A circle drawn from that center touching the tips of the shadows is the path where the shadow tip of the gnomon (standing at the center of the directions) rotates. The <term>rationale</term> <note>Vasana: the geometric or logical proof</note> for this was already stated by us in the previous verse. 

Regarding the "distance of the midday shadow," he says: the distance between the "gnomon and the circle"—meaning the distance between the base of the gnomon and the circle of the shadow's rotation. That distance, whether north or south, is taken as the measure of the midday shadow on the meridian line.

Here too, the rationale was shown in the previous verse. It is appropriate because it shows the structure of the shadow's circumference. The author explains in two verses the answer to how one who sees the shadow tip can know the directions even if they know the declination and latitude. ||2-3||

**V. M. [Commentary]:** On a desired day, having observed three shadows of the gnomon (placed at the center of the directions) at different times, one should draw three circles with a compass using those three tip-points as centers. By their intersection, produce two <term>fish-figures</term>. The intersection of the lines passing through the mouth and tail of these fish is the South direction in the northern hemisphere. If, in a place with <term>low latitude</term> <note>Jinālpākṣa: latitude less than 24 degrees</note>, the shadow tip is sometimes south of the gnomon's base, then that intersection is the North direction. The circle whose circumference is formed by the intersection of the lines emerging from the mouth and tail of the two fish touches the shadow tips; thus, that circumference is the shadow's path. The distance between the gnomon's base and the shadow-rotation circle is the midday shadow, which may be north or south. In a place with high latitude, the midday shadow is always north.

<header>In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta</header>

It occurs that in the Northern Hemisphere, in a place with a low latitude <note>specifically less than 24 degrees</note>, when the sun's northern declination is greater than the latitude, the midday shadow of the gnomon becomes south-facing. In the *Surya-siddhanta* <note>The "Sun Treatise," a foundational text of Indian astronomy</note> it is also stated: "On a desired day, having marked three points of the shadow at morning, noon, and evening, one should find the path of the shadow's rotation using the 'three-touch' line formed by the intersection of two 'fish' figures." Similarly, Lalla Acharya states: "The circle drawn from the intersection of the cords emerging from the mouth and tail of the 'fish' figures, which touches the tips of the three shadows, defines the path that the shadow line does not leave." Sripati also speaks in accordance with the teachers, saying: "From the intersection of the cords passing through the bellies of the two 'fish,' a circle is formed touching three points; the shadow of the central gnomon does not leave that circumference." This refers to the center of the shadow's rotation being either north or south of the midday shadow. ||2-3||

## Rationale

If the sun's declination were fixed for a single day, then the ray-lines originating from the center of the sun at every point on its daily path and passing through the tip of the gnomon would strike the horizontal surface of the horizon. The shadows extend from the base of the gnomon to these points. By observing the nature of the shadow, it is proven that a cone <term>suci|literally 'needle,' here meaning a geometric cone</term> is formed with the gnomon tip as the apex and the daily path of the sun as the base. The path of the shadow's rotation is the curve produced when this cone is intersected by the horizontal plane of the horizon. 

At the North Pole <term>Meru</term>, the horizon is the celestial equator, which is parallel to the sun's daily path. Therefore, the oblique cone formed from the gnomon tip is cut by a plane parallel to its base, producing a circular intersection. Thus, it is proven that at the Pole, the shadow path is always a circle. The fact that teachers like the author of the *Surya-siddhanta*, Lalla, and Brahmagupta accepted the shadow path as always being a circle is only strictly accurate at the Pole. Elsewhere, in places with latitude, depending on the height of the gnomon, the shadow path can be a circle, a straight line, a parabola, an ellipse, or a hyperbola. At the equator on the day of the equinox, because the sun moves along the celestial equator and the gnomon tip lies in that same plane, no cone is formed; instead, the intersection of the equatorial horizon and the celestial equator results in a straight line. Seeing that the shadow path is not always a circle, Bhaskara Acharya, in the *Siddhanta-shiromani*, refuted the circular shadow path, stating "the shadow rotation from three points is not always [circular]," etc. ||2-3||

## Now, determining directions based on the shadow path line

**Hindi Commentary:** On a desired day, on ground leveled with water, one should place a gnomon at the center of a circle. Having marked the shadows at three different times, one should draw three circles from those points using a compass <term>karkata|literally 'crab,' referring to a compass tool</term>. By their intersection, two "fish" shapes <note>vesica piscis shapes used in geometric construction</note> are formed. Where the two lines passing through the mouths and tails of these fish intersect, that point should be understood as the South direction in the Northern Hemisphere. If, in a place with low latitude (less than twenty-four degrees), the intersection falls in a southern shadow relative to the gnomon base, then that should be understood as the North direction...

It is required that the circle formed by joining the lines passing through the mouths and tails of the two "fish" shapes <note>A geometric construction method using intersecting arcs, known as *matsya* or "fish" in Indian geometry</note> is the circle that touches the tip of the shadow (**Shadow Rotation Circle**). Therefore, that circular line itself is the path of the shadow's rotation. The distance between the base of the <term>Gnomon</term> <note>A vertical pillar or rod used to cast a shadow for astronomical measurements</note> and the shadow rotation circle is the midday shadow; it can be either North or South. In regions where the latitude is greater than 24 degrees, the midday shadow is always North. In the Northern Hemisphere, in regions with low latitude, when the Sun's northern declination is greater than the latitude, the shadow of the gnomon at midday faces South. In the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit astronomical text</note>, this is similarly stated as "from the desired hypotenuse in the middle, East and West, etc." Lallacharya also states this in the Sanskrit commentary through verses such as "the union of the ropes emerging from the tail and mouth of the fish," as well as "from the union of the lines going through the two bellies of the fish," and "of the gnomon's shadow and the rotation circle." Sripati also speaks in accordance with the teacher's words. || 2-3 ||

## Proof

If the Sun's declination is considered constant for one day, then the shadow extends from the base of the gnomon to the points where the ray-lines passing from the Sun's centers on the diurnal circle through the tip of the gnomon hit the surface of the horizon. By observing the nature of these shadows, it is proven that if you create a cone with the tip of the gnomon as the apex and the diurnal circle as the base, the path of the shadow's rotation is the curve formed by the intersection of that cone with the surface of the horizon. 

For those living at the Meru <note>The North Pole</note>, the horizon circle is the celestial equator; it is parallel to the diurnal circle. Therefore, the oblique cone based on the diurnal circle from the gnomon's tip, when cut by the horizon surface (which is parallel to the equatorial plane), creates a circular intersection. This proves that at the Pole, the shadow's path is always circular. The authors of the *Surya Siddhanta*, Lallacharya, Brahmagupta, and other teachers who accepted the shadow's path as circular, can only be correct regarding the Pole. This is because elsewhere, in regions with latitude, the shadow rotates in various curves—lines, circles, parabolas, ellipses, or hyperbolas—depending on the gnomon's slant. 

At the equator on the day of the equinox, because the Sun moves along the celestial equator and the tip of the gnomon lies in the equatorial plane, there is an absence of a cone. Therefore, the intersection line of the equatorial horizon and the equatorial plane (the vertical line at the equator) becomes the shadow line. Seeing that the shadow rotation does not always occur in a circle in all countries, Bhaskaracharya, in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, refuted the circular shadow path with the verse "the rotation of the arm is not sufficient, it is not true," which is very correct. || 2-3 ||

## Now, he speaks of calculating the shadow of a twelve-digit gnomon:

> In the shadow circle, the Sun's shadow is the hypotenuse; its square is equal to the sum of the squares.
> As with the gnomon, the shadow here is described separately by its difference and sum. || 4 ||

**The gnomon is the square root of the difference between the square of the shadow and the square of the base <note>the "bhuja" or north-south distance</note> in the east-west direction.**
**That east-west shadow is the upright <note>the "koti" or perpendicular</note> representing the distance between the base and the tip of the shadow. ||5||**

*Vasanabhashya* <note>The author's own explanatory commentary</note>— Methods for determining the eastern direction using three points even without knowing the declination or latitude have been stated. Now, the author explains how to determine the directions using a single point generated by that process. This is explained in two half-verses. The meaning is as follows: he describes how the solar amplitude <term>arkagra</term><note>The distance of the sun at rising/setting from the east-west line</note> behaves within the circle of the shadow. The solar amplitude is multiplied by the hypotenuse and divided by the radius. By establishing the solar amplitude through the dimensions of the celestial sphere, a proportion is made: if the solar amplitude is this much in a circle of radius <term>trijya</term>, how much would it be in the circle of the desired shadow's hypotenuse? The result is the solar amplitude in digits <note>angulas</note> for the shadow-circle. Then, by taking the difference or sum of that with the local equinoctial shadow <note>the shadow at noon on the equinox</note> of a twelve-digit gnomon, depending on whether the sun is in the northern or southern hemisphere, the "base" <term>bhuja</term> is produced.

Regarding where the gnomon stands in relation to this, he says: "Of the east-west..." The shadow of the gnomon at the tip of this base, the square of that shadow and the square of the base—the square root of the difference of those two squares is the east-west upright. Where does this occur? He says: "The upright is the distance between the shadow and the tip of the base." The meaning is this: for a gnomon situated on level ground, its shadow is the hypotenuse. The "base" calculated as described should be applied in the opposite direction from the foot of the gnomon so that the gnomon stands at the tip of the base. If the base is north, it is applied south, and vice versa. Then, subtracting the square of the base from the square of the hypotenuse, the square of the upright remains; its square root is the upright, which lies in the east-west direction.

The underlying logic <term>vasana</term> is this: having drawn a circle with the hypotenuse of the desired shadow as the radius and marking the directions, one should place a string equal to the solar amplitude from the east and west points, either to the north or south. Having placed that rising-setting line within the circle, a point should be made at its end on the north-south line. By making points for the solar amplitudes and using the "two-fish" method <note>a geometric construction using intersecting arcs to find a perpendicular</note> from those three points, a point is found where the strings from the "mouth" and "tail" meet. One should place the three points within that point, or a circle is produced. That circle on the ground represents the diurnal path <term>ahoratravritta</term> where the foot of the large gnomon wanders.

The "base" is defined as the distance between the foot of the gnomon and the east-west line. Therefore, at sunrise or sunset, the base is exactly equal to the solar amplitude. This applies everywhere in regions with latitude and at the equator. At the equator, the entire amplitude is the base for the whole day, so the foot of the gnomon never leaves the rising-setting line. In regions with latitude, this is due to the latitude. Because of the obliquity of the equinoctial circle and the corresponding diurnal circle, the solar amplitude becomes the base in the northern hemisphere. If the gnomon is north of the east-west line, or if it is south and the value is greater than the solar amplitude, it is subtracted at the base of the gnomon; however, the difference remains. In the shadow-circle, the equinoctial shadow is always the base-offset <term>shankutala</term>. Therefore, the difference is stated with respect to that. In the southern hemisphere, the foot of the gnomon is always at a distance equal to the sum of the southern solar amplitude and the base-offset from the rising-setting line. Thus, their sum is always the base derived from the equinoctial shadow. When the base is in the north, it must be north of the east-west sine. The construction of the figure can be done sequentially from the foot of the gnomon, or inversely from the base. Thus, the distance between the center of the circle and the foot of the gnomon is the shadow... and the east-west distance of the gnomon's foot is [the root of] the square of the hypotenuse minus the square of the base—

The author now provides the answer to the question of how one who knows the directions might understand the rotation of the gnomon's shadow. ||4-5||

**Commentary:**—The Sun's *Agra* <note>amplitude; the distance of the rising sun from the East-West line</note> multiplied by the shadow-hypotenuse and divided by the radius (the *Trijya*) results in the Sun's *Agra* within the shadow-circle (the *Karnavrttagra*). The equinoctial shadow (*Palabha*) is always considered to be in the South. Their difference or sum (the difference if the *Karnavrttagra* and *Palabha* are in different directions, and their sum if in the same direction) results in the *Bhuja* <note>the distance from the East-West line to the tip of the shadow</note> in the direction of the calculation. ||4||

# Here is the Rationale

The *Agra* is the distance between the East-West line and the line connecting the points of rising and setting. The perpendicular dropped from the base of the gnomon onto the rising-setting line is the *Shankutala* <note>the distance from the center of the diurnal circle to the East-West line</note>. By the combination of the *Agra* and the *Shankutala*, the *Bhuja* is formed as a perpendicular from the base of the gnomon to the East-West line. If, in a circle with the radius of the *Trijya*, the *Agra* is obtained, then what is obtained in the circle of the shadow-hypotenuse? The *Agra* in the shadow-hypotenuse circle = $\frac{Agra \times Shadow-Hypotenuse}{Radius}$. It is demonstrated how, in the sphere of the shadow-hypotenuse, the *Shankutala* becomes equal to the *Palabha* (equinoctial shadow). Now, $\frac{Palabha \cdot Gnomon}{12}$ is the *Shankutala*. However, by substituting the Gnomon as $\frac{12 \times Radius}{Shadow-Hypotenuse}$, we get $\frac{Palabha \cdot 12 \cdot Radius}{12 \times Shadow-Hypotenuse} =$ *Shankutala*. Converting this to the radius of the shadow-hypotenuse: $\frac{Palabha \cdot 12 \cdot Radius \times Shadow-Hypotenuse}{12 \times Shadow-Hypotenuse \times Radius} =$ *Palabha* = *Shankutala*. Therefore, in the shadow-hypotenuse sphere, the *Bhuja* is formed by the combination of the *Agra* and the *Palabha*. Since: *Agra* $\pm$ *Shankutala* = *Bhuja*.
Bhaskaracharya <note>the 12th-century mathematician-astronomer</note>, accepting the *Bhuja* as the distance between the shadow-tip and the East-West line, considered the *Palabha* as North in the inverted sphere. The Teacher <note>referring to the author of the current text</note>, accepting the *Bhuja* as the distance between the base of the small gnomon and the East-West line, has kept the *Agra* and *Palabha* in their actual directions, relating the *Bhuja* to the tip. ||4||

# Now, the calculation of the Bhuja for a twelve-digit gnomon is described

**Hindi Commentary:**—Multiplying the Sun's *Agra* by the shadow-hypotenuse and dividing by the radius gives the Sun's *Agra* in the shadow-circle. The *Palabha* is always in the South direction. By taking the difference or sum of these two (the difference if the *Karnavrttagra* and *Palabha* are in different directions, and the sum if in the same direction), the *Bhuja* of the calculated direction is obtained. ||4||

The *Agra* is the difference between the rising-setting line and the East-West line. From the base of the gnomon to the East-West line...

The vertical gnomon <term>Shanku: a gnomon or vertical pillar used in ancient astronomy to measure time and latitude via its shadow</term> stands above the base. By adjusting the <term>Agra: the sine of amplitude, or the distance of the sun's rising point from the east-west line</term> and the base of the gnomon, we find the <term>Bhuja: the base or the north-south component of the shadow</term> which is the perpendicular from the gnomon's base to the east-west line. If we find the amplitude-sine relative to the radius, then what is it relative to the shadow-hypotenuse? From this we get the amplitude-sine on the circle of the shadow-hypotenuse = $\frac{\text{Agra} \times \text{Shadow-Hypotenuse}}{\text{Radius}}$. However, in the sphere of the shadow-hypotenuse,

the <term>Palabha: the equinoctial midday shadow</term> is equal to the base of the gnomon. For example: $\frac{\text{Palabha} \times \text{Gnomon}}{12} = \text{Gnomon Base}$, therefore $\frac{12 \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Shadow-Hypotenuse}} = \text{Gnomon}$.

Thus, by substitution: $\frac{\text{Palabha} \times 12 \times \text{Radius}}{12 \times \text{Shadow-Hypotenuse}} = \text{Gnomon Base}$. Converting this into the sphere of the shadow-hypotenuse:

$\frac{\text{Palabha} \times 12 \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Shadow-Hypotenuse}}{12 \times \text{Shadow-Hypotenuse} \times \text{Radius}} = \text{Palabha} = \text{Gnomon Base}$. Therefore, in the sphere of the shadow-hypotenuse, the *Bhuja* (north-south component) is formed by the adjustment of the *Agra* (amplitude) and the

*Palabha* (equinoctial shadow). <note>Bhaskaracharya (1114–1185 AD) was a legendary Indian mathematician and astronomer.</note> Bhaskaracharya accepted the distance between the tip of the shadow and the east-west line as the *Bhuja*, treating the amplitude-sine on the shadow-hypotenuse circle as the inverted sphere and the *Palabha* as North. Here, the Teacher <note>Referring to Brahmagupta, the author of the original text.</note> accepts the distance between the base of the small gnomon and the east-west line as the *Bhuja*, and has established the *Agra* and *Palabha* according to their actual directions. The phrase "at the end of the *Bhuja*" connects to what follows. ||4||

**Scholarly Commentary:** The base of the gnomon should be understood as the tip of the *Bhuja* extending in its respective direction from the east-west line. The square root of the difference between the squares of the shadow and the *Bhuja* is the distance between the tip of the shadow and the tip of the *Bhuja*; this is the east-west <term>Koti: the perpendicular or the east-west component of the shadow</term>. ||5||

---

### Mathematical Proof

The *Bhuja* is the perpendicular from the base of the gnomon to the east-west line; this is the distance between the shadow-tip of a gnomon at the center of the directions and the east-west line. The shadow-hypotenuse of the gnomon at the center of the directions is the hypotenuse. The *Bhuja* is the perpendicular from the shadow-tip to the east-west line. The distance from the end of the *Bhuja* to the center of the directions (the center of the circle) along the east-west line is the *Koti*. Therefore, $\sqrt{\text{Shadow}^2 - \text{Bhuja}^2} = \text{Koti}$. Bhaskaracharya also says the same in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*: "The distance between the shadow-tip of the gnomon at the intersection of the direction-lines and the east-west line..." etc. ||5||

The shadow-hypotenuse of the gnomon at the center of the directions, from the shadow-tip...

# Chapter on the Three Problems

On the east-west line, the <term>Bhujā</term> <note>the north-south side of the shadow triangle</note> is the perpendicular; from the tip of this <term>Bhujā</term> to the center of the directions along the east-west line is the <term>Koṭi</term> <note>the east-west side of the shadow triangle</note>. In this right-angled triangle, $\sqrt{Shadow^2 - Bhujā^2} = Koṭi$. Bhaskaracharya also states this in the *Siddhānta Shiromaṇi* <note>A foundational 12th-century astronomical text</note> with the phrase: "The shadow of the gnomon placed at the intersection of the directional lines [reaches] the middle of the east-west line." || 5 ||

->Now he describes the relative positions of the gnomon and the shadow<-

> By placing the tip of the shadow at the center of the directions, the gnomon moves according to the direction.
> For a gnomon standing at the center of the directions, the tip of the shadow moves in the opposite manner. || 6 ||

<term>Commentary</term> <note>original: "Vā. Bhā." or Vāsanābhāṣya, the author's own explanatory commentary</note>—If someone asks, after marking a desired point for the shadow-tip, "Where must the gnomon be placed so its shadow-tip falls here?" the first half of the verse provides the answer: "by placing the tip of the shadow at the center." Having determined the directions as before, and with the <term>Bhujā-sine</term>, <term>Koṭi</term>, and the instantaneous shadow-hypotenuse established, one should lay them out on the east-west line of the questioned shadow-tip. From that tip, along the east-west line: if the sun is in the eastern sky, extend a cord equal to the <term>Koṭi</term> digits toward the east. If it is in the western sky, extend it toward the west. From the end of that <term>Koṭi</term>, extend a cord equal to the <term>Bhujā</term> digits toward the north <insert>if the sun is north</insert> or toward the south <insert>if the sun is south</insert>. Place the gnomon at the end of that cord; the shadow of the gnomon placed there will match the question. In this way, the gnomon "moves" according to the direction. Otherwise, the logic is this: in the forenoon, the shadow must necessarily face west.

Since the tip is placed at the center of the directions, the gnomon must necessarily be to the east of the center; thus, the <term>Koṭi</term> is extended eastward. It is said the gnomon moves according to the direction. The <term>Bhujā</term> is applied from the end of the <term>Koṭi</term> or the gnomon-tip, either to the north or south. Since when the sun is north or south of the prime vertical, the gnomon is also there, the shadow of that gnomon will face west and reach the center point. In the afternoon, everything occurs in the opposite way. However, for one who places the gnomon at a desired spot and asks for the shadow-tip based on the shadow's length in digits, the answer is in the second half of the verse. Having determined the directions, the <term>Koṭi</term> and <term>Bhujā</term> are found. Then, place the gnomon at the center of the directions. From its base, the <term>Koṭi</term> should be extended westward in the forenoon and eastward in the afternoon. From that end, the <term>Bhujā</term> should be applied in the opposite direction: north as south, and south as north. The shadow-tip will be at the end of that. Thus it is said: "the tip of the shadow moves in the opposite manner." The logic here is: for a gnomon on the east-west line, the shadow in the forenoon faces west; therefore, the <term>Koṭi</term> is extended to the west. Since we seek the shadow-tip, and in the afternoon it faces east, it is extended [east].

There too, to find the shadow-tip, the <term>Bhujā</term> is also applied inversely. Because if the sun is north of the prime vertical line, the shadow-tip is to the south. When the sun is to the south, the shadow-tip is to the north. If one places that shadow-tip, the sun will be positioned on the prime vertical. In a place with latitude <note>as opposed to the equator</note>...

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>The "Three Problems" refer to the determination of time, place, and direction using a gnomon's shadow.</note>

-> Page 273 <-

Having tied one end of a string at the intersection of the **meridian circle** <note>original: "yamya-uttara mandala"</note> and the **equinoctial circle** <note>original: "vishuvad-mandala"</note>, one should tie the second end on that same meridian circle at an equal distance to the north of the **prime vertical** <note>original: "sama-mandala"</note>. As long as that remains, the **Sine of Latitude** <term>Akshajya: the sine of the observer's latitude</term> is defined by the string passing through the center of the earth and bisecting the prime vertical; one should then attach the **plumb-line** <note>original: "avalambaka"</note> at its end. The string that is directed south-to-north from the center of the earth is the **Sine of Co-latitude** <term>Lambajya: the sine of the angle complementary to the latitude</term> of one's own location. We have already explained this matter in the *Chapter on the Sphere* <note>original: "Goladhyaya"</note>.

In that context, the Co-latitude is the vertical side <note>original: "koti"</note> and the Latitude is the horizontal side <note>original: "bhuja"</note>. The square root of the sum of their squares is the **Equinoctial hypotenuse** <note>original: "vishuvat-karna"</note>, which is the radius, because on that day the equinoctial circle itself is the diurnal circle. On other days, the circle of the shadow's hypotenuse is different; even at noon, it is not the equinoctial hypotenuse, but rather the **Sine of Altitude** <note>original: "unnata-jiva"</note> in the vertical circles. The vertical side of the **gnomon** <term>Shanku: a vertical pillar used to measure shadows</term> is called the **Sine of Zenith Distance** <note>original: "drig-jya"</note>.

With respect to the gnomon and the Sine of Altitude, that is called the Sine—and with respect to its vertical side, it is called the horizontal side, because that vertical circle rotates facing the planet. It does not leave the **Zenith** <note>original: "kha-svastika"</note> above and below the prime vertical—this matter was detailed by us in the *Chapter on the Sphere* regarding its construction. Therefore, it is well said: the gnomon is the vertical side of the Sine of Altitude; synonymously, the shadow is the Sine of Zenith Distance; the horizontal side and the Sine of Zenith Distance are synonyms. The hypotenuse is called the circle of the shadow. Both the shadow-circle and the hypotenuse are called the **Radius** <term>Trijya: the standard radius used in Indian trigonometry, often 3438 minutes</term> at the equinox.

Then, one should multiply both by the square of the Radius. After that, the sum of the squares should be used as the divisor in both places. The result for the square of the gnomon is the Sine of Co-latitude; for the square of the equinoctial shadow, it is the Sine of Latitude. Having converted those Sines of Co-latitude and Latitude into arcs, their degrees should be calculated separately. This is the **rationale** <note>original: "vasana"</note> of the **Rule of Three** <note>original: "trairashika"</note>.

It is as follows:
The gnomon of twelve digits is the vertical side; the equinoctial shadow is the horizontal side. The sum of their squares is the square of the equinoctial hypotenuse.
*   If by the square of the equinoctial hypotenuse, the square of the gnomon-side is obtained...
*   Then by the square of the Radius-hypotenuse, what is the square of the gnomon-side?
The result is the square of the Sine of Co-latitude.

Then, by the square of the equinoctial hypotenuse, the square of the equinoctial shadow-side is obtained. Then, the square of the horizontal side is the difference between the square of the Radius-hypotenuse and the square of the vertical side. The result is the square of the Sine of Latitude. The square roots of these are the Sine of Co-latitude and the Sine of Latitude. Alternatively, the Radius is divided separately by the equinoctial hypotenuse or the shadow-hypotenuse.

Here too is the Rule of Three:
*   If for the equinoctial hypotenuse, the vertical side is twelve...
*   Then for the Radius-hypotenuse, what is it?
The result is the Sine of Co-latitude.
*   Then, if for the equinoctial hypotenuse, the horizontal side is the equinoctial shadow...
*   Then for the Radius-hypotenuse, what is the horizontal side?
The result is the Sine of Latitude.

Therefore, one should multiply the Radius separately by twelve and the equinoctial shadow, and divide by the equinoctial hypotenuse. This is proven.

Or there is another method:
When the **Versine** <term>Utkramajya: 1 - cos(x)</term> of the degrees of Co-latitude is subtracted from the Radius, it becomes the Sine of Latitude. When it is subtracted from the Versine of the Latitude, it becomes the Sine of Co-latitude.

The rationale here is:
The degrees of Co-latitude situated above the southern horizon in the meridian circle—the **Sine** <note>original: "kramajya"</note> of those is the Sine of Co-latitude, as shown before. Having doubled that, the arrow <note>the versed sine</note> of the arc situated above is the Versine of the degrees of Co-latitude. When that is subtracted from the Radius, the remaining sine-segment is equal to the Sine of Latitude. This arises from the string passing through the center of the earth and the middle of the prime vertical.

This is the method for either sine:
*   When the degrees of Latitude are subtracted from ninety, the degrees of Co-latitude remain. Their sine is the Sine of Co-latitude.
*   When the degrees of Co-latitude are subtracted from ninety, the degrees of Latitude remain. Their sine is the Sine of Latitude.

The connection between the Sine of Latitude and Sine of Co-latitude will follow hereafter; this is the rationale here.

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

At Mount Meru <note>the North Pole</note>, the degrees of latitude are ninety. Because the Pole Star is situated directly overhead, the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>the shadow-length at the equinox</note> is attached to the horizon, and thus there is an absence of degrees of latitude <note>meaning the sun does not rise above the horizon in the same way</note>. At the terrestrial equator <note>literally "the place without latitude"</note>, there is no latitude; because the two poles are attached to the horizon, the colatitude is ninety degrees. Because the Pole Star is situated there, at the interval of half a circle, the sum of the latitude and colatitude is ninety degrees. Therefore, by the movement along the meridian circle passing through the south of the center of the prime vertical, the horizon's zenith is ninety degrees. When the degrees of latitude are subtracted from these, the remaining degrees are the colatitude. Conversely, when the degrees of colatitude are subtracted, the remaining parts are the latitude. It is known sequentially that the sine of one's own parts becomes that specific sine; this is explained here. Therefore, it is proven. One should also demonstrate the field as it stands on the globe.

Now, another method of calculation:
Multiply by the gnomon's shadow and divide by twelve <note>the standard height of a gnomon</note>. Divide the sine of latitude multiplied by twelve by the equinoctial shadow. The result is the <term>sine of colatitude</term> <note>Lambajya: the sine of the angle between the zenith and the celestial equator</note>. If one multiplies the sine of colatitude by the equinoctial shadow and divides by twelve, the result is the sine of latitude. The logic here is: if the equinoctial shadow is the base and twelve is the perpendicular, then the sine of latitude is the result. If the sine of colatitude is the result when twelve is the perpendicular and the equinoctial shadow is the base, then what is the base for the sine of colatitude as the perpendicular? The result is the sine of latitude. This is proven.

Alternatively, by knowing one, the second can be calculated: subtract the square of the sine of colatitude from the square of the <term>radius</term> <note>Trijya: the total sine</note> and the square root is the other; or subtract the square of the sine of latitude from the square of the radius and the square root is the sine of colatitude. Since the sine of latitude is the base, the sine of colatitude is the perpendicular, and the radius is the hypotenuse. Therefore, it is proven: subtracting the square of the perpendicular from the square of the hypotenuse and taking the root gives the base; subtracting the square of the base gives the perpendicular.

Thus, when the sun <note>literally "the hot-rayed one"</note> enters the <term>meridian circle</term> <note>Yamyottaramandala: the north-south circle</note> at the equinox, one may demonstrate the sines of zenith distance and altitude in many ways. Now, he directs how to find them elsewhere at midday. By this half-verse, the calculation of the sine of altitude is always the same elsewhere. Just as the sines of zenith distance and altitude are made from the equinoctial shadow and equinoctial hypotenuse, so on any desired day, they should be made using the midday shadow and its hypotenuse, and their arc-parts should be calculated. Those parts which are the zenith distance are the latitude for that day. The sun reaches midday from the center of the prime vertical by that many degrees of direction on that day; this means that however many degrees it is "bent" <note>zenith distance</note>, it is that many degrees "raised" <note>altitude</note>.

Even at any desired time, the sines of zenith distance and altitude should be calculated using the shadow of that moment or the hypotenuse of that shadow. There, the sine of altitude is the <term>gnomon</term> <note>Shanku: the vertical pillar</note>, and the sine of zenith distance is the shadow. The degrees of those two are the degrees of zenith distance and altitude at that time. Just as at the equinoctial midday, the degrees of zenith distance and altitude that are calculated are also in the <term>vertical circle</term> <note>Drigmandala</note>, because the meridian circle is always the vertical circle in the middle. There, the degrees of zenith distance are the interval between the prime vertical and the equinoctial circle. Because of the existence of this interval, the sun having gone to the equinoctial circle on that day, the distance from the equinox is the planet's declination. On this day, due to the midday declination, the degrees of zenith distance become less or more than the degrees of latitude.

---

From that twelve <note>the gnomon</note>, they are less or more; they belong to the midday shadow and its hypotenuse. Therefore, the sines of zenith distance and altitude are joined to the equinox by the shadow and hypotenuse of one's own center. They are also joined at other times and at midday. Because the circle of directions revolves facing the planet. Above and below the prime vertical, one's own zenith is not abandoned. If for the hypotenuse of the desired shadow there is a gnomon of twelve, then for the hypotenuse of the radius, what is the shadow? Thus the sine of zenith distance is obtained. In this way, because the signs of the zodiac etc. are situated in the vertical circle, everything is proven. One should demonstrate this as it stands on the globe. He now gives the answer to the question: "Who knows the sun through the midday shadow or knows the degrees of latitude?"

### Now, the calculation for the Sine of Co-latitude and the Sine of Latitude is described:

**Sanskrit Commentary:** Here, the word <term>Gnomon</term><note>Sanskrit: Sanku; a vertical pillar used to cast a shadow for astronomical measurements.</note> refers to a gnomon of twelve digits, and the word <term>Shadow</term><note>Sanskrit: Chhaya</note> refers to the <term>Equinoctial Shadow</term><note>Sanskrit: Palabha; the shadow cast by a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox.</note>. When the squares of twelve and the equinoctial shadow are each multiplied by the square of the radius and divided by their sum (the sum of the squares of twelve and the equinoctial shadow), the square roots of these results are, respectively, the Sine of Co-latitude and the Sine of Latitude. The degrees of their arcs are the degrees of co-latitude and latitude. || 9 ||

12-digit Gnomon = Perpendicular, Equinoctial Shadow = Base, Equinoctial Hypotenuse = Hypotenuse. } The "Latitude-Triangle" formed by these perpendicular, base, and hypotenuse  
Sine of Co-latitude = Perpendicular, Sine of Latitude = Base, Radius = Hypotenuse. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;} are similar; therefore, we use a proportion.

$\frac{\text{12² × Radius²}}{\text{Equinoctial Hypotenuse²}}$ = Sine of Co-latitude², and $\frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow² × Radius²}}{\text{Equinoctial Hypotenuse²}}$ = Sine of Latitude². ### Chapter on the Three Problems

The two <term>sine</term> values (the Sine of Latitude and the Sine of Co-latitude) are produced thus: the <term>Radius</term> minus the <term>Versine</term> of the Co-latitude equals the Sine of Latitude; and the Radius minus the Versine of the Latitude equals the Sine of Co-latitude. || 10 ||

->The Proof Here<-

In the previous verse, I derived the Sine of Co-latitude and Sine of Latitude by taking the square root of the ratio of their squares. Here, their derivation is shown through a simple proportion: Radius — Versine of Co-latitude = Sine of Latitude; Radius — Versine of Latitude = Sine of Co-latitude. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, <note>A major 11th-century astronomical treatise</note> Sripati states: "The Versine of the degrees of Co-latitude and Latitude subtracted from the Radius results in the other." Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the famous 12th-century mathematician</note> also says the same thing in reverse: "The Sines of the two—the arc and its complement—subtracted from the Radius, or those themselves, are the Sines of the complement and the arc." || 10 ||

---

Now, the calculation of these two (the Sine of Co-latitude and Sine of Latitude) is explained by another method.

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiplying the Radius separately by twelve and by the <term>Equinoctial Shadow</term> <note>Palabha: the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note> and dividing by the <term>Equinoctial Hypothenuse</term> results in the Sine of Co-latitude and the Sine of Latitude. Alternatively, subtracting the Versine of the Co-latitude from the Radius gives the Sine of Latitude, and subtracting the Versine of the Latitude from the Radius leaves the Sine of Co-latitude. || 10 ||

->Proof<-

In the previous verse, the squares of the Sine of Co-latitude and Sine of Latitude were brought forth by the ratio of squares and then the square root was taken. Here, the calculation of both is by simple proportion: Radius — Versine(Co-lat) = Sine(Lat); Radius — Versine(Lat) = Sine(Co-lat). In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Sripati, with the words "The Versine of the degrees of Co-latitude and Latitude," etc., and Bhaskaracharya, through the inverse of "The Sines of the two—the arc and its complement," etc., say the same thing. || 10 ||

### Again, the Sine of Co-latitude and Sine of Latitude are stated by another method:

Subtracting the degrees of Co-latitude and Latitude from ninety and then calculating the Sine gives the other Sine. That is to say: the Sine of (90 minus Co-latitude) is the Sine of Latitude; the Sine of (90 minus Latitude) is the Sine of Co-latitude. Alternatively, the Sine of Latitude and Sine of Co-latitude multiplied by the gnomon and the shadow (twelve and the Equinoctial Shadow) and divided by the shadow and twelve (the Equinoctial Shadow and twelve) results in the other Sines. || 11 ||

->The Proof Here<-

Sine (90 — Latitude) = Sine of Co-latitude; Sine (90 — Co-latitude) = Sine of Latitude. Or:
(Sine of Latitude $\times$ 12 / Equinoctial Shadow) = Sine of Co-latitude; and (Equinoctial Shadow $\times$ Sine of Co-latitude / 12) = Sine of Latitude. Thus, what the Teacher has stated is proven. || 11 ||

->Now, the Sine of Co-latitude and the Sine of Latitude are explained by another method.<-

### Mathematical Proof

Sine (90° — Latitude) = Sine of Co-latitude, Sine (90° — Co-latitude) = Sine of Latitude, or:

(Sine of Latitude × 12) / Palabha = Sine of Co-latitude; (Palabha × Sine of Co-latitude) / 12 = Sine of Latitude. Thus, the teacher's statement is proven. ||11||

->Now, it is stated by another method:<-

Sanskrit Commentary—By subtracting the square of the Sine of Co-latitude or Sine of Latitude from the square of the <term>Trijya</term><note>The radius of the celestial sphere, often taken as 3438 minutes in Indian astronomy</note>, the square root of the remainder is the other (i.e., subtracting the square of the Sine of Co-latitude gives the Sine of Latitude, and subtracting the square of the Sine of Latitude gives the Sine of Co-latitude). In the same way, the calculation of the Sine of Altitude and Sine of Zenith Distance should always be done; specifically, the square root of the square of the Sine of Zenith Distance subtracted from the square of the Radius is the Sine of Altitude, and the square root of the square of the Sine of Altitude subtracted from the square of the Radius is the Sine of Zenith Distance. The arcs of these two values become the degrees of altitude and degrees of zenith distance respectively. ||12||

### Here is the Proof:

√Radius² — (Sine of Co-latitude)² = Sine of Latitude; √Radius² — (Sine of Latitude)² = Sine of Co-latitude; Sine of Zenith Distance = <term>Drigjya</term><note>The Sine of the zenith distance</note>;
Sine of Altitude = <term>Shanku</term><note>The Gnomon or the Sine of altitude</note>; √Radius² — (Shanku)² = Drigjya; √Radius² — (Drigjya)² = Shanku.
Thus ends the proof. ||12||

->Now, the Sine of Co-latitude and the Sine of Latitude are explained by another method.<-

Hindi Commentary—Alternatively, the square root of the remainder after subtracting the square of the Sine of Co-latitude from the square of the Radius is the Sine of Latitude. The square root of the remainder after subtracting the square of the Sine of Latitude from the square of the Radius is the Sine of Co-latitude. In the same manner, one should bring forth the Sine of Altitude and the Sine of Zenith Distance. That is, the square root of the remainder after subtracting the square of the Sine of Zenith Distance from the square of the Radius is the Sine of Altitude (Shanku), and the square root of the remainder after subtracting the square of the Sine of Altitude from the square of the Radius is the Sine of Zenith Distance (Drigjya). The arcs of these two are the degrees of altitude and degrees of zenith distance. This concludes verse 12.

# Chapter on the Three Problems: Page 239

### Mathematical Proof <note>Sanskrit: Upapatti</note>

$\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Sine of Latitude}^2} = \text{Sine of Co-latitude}$, and $\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Sine of Co-latitude}^2} = \text{Sine of Latitude}$.
$\text{Radius} - \text{Sine of Altitude} = \sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Gnomon}^2} = \text{Sine of Zenith Distance}$.
<note>The text uses "Drig-jya" for Sine of Zenith Distance and "Shanku" for the Gnomon/Sine of Altitude.</note>
$\text{Radius} - \text{Sine of Zenith Distance} = \sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Sine of Zenith Distance}^2} = \text{Gnomon}$.
Thus ends the derivation. || 12 ||

->Now, he explains the method for finding the local latitude when the zenith distance and declination at midday are known.<-

> **The sum or difference of the zenith distance and the declination at the desired midday [gives the latitude]. In the signs beginning with Libra, [take the sum]. In the signs beginning with Aries, the difference [gives] the latitude when the shadow is toward the south.** || 13 ||

**Vasanabhashya (Author's Commentary):**—The method for bringing forth the Sine of Latitude and Sine of Co-latitude by means of the midday shadow on the equinox was stated previously. Now, by this verse, he demonstrates the method for bringing them forth using the shadow of any desired day. Just as on the day of the equinox, the latitude is determined by the equinoctial shadow and the equinoctial hypotenuse, so too, the degrees of zenith distance <term>Natamsha: degrees of "bending" or distance from the zenith</term> are determined by the desired midday shadow and its hypotenuse. Those which are the degrees of co-latitude are called the degrees of altitude. Then, having calculated the Sine of Declination for that specific midday, those arc-parts are made into degrees of declination.

Then, if the Sun is in the six signs beginning with Aries <note>The Northern Hemisphere signs</note>, the sum of the zenith distance and the declination should be made; these become the latitude of one's own country. Or, if the Sun is in the Southern Hemisphere <note>The signs beginning with Libra</note>, the difference of these becomes the local latitude. This applies if the midday shadow is northern—meaning the shadow at midday faces north.

Regarding "the difference in the signs beginning with Aries": Now, if the midday shadow faces south, the difference between the zenith distance and the declination becomes the local latitude. This occurs when the Sun is in the signs beginning with Aries. This is possible in places where the latitude is less than 24 degrees <note>The maximum declination of the sun</note>; in the Southern Hemisphere, a southward shadow is never possible.

By subtracting the local latitude from 90 degrees, the remaining parts are the co-latitude, as explained before. The logic <note>Vasana</note> is as follows: The degrees between the Prime Vertical <term>Samamandala: the east-west circle passing through the zenith</term> and the Celestial Equator <term>Vishuvadmandala</term> along the meridian are the local latitude degrees. In the Northern Hemisphere, these are decreased daily by the degrees of declination because the Sun moves closer to the Prime Vertical. Therefore, the declination is added back to the zenith distance to recover the latitude. In the Southern Hemisphere, the latitude degrees are increased daily by the declination to become the zenith distance, as the Sun moves further from the Prime Vertical. Thus, the declination is subtracted from the zenith distance to leave the latitude. This is how it is proven.

Furthermore, where the Sun reaches midday to the north of the Prime Vertical—where the northern declination is greater than the latitude—the shadow at midday will face south. In that case, the latitude is found by subtracting the zenith distance from the declination. Therefore, it was said "the difference in the signs beginning with Aries." Thus, everything is proven. One should demonstrate this by sketching the local latitude and the celestial spheres.

Now, he speaks a verse in response to the question of one who understands the "ascensional differences" <term>Charakhandaka: tables used to calculate the variation in day length</term>.

<header>In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta</header>

**Sanskrit Commentary:** When the Sun is in the signs beginning with Aries or Libra <note>the vernal and autumnal equinoxes</note>, the latitude <term>Akshansha: the angular distance north or south of the earth's equator</term> is found by the sum or difference of the zenith distance <term>Natansha: the angular distance of a celestial body from the zenith</term> and the declination <term>Krantyansha: the angular distance of the sun north or south of the celestial equator</term> at midday of the desired day. When the Sun is in the signs beginning with Aries <note>the Northern Hemisphere</note> and the midday shadow is toward the south, the difference between the zenith distance and the declination is the latitude. ||13||

### Geometrical Proof

In the Northern Hemisphere at midday, when the Sun is situated on the meridian between the Zenith <note>Khasvastika: the point directly overhead</note> and the Celestial Equator <note>Niraksha-khasvastika: the zenith of a place on the equator</term>, the distance from the Sun to the Celestial Equator is the Sun's declination. The distance from the Sun to the Zenith is the Sun's zenith distance. By adding these two, the distance from the Zenith to the Celestial Equator—which is the latitude—is obtained. In the Southern Hemisphere, when the Sun is south of the Celestial Equator, the latitude is found by subtracting the declination from the zenith distance. In the Northern Hemisphere, if the Sun is north of the Zenith, the latitude is found by subtracting the zenith distance from the declination. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*:
> "The degrees of zenith distance combined with northern declination, or differentiated otherwise, become the degrees of latitude in one's own location."

By this, Shripati <note>an 11th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>, and also Bhaskaracharya <note>the famous 12th-century mathematician</note> in the following:
> "The difference between the degrees of zenith distance and declination when they are in the same direction, and their sum when they are in different directions, shall be the latitude,"

both affirm exactly what was stated by the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note>. ||13||

Now, the method for knowing the latitude from the knowledge of the zenith distance and declination at midday is explained.

**Hindi Explanation:** When the Sun is in Aries etc., or Libra etc.—that is, in the Northern or Southern Hemispheres—the sum or difference of the zenith distance and declination at midday of the desired day is the latitude. When the Sun is in Aries etc., and the midday shadow is southern, the difference between the zenith distance and declination is the latitude. ||13||

### Proof

In the Northern Hemisphere at midday, when the Sun is on the meridian between the Zenith and the Celestial Equator, the distance from the Sun to the Celestial Equator is the Sun's declination, and the distance from the Sun to the Zenith is the Sun's zenith distance. Adding these two results in the latitude (the distance from the Zenith to the Celestial Equator). In the Southern Hemisphere, when the Sun is south of the Celestial Equator, subtracting the declination from the zenith distance gives the latitude. In the Northern Hemisphere, if the Sun is north of the Zenith, subtracting the zenith distance from the declination gives the latitude. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*:
> "The degrees of zenith distance combined with northern declination, or differentiated otherwise, become the degrees of latitude in one's own location."

By this, Shripati, and in the *Siddhanta-shiromani*:
> "The difference between the degrees of zenith distance and declination when they are in the same direction, and their sum when they are in different directions, shall be the latitude,"

Bhaskaracharya also says exactly what the Teacher stated. ||13||

# Chapter on the Three Problems

The *charakhandas* <note>portions of ascensional difference</note> are determined according to the verse beginning with "The sines of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini..." from the *Siddhanta Shekhara* <note>An 11th-century astronomical treatise by Sripati</note>. I shall state them here exactly as prescribed by the ancient teachers. ||54||

### Now, the method for calculating the rising times at the equator (Lankodaya) is described:

> The half-day radius of Gemini, multiplied by the sines of the respective signs and divided by the half-day radius of Aries and the others; the arcs of the results are the rising times at the equator in *pranas* <note>respirations, a unit of time where 1 respiration = 4 seconds</note>. ||55||

**Commentary:** The half-day radius of Gemini is multiplied by the sines of Taurus and Gemini. This is then divided by the half-day radius of Aries and the others. By taking the arcs of the resulting values and subtracting the preceding ones from the succeeding ones, the rising times at the equator (*Lankodaya-pranas*) are obtained. For Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, these are calculated in direct order; for Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, they are the same but in reverse order; for Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius, they follow the direct order again; and for Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces, they are in reverse order.

The **rationale** <term>Vasana: the underlying geometric or logical explanation</term> should be demonstrated on the armillary sphere at a point below the north and south celestial poles. Specifically: one should fix three diurnal circles at the ends of the declinations of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini to the north of the equator on the globe. These same circles serve for Cancer, Leo, and Virgo in reverse order. Similarly, one should fix three diurnal circles for the three signs starting with Libra to the south of the equator. These will serve for Capricorn and the others in reverse order.

Then, one should fix a circle passing through the north and south poles with a radius equal to the sine of Aries in the center of the celestial sphere. Its center lies on the east-west line emerging from the Earth. Similarly, another should be fixed with the sine of Taurus as the radius, and another with the sine of Gemini (which is equal to the total radius/trizyā) at the ends of the meridian circle.

In all three circles, because of the calculation of their own sines, the declination sine is the vertical side (sine) and the horizontal side (cosine) is to be determined. For Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, the half-day radii are the cosines of the diurnal circles. Once these circles of varying radii are known, this operation involves two sets of proportions <term>Trairashika: the Rule of Three</term> to bring them to the scale of the standard radius.

For example: If for the hypotenuse of the Gemini circle (the standard radius), the cosine is the half-day radius of Gemini, then what is the cosine for the hypotenuse of the Aries sine? In the first proportion, the result is the divisor in the diurnal circle. Because they are equal, the multiplication of the half-day radius of Gemini by the sine of Aries is divided by its own day-radius. The result is the radius... <note>The text here describes the geometric projection of the celestial equator onto the diurnal circles to find the time it takes for each sign to rise</note>. This is demonstrated here like a geometric figure. Specifically: on the ecliptic, one end of a string is tied at the end of Aries and the other at the beginning of Pisces to the south of the equator.

Similarly, from the end of Aries, Aquarius and others are to be joined. Likewise for the end of Gemini and Capricorn. These strings represent the diameters of the previously described circles. Those which are vertical and intersected by the east-west strings are the hypotenuses. Then, having tied three strings at the ends of the declinations on the eastern horizon of the equator, and standing on the western side, one should tie others on the horizon at the ends of the declinations. There, those are the rising-setting strings. Because the horizon and the prime vertical are the same at the equator, the distance between those two strings on the east-west line...

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
## Page 284

From the center of the circle, one should fasten two strings of the same measure, extending from south to north. The <term>sine of declination</term> <note>Kranti-jya: the distance of a point on the ecliptic from the celestial equator</note> and the <term>sine of the longitude</term> <note>Bhuja-jya</note> are calculated separately. Then, having tied a string at the end of Aries, one should bring it upward and fasten it at the tip of its own declination. In this same way, for Taurus and Gemini, those separate "upright" sides <note>Kotis: the vertical sides of the right-angled triangles formed in the celestial sphere</note> were previously shown. By the rising of their respective upright sides, the rising of Aries and the others occurs. Because the entire cage of stars <note>Bhapunjara: the celestial sphere or stellar firmament</note> rotates according to the celestial equator, the arcs of those upright sides are calculated. Since the cage of stars rises in a circular motion, the resulting arcs are determined. 

Because all three signs up to Gemini rise through the upright side of Gemini, and two signs rise through the upright side of Taurus, one desires to know the individual rising measures. Therefore, the differences between the arcs are applied. The minutes of the arc become the <term>respirations</term> <note>Pranas: a unit of time equivalent to 4 seconds, based on the duration of a single breath</note>, because it was previously established that the celestial sphere rotates by one respiration. For Cancer and the following signs, the explanation <note>Vasana: the underlying logic or demonstration</note> should be applied in order; for Libra and the following signs in the south, and for Capricorn and the following, it should be applied in reverse order.

Specifically, the respirations for Aries are 1670 <note>original: "kha-muni-rasa-indavah" (0-7-6-1 in reverse notation)</note>. The respirations for the rising of Taurus are 1795 <note>original: "shara-nava-aga-chandrah" (5-9-7-1)</note>. The respirations for the rising of Gemini are 1935 <note>original: "panca-agni-nava-shashinah" (5-3-9-1)</note>. For Aries: 1670; for Taurus: 1795; and for Gemini: 1935. Now, showing the rising times at the equator <note>Niraksha-udaya</note> by another method, the author speaks a verse:

**V. Ma.** — The half-day radius of Gemini <note>the maximum day-radius</note> multiplied by those sines <note>the sines of the longitude of the three signs starting with Aries</note> and divided by the half-day radius of the beginning of the sign <note>the day-radius of Aries etc.</note> gives results whose arc-differences are the rising times at the equator <note>Lankodaya-pranas</note>. ||15||

->**Here is the Proof:**<-

When the starting point of a zodiac sign arrives at the equatorial horizon, the time interval until the end point of that sign arrives at that same horizon is the measure of the "rising at Lanka" <note>Lankodaya: the rising time of a sign at the Earth's equator</note> for that sign. In other words, a <term>declination circle</term> <note>Dhruvaprota-vritta: a great circle passing through the celestial poles</note> should be drawn over the start of the sign and another over the end of the sign. The arc on the equatorial circle <note>Nadivritta</note> between these two is the rising measure of that sign. This becomes clear from the following diagram:
