# Chapter on Problems of Time and Direction

The term *dyuca* refers to the arc of the minimum diurnal sine <note>original: "परमाल्प द्युज्याचापम्"; this refers to the sine of the declination at the solstices</note>. In the spherical triangle *Dhru-Go-Me* <note>Pole-Equinox-Aries</note>, by proportion, the sine of the rising time of Aries is equal to: (Minimum Diurnal Sine × Sine of Aries) / Diurnal Sine at the end of Aries. Similarly, in the spherical triangle *Dhru-Go-Vri*, the proportion is: (Minimum Diurnal Sine × Sine of Taurus) / Diurnal Sine at the end of Taurus = Sine of (Rising of Aries + Rising of Taurus). In the spherical triangle *Dhru-Go-Mi*, the proportion is: (Minimum Diurnal Sine × Sine of Gemini) / Diurnal Sine at the end of Gemini. Since the Diurnal Sine at the end of Gemini is equal to the Minimum Diurnal Sine, this equals the Sine of Gemini, which is the Radius <note>original: "त्रि" or "Trijya"</note>. Here, the Sines of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini are the sines of the signs starting from Aries. When the arcs of these results are subtracted successively, they become the rising times at the equator <term>Lankodaya</term> <note>The time it takes for a zodiac sign to rise above the horizon at the Earth's equator</note> for Aries and the following signs. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, it is stated: "The sines of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, multiplied by the final diurnal sine and divided by their respective diurnal sines, give the arcs in breaths <term>Prana</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 4 seconds</note>; these, when subtracted from one another, are the equatorial risings." Similarly, in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*: "The sines of Aries and the rest, multiplied by the radius and divided by their respective diurnal sines, or converted to arcs and subtracted as before, give the rising breaths of Aries and the rest." Bhaskaracharya also follows the same sequence as taught by the previous teachers. || 15 ||

### Now the method for calculating the Equatorial Risings (Lankodaya) is explained.

**Hindi Commentary** — Multiply the sines of the signs starting from Aries by the diurnal sine of the end of Gemini (the minimum diurnal sine), and divide by their respective diurnal sines. The arcs of the resulting values, when subtracted successively, provide the equatorial rising times for Aries and the subsequent signs. || 15 ||

### Mathematical Proof (Upapatti)

When the starting point of a zodiac sign reaches the horizon of Lanka (the equator), the time that elapses until the end point of that sign reaches the same horizon is called the equatorial rising time <term>Lankodaya-mana</term> of that sign. In other words, if we draw hour circles <note>original: "ध्रुव प्रोतवृत्त"</note> through the beginning and end of a sign, the arc of the celestial equator <note>original: "नाड़ी वृत्त"</note> contained between these two hour circles is the rising time. This is clear from diagram (A) described in the Sanskrit proof. For example: *Go* = Equinoctial point (beginning of Aries); *Me* = End of Aries (beginning of Taurus); *Vri* = End of Taurus (beginning of Gemini); *Mi* = End of Gemini. *Dhru* = Celestial Pole. *Go-Me* = Longitude of Aries; *Go-Vri* = Longitude of Taurus; *Go-Mi* = Longitude of Gemini. *Go-Ma* = Rising time of Aries; *Na-Ma* = Rising time of Taurus; *Ma-Ca* = Rising time of Gemini. *Dhru-Me* = Arc of the diurnal sine at the end of Aries; *Dhru-Vri* = Arc of the diurnal sine at the end of Taurus; *Dhru-Mi* = Arc of the diurnal sine at the end of Gemini (minimum diurnal sine). In the spherical triangle *Dhru-Go-Me*, by proportion: (Minimum Diurnal Sine × Sine of Aries) / Diurnal Sine at the end of Aries = Sine of the rising of Aries. Similarly, in the spherical triangle *Dhru-Go-Vri*, by proportion: (Minimum Diurnal Sine × Sine of Taurus) / Diurnal Sine at the end of Taurus = Sine of (Rising of Aries + Rising of Taurus). In the spherical triangle *Dhru-Go-Mi*, by proportion:

->Now he describes another method for calculating the rising times at the equator.<-

### From the square of the Sine, subtract the square of the Declination-Sine; the square root of that, multiplied by the Radius
### and divided by the radius of the diurnal circle, gives the arcs; their differences are the rising times. || 16 ||

**Vasanabhashya (Author's Commentary):** — One should take the square root after subtracting the square of the <term>Kranti-jya</term><note>Sine of declination.</note> from the square of the Sine of Aries. Multiply that by the Radius and divide by the <term>Svahoratrardha</term><note>The radius of the diurnal circle (day-radius) for that specific point.</note>. The result is the produced <term>Koti</term><note>The horizontal component or cosine-like value in this spherical geometry.</note> radius of the rising of Aries. Similarly, using their respective Sines and Declination-Sines, the rising-cosines for Taurus and Gemini are found. Then, having converted those into arcs and subtracting them from one another as before, they become the <term>Pranas</term><note>Units of time; one respiration or 4 seconds.</note> of the rising at the equator. Alternatively, the <term>Vasana</term><note>Geometrical explanation or "realization" of the proof.</note> produced by this method is: in the previously shown circles, the Sine of the sign is the hypotenuse and the Declination-Sine is the upright side (<term>Bhuja</term>). Then, by subtracting the squares of the upright sides from the squares of the hypotenuses, the squares of the horizontal sides (<term>Koti</term>) remain. Their square roots are the horizontal sides, which are produced as the diurnal radii. Then a proportion is applied: if in the diurnal circles there are these many horizontal sides, then how many would there be in the Radius-circle? These individual results are the horizontal sides in the Radius-circle for the risings of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, which are situated north of the transverse celestial equator. Therefore, the Sines of the signs themselves are not their rising times in <term>Pranas</term>. Otherwise, at the equator, the rising of a sign would always be five <term>Ghatikas</term><note>A sign (30 degrees) would rise in exactly 2 hours if the ecliptic weren't tilted.</note>. The remaining explanation is provided in the previous verse. Intending to address the question of how the <term>Lagna</term><note>The ascendant or rising point.</note> is calculated, he provides the verse for calculating local rising times using the equatorial risings and the local <term>Chara-khandas</term><note>Ascensional differences.</note>.

**Vijnanabhashya (Scientific Commentary):** — From the square of the Sine (the Sine of the signs Aries, etc.) minus the square of the Declination-Sine, the square root is taken. That, multiplied by the Radius and divided by the radius of the diurnal circle, gives the arcs. By successively subtracting those arcs, the values for the <term>Lankodaya</term> (equatorial risings) are obtained. || 16 ||

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>The "Three Problems" refer to the fundamental astronomical determinations of time, place, and direction.</note>

Two triangles are formed by the sines of the declination degrees. The sine of the longitude at the end of Aries is the hypotenuse. The sine of the declination is the base, and the line at its root—which Kamalākara calls the sine of the equatorial rising degrees—is the perpendicular.
$\sqrt{\text{Sine of Aries End}^2 - \text{Declination}^2} = \text{Sine of Equatorial Rising Degrees}$.
Similarly, from the pole to the celestial intersection <note>the equinox</note>, there are ninety degrees on the polar circle passing through the intersection. On the polar circle above the end of Aries, from the tip of the pole to the intersection of the two polar circles, there are ninety degrees. At the end of Aries, in the two triangles called the "Equinoctial Parts," there is a similarity of sine-areas elsewhere (where the radius is the hypotenuse, the sine of the right ascension is the base, and its cosine is the perpendicular; this circle of three sides). From the center of the sphere to the root of the sine of declination is the hypotenuse of the diurnal circle, and the sine of the equatorial rising degrees is the base. From the center of the sphere to the root of the sine of the longitude is the perpendicular; this triangle of three sides is similar to the previous one. Therefore, by proportion: if the sine of the equatorial rising degrees is obtained by the radius of the diurnal circle, then what is obtained by the total radius? This gives me the sine of the right ascension of the end of Aries, or the sine of the rising at Lanka <note>Lanka represents the terrestrial equator in Indian astronomy</note> = $\frac{\text{Sine of Equatorial Rising Degrees} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Diurnal Radius of Aries}} = \frac{\sqrt{\text{Sine of Aries End}^2 - \text{Declination}^2} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Diurnal Radius of Aries}}$ = Sine of the rising of Aries.

In the same way, $\frac{\sqrt{\text{Sine of Taurus End}^2 - \text{Declination of Taurus End}^2} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Diurnal Radius of Taurus}}$ = Sine (Rising of Aries + Rising of Taurus).
The same applies at the end of Gemini. When these arcs are subtracted from one another in succession, they become the measures of the rising times at Lanka for Aries and the following signs. In the *Siddhānta Śekhara*, Śrīpati says: "From the square of the sine <note>original: *shinjini*</note> diminished by the square of its declination, take the square root; multiply that by the radius and divide by the respective diurnal sines. The arcs of those results, when subtracted from one another in order, are the measures of the risings at the equator." By this, and by the teacher Bhāskara <note>Bhāskara II</note> who said: "The sine of the longitude of one sign, or of two, or of three, squared and diminished by the square of their respective declinations, etc.," the same method taught by the ancient masters is being described. || 16 ||

And the ninety degrees up to the intersection of the celestial equator, the triangle formed by these <term>equinoctial parts</term><note>The degrees of right ascension at the end of Aries</note>—specifically the <term>sine-area</term><note>A geometric representation of sines where the radius is the hypotenuse, the sine of the equinoctial parts is the base, and its cosine is the upright</note>—is similar to the triangle formed from the center of the sphere to the base of the <term>declination-sine</term><note>krāntijyā</note>, where the <term>day-radius</term><note>dyujyā</note> is the hypotenuse, the <term>sine of the rising degrees at the equator</term> is the base, and the distance from the center of the sphere to the base of the <term>sine of the longitude</term> is the upright. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati says, "From that which is deprived of the square of the declination-sine," etc. In his Sanskrit commentary, Bhaskaracharya also says, "That which is the third of a sign," etc., agreeing with the teachings of the ancient Teachers. || 16 ||

### Now he describes the method for finding the rising times at one's local latitude:

> The rising times at the equator, decreased or increased by the <term>ascensional difference</term><note>carāsu: the difference in time between the rising of a star at the equator and at a specific latitude</note> in direct and inverse order, become the rising times at the local latitude. These should be calculated after determining the sun's true position for that time. || 17 ||

**Vāsanā-bhāṣya (Commentary):** "Decreased or increased by the segments of the ascensional difference"—in what way? In direct and inverse order. The previously mentioned equatorial rising times are modified by the <term>breath-units</term><note>asu: a unit of time equal to 4 seconds</note> of the ascensional difference. What happens when this is done? They become the "rising breaths." This means the rising times of the zodiac signs at one's local latitude. There are twelve of these. This is what is meant: having placed the equatorial rising times of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini in order, and then in inverse order, the segments of the ascensional difference are placed beside them. Then, the three segments of the ascensional difference are subtracted from them respectively. Then, for the signs starting with Aries in inverse order, the segments of the ascensional difference are added in inverse order. In this way, the values for Aries and the other signs become the rising times at the local latitude. For the signs starting with Libra, the process is reversed. Thus it results that the rising time of Aries is equal to that of Pisces; similarly Taurus equals Aquarius, Gemini equals Capricorn, Cancer equals Sagittarius, Leo equals Scorpio, and Virgo equals Libra. "Having made the sun's position for that time"—this refers to a calculation that will be connected to the following section. The underlying logic (<term>vāsanā</term>) is this: the uprights of Aries etc., which reach the <term>unmaṇḍala</term><note>the six-o'clock circle or equatorial horizon</note>, were shown previously. The breaths of those arcs situated on their respective diurnal circles are the rising times described for Aries etc. Furthermore, at the local latitude, due to the oblique latitude and the celestial equator, the rising uprights of the first three signs (Aries etc.) on their diurnal circles are diminished. Because of that diminution, the arcs are also diminished. This diminution in one's own diurnal circle is equal to the segment of the ascensional difference. Therefore, those segments of ascensional difference are subtracted from the equatorial rising times of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini. As far as the celestial equator—

The segment equal to the rising interval of a quadrant does not remain constant. It is not necessary that the quadrant of the circle always rises exactly in Capricorn. The time taken for the rising of the remainder of the first quadrant of the equatorial circle, combined with the second quadrant, is the same as the third and fourth quadrants of the ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: the sun's apparent path</term> starting from Cancer; these should be applied inversely like the first quadrant. One should demonstrate this on the globe as well. The collection of these points is included here to facilitate the understanding of the rising times of the signs.

**Scientific Commentary**—Those rising times at the equator <note>original: "nirakṣodayāḥ"</note> for the three groups starting with Aries, calculated previously, should be placed in direct and reverse order. By subtracting or adding the ascensional differences <term>Ascensional Difference: the difference between the rising time of a star at the equator and at a specific latitude</term> in direct and reverse order respectively, the rising breaths <note>original: "udayaprāṇāḥ" - a unit of time where 1 breath equals 4 seconds</note> of the first six signs starting from Aries are obtained for one's local latitude. Consequently, these same values in reverse order become the rising breaths for the six signs starting from Libra. The phrase "having calculated the true position of the sun" connects to the subsequent text.

## The Mathematical Rationale

The difference between the rising of the sun at the equator and at one's local latitude is the ascensional difference <note>original: "cara"</note>. The starting point of Aries rises simultaneously at the local horizon and the equatorial horizon. However, the end point of Aries first touches the local horizon and later reaches the equatorial horizon; therefore, the local rising time of Aries is the equatorial rising time minus the segment of the ascensional difference. The same applies to Taurus and Gemini. From Cancer onwards, because the segments of the ascensional difference are decreasing, they result in an addition. From Libra onwards, because the equatorial horizon <note>original: "unmaṇḍala"</note> lies below the local horizon, the segments of the ascensional difference are added. From Capricorn onwards, as the segments are decreasing, they are subtracted.

In the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A major 12th-century astronomical treatise</note>, the teacher Bhaskaracharya says: "By subtracting or adding their own segments of ascensional difference in direct and reverse order from the equatorial rising times in direct and reverse order, the rising times for the six signs starting with Aries at one's local latitude are found; for the signs starting with Libra, these same values are applied in reverse." This confirms exactly what the author has stated. // 17 //

->Now the method for calculating local rising times is explained.<-

## Rationale

The difference between the sun's rising at the equator and its rising at the local latitude is the "Chara" (ascensional difference). In one's own country and at the equator, the initial point of Aries rises at the same time. The end point of Aries reaches the local horizon first, and after the interval of the ascensional difference, it reaches the equatorial horizon. Therefore, subtracting the ascensional difference from the equatorial rising value of Aries gives the local rising value of Aries. The same applies to Taurus and Gemini. In the signs starting with Cancer, they are added due to the decreasing nature of the ascensional difference segments.

### Now he describes the calculation of the Ascendant at one's own location:

->**The minutes of the portion of the sign already traversed by the Sun, multiplied by the rising time of that sign at that location,**<-
->**And divided by the total minutes in a sign (1800), should be subtracted from the respiration-units (pranas) of the given time.**<-
->**Having added the remaining portion of the sign, from the remaining respiration-units, as many**<-
->**Rising times as can be subtracted in order from the Sun's position, that many signs should be added to the Sun.**<-
->**The remainder, multiplied by thirty and divided by the rising time of the next sign which was not subtracted,**<-

**Vasanabhashya (Commentary):** At whatever desired time during the day one wishes to calculate the Ascendant, one should first determine the instantaneous position of the Sun for that time. Take the minutes (*kala*) of the sign already traversed by the Sun and multiply them by the rising times (*udayasus*) of that specific location—meaning the rising time of the sign occupied by the Sun. Divide this by the minutes in a sign, which is 1800. The result is in respiration-units (*asus*). These obtained units should be subtracted from the units of the time elapsed since sunrise (the "question time"). In the Sun's position, the portion of the sign not yet traversed should also be added in degrees, or it becomes devoid of degrees. Then, from the remaining units of the question time, subtract in order the rising times of the signs following the one occupied by the Sun, as many as can be subtracted. Add that same number of signs to the Sun's position. For the remaining units from which a full sign's rising time cannot be subtracted, multiply those units by thirty and divide by that unsubtracted rising time. The result is in degrees and minutes. By adding this to the Sun—either to the portion already traversed or to the signs already cleared—the Ascendant (*Lagna*) for that moment in the heavens is found.

Now, if one calculates the Ascendant for a time during the night, one should add six signs to the instantaneous Sun and perform the calculation using the portion traversed and the rising times of the subsequent signs, just as was done for the daytime. Because this method is not widely known, I have explained this meaning in detail.

The underlying logic (*vasana*) is as follows: wherever the intersection of the ecliptic <note>Sanskrit: *apamandala*; the sun's path</note> and the horizon circle occurs, at that point on the ecliptic, the Ascendant is formed; therefore, it is called the *Lagna* <note>literally "the point of contact"</note>. The teacher has stated in the *Goladhyaya* (Chapter on the Sphere) that the intersection of the horizon and the ecliptic is the Ascendant, and I have explained it there as well. At the time of sunrise, the Sun is at the point of the ecliptic that is the Ascendant, because at that time that portion of the sign is attached to the horizon. As the Sun moves further away from that time of sunrise, the Sun, increased by the portion of the ecliptic situated between the horizon and the Sun's position, becomes the Ascendant with its degrees. Thus it increases. How is this known? By the statement "the minutes of the traversed sign," etc. That is to say, the degrees etc. situated ahead of the Sun in the sign it occupies are traversed by time as they rise; therefore, the minutes of the sign etc. from the rising of the Sun's position, by their own rising time, become the respiration-units of the Ascendant's portion. # Chapter on the Three Problems

The resulting breaths <note>Prana: a unit of time equal to 4 seconds</note> are calculated from the minutes of the arc already traversed; these are suitable for the new calculation. When the Sun has risen above the horizon, the portion of the sign already traversed is given.

By this, the portion of the Ascendant at that specific time is grasped. Now, from the breaths of the given time <note>the time elapsed since sunrise</note>, as many intervening rising periods <note>Udayas: the time it takes for a zodiac sign to rise</note> as can be subtracted are considered to have risen in the calculation circle; these are then added to the Sun's position. Thus, the portion of the Ascendant is grasped. The sign whose rising breaths cannot be fully subtracted is the one currently situated at the rising point <note>the horizon</note>. To find its specific degrees, a rule of three is applied: if thirty degrees correspond to the total rising breaths of that sign, how many degrees correspond to the remaining breaths? The resulting degrees, minutes, etc., are also added to the Sun. By this process, the segment of the ecliptic between the horizon and the Sun's position is captured. This calculation is done using the Sun's position at that specific moment, because the hours of a solar day are determined by considering the motion of the Sun relative to the stars; otherwise, if one only used the daily motion, the sixty hours would be purely sidereal. This is not the case, as in calculations involving motion, the Ascendant, and shadows, we use civil <note>Savana</note> hours. Therefore, the Sun's position must be calculated for that specific moment, because in one solar day, the difference between the Sun's civil day and the sidereal day is exactly one day. Even if the time is after sunset—the Sun's position at sunset should be used. This is the direct method for calculating the rising of the segments of the celestial circle. All of this should be demonstrated on a globe, whether for a location on the equator or to the north or south. The answer to the question "How does one know the hours from the Ascendant?" is given in three verses:

**Explanatory Commentary:** Having calculated the Sun <gloss>the Sun's position</gloss> for the specific time, the time for the remaining portion of the sign <gloss>the portion yet to be traversed</gloss> is found by subtracting the minutes already traversed. These are multiplied by the rising breaths of that sign <gloss>the rising time of the sign the Sun is currently in for that specific latitude</gloss> and divided by the total minutes in a sign <note>1800 minutes</note>. The resulting breaths are subtracted from the desired time breaths <gloss>the time elapsed since sunrise</gloss>. After adding the remaining portion of the sign <gloss>the degrees to be traversed</gloss> to the Sun, one should subtract the rising periods of the subsequent signs one by one from the remaining breaths as long as possible, and add those signs to the Sun <gloss>join them</gloss>. From the remaining breaths, multiply by thirty and divide by the rising breaths of the next (unsubtracted) sign <gloss>the rising breaths of the sign that was too large to subtract</gloss>. The resulting degrees and minutes should be added to the Sun <gloss>joined</gloss>. When this is done, the result is the Ascendant (Lagna). ||18-20||

### Mathematical Proof:

The Ascendant is the intersection of the rising horizon and the ecliptic. A proportion is made using the remaining minutes of the sign in which the Sun is located: if the total minutes of a sign correspond to the rising breaths of that sign, then how many breaths correspond to the Sun's remaining minutes? These are the "Sun's remaining breaths." These breaths are subtracted from the desired time <gloss>which consists of the Sun's remaining breaths, the Ascendant's elapsed breaths, and the sum of the rising breaths of the signs in between</gloss>. Then, the sum of the rising breaths of the signs between the Sun and the Ascendant remains. Here, as many full rising signs as possible are subtracted. From the remainder, a proportion is used: if the rising breaths of the unsubtracted sign <gloss>the sign whose rising value was not fully subtracted</gloss> correspond to thirty degrees, then what do the remaining breaths correspond to? # In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

...the Ascendant is formed by adding the signs starting from Aries. However, due to the <term>grossness</term><note>original: "sthulatva" - referring to mathematical imprecision or lack of infinitesimal refinement</note> of the signs, their rising times (<term>udayasavas</term>) are also imprecise. All ancient scholars calculated the Ascendant based on the rising times of their local latitudes, which is why those calculations are not entirely accurate. For this reason, Bapudeva Sastri provided a corrected method for calculating the Ascendant in his commentary on the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, but even that is not perfectly accurate. Mahamahopadhyaya Pandit Sudhakar Dwivedi has refuted that method. 

He established a pure method for calculating the Ascendant with the following verse: 
"One should determine the desired position of the Sun and the degrees of the complement of declination through the right ascension of the mid-heaven. Using the <term>Yasti</term><note>a mathematical sine-related variable</note> multiplied by the sine of twenty-four degrees, and the right ascension... adjusted by one's own latitude... for the northern and southern celestial hemispheres, the arc should be calculated. The sum of these two arcs results in the <term>Sayana Lagna</term><note>the tropical Ascendant</note>; this is the clear calculation for wise astronomers." 

The ancient authors of the *Surya Siddhanta* and others calculated the Ascendant only from the <term>Nirayana</term><note>sidereal</note> Sun, which is also a flaw in their work. I have developed six new methods for calculating the Ascendant; to understand them, one should consult my book titled *Lagnanayana* (Calculation of the Ascendant). || 18-19-20 ||

---

-> **Now, the method for calculating the Ascendant at one's local latitude is described.** <-

**Hindi Commentary:** Having determined the instantaneous position of the Sun (<term>Ravi</term>), multiply its remaining minutes of the sign (<term>bhogyakala</term>) by the local rising time of that sign and divide by the total minutes of a sign (1800). Subtract the resulting time units (<term>asu</term>) from the desired elapsed time (<term>ishtakala</term>). Add the remaining signs to the Sun. From the remaining time units, subtract the rising times of subsequent signs in order. Multiply the remainder by thirty and divide by the rising time of the next (un-subtracted) sign. Add the resulting degrees and minutes to the Sun; this process yields the Ascendant. || 18-19-20 ||

### Mathematical Proof (Upapatti)

The point where the ecliptic meets the eastern horizon—that is, the intersection point of the horizon and the ecliptic—is the Ascendant (<term>Lagna</term>). We calculate the ratio based on the remaining minutes of the sign in which the instantaneous Sun is located. If the total minutes of a sign correspond to the local rising time of that sign, then what will the remaining minutes of the Sun correspond to? This gives the Sun's remaining rising time. Subtract this from the desired elapsed time (which is the sum of the Sun's remaining rising time, the Ascendant's elapsed rising time, and the rising times of the signs between the Sun and the Ascendant). From the remainder, subtract as many full rising times of signs as possible. From the final remainder, use the ratio: "If thirty degrees are obtained in the rising time of the next sign, then what is obtained in the remaining time units?" Add the resulting degrees to the sum of the preceding signs starting from Aries to find the Ascendant. 

However, because the signs are treated as large units, their rising times are imprecise. All ancient teachers calculated the Ascendant based on these imprecise rising times, which is why it is not correct. Therefore, the reviser Bapudeva Sastri provided a "pure" calculation in his notes on the *Siddhanta Shiromani*. But that too is not quite right; Mahamahopadhyaya Pandit Sudhakar Dwivedi refuted it. He established his own pure method for calculating the Ascendant through the Sanskrit verses starting with "One should determine through the right ascension of the mid-heaven..." as written in the proof. The *Surya*...

# Chapter on the Three Problems (Direction, Place, and Time)

Ancient teachers such as Brahmagupta and others calculated the Ascendant <note>Lagna: the point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon</note> using the sidereal zodiac <note>Nirayana: the fixed zodiac</note>, which is not appropriate. It is proper to calculate the Ascendant using the tropical zodiac <note>Sayana: the zodiac that accounts for the precession of the equinoxes</note>, as many other teachers have done. I have formulated six original methods for calculating the Ascendant; for those, please refer to my book *Lagnanayanum*. Thus ends the commentary on verses 18-20.

->Now, he describes the calculation of time from the Ascendant:<-

> Multiply the minutes of the sign already traversed by the Sun by its respective rising time <note>Udaya: the time it takes for a zodiac sign to rise at a specific latitude</note> and divide by the total minutes in a sign (1800).
> The resulting breaths <note>Prana: a unit of time equal to 4 seconds</note> should be set aside. Then, add the remaining portion of the sign to the Sun's position. ||21||
>
> One should continue adding whole signs to the Sun until it equals the number of signs in the Ascendant.
> Sum the rising times (in breaths) of these added signs and add them to the breaths previously set aside. ||22||
>
> Multiply the remaining minutes of the Ascendant sign by its rising time and divide by the total minutes in a sign.
> Add these resulting breaths to the total. These breaths represent the time elapsed since sunrise. This process should be repeated for accuracy. ||23||

**Sudhakara's Commentary:** Just as the Ascendant is calculated from time, the calculation of time from the Ascendant is established here in reverse through these three verses. When someone asks for the time based on a specific desired Ascendant, one must take the minutes of the sign already traversed by the Sun at sunrise. Multiply those by the rising time of that specific sign and divide by the "house minutes," meaning 1800. The resulting breaths are placed to one side. Then, add the remaining portion of that sign to the Sun and continue adding subsequent whole signs until reaching the sign of the Ascendant. Sum the rising breaths of those intervening signs and add them to the previously stored breaths. Then, take the degrees and minutes by which the Ascendant exceeds the start of its sign; multiply those minutes by the rising time of that sign and divide by 1800. Add these breaths to the previous sum to find the time elapsed in the day. Because the Sun's position changes, these breaths are initially "gross" <note>Sthula: approximate</note>; therefore, the text says "repeatedly" <note>Asakrit</note>. One must recalculate the Sun's true position for that elapsed time and repeat the process until the time stabilizes. If the time is after sunset, one should use the Sun increased by six signs <note>180 degrees</note> and proceed as before. The logic <note>Vasana</note> is the same: the time is the portion of the equator that rises between the Sun's position on the horizon and the Ascendant's position.

**Vijnanamaya Commentary:** Regarding the minutes traversed by the Sun: take the minutes remaining to be traversed in the Sun's current sign. Multiply by the rising time of that sign and divide by the 1800 minutes of a sign. The resulting breaths are the "breaths to be traversed"; set them aside. Then, for all the signs occurring before the Ascendant sign, add those signs to the Sun...

One should add and combine the previously calculated "remaining portions" <note>original: bhogyāsu; the time remaining for a zodiac sign to rise</note> into the time-measures (Asus) <note>term: Asu; a unit of time equal to four seconds, or the time taken for one breath</note> and establish them. The product of the remaining minutes of the arc and the rising time: the minutes already passed by the Lagna <note>term: Lagna; the rising point of the ecliptic on the eastern horizon, or the Ascendant</note> and the rising time-measures of that sign—the product of these two, divided by 1800 minutes <note>the total minutes in one zodiac sign (30 degrees)</note>, gives the time-measures passed by the Lagna. These should be added to the previously calculated time-measures; then the desired "Ghatika-measures" <note>term: Ghatika; a unit of 24 minutes</note> are obtained. Because these Ghatikas are based on the civil solar day <note>original: sāvanārka</note> starting from sunrise, this calculation must be performed repeatedly (iteratively) to reach precision, or by using the desired civil time.

---

### Here is the Proof:

> "Here," the time elapsed from the Lagna is the sum of the Sun's remaining portion, the portion already passed by the rising sign, and the rising times of the intermediate signs. According to Bhaskara's method for calculating time from the Lagna <note>referring to the 12th-century mathematician Bhaskaracharya</note>, the civil time-measure is the sum of the time-measures of the Sun's remaining portion, the Lagna's passed portion, and the rising times of the signs between them. This represents the interval on the diurnal circle between the horizon and the position of the Sun at that moment, which is clearly visible on the celestial sphere.

<margin>
L = Lagna (Ascendant)
R = Sun at that moment
K = End of the Sun's sign
C = Beginning of the Lagna's sign
KC = Intermediate signs
RS = Desired civil time (Ghatikas)
S = Intersection of the diurnal circle passing through the Sun and the horizon.
</margin>

In this context, within the arc RS (measured in breaths/Asus), there exist the arcs RK, KC, and CL. For this reason, the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> stated:
Arc RK = $\frac{\text{Unpassed minutes of Sun's sign} \times \text{Rising time of sign}}{\text{1800}}$ = Remaining portion (Bhogyāsu).
Similarly, the time passed by the Lagna (Arc CL) = $\frac{\text{Rising time of sign} \times \text{Minutes passed by Lagna}}{\text{1800}}$.
By adding these to the rising times of the full intermediate signs (KC), the total measure of the Sun's civil time is found. Because these time-measures are variable, the exact civil time is found through iterative calculation <note>original: asakṛt-karma; a method of successive approximations</note>. Therefore, Bhaskaracharya stated in the section on the Celestial Sphere: "If the desired time-measures for the Lagna are civil (Savana), they must be determined by the position of the Sun at that specific moment." || 21-22-23 ||

# Chapter on the Three Problems

Now, from this text, we determine the desired time by first finding the instantaneous position of the Sun and the Ascendant.

According to the logic of the celestial sphere, the "desired time" is defined as the duration within the diurnal circle above the instantaneous center of the Sun up to the horizon. When the Sun is above the rising horizon during this desired time, it is calculated as the sum of the Sun’s "remaining breath-time" <note>original: *bhogyasu*; the time taken for the remaining portion of the current zodiac sign to rise</note>, the Ascendant’s "elapsed breath-time" <note>original: *bhuktasu*; the time already passed in the rising sign</note>, and the rising times of the intervening zodiac signs. Therefore, the Teacher states that one should multiply the Sun’s remaining degrees by the rising time of the current sign and divide by the total minutes in a sign (1800). The resulting quotient is the Sun’s remaining breath-time. To this, one adds the Ascendant’s elapsed breath-time—calculated by multiplying the elapsed degrees of the Ascendant by the sign's rising time and dividing by 1800—and the rising times of the intermediate signs to establish the "Solar Desired Ghatis" <note>A *ghati* is a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. However, because the Solar Desired Ghatis are variable, the Teacher applies "repeated operations" <term>Asakrit Karma: an iterative mathematical process used to reach a precise value</term> here.

The Teacher’s intent in mentioning "single operations" <term>Sakrit Karma: a direct, non-iterative calculation</term> is that the "Sidereal Ghatis" <note>time measured relative to the stars</note> are unknown; only the Solar Desired Ghatis are known. Thus, the Sidereal time cannot be known through the aforementioned method alone. Therefore, the desired time is fixed through a direct calculation. Bhaskaracharya also states in the *Chapter on the Celestial Sphere* <note>Goladhyaya</note>: "If the desired ghatis for the Ascendant are Solar, they should be made through the calculation of the instantaneous Sun," which is described there in detail. || 21-22-23 ||

### Now, the Inverse Ascendant and the calculation of time from it are stated:

> If the question is asked before sunrise, the Sun minus the breath-times of the question and the elapsed signs becomes the Ascendant.
> By thus reducing the Sun until it equals the Ascendant, the time before sunrise is found. || 24 ||

<term>Vatshya Bhashya: The commentary of Vatshya</term> — When the calculation is made before sunrise, the operation is performed as before using the ghatis remaining in the night and their own rising times, specifically using the "elapsed signs." This means: write down the elapsed degrees of the instantaneous Sun and convert them into minutes. Multiply this by the rising time of the sign occupied by the Sun, and divide by 1800. The result is in "breaths" <note>Prana: a unit of time</note>. Subtract these breaths from the total, and subtract the elapsed signs from the Sun. From the remainder, subtract the rising times of the signs for as long as they can be subtracted. Subtract the same number of signs from the Sun. From the remaining "question-breaths," multiply by thirty etc., to find the result; subtract this also from the Sun to find the Ascendant at the end of the night. <term>Vasanamukha: The introduction to the rationale</term> In the end, the Ascendant is found; therefore, the Sun diminished by the elapsed portion of the zodiac becomes the Ascendant. One should show the Moon on the sphere. In the second part, he explains the calculation of time from the Ascendant at the end of the night.

Just as the Sun is diminished by time, it attains a reduction by the rising times of the local signs; thus, by inverse calculation, it becomes equal to the Ascendant <unclear>at</unclear> the marked time. This means: the time comprised of the elapsed degrees of the Ascendant, the elapsed degrees of the Sun, and the rising times of the intervening signs is the time remaining in the night. The Sun, when reduced, becomes equal to the Ascendant. Here too, one must add the segment of the ecliptic situated below the horizon as before. To the question of one who does not know the truth <unclear>through</unclear> the passing shadow, he will give the answer in many ways, starting with this one.

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
### [The Corrected Treatise of Brahma]

The author presents a half-verse explaining the method for bringing forth the remaining parts of the zodiacal signs and the divisor:

**Scientific Exposition:**—When the ascendant <note>The *Lagna*, or the point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon</note> is desired before sunrise using the given breath-intervals <note>*Asu*: a unit of time equal to one respiration or 4 seconds</note> of the query, the Sun is decreased by the degrees and signs already traversed; that becomes the ascendant. For calculating the time from the ascendant, the Sun and the ascendant are made equal, and thus the desired time before sunrise is found. 

This is what is meant: Multiply the degrees already traversed by the Sun at that time by the rising time of the sign occupied by the Sun, divide by thirty, and subtract the result from the desired breath-intervals. Then, subtract the signs traversed from the Sun. From the remaining breath-intervals, subtract the rising times of as many untraversed signs as possible, and subtract the same number of signs from the Sun. Multiply the remaining breath-intervals by thirty and divide by the rising time of the next sign; subtract the resulting degrees from the Sun. This gives the ascendant during the remainder of the night. 

To calculate the time from the ascendant thus obtained, the Sun—reduced by the time as before—is brought to the state of the ascendant using the rising times of the signs of the local latitude. When the Sun is thus made equal to the ascendant by this inverse process, the time elapsed in the remainder of the night becomes clear. This means that by combining the traversed degrees of the ascendant and the rising times of the intervening signs through repeated calculation, the precise time in the remainder of the night is found. The Sun, devoid of the untraversed degrees and signs, becomes equal to the ascendant. || 24 ||

The logic <term>Upapatti: mathematical proof or rationale</term> here should be understood as being in the form of a commentary. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara* [Crest-jewel of Siddhantas], Shripati says: "Even before sunrise, the Sun, deprived of the signs and degrees passed and the rising times of the preceding signs, is the ascendant; when the Sun is made equal to that, it is the time." This, and Bhaskara's statement in the *Shiromani* [Crown of Treatises] beginning with "In the subtraction of the traversed breaths, the inverse ascendant..." etc., is exactly in accordance with what the Teacher <note>Referring to Brahmagupta, the original author</note> has said. || 24 ||

---

-> Now the inverse ascendant and the calculation of time from it are described. <-

**Hindi Exposition:**—If the ascendant is desired before the given breath-intervals, then the ascendant is found by subtracting the traversed degrees and signs from the Sun. Multiply the traversed degrees of the Sun at that time by the rising value of the sign in which the Sun is located, divide by thirty, subtract the quotient from the desired breath-intervals, and also subtract the traversed signs from the Sun. Subtract as many untraversed sign-rising values as possible from the remaining breath-intervals and subtract the same number of signs from the Sun. Multiply the remaining breath-intervals by thirty and divide by the rising value of the incomplete sign; subtract the resulting degrees from the Sun to find the ascendant in the remainder of the night. 

From the ascendant of the remainder of the night thus obtained, the precise desired time in the remainder of the night is found through repeated calculation using the sum of the rising values of the untraversed degrees and the signs between the Sun and the ascendant. || 24 ||

The logic for this is in the form of the commentary itself. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, through the verse written in the Sanskrit logic beginning with "Even before sunrise, the Sun...", Shripati and Bhaskaracharya (in the *Siddhanta-shiromani* with "In the subtraction of the traversed breaths...") have said the same in accordance with the Teacher. || 24 ||

## Now, he describes the Desired Sine of Altitude (Ishtashanku).

> From the elapsed or remaining time of the day, whichever is less, and based on the northern or southern hemispheres, using the half-equinoctial rising <note>original: "charardhaih"</note>;
> The sine of that time, decreased or increased accordingly, multiplied by the radius of the diurnal circle, ॥25॥
>
> And divided by the radius <note>original: "trijya"</note>, then increased or decreased by the earth-sine <note>original: "kshitijya"</note> in the northern and southern hemispheres respectively, becomes the divisor.
> This divisor, multiplied by the colatitude <note>original: "avalambaka"</note> and divided by the radius, is the Sine of Altitude <note>original: "shanku"</note>. ॥26॥

**Author’s Commentary (Vasana-bhashya)** — At whatever desired time one wishes to <term>calculate</term> the shadow of the elapsed day: take the time elapsed since sunrise or the time remaining until sunset, whichever is less. One should calculate the sine of that elapsed time of the day. How? By using the half-equinoctial rising <note>the difference between the local rising time and the equatorial rising time</note>. In the northern hemisphere, subtract the half-rising from the time; in the southern, add it. Then, that sine is multiplied by the radius of the diurnal circle and divided by the total radius. This result is then increased or decreased by the earth-sine <note>original: "kujya" or "kshitijya"</note> respectively, depending on whether the sun is in the northern or southern hemisphere. This result is the "divisor."

Here, the underlying logic <note>original: "vasana"</note> regarding the application of the local latitude should be demonstrated by arranging the celestial sphere. It is as follows: Having marked the diurnal circle of the desired day with time-units (ghatikas), and having tied the north-south cords as before, one should fix the rising-setting line in the middle of the eastern and western points of the horizon and the 6-o'clock circle <note>original: "unmandala"</note>. Having fixed the 6-o'clock circle, one should tie the equatorial rising-setting line extending east-west at the intersection of the diurnal circle.

In this state, however many time-units have elapsed from the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle, one should calculate that along the diurnal circle and mark a sign at the end of it. That represents the position of the Sun at that time. From those time-units, the half-rising units are subtracted in the northern hemisphere because the sines begin from the 6-o'clock circle, which is above or below the horizon. The 6-o'clock circle is separated from the horizon by the half-rising <note>charadala</note>. Thus, by subtracting this from the portion of the diurnal circle, the sine of the remaining time-units is measured from the 6-o'clock circle.

In the southern hemisphere, the half-rising units are added to the elapsed time because the 6-o'clock circle is below the horizon. To find the sine starting from the 6-o'clock circle, the portion of the diurnal circle intercepted by the 6-o'clock circle must be included.

Since the calculation is initially imagined on the circle of the total radius, it must be converted to the specific diurnal circle. For that, this rule of three is used: "If this is the sine in the circle of the total radius, what would it be in the diurnal circle?" The result is the sine of the distance between the Sun and the 6-o'clock circle on the diurnal circle.

But we desire the sine of the distance from our own horizon. Therefore, in the northern hemisphere, it is added to the earth-sine because the Sun is above the horizon; in the southern hemisphere, it is subtracted from the earth-sine to find the sine relative to one's own horizon. This is called the "desired sine" on the diurnal circle. This "earth-sine" is called *kujya* in the works of Aryabhata and others, as well as in our own Siddhanta.

---

A cord of that measure, when the Sun is at the beginning of Aries or Libra, is increased by the earth-sine and doubled. One end of that cord is tied to the Sun's disk on the diurnal circle, and the second end is tied below the equatorial horizon...

One should fasten the arc like a bow upon the diurnal circle itself. There, the segment defined by the line ending at the local rising point is the <term>Cheda</term> <note>divisor or hypotenuse of the day-radius</note>. The sine defined by the intersection of that same line with the line of the equatorial rising point is called the <term>Jiva</term> <note>sine</note>. The sine of the interval between the Sun and the celestial equator was shown previously. With the <term>Cheda</term> acting as the radius, one should place the north-south meridian circle, making a line between the rising and setting points of the <term>Cheda</term>. In this arrangement, the <term>Cheda</term> is the hypotenuse, the <term>Shanku</term> <note>gnomon or vertical sine</note> is the upright, and the base of the gnomon is the side. Just as at the equinoctial midday, where the radius is the hypotenuse, the sine of the co-latitude is the upright, and the sine of the latitude is the side of the meridian circle—by this fundamental principle, all calculations for the shadow's path are derived. All of this should be demonstrated on the <term>Gola</term> <note>armillary sphere</note>. Now, he speaks a verse to provide the answer for calculating the gnomon.

The <term>Cheda</term> multiplied by the sine of the co-latitude and divided by the radius is the <term>Shanku</term>. The <term>Cheda</term> is brought forth as the interval; it becomes the <term>Shanku</term> when multiplied by the sine of the co-latitude and divided by the radius. Here is the <term>Vasana</term> <note>geometrical explanation/rationale</note>: Having tied one end of a string to the point marked by the Sun on the diurnal circle, let the second end hang down by attaching a weight. Then, measuring from the center of the Earth, tie a second string to the horizon where it touches the hanging string. Where those two strings intersect is the base of the gnomon. From there, up to the Sun is the gnomon; to the center of the Earth-sphere is the shadow; to the base of the gnomon's <term>Cheda</term> is the gnomon-floor; and the <term>Cheda</term> is the hypotenuse. This is a proportion: if when the radius is the hypotenuse, the sine of the co-latitude is the gnomon, then in this north-south circle, how much is the gnomon when the <term>Cheda</term> is the hypotenuse? The result is the gnomon for the desired time of day. The same rationale applies to the afternoon. Because of their equality, the Sun's shadows [at corresponding times] are the same. All of this should be demonstrated on the sphere. Now, he speaks a half-verse to calculate the shadow by a second method.

**V. Bha.** <note>Commentary by Vishnu Bhaskara</note> — Of the day's past or remaining time (whichever is less, meaning the <term>Unnata-kala</term> or time since sunrise/before sunset), in the northern or southern hemispheres, the sine of that time decreased or increased respectively by the half-ascensional difference, multiplied by the day-radius and divided by the radius, gives the <term>Kala</term>. That, when added to or subtracted from the <term>Kujya</term> <note>earth-sine</note> in the north and south hemispheres, becomes the <term>Cheda</term> (also called <term>Ishtahriti</term>). The <term>Cheda</term> multiplied by the sine of the co-latitude and divided by the radius results in the desired <term>Shanku</term> (gnomon). || 25-26 ||

### Here is the Proof:

From the eastern half of the meridian circle, before midday, the time elapsed since the Sun was at the rising horizon is the "day-past." From the Sun to the setting horizon is the "day-remaining." Here, the day-past is less than the day-remaining, so that is the <term>Unnata-kala</term> <note>elevated time</note>. This spans from the intersection of the hour circle and the celestial equator (passing through the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle) to the intersection of the hour circle and the celestial equator passing through the Sun. In the northern hemisphere, on the hour circle passing through the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle...

# Chapter on the Three Problems
## (Triprasna-adhikara)

From the eastern point of intersection, at a distance of the <term>ascensional difference</term> <note>the difference between the time of sunrise at the equator and at a specific latitude</note>, when the sun is below the horizon during the <term>elapsed time since sunrise</term> <note>unnata-kala</note>, that ascensional difference is subtracted. Then, the arc of the cord from the eastern intersection to the point where the hour circle passing through the sun meets the celestial equator is formed; the sine of this arc is called the **"Sutra"** <term>Sutra-samjnaka</term>. In the southern hemisphere, the hour circle passing through the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle meets the celestial equator at a distance of the ascensional difference from the eastern point. During the elapsed time since sunrise, by adding the ascensional difference, the "Sutra arc" is formed. Its sine, the **Sutra**, is effectively the perpendicular from the intersection of the sun's hour circle and the equator onto the east-west line. From the pole to the eastern point on the <term>unmandala</term> <note>the six-o'clock circle or equatorial horizon</note> is 90 degrees. From the pole to the intersection of the sun's hour circle and the equator is also 90 degrees on the hour circle. The "Sutra arc" lies on the celestial equator. In the triangle formed by these three sides (where the <term>radius</term> <note>Trijya</note> is the hypotenuse, the **Sutra** is the base, and the cosine of the Sutra is the upright), the arc from the pole to the sun is the <term>arc of the day-radius</term> <note>Dyujya-chapa</note>. From the pole to the intersection of the *unmandala* and the diurnal circle is also the <term>arc of the day-radius</term>. The arc within the diurnal circle between the hour circle and the *unmandala* is similar to the sine-area of this triangle (where the <term>day-radius</term> <note>Dyujya</note> is the hypotenuse, the perpendicular from the sun to the equatorial sunrise-sunset line is the base called **"Kala"**, and the distance from the base of the *Kala* to the center of the diurnal circle is the upright). Therefore, by proportion: if the **Sutra** is obtained from the **Radius**, what is obtained from the **Day-radius**? Thus, **Kala** $= \frac{\text{Sutra} \times \text{Day-radius}}{\text{Radius}}$. The perpendicular from the sun to its own sunrise-sunset line is the <term>desired divisor</term> <note>Ishta-hriti</note>. The distance between the sun's own sunrise-sunset line and the equatorial sunrise-sunset line is the <term>earth-sine</term> <note>Kujya</note>. In the northern hemisphere, because the sun's sunrise-sunset line is below the equatorial one, the **Kala** plus the **Earth-sine** equals the **Desired Divisor**. In the southern hemisphere, the **Kala** minus the **Earth-sine** is the **Desired Divisor**. Furthermore, another "latitude triangle" <note>Aksha-kshetra</note> is formed where the **Radius** is the hypotenuse, the <term>sine of latitude</term> <note>Akshajya</note> is the base, and the <term>sine of colatitude</term> <note>Lambajya</note> is the upright. Similarly, a second latitude triangle is formed where the **Desired Divisor** is the hypotenuse, the <term>desired sine/gnomon</term> <note>Ishta-shanku</note> is the upright, and the <term>gnomon's shadow-base</term> <note>Shankutala</note> is the base. Because these are similar, by proportion: if the **Sine of Colatitude** is obtained from the **Radius**, what is obtained from the **Desired Divisor**? Thus, **Desired Sine (Gnomon)** $= \frac{\text{Sine of Colatitude} \times \text{Desired Divisor}}{\text{Radius}}$. This proves what the Teacher has stated. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya says:

> "Then, from the elapsed time since sunrise, subtract or add the ascensional difference respectively for the North and South hemispheres; the sine of that is the **Sutra**. This multiplied by the **Day-radius** and divided by the **Radius** is called **Kala**." This is exactly in accordance with what the Teacher has said.

---

-> Now the method for finding the <term>Desired Sine (Gnomon)</term> is described. <-

**Hindi Commentary:** — The smaller value between the time passed since sunrise and the time remaining until sunset is the <term>elapsed time</term> <note>unnata-kala</note>. In the northern hemisphere, subtracting the <term>half-ascensional difference</term> <note>charardha</note> from the elapsed time, and in the southern hemisphere, adding the half-ascensional difference to the elapsed time, gives a value whose <term>sine</term> (Sutra) is multiplied by the <term>day-radius</term> and divided by the <term>radius</term> to get the **Kala**. In the northern hemisphere, adding the <term>earth-sine</term> <note>kujya</note> to the **Kala**, and in the southern hemisphere, subtracting the **earth-sine** from the **Kala**, gives the divisor (<term>desired divisor</term>). Multiplying the desired divisor by the <term>sine of colatitude</term> and dividing by the <term>radius</term> results in the **Desired Sine (Gnomon)**. || 25-26 ||

<header>Chapter on the Conjunction of Planets</header>

### Rationale

The time elapsed since sunrise to the point where the Sun is located before noon is the "day-past" time <note>Sanskrit: *dinagata kala*</note>. Conversely, the time remaining until sunset is the "day-remaining" time. Here, if the day-remaining time is less than the day-past time, then that (the day-remaining) is considered the "elevated time" <note>Sanskrit: *unnata kala*; the time the sun is above the horizon</note>. If the day-past time is less than the day-remaining, then that (the day-past) is the elevated time. This occurs on the celestial equator <note>Sanskrit: *nadivritta*</note> between the intersection of the hour circle <note>Sanskrit: *dhruvaprotavritta*</note> passing through the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle, and the hour circle passing through the planet's position.

In the Northern Hemisphere <note>Sanskrit: *uttara gola*</note>, the hour circle passing through the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle meets the celestial equator below the East point by the amount of the ascensional difference <note>Sanskrit: *charantara*</note>. Therefore, by subtracting the ascensional difference from the elevated time, we obtain the arc of the celestial equator from the East point to the hour circle of the planet; this is called the "sine-arc" <note>Sanskrit: *sutrachapa*</note>. Its sine is designated as the "string" <note>Sanskrit: *sutra*</note>.

In the Southern Hemisphere <note>Sanskrit: *dakshina gola*</note>, the intersection occurs above the East point by the ascensional difference. Therefore, by adding the ascensional difference to the elevated time, the sine-arc is formed. Its sine (the perpendicular line from the intersection of the planet's hour circle and the equator to the East-West line) is the "string."

A triangle is formed by these three sides: 90 degrees on the six-o'clock circle <note>Sanskrit: *unmandala*</note> from the pole to the East point; 90 degrees on the hour circle from the pole to the equator; and the sine-arc on the equator. The geometric figure of this triangle (where the Radius is the hypotenuse, the "string" is the base, and the cosine of the string is the upright) is similar to the geometric figure formed by: the arc of the diurnal radius <note>Sanskrit: *dyujyachapa*</note> from the pole to the Sun; the diurnal radius on the six-o'clock circle from the pole to the intersection of the horizon; and the arc between the hour circle and the diurnal circle.

Therefore, we calculate the proportion: if for the Radius <note>Sanskrit: *trijya*</note> we get the "string," then what do we get for the diurnal radius? From this, the *kala* <note>a specific mathematical segment</note> is derived:
$\frac{\text{String} \times \text{Diurnal Radius}}{\text{Radius}}$ = *Kala*

The perpendicular line from the Sun to the local rising-setting line is the "desired day-radius" <note>Sanskrit: *ishtahriti*</note>. The difference between the local rising-setting line and the equatorial rising-setting line is the "earth-sine" <note>Sanskrit: *kujya*</note>, which is a segment of the *ishtahriti*. In the Northern Hemisphere, the local rising-setting line is below the equatorial one; therefore, by adding the earth-sine to the *kala*, the *ishtahriti* is obtained. In the Southern Hemisphere, by subtracting the earth-sine from the *kala*, the *ishtahriti* is obtained.

One "latitude-triangle" <note>Sanskrit: *akshakshetra*</note> is formed by these three sides: Radius (hypotenuse), Sine of Latitude (base), and Cosine of Latitude (upright). A second latitude-triangle is formed by: *Ishtahriti* (hypotenuse), Desired Gnomon <note>Sanskrit: *ishtashanku*</note> (upright), and the Gnomon-base <note>Sanskrit: *shankutala*</note> (base). Both latitude-triangles are similar. Therefore, we calculate the proportion: if for the Radius we get the Cosine of Latitude <note>Sanskrit: *lambajya*</note>, then what do we get for the *ishtahriti*? From this, the measure of the Desired Gnomon is derived:
$\frac{\text{Cosine of Lat.} \times \text{Ishtahriti}}{\text{Radius}}$ = Desired Gnomon

This validates the teachings of the ancient masters. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, **Bhaskaracharya** also says the same in accordance with the masters in the Sanskrit rationale verse beginning with **"Mathocchatanunayuttaccharottha..."** <note>original: "मथोच्चतादूनयुताच्चरोत्थ"</note> etc. ||25-26||

It uses the principles of similar triangles and celestial circles to explain how to derive solar position based on hemispheric latitude and time.</summary>

# Chapter on the Triple Inquiry

->Now, he describes another method for finding the Great Gnomon and the Sine of Altitude (Drigjya):<-

> The divisor multiplied by twelve and divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse is the gnomon.
> The square root of the square of the radius minus the square of the gnomon is the Sine of Altitude. || 27 ||

**Vāsanābhāṣya (Author's Commentary):** Alternatively, the previously calculated divisor <note>Hriti</note> multiplied by twelve and divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>Palakarna; the hypotenuse of a shadow cast at the equinox</note> results in the gnomon. The underlying logic <note>Vāsanā</note> is as follows: if in the circle of the equinoctial hypotenuse-radius, twelve is the vertical side <note>Koti</note>, then what will it be in the circle of the divisor-radius? The result is the vertical side called the gnomon. Here, at the equinoctial noon, the equinoctial hypotenuse is imagined in place of the radius of the meridian circle, and twelve is the vertical gnomon. It was said previously that this is the base of the gnomon. This is all logically consistent. Now, to find the shadow of the resulting Great Gnomon, he speaks the second half of the verse.

The square root of the square of the radius minus the square of the gnomon is the Sine of Altitude. From the square of the radius, subtract the square of the gnomon just calculated; the square root of that is the Sine of Altitude <note>Drigjya</note>. The Sine of Altitude is also called the shadow <note>in the context of the celestial sphere</note>. The logic is that in the diurnal circle, the hypotenuse extends to the center of the marked point. The vertical line from the Sun's position to the horizon line passing through the Earth's center is the gnomon-side <note>Koti</note>. From the base of that vertical to the Earth's center is the Sine of Altitude, which is the shadow-side <note>Bhuja</note>. By subtracting the square of the vertical side from the square of the hypotenuse, the root is the horizontal side. All this should be demonstrated on the armillary sphere. Thus, having brought forth the Great Gnomon and its shadow, he gives half a verse to find the twelve-digit shadow. || 27 ||

**Vijnanabhashya (Scientific Commentary):** The divisor <note>Hriti</note> multiplied by twelve and divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>Palakarna</note> is, by another method, the gnomon. The square root of the square of the radius <note>Trijya</note> minus the square of that gnomon is the Sine of Altitude. || 27 ||

---

### Mathematical Proof

| | |
|----------|----------|
| The equinoctial shadow is the base, the 12-digit gnomon is the vertical, and the equinoctial hypotenuse is the hypotenuse. | } Because these two "Latitude Triangles" <note>Akshakshetra</note> |
| The gnomon-base is the base, the desired gnomon is the vertical, and the divisor (Hriti) is the hypotenuse. | } are similar, the proportion is: |

If for an equinoctial hypotenuse, a 12-digit gnomon is obtained as the vertical side, then for the "divisor" <note>Hriti</note> as the hypotenuse, what is obtained?

Desired Gnomon $= \frac{12 \times \text{Divisor}}{\text{Equinoctial Hypotenuse}}$. Then, the Sine of Altitude is the base. The desired gnomon is the vertical. The radius is the hypotenuse. In the shadow-triangle produced by these sides: $\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Gnomon}^2} =$ Sine of Altitude. Thus, what was stated by the Teacher is proven.

->Now, the gnomon and the sine of zenith distance are described by another method:<-

# Mathematical Proof

Equinoctial shadow (Palabha) = Base, 12-digit gnomon = Perpendicular, Equinoctial hypotenuse (Palakarna) = Hypotenuse } These two are similar right-angled triangles of the latitude (Akshakshetra).
Gnomon-projection (Shankutala) = Base, Desired gnomon (Ishtashanku) = Perpendicular, Divisor (Hriti) = Hypotenuse }

Therefore, we apply the rule of proportion: If for the Equinoctial hypotenuse we get a 12-digit gnomon, then what do we get for the Divisor (desired hypotenuse)? This gives the desired gnomon: $\frac{12 \times \text{Hriti}}{\text{Palakarna}}$ = Desired Gnomon.
The Sine of zenith distance (Drigjya) = Base, Desired gnomon = Perpendicular, Radius (Trijya) = Hypotenuse.

In this shadow-triangle, $\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Gnomon}^2}$ = Sine of zenith distance. Thus, the teacher's statement is proven. || 27 ||

->Now the shadow's hypotenuse is described:<-

> **The sine of zenith distance multiplied by twelve and divided by the gnomon results in the shadow.**
> **The radius divided by the 'divisor' and multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse is the hypotenuse [of the shadow]. || 28 ||**

**Sanskrit Commentary:** Having calculated the sine of zenith distance as previously brought forth, multiply it by twelve and divide by the gnomon to obtain the shadow—the phrase "of a twelve-digit gnomon" is understood to complete the sentence. Alternatively, by this same sine of zenith distance, if multiplied by the height of trees, mountains, etc., the shadow of that object at that time is found. Here the <term>Rule of Three</term><note>Trairashika: a mathematical proportion involving three known values to find a fourth</note> logic is: if for a large gnomon the sine of zenith distance is the shadow, then what is it for a twelve-digit gnomon? The result is the shadow of a twelve-digit gnomon, because for practical use, the definition of a gnomon was established in the Chapter on Instruments. It should be seen in the original text: "A twelve-digit shadow-gnomon with a thick base and pointed tip..." Alternatively, another method for finding the shadow without using the 'divisor' is stated in the second half of the verse:

The <term>Radius</term> divided by the 'divisor' and multiplied by the <term>Equinoctial Hypotenuse</term> is the hypotenuse. One should multiply the radius by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divide by the 'divisor'; the result is the hypotenuse of the shadow at that time. By subtracting the square of the twelve-digit gnomon from the square of the shadow's hypotenuse and taking the square root, the shadow of the twelve-digit gnomon is found—this is the logic. This is explained through the center of the earth without inversion: if for the shadow-hypotenuse the twelve-digit gnomon is the perpendicular, then for the radius-hypotenuse on the vertical circle, what is the perpendicular? The result is the large gnomon at that time. Then a second proportion: if at the equinoctial midday on the meridian circle the Co-latitude sine is the perpendicular for a radius-hypotenuse, then for the desired gnomon as the perpendicular, what is the hypotenuse on the 'divisor' radius? The result is the 'divisor'. Here, in place of the Co-latitude sine, twelve is assumed as the perpendicular, and in place of the radius, the equinoctial hypotenuse is used. Thus, in the first proportion, twelve is the multiplier, and in the second, it is the divisor; they cancel out. The equinoctial hypotenuse remains the multiplier of the radius, and the shadow-hypotenuse is the divisor, the result being the 'divisor'. When the radius is divided by the 'divisor'...

**Tri. Bha.** — The sine of zenith distance <term>Drig-jya: the sine of the angular distance of a celestial body from the zenith</term> multiplied by twelve and divided by the gnomon <term>Shanku: a vertical pillar or gnomon used to measure shadows, traditionally 12 digits high</term> results in the shadow. ->**Here is the Proof:**<-

Shadow = Base. Twelve-digit gnomon = Perpendicular. Shadow's hypotenuse = Hypotenuse.
Sine of zenith distance = Base. Desired gnomon = Perpendicular. Radius = Hypotenuse. } Because these two shadow-triangles are similar, the proportion is: if the sine of zenith distance is obtained by the gnomon, then what is obtained by a twelve-digit gnomon?
Shadow = $\frac{\text{Sine of zenith distance} \times 12}{\text{Gnomon}}$.
Similarly, if the radius is obtained by the gnomon, then what is obtained by a twelve-digit gnomon?
Shadow's hypotenuse = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times 12}{\text{Gnomon}}$.
However, since $\frac{12 \times \text{Hati}}{\text{Palakarna}} =$ Gnomon, by substituting this value for the gnomon, the Shadow's hypotenuse = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times 12}{\frac{12 \times \text{Hati}}{\text{Palakarna}}} = \frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Palakarna}}{\text{Hati}}$.
By this, what the Teacher <note>referring to the original author of the treatise</note> stated is proven.
Sripati <note>An 11th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> also says the same as the Teacher: "If the radius is multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divided by the divisor, the desired hypotenuse is found."
The shadow and shadow's hypotenuse arrived at by the two previous proportions are exactly what Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the famous 12th-century mathematician</note> stated: "The sine of zenith distance and the radius, multiplied by the Sun [12] and divided by the gnomon, become the shadow and its hypotenuse." ||28||

->Now he describes another method for bringing forth the shadow hypotenuse and the desired <term>Antya</term><note>The 'final' sine or chord at a given time</note><-

->**Or, the radius multiplied by twelve and divided by the gnomon is the hypotenuse.**<-
->**The sine, increased or decreased by the sine of the earth-sine, is the sine in Aries or Libra etc.**<- <note>This refers to the calculation of the 'Antya' or 'Ista-jya' depending on whether the sun is in the northern or southern hemisphere.</note> ->**|| 29 ||**<-

**Vasanabhashya (Commentary on the Meaning):** One should multiply the radius by twelve and divide by the large gnomon. The result is the shadow hypotenuse. Alternatively, it is stated in this way: this proof follows if, for the large gnomon as the vertical side, the east-west hypotenuse-radius of twelve digits is the vertical side, then what is the result? Thus the shadow hypotenuse is proven. In the field of the visible circle, he then speaks the second half of the verse to bring forth the sine. "The sine, increased or decreased by the sine of the earth-sine, is the sine in Aries or Libra etc." The sine of the lesser of the elapsed or remaining time of day, decreased or increased by the <term>Carardha</term><note>Half the variation of the day's length</note> in the northern or southern hemispheres, is taken here. By this, the meaning is: the sine in Aries etc., when added to the sine of increase/decrease, becomes the named sine. When the Sun is in the six signs starting with Libra, it becomes the sine when decreased by the sine of increase/decrease. The reasoning here is: having subtracted the segment of the diurnal circle between the horizon and the sun (called the half-variation) from the hypotenuse, the sine of the remainder is calculated. The sine up to the <term>Unmandala</term><note>The equatorial horizon</note> is the sine produced in the circle of the radius, as shown previously. The sine of increase/decrease is added to the sine of the half-variation segment in the northern hemisphere because it is situated below the horizon; in the southern hemisphere, it is subtracted because it is situated above the horizon from the equatorial horizon. By doing this, the sine of the interval from the horizon is in the circle of the radius; this is the meaning of the resulting divisor. One should show the field as before. Because of the difference in the arrangement made with the standardized divisor, he now speaks the half-verse to bring forth the divisor. || 29 ||

**Vimalabhashya (Clear Commentary):** The radius multiplied by twelve and divided by the gnomon—or by another method—becomes the shadow hypotenuse. The sine (of the arc of the formula from half the sum of the lesser of the day past or day remaining and the half-variation according to the hemisphere) when added or subtracted by the sine of increase/decrease (the <term>Carajya</term>) in Aries or Libra (Northern and Southern hemispheres) then becomes the sine (the desired <term>Antya</term>). || 29 ||

->**Here is the Proof:**<-

&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; If the radius is obtained by the gnomon, then what is obtained by twelve?
&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Radius × 12
Shadow Hypotenuse = -----------. The secondary circle passing through the poles, which passes through the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle, meets the equinoctial circle at a distance from the East point—below in the Northern hemisphere and above in the Southern hemisphere—from that point.

### Chapter on the Three Problems

(From the intersection of the <term>celestial equator</term><note>nāḍīvṛtta</note> and the <term>hour circle</term><note>dhruvaprōtavṛtta</note> passing through the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle), a line parallel to the East-West line should be drawn. Upon that, a perpendicular should be dropped from the intersection of the hour circle passing through the planet and the celestial equator; this is the <term>desired day-radius</term><note>iṣṭāntyā: the portion of the day-radius corresponding to a specific time</note>. Whichever is less between the time passed and the time remaining in the day is the <term>elevated time</term><note>unnata-kāla: time since sunrise or until sunset</note>. In the Northern and Southern hemispheres, when this is decreased or increased by the <term>ascensional difference</term><note>carārdha: the difference between the 6-hour arc and the actual half-day length</note>, it becomes the "chord-arc" (from the intersection of the planet's hour circle and the equator up to the East point). The sine of this is the "chord" (the perpendicular from the intersection of the planet's hour circle and the equator onto the East-West line). The distance between the previously drawn parallel line and the East-West line is the <term>sine of ascensional difference</term><note>carajyā</note>. In the Northern and Southern hemispheres respectively, when the "chord" is added to or subtracted from the sine of ascensional difference, it becomes the <term>desired day-radius</term><note>iṣṭāntyā</note>. Here, the Teacher <note>referring to the author of the primary text being commented upon</note> calls the "chord" by the name *Jīvā* and the "desired day-radius" by the name *Jyā*. In the *Siddhānta Śekhara*, Śrīpati says: <note>original Sanskrit: "dvādaśabhirguṇite yadi vā'smin..."</note> "If multiplied by twelve or in this case, know the hypotenuse by dividing by the gnomon," and also "As before, from the elevated time, increased or decreased by the half-ascensional difference... it becomes the *Jyā* when multiplied by the day-radius. Then divided by the radius... the gnomon is found as before." What the Teacher says in the verse "multiplied by twelve etc." and the subsequent verse "multiplied by half the diurnal circle etc." is exactly in accordance with these two. ||26||

---

->Now, another method for calculating the shadow's hypotenuse and the desired day-radius is stated.<-

**Hindi Commentary—**By multiplying the <term>radius</term><note>trijyā</note> by twelve and dividing by the <term>gnomon</term><note>śaṅku</note>, or by another method, the <term>shadow's hypotenuse</term><note>chāyākarṇa</note> is obtained. In the *Jīvā* (the sine of the "elevated time"—the lesser of time passed or remaining—decreased or increased by the ascensional difference according to the hemisphere), by adding or subtracting the sine of ascensional difference in the Northern and Southern hemispheres respectively, the *Jyā* (desired day-radius) is obtained. ||26||

---

->**Mathematical Proof**<-

If we obtain the radius in the gnomon, then what do we get in twelve? From this proportion, the shadow's hypotenuse is derived: 
<margin>Radius × 12 / Gnomon = Shadow's Hypotenuse</margin> 
The intersection of the hour circle passing through the horizon-diurnal circle intersection lies at the distance of the ascensional difference from the East point in the Northern hemisphere, and can lie at the distance of the ascensional difference in the Southern celestial equator. From that point (the intersection of the hour circle and the equator), draw a line parallel to the East-West line. Beyond that, the distance from the intersection point of the planet's hour circle and the equator is the "desired day-radius." The lesser of the radius and the remaining day is the elevated time. By decreasing or increasing that by the ascensional difference in the Northern and Southern hemispheres respectively, the sine of the result (the perpendicular line from the intersection of the planet's hour circle and the equator onto the East-West line) is the "chord." The difference between the parallel line and the East-West line is the sine of ascensional difference. In the Northern and Southern hemispheres, to the "chord," the sine of ascensional difference...
