Header: In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

By adding or subtracting in order, the desired *antya* <note>The *antya* is a specific chord used in calculating the position of a planet relative to the horizon</note> is found. Here, the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> calls the formula by the name *jiva* <note>sine</note> and refers to the desired *antya* as *jya*. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, Shripati says "multiplied by twelve" etc., and in the Sanskrit commentary on "the difference between the risen time and half the variation of the day," he speaks in accordance with the Teacher's statement "multiplied by twelve" and the subsequent verse "multiplied by half the day-night radius" etc. ||29||

### Now he describes the calculation of the divisor and other elements again:

> Either that [antya] multiplied by half the day-night radius and divided by the radius is the divisor (*cheda*).
> The gnomon and other parts are as before; the sine multiplied by the product of half the day-night radius... ||30||

**Vasanabhashya (Author's Commentary):**—The word *jya* <note>sine</note> carries over here. One should multiply the sine by half the day-night radius and divide by the radius. The result is the *cheda* <note>the divisor, often representing the *ishta-dhriti* or the sine of the altitude on the prime vertical</note>. The logic here is based on the Rule of Three: if in a circle with the full radius this much is the sine, then in the day-night circle <note>the diurnal circle of the planet</note>, how much would it be? The result is called the *cheda* of the desired sine in the day-night circle. With that divisor, one should demonstrate the gnomon and other elements in the sphere or in the field as before.

The gnomon and others are as before; the sine multiplied by the product of half the day-night radius and multiplied by the square of the radius, or by the equinoctial hypotenuse, becomes the hypotenuse. This text is already explained by "the gnomon and others as before." Regarding the product of the sine and the day-night radius—that is, their mutual multiplication—he asks what the square of the radius of the northern solar path becomes by that product. ||30||

**Vimalabhashya (Explanatory Commentary):**—That (the previously calculated desired *antya*) multiplied by half the day-night radius (<term>dyujya</term> <note>the radius of the diurnal circle</note>), divided by the radius (<term>trijya</term> <note>the radius of the great circle, usually 3438'</note>), or by another method, becomes the divisor (<term>ishta-dhriti</term> <note>the "desired support," a specific sine value used in shadow calculations</note>). Then, as before, the gnomon (<term>shanku</term>) and other values are derived. The phrase "the sine multiplied by the product of half the day-night radius" connects to the next verse. ||30||

### Here is the Geometric Proof:

The line from the center of the Earth to the intersection of the declination circle passing through the planet and the celestial equator is the radius. The perpendicular dropped from the intersection of the declination circle and the equator onto the line parallel to the east-west line is the <term>ishta-antya</term>. The line at its base forms one triangle with these three sides. 

From the center of the planet's diurnal circle, the line to the planet is the *dyujya* (day-night radius). The perpendicular from the planet to its own rising-setting line is the *ishta-dhriti*. The line at its base forms a second triangle with these three sides. Because these two triangles are similar, the proportion is: if for the <term>trijya</term> (radius) we get the <term>ishta-antya</term>, then for the <term>dyujya</term> (day-night radius), what do we get? By this we arrive at the *ishta-dhriti*:

= $\frac{\text{ishta-antya}\cdot\text{dyujya}}{\text{trijya}}$

From this, the gnomon and other values are derived just as before. ||30||

# Chapter on the Three Problems

Now, the calculation of the divisor and other factors is stated:

**Hindi Commentary:** By multiplying the previously calculated "desired end-point" <note>Istāntyā</note> by the "radius of the diurnal circle" <note>Dyujyā</note> and dividing by the "radius of the sphere" <note>Trijyā</note>, the "divisor" <note>Istahrti</note> is obtained. From that, the "gnomon" <note>Shanku</note> and other values are derived as before. The phrase "The product of the sine and the half-day-diameter" relates to the following verse. ||30||

->**Geometric Proof**<-

The line connecting the center of the Earth to the intersection of the secondary circle passing through the planet and the celestial equator is the radius. The perpendicular line dropped from that intersection onto the east-west line is the "desired end-point." The line from the center of the Earth to the base of this perpendicular forms a triangle with these three sides. 

In the second triangle: the line from the center of the diurnal circle to the planet is the "radius of the diurnal circle"; the perpendicular from the planet to the rising-setting line is the "divisor"; and the line from the center of the diurnal circle to the base of the divisor is the third side. These two triangles are similar. Therefore, we use the rule of proportion: if for the "radius of the sphere" we get the "desired end-point," then what do we get for the "radius of the diurnal circle"? This yields the "divisor."

Desired End-point × Radius of Diurnal Circle
-------------------------------------------- = Divisor
Radius of the Sphere

From this, the knowledge of the gnomon and other values is easily attained as before. ||30||

->**Now, another method for finding the hypotenuse of the shadow and the gnomon is stated**<-

> The hypotenuse of the shadow may be found by multiplying the square of the radius by the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>the hypotenuse of the shadow at noon on the equinox</note>. Or, the gnomon is the product of the sine and the cosine of latitude <note>Lambaka</note> divided by the square of the radius. ||31||
>
> Or, the gnomon is the product of the sine and the radius divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse. The shadow is the square root of the difference between the square of the hypotenuse and the square of twelve <note>the standard height of the gnomon</note>. ||32||

**Vāsanā Commentary:** Here, the logic is established by imagining three rules of proportion in reverse from the center of the Earth. For example: if for the hypotenuse of the shadow the gnomon is twelve, then for the radius-hypotenuse, what is the gnomon? The result is the "Great Gnomon." Then, if for the cosine of latitude the hypotenuse is the radius, then for this gnomon-side, what is the hypotenuse in the north-south circle? The result is the "divisor." Third: if this is the divisor in the diurnal circle, what would it be in the radius-circle? The result is the sine. 

In this setup, where the cosine of latitude is replaced by twelve (the gnomon) and the radius is replaced by the equinoctial hypotenuse, in the first proportion twelve is the multiplier and in the second it is the divisor; being equal, they cancel out. The multipliers remain the square of the radius, and the divisor is the product of the equinoctial hypotenuse and the radius of the diurnal circle; the result is the sine. <unclear>Then</unclear>, if that same dividend is divided by the product of the sine and the radius of the diurnal circle, the result is the hypotenuse of the shadow. All this should be demonstrated on the armillary sphere. 

Regarding the alternative method for the gnomon, it says: "the gnomon is the product of the sine and the cosine of latitude divided by the square of the radius." Alternatively, the sine and the radius of the diurnal circle <insert>137</insert>... it is appropriate to take the gnomon using the cosine of latitude of the place as long as the sun is below the six-o'clock circle <note>Unmandala</note> and above the horizon...

The sine of the arc <note>original: "jīvā"</note> is also taken here, and it starts from the 6 o'clock circle <note>term: "unmaṇḍala" - the equatorial horizon or the circle passing through the celestial poles and the east-west points</note> downwards. From the respirations <note>term: "prāṇa" - a unit of time equal to 4 seconds, the time taken for one breath</note> of the ascensional difference <note>term: "caradala" - the difference between the equatorial and oblique ascension</note>, the elapsed or remaining respirations are subtracted, by which the sine of the segment of the diurnal circle <note>term: "svāhorātravṛtta" - the daily path of a planet</note> within the 6 o'clock circle is called the sine. This means the ascensional difference of the Sun below the 6 o'clock circle. And the "sine of decrease and increase" <note>term: "kṣayavṛddhijyā" - a specific sine used in calculating day length</note> is the sine of the segment of the diurnal circle between the horizon and the 6 o'clock circle; therefore, the latitude-offset <note>term: "avalambana"</note> is subtracted from the sine of decrease and increase. By this, the sine-segment of the diurnal circle above the horizon and below the Sun is collected; that is what is called the sine. Therefore, it is said that the sine of decrease and increase is diminished by that sine. When that same latitude-offset is divided by the radius of the diurnal circle, then it becomes the earth-sine <note>term: "kṣitijā"</note> converted to the diurnal circle. Therefore, by subtracting its own latitude-offset from it, the divisor <note>term: "cheda"</note> is formed. Now, if the time of the query and the ascensional difference are equal, then the Sun is exactly on the 6 o'clock circle; there, in relation to the diurnal circle, the divisor of the earth-sine is the height of the Sun when the Sun is on the 6 o'clock circle.

Then, in the radius of the diurnal circle, the sine of decrease and increase is the sine by addition. The height is just that much, and with that radius, one should show the circle as before, passing through the north and south. For that also, the cosine of the instantaneous gnomon <note>term: "śanku-koṭi"</note>, the gnomon-base <note>term: "śankutala"</note>, the sine as the side <note>term: "bhujā"</note>, etc., the logic of the rule of three <note>term: "trairāśika-vāsanā"</note> should be applied. With the formulas stating that the divisor is multiplied by the latitude-sine, etc., the rest is as previously stated; therefore, all is proven. One should demonstrate this on the armillary sphere <note>term: "gola"</note> as it stands. Now, he describes the calculation of the two sines within the half-day. // 31 //

Alternatively, having multiplied the product of the sine and the diurnal circle by twelve, one should divide by the product of the radius and the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>term: "viṣuvat-karṇa" - the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow</note>. The result is the great gnomon. The logic here is based on the first half. In the second rule of three, the difference is that the equinoctial hypotenuse is in the place of the radius, and twelve is the upright <note>term: "koṭi"</note> in the place of the latitude-sine. Therefore, it is proven. One should show this on the sphere. Now, he describes the calculation of the shadow and the shadow-hypotenuse <note>term: "chāyā-karṇa"</note> in the latter half of the verse. Subtracting the square of twelve from the square of the hypotenuse, the square root is the shadow. By subtracting the square of the gnomon (twelve) from the square of the shadow-hypotenuse, the root of that is the instantaneous shadow of the gnomon. The logic here is that the shadow-hypotenuse is the hypotenuse, twelve is the gnomon (the upright), and the shadow is the side; therefore, by subtracting the square of the upright from the square of the hypotenuse, the root is the side—this is proven. In this way, it should be applied to the shadow-hypotenuse of a gnomon of any desired height, such as trees, houses, or mountains. Now, for the day when the time of query is less than the ascensional difference, in the northern hemisphere, he speaks an Āryā verse to calculate the divisor and the sines. // 32 //

<term>Scientific Commentary</term>—The square of the radius <note>original: "trijyā-varga"</note> multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>original: "pala-karṇa"</note> and divided by the product of the sine and the radius of the diurnal circle <note>original: "dyujyā"</note>, or alternatively, the hypotenuse <note>shadow-hypotenuse</note> is found. The product <note>of the "iṣṭāntyā" and the diurnal circle radius</note> multiplied by the latitude-sine and divided by the square of the radius, or alternatively, the desired gnomon is found. Or, that product multiplied by twelve and divided by the product of the radius and the equinoctial hypotenuse gives the desired gnomon. By subtracting the square of twelve from the square of the shadow-hypotenuse, the square root should be taken; then the shadow is found. // 31-32 //

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

**Vāsanā Commentary** — When the time elapsed since sunrise or remaining until sunset is small, and the breaths <note>prāṇa: a unit of time equal to 4 seconds</note> of the query-time occur in the Northern Hemisphere <note>original: "uttaragole"</note>, then a reverse subtraction should be performed from the breaths of the ascensional difference <note>caradala: the difference between the local and equatorial rising times</note> of that day. The sine <note>jyā</note> of the remaining breaths is calculated; this is called the *jīva*. Then, multiply that by the radius of the diurnal circle <note>svāhorātrārddha</note> and divide by the radius <note>vyāsārddha/trijyā</note>. The result is called the *hṛta*. The *hṛta* should be subtracted from the earth-sine <note>kṣitijā/kujyā</note>; this becomes the divisor <note>cheda</note>. The sine of the increase/decrease <note>kṣayavṛddhijyā</note> minus the *jīva* becomes the "risen sine" <note>jyārutthā</note>. 

Now, if the time of query is equal to the ascensional difference, then the earth-sine itself is the divisor, and the sine of increase/decrease is the "risen sine." Just as the shadow calculations were described previously using the divisor and the sine, they should be performed here for the time as well; this occurs in the Northern Hemisphere. 

The reasoning <note>vāsanā</note> here is as follows: In the Northern Hemisphere, the time of the ascensional difference is subtracted from the elapsed or remaining time. Because the Sun is above the celestial equator, and the portion of the diurnal circle is below the horizon-line <note>uadayāsta-sūtra</note>, the difference is subtracted because the celestial equator is above the local horizon. When the radius of the diurnal circle is taken as the radius, the earth-sine follows that proportion. The logic remains consistent for both Northern and Southern hemispheres. The terms "midday sine" <note>dyudalāntyajyā</note> and "final sine" <note>antyā</note> are used later because that is the maximum increase. On the day of the equinox, there is no declination, so the diurnal radius equals the total radius because the horizon and the celestial equator coincide. On that day, there is no ascensional difference. At the equator <note>nirakṣa</note>, the rising-setting line is the East-West line; therefore, the radius itself is both the midday sine and the final sine. All these variations of shadow calculations should be demonstrated on the globe. At the equator, all types of shadow calculations are possible. Now, he speaks in two verses regarding the midday sine and shadow calculations. ||33||

---

**Vivaraṇa Commentary** — If the number of breaths at the time of query is small and the breaths of the half-ascensional difference are many, then in the Northern Hemisphere, one should subtract the query-breaths from the ascensional breaths. The sine of the remainder is called the *sūtra*. That multiplied by the diurnal sine and divided by the radius becomes the *kalā*. The earth-sine <note>kṣitijā</note> minus that *kalā* becomes the divisor <note>cheda</note>. The sine of increase/decrease <note>carajyā</note> minus the *sūtra* is the "desired final sine" <note>iṣṭāntyā</note>. Then, using the divisor and the final sine, the calculation of the gnomon <note>śaṅku</note> and other elements should be done as before. ||33||

---

### Rationale/Proof

> Following the rule stated by Bhāskara <note>Bhāskara I or II, famous Indian mathematicians</note>: "Where a subtraction is to be made but the value to be subtracted is greater, it is a reverse subtraction," this is clearly a case of reverse subtraction. Lallācārya <note>8th-century astronomer</note> also says: "If the breaths of the elapsed time are less than the Sun's ascensional difference in the Northern Hemisphere, then subtract the elapsed time from the ascensional difference. The sine of the remainder multiplied by the diurnal sine... is declared the desired divisor." Similarly, Śrīpati <note>11th-century polymath</note> in the *Siddhānta-śekhara* says: "If the desired breaths are not more than the ascensional difference in the Northern Hemisphere, they are subtracted from the ascensional difference... the divisor is then calculated by the stated method." Thus, what I have said is consistent with these authorities. ||33||

# Chapter on the Three Problems

->Now, something specific is said regarding the "Desired Divisor" and the "Desired Antya"<-

**Hindi Commentary** — If the number of *Ishtasu* <note>desired respiration units/time</note> is small and the number of *Charasu* <note>ascensional difference in time units</note> is large—that is, if the *Charasu* exceeds the *Ishtasu*—then in the Northern Hemisphere, subtracting the *Ishtasu* from the *Charasu* gives a remainder whose sine is called the *Sutra*. Multiplying this by the *Dyujya* <note>radius of the diurnal circle</note> and dividing by the *Trijya* <note>radius of the prime circle/3438'</note> results in the *Kala*. Subtracting this from the *Kujya* <note>earth-sine</note> gives the *Ishtahriti* <note>the desired divisor/hypotenuse of the gnomon</note>. Subtracting the sine of the *Sutra* from the *Charajya* <note>sine of ascensional difference</note> gives the *Ishtantya*. Then, using this *Ishtahriti* and *Ishtantya*, one should calculate the *Shanku* <note>gnomon/altitude</note> as previously described. ||33||

## Mathematical Proof

According to the method stated by Bhaskara, "Wherever a subtraction is required but the value to be subtracted is greater, it is done by reverse subtraction," this is clear. Lallacharya says the same in the Sanskrit proof starting with "If they become smaller," following the teachings of the ancient masters. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati has also stated exactly what Lalla said in the verse starting with "The desired breaths from the fraction of the ascensional difference." ||33||

## Now, the method for calculating the Divisor and the Antya is stated:

->The half-diameter of the diurnal circle, increased or decreased in the North and South respectively by the Earth-sine,<-
->Is the midday divisor. The radius increased or decreased by the sine of ascensional difference is the *Antya*.<- ||34||

**Vasanabhashya (Explanatory Commentary)** — The half-diameter of the diurnal circle for the desired day, when added to the daily *Kshitijya* <note>Earth-sine</note> in the signs starting with Aries <note>Northern Hemisphere</note> and subtracted in the signs starting with Libra <note>Southern Hemisphere</note>, becomes the midday divisor (*Dyudalantya-jya*). Similarly, the radius (*Vyasardha*) increased by the sine of ascensional difference in the Northern Hemisphere is the *Antya*; in the Southern Hemisphere, it is decreased to become the *Antya*. On the day of the Equinox, the midday divisor and the *Antya* are equal to the radius. 

The logic (*Vasana*) here: in the previous diagram, where the intersection occurs with the rod below the line of the equator's rising, tie one end of a string there and take the second end upward to the intersection of the meridian and the diurnal circles. That half-diameter of the diurnal circle sits slanted in a location with latitude. There, the distance between the rising-setting lines of the equator is added in the Northern Hemisphere. Then, dividing by the radius, the result is the "Great Gnomon" (*Brihad-shanku*). 

The logic follows two rules of three: 
1. If in the circle of the radius this is the sine, then in the diurnal circle, what would it be? The result is the divisor (*Chheda*). 
2. If for the radius-hypotenuse the *Lambajya* <note>sine of colatitude</note> is the upright, then for this obtained divisor, what is the upright? The result is the Great Gnomon. This should be demonstrated in the actual geometric figure. Now, another way of bringing forth the gnomon is stated by Aryabhata. ||34||

**Vividhabhashya (Detailed Commentary)** — In the Northern and Southern hemispheres, the half-diameter of the diurnal circle (**Dyujya**) increased or decreased respectively by the Earth-sine (**Kujya**) becomes the **Midday Divisor** (*Dyudalantyajya*). Similarly, in the two hemispheres, the radius (*Trijya*) increased or decreased by the sine of ascensional difference (**Charajya**) becomes the **Antya**. ||34||

### Here is the Proof:

The <term>hour circle</term><note>dhruvaprota-vrtta: a circle passing through the celestial poles</note> passing through the intersection of the horizon and the <term>diurnal circle</term><note>ahoratra-vrtta: the daily path of a star or planet</note> meets the <term>equinoctial circle</term><note>nadivrtta: the celestial equator</note> at a distance of the <term>ascensional difference</term><note>cara: the difference between the equatorial and local rising times</note> below or above the East cardinal point in the Northern and Southern hemispheres respectively. Parallel lines to the East-West line should be drawn through those points. The perpendicular line from the intersection of the planet's hour circle and the equinoctial circle onto those parallels is the <term>desired Antya</term><note>istāntyā: a specific sine value used in spherical trigonometry</note>. The distance between the East-West line and its parallel lines is the <term>sine of the ascensional difference</term><note>carajya</note>.

At midday, because the Sun is situated on the <term>meridian</term><note>yamyottara-vrtta</note>, the intersection of its hour circle and the equinoctial circle is the <term>zenith of the equator</term><note>niraksa-svastika</note>. Therefore, the perpendicular line from that point to the parallel of the East-West line is simply the vertical line of the equator. Thus, in the Northern hemisphere, by adding the segment of the equatorial vertical line (which is the <term>sine of the ascensional difference</term>) to the <term>radius</term><note>trijya</note> extending from the Earth's center to the equatorial zenith, the perpendicular <term>Antya</term> from the equatorial zenith to the parallel line is formed. In the Southern hemisphere, that value is found by subtracting the <term>sine of the ascensional difference</term> from the radius.

Similarly, in the Northern and Southern hemispheres, by adding or subtracting the <term>earth-sine</term><note>kujya</note>—which lies between the equatorial and local rising/setting lines—to the <term>radius of the diurnal circle</term><note>dyujya</note>, the result is the <term>Hrti</term><note>hrti: the hypotenuse of the gnomon shadow at noon</note>, which is the perpendicular distance to the local rising/setting line at midday.

In the *Siddhanta-Shekhara*:
> "The half-day-diameter <note>dyujya</note> increased or decreased by the earth-sine <note>kujya</note> is the midday-Hrti; the radius <note>trijya</note> with the sine of the ascensional difference <note>carajya</note> becomes the Antya, according to the Sun's hemisphere."

By this, Sripati <note>an 11th-century mathematician</note>, and Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, 12th-century astronomer</note> in:
> "The diurnal radius modified by the earth-sine is the Hrti; the radius modified by the sine of the ascensional difference is the Antya,"

are merely stating what was taught by the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta, the author of the original text</note>. ||34||

### Now, the Hrti and Antya are explained:

**Hindi Commentary:** In the Northern hemisphere, adding the <term>earth-sine</term> to the <term>diurnal radius</term>, and in the Southern hemisphere, subtracting the <term>earth-sine</term> from the <term>diurnal radius</term>, gives the **Hrti** (Midday-Hrti). Similarly, in the Northern hemisphere, adding the <term>sine of the ascensional difference</term> to the <term>radius</term>, and in the Southern hemisphere, subtracting it from the <term>radius</term>, gives the **Antya** (at midday). ||34||

### Proof

The hour circle passing through the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle meets the equinoctial circle at a distance of the ascensional difference below or above the East cardinal point in the Northern and Southern hemispheres respectively. From the intersection of the planet's hour circle and the equinoctial circle, the perpendicular line dropped onto the lines parallel to the East-West line is the "desired Antya." At midday, the Sun stays in the meridian; therefore, the perpendicular line from the intersection of the Sun's hour circle (meridian) and the equinoctial circle (the equatorial zenith) to the parallel of the East-West line is the equatorial vertical line itself. By adding the segment of the equatorial vertical line (the <term>sine of the ascensional difference</term>) to the radius from the Earth's center to the equatorial zenith in the Northern hemisphere, and subtracting it in the Southern hemisphere, the perpendicular line from the equatorial zenith to the parallel line is the **Antya**.

This occurs. Similarly, at midday, the <term>radius of the diurnal circle</term> <note>original: "dyujya"</note>—which is the circle of the day and night located at the center of the celestial sphere relative to the equatorial rising and setting line—is adjusted. By adding or subtracting the <term>earth-sine</term> <note>original: "kujya"; the distance between the horizon and the equatorial rising/setting line</note> according to the direction of the celestial hemisphere, the perpendicular line from the Sun to the local rising and setting line is found; this is called the <term>Hriti</term> <note>The "Hriti" is a specific sine-segment used in Indian trigonometry to calculate the sun's altitude</note>.

In the text *Siddhanta-Shekhara*, the scholar Sripati expresses this same principle in the verse beginning with "The half-day-radius joined with the earth-sine..." and Bhaskaracharya also confirms the teacher's words with the verse "By the earth-sine, the day-radius becomes the Hriti." ||34||

## Now, another method for calculating the desired shadow-hypotenuse is described:

> The midday-radius multiplied by the midday-shadow-hypotenuse and divided by the divisor <note>the "cheda" or instantaneous sine-altitude</note> results in the shadow-hypotenuse. Alternatively, the midday-radius multiplied by the midday-shadow-hypotenuse and divided by the sine-altitude results in the shadow-hypotenuse. ||35||

**Bhaskara’s Commentary:** Multiply the previously calculated midday-radius <note>the sine of the solar altitude at noon</note> by the midday shadow-hypotenuse of that day, and divide by the "divisor" <note>the sine of the altitude at the desired time</note>. The result is the shadow-hypotenuse for that specific time. The removal of the shadow is as explained before. The logic <note>vasana</note> is as follows: at midday, the midday-radius itself is the divisor. To find what the divisor is for a desired shadow-hypotenuse, one multiplies by the midday-hypotenuse and divides by the shadow-hypotenuse to get the divisor. One should demonstrate all these lines—the midday-radius and others—on the armillary sphere.

The second half of the verse explains another way to bring about the shadow-hypotenuse: "The midday-radius multiplied by the midday-shadow-hypotenuse and divided by the sine..." Or, multiply the previously calculated radius by the midday-shadow-hypotenuse and divide by the sine. The result is the instantaneous shadow-hypotenuse. The logic here is identical to the first half, because at midday, the radius is transformed into the diurnal circle's midday-radius. The sine at the desired time, transformed into the diurnal circle, is called the "divisor." Therefore, the rule of three <note>trairashika</note> logic applies here; the distinction is only in terminology. Thus, the method for finding the divisor from the remaining part of the day was told; now, a verse is given to find the divisor from the "natakala" <note>the time elapsed since noon</note> using the midday-radius. ||35||

**Vishnu’s Commentary:** The midday-radius (Hriti) multiplied by the midday-shadow-hypotenuse and divided by the divisor (the desired Hriti) gives the desired shadow-hypotenuse. Alternatively, the midday-radius multiplied by the midday-shadow-hypotenuse and divided by the sine (the desired radius) gives the desired shadow-hypotenuse. ||35||

### Mathematical Proof

Now, the Midday Sine-Altitude = $\frac{12 \times Radius}{Midday Shadow-Hypotenuse}$

Therefore, if by multiplying the Hriti one obtains the Midday Sine-Altitude, then by the desired Hriti, what is obtained?

The resulting Desired Sine-Altitude = $\frac{Midday \times Desired}{Hriti}$

By substituting the Midday Sine-Altitude = $\frac{12 \times Radius \times Desired}{Midday Shadow-Hypotenuse \times Hriti}$

$= \frac{12 \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Midday Shadow Hypotenuse}} \cdot \frac{\text{Desired Antya}}{\text{Antya}}$—Then, according to the statement of Bhaskara <note>referring to Bhaskara I or II, likely the latter given the commentary style</note>: "The sine of altitude multiplied by the radius and divided by the gnomon's shadow in the circle results in the hypotenuse of the shadow."

Thus $= \frac{12 \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Desired Gnomon}} = \text{Desired Hypotenuse} = \frac{12 \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Midday Shadow Hypotenuse} \times \text{Hriti}}{12 \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Desired Hriti}}$

$= \frac{\text{Midday Shadow Hypotenuse} + \text{Hriti}}{\text{Desired Hriti}} = \frac{\text{Midday Shadow Hypotenuse} \cdot \text{Antya}}{\text{Desired Antya}} \therefore \frac{\text{Hriti}}{\text{Desired Hriti}} = \frac{\text{Antya}}{\text{Desired Antya}}$

By this much, the teacher's <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> statement is proven. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, Sripati says the same thing as the teacher with the verse: "The first [hypotenuse] multiplied by the hypotenuse arising at midday and divided by the divisor, or the *Antya* multiplied by the midday hypotenuse and divided by the sine, is the hypotenuse." ||35||

->Now, another method for calculating the Desired Shadow Hypotenuse is described.<-

**Hindi Commentary:**—Multiply the <term>Hriti</term> <note>The hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow or a specific celestial chord</note> by the <term>Midday Shadow Hypotenuse</term> and divide by the <term>Desired Hriti</term>; the result is the Desired Shadow Hypotenuse. Alternatively, multiply the <term>Antya</term> <note>The maximum sine of the diurnal arc</note> by the Midday Shadow Hypotenuse and divide by the Desired Antya to find the Desired Shadow Hypotenuse. ||35||

### Mathematical Proof

$\text{Midday Gnomon} = \frac{\text{Radius} \cdot 12}{\text{Midday Shadow Hypotenuse}}$

Then we apply the proportion: If for the *Hriti* we obtain the Midday Gnomon, then what do we obtain for the Desired Hriti? From this, the <term>Desired Gnomon</term> is found: $\frac{\text{Midday Gnomon} \cdot \text{Desired Hriti}}{\text{Hriti}} = \text{Desired Gnomon}$.

Substituting the value of the Midday Gnomon into this:
$\frac{\text{Radius} \cdot 12 \cdot \text{Desired Hriti}}{\text{Midday Shadow Hypotenuse} \cdot \text{Hriti}} = \frac{\text{Radius} \cdot 12}{\text{Midday Shadow Hypotenuse}} \cdot \frac{\text{Desired Antya}}{\text{Antya}} = \text{Desired Gnomon}$.

Then by proportion: $\frac{\text{Radius} \cdot 12}{\text{Desired Gnomon}}$
$= \text{Desired Hypotenuse} = \frac{\text{Radius} \cdot 12 \cdot \text{Midday Shadow Hypotenuse} \cdot \text{Hriti}}{\text{Radius} \cdot 12 \cdot \text{Desired Hriti}} = \frac{\text{Midday Shadow Hypotenuse} \cdot \text{Hriti}}{\text{Desired Hriti}} = \frac{\text{Midday Shadow Hypotenuse} \cdot \text{Antya}}{\text{Desired Antya}}$

$\therefore \frac{\text{Hriti}}{\text{Desired Hriti}} = \frac{\text{Antya}}{\text{Desired Antya}}$

Thus, the teacher's statement is proven. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, the verse "The first multiplied by the hypotenuse arising at midday..." etc., as written in the Sanskrit proof, shows that Sripati is merely repeating what the Teacher (Brahmagupta) said. ||35||

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of spherical trigonometry and gnomon shadow calculations (Triprasna) from the previous section, focusing on the derivation of the 'Cheda' (divisor) or 'Ishtahriti' (instantaneous sine) using the time elapsed since noon.</meta>

<page-num>315</page-num>
<header>Chapter on the Three Problems</header>

The number of ghatikas <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> between the current time and midday are called the "noon-elevated" ghatikas. The versed sine <note>original: "utkramajya"; a trigonometric function</note> of those ghatikas, when converted to arc-units, is called the Versed Sine of the Hour Angle <note>original: "natotkramajya"</note>. Then, one should multiply that Versed Sine of the Hour Angle by the radius of the diurnal circle <note>original: "svahoratrardha"</note> and divide by the radius of the celestial sphere <note>original: "vyasardha"</note>. The result obtained is subtracted from the "Noon-End Versed Sine" <note>original: "dyudalantyotkramajya"</note>; the remainder is the Divisor <note>original: "cheda"</note>. 

Through this divisor, the shadow calculations are made. When the given ghatikas exceed fifteen ghatikas <note>representing 6 hours or 90 degrees from noon</note>, then the versed sine of fifteen ghatikas becomes the radius. For the remaining ghatikas, one should take the sine <note>original: "kramajya"</note> and add it to the radius. 

The rationale <note>original: "vasana"</note> for this is as follows: In the diurnal circle, at the point marked by the Sun, tie one end of a string. Lead the second end to the middle of the meridian circle—not in the other direction—and tie it at the same height on the diurnal circle. That string, stretched east-west, stays like a chord. The segment of the diurnal circle arc defined by this, which acts as a "bow-string" <note>the versed sine</note>, is the Versed Sine of the Hour Angle on the Noon-End string. This is produced in the circle of the radius. Therefore, it is transformed into the diurnal circle. 

The proportion is: "If in the circle of the radius this much is obtained, then in the diurnal circle, how much?" The result is the Versed Sine of the Hour Angle produced in the diurnal circle. When that is subtracted from the Noon-End Versed Sine, a portion of the Noon-End Versed Sine remains which is equal to the Divisor; that itself is the sine produced in the diurnal circle for those ghatikas. 

When the Sun's own horizon-distance is fifteen ghatikas, the Sun is on the six-o'clock circle <note>original: "unmandala"</note>. There, the Versed Sine of the Hour Angle is equal to the radius. When transformed into the diurnal circle, the result is simply the radius of the diurnal circle. When the hour angle ghatikas exceed fifteen, the Sun is between the horizon and the six-o'clock circle. There, below the six-o'clock circle, the sine <note>standard sine</note> begins again. Here, the sine of the ghatikas exceeding fifteen is added to the radius. By this, the Versed Sine of the Hour Angle in the diurnal circle for the ghatikas situated between the Sun and midday is found. Therefore, it is proven that this should be demonstrated on the armillary sphere as it stands. 

Now, he describes the calculation of the sine of the hour angle, the divisor, and the shadow quantity in verse 36:

**V. Ma.**—The Versed Sine of the Hour Angle from midday is found thus: multiply the versed sine of the hour angle (the time from midday to the desired time) by the radius of the diurnal circle (day-sine) and divide by the radius (tri-sine). The Noon-End Versed Sine (hridi) <unclear>java</unclear> (by another method) diminished by that result becomes the Divisor (desired-hriti). ||36||

---

->The Proof<-

At the point where the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle meets the polar circle and the equatorial circle <note>original: "nadivritta"</note>, a line parallel to the east-west line should be drawn. Above that, the vertical line from the celestial equator is the "Antya" <note>the total versed sine of the day-arc</note>. The vertical line from the intersection of the polar circle and equatorial circle above the planet is the "Ishtantya" <note>the instantaneous versed sine</note>. The perpendicular from the intersection of the polar circle and equatorial circle above the planet to the equatorial-zenith line is the Sine of the Hour Angle. From its base to the celestial equator is the Versed Sine of the Hour Angle. The Versed Sine of the Hour Angle subtracted from the "Antya" results in the "Ishtantya". Then, by proportion: "If the Antya is obtained for the Radius, then what is obtained for the Day-Sine?" This gives the Desired Divisor <note>original: "ishtahriti"</note>.

| Ishtantya × Day-Sine | | (Antya — Versed Sine of Hour Angle) × Day-Sine | | Antya × Day-Sine | | Versed Sine × Day-Sine |

<vocab>
**Versed Sine of the Hour Angle (Natotkramajya):** The distance from the meridian to the planet's position measured as a versed sine.
**Radius of the Diurnal Circle (Svahoratrardha):** The radius of the path the sun takes across the sky on a specific day.
**Radius (Vyasardha/Trijya):** The standard radius of the celestial sphere (usually 3438 minutes of arc).
**Noon-End Versed Sine (Dyudalantyajya):** The versed sine of the half-day arc.
**Divisor (Ishtahriti):** A mathematical value used to calculate the length of a shadow at a specific time.
**Horizon (Kshitija):** The circle where the sky meets the earth.
**Equatorial Circle (Nadivritta):** The celestial equator.
**Instantaneous Versed Sine (Ishtantya):** The specific versed sine value for a given moment.
</vocab>

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

$\frac{\text{Versed Sine of Hour Angle} \cdot \text{Day-Radius}}{\text{Radius}} = \text{Hriti} - \frac{\text{Versed Sine of Hour Angle} \cdot \text{Day-Radius}}{\text{Radius}}$

By this much, the teacher's statement is proven. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara* <note>A major astronomical treatise by Sripati, c. 1039 CE</note>, it is said: "The versed sine of the hour angle multiplied by the day-radius and divided by the radius, then subtracted from the noon-radius, results in the Hriti." By this, Sripati says exactly what is consistent with the teacher's <note>Brahmagupta's</note> instruction. ||36||

-> Now, another method for finding the Desired Hriti is described <-

**Hindi Commentary:** The versed sine of the hour angle <term>Nato-tkramajya: the versed sine of the time elapsed since or remaining until noon</term> at the desired time is multiplied by the day-radius <term>Dyujya: the radius of the sun's diurnal path</term> and divided by the radius <term>Trijya: the standard radius of 3438 minutes</term>. Subtracting the resulting quotient from the total Hriti <note>the hypotenuse of the sun's position relative to the celestial equator</note> gives the Desired Hriti. ||36||

-> Mathematical Proof <-

Draw a line parallel to the East-West line from the point where the diurnal circle intersects the horizon. The perpendicular line from the intersection of the diurnal circle and the hour circle to that line is the "Desired Antya" <note>the versed sine of the semi-diurnal arc</note>. The perpendicular from the intersection of the diurnal and hour circles to the vertical line of the equator is the sine of the hour angle. The distance from the base of the sine of the hour angle to the celestial zenith is the versed sine of the hour angle. By subtracting the versed sine of the hour angle from the total Antya, we get the Desired Antya. Then we apply the proportion: if we get the Desired Antya in the Radius, what do we get in the Day-Radius? From this proportion, the Desired Hriti is derived:

$\frac{\text{Desired Antya} \cdot \text{Day-Radius}}{\text{Radius}} = \frac{(\text{Antya} - \text{Versed Sine of Hour Angle}) \cdot \text{Day-Radius}}{\text{Radius}}$

$= \frac{\text{Antya} \cdot \text{Day-Radius}}{\text{Radius}} - \frac{\text{Versed Sine of Hour Angle} \cdot \text{Day-Radius}}{\text{Radius}}$

$= \text{Hriti} - \frac{\text{Versed Sine of Hour Angle} \cdot \text{Day-Radius}}{\text{Radius}}$

$=$ Desired Hriti. Thus, the teacher's statement is proven. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, Sripati says the same in the verse "The versed sine of the hour angle multiplied by the day-radius..." etc. ||36||

-> Now he describes another method for the Desired Antya and the different methods for calculating the shadow <-

**The Antya minus the versed sine of the hour angle becomes the divisor for the six sines separately.**
**With these two sines, there are thirty-six methods for calculating the shadow. ||37||**

**Vasanabhashya (Explanation):** This Antya, which was just brought forth, when diminished by the versed sine of the hours, becomes the radius <note>in a transformed coordinate system</note>. With that, the shadow calculations are performed as before. The logic here is shown through the noon-Antya-sine formula. By dividing these into parts, the variations arise. Why? Because of the variations from noon onwards. The teacher has provided six shadow calculations for each separately. Thus, from the hours of elevation <note>time since sunrise</note>, there are eighteen shadow calculations using the sine. Similarly, from the hour angle <note>time from noon</note>, there are <unclear>sine</unclear> and Antya-sine calculations, totaling eighteen, which makes thirty-six in all. # In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

By the phrase "twelve squares," four methods for bringing forth the shadow from the hypotenuse are established. From the divisor and the gnomon, two methods are already proven; therefore, there are six methods here for bringing forth the shadow from the divisor. The method "The sine multiplied by the half-day diameter and divided..." is not the only one. From the hypotenuse, the gnomon is the product of the cosine and the sine divided by the radius; from that gnomon, by the rule "the sine of the amplitude multiplied by twelve" and "or multiplied by twelve," two methods arise. By the rule "or the product multiplied by the sun (twelve)," two more methods arise from the gnomon as before. By the rule "the sine divided, or the last sine multiplied by the noon hypotenuse is the hypotenuse," one method arises from the hypotenuse. ## Here is the Proof:

The hour circle <term>dhruvaprota-vritta: a circle passing through the celestial poles</term> passing over the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle meets the celestial equator <term>nadivritta</term> below the east point in the northern hemisphere and above it in the southern hemisphere. From those two points, two lines should be drawn parallel to the east-west line. The perpendicular lines from the intersection of the hour circle and the celestial equator passing over the planet situated on those lines are the "desired last sines" <term>ishtantya</term> in the two hemispheres. At midday, the planet is on the meridian circle; therefore, the hour circle over the planet is the meridian itself, and its intersection with the celestial equator is the equatorial zenith. The perpendicular lines from the equatorial zenith onto the parallel lines are the "last sines" <term>antya</term> in the two hemispheres. The perpendicular from the intersection of the hour circle and celestial equator (over the planet at the desired position) onto the equatorial vertical line is the sine of the hour angle <term>natakala-jya</term>. From its base to the equatorial zenith is the versed sine of the hour angle <term>natakala-utkramajya</term>. The segment of the equatorial vertical line from the equatorial zenith to the parallel line is the "last sine" <term>antya</term>. The segment of the equatorial vertical line from the base of the sine of the hour angle to the parallel line is equal to the "desired last sine" <term>ishtantya</term>. If the versed sine of the hour angle is subtracted from the "last sine," then that same segment (from the base of the hour angle sine to the parallel line) becomes the "desired last sine." This is clearly observed on the globe. Thus, in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A major 12th-century work by Bhaskara II</note>, it is said: "The last sine diminished by the versed sine of the hour angle, which is the arrow, becomes the intended last sine," which is stated in exact accordance with the Teacher's <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> words. ||37||

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>The "Three Problems" (Triprasna) refer to the determination of direction, place, and time through the study of shadows.</note>

By the rule "multiplied by..." <note>original: *gunita*</note> there are two ways to find the shadow from the two gnomons. By "multiplied by twelve..." <note>original: *gunitam va dvadasabhih*</note> there are two ways to calculate the hypotenuse of the shadow from these two gnomons. By the rule "the divisor divided by the midday radius multiplied by the midday hypotenuse..." <note>original: *chedahrta dyudalantya dinarddhakarnaghni*</note> etc., there is one way to find the shadow hypotenuse from the divisor. Thus, there are four ways to find the shadow hypotenuse from the divisor. By "subtract from the square of twelve in the hypotenuse calculation..." <note>original: *karnahrteh sasodhaya dvadasavarge*</note> there are four ways to find the shadow from the shadow hypotenuse. Two ways are already established from the gnomon generated by the divisor. Therefore, there are six ways to find the shadow from the divisor. By "the sine multiplied by the half-day-circle..." <note>original: *jya svahoratrardhagatahrta*</note> etc., there is one way based on the hypotenuse. By "the product of the vertical sine..." <note>original: *lambaguno va ghatah sankuh*</note> etc., the sine of the amplitude <term>Hrijjya: the sine of the amplitude of the sun at the horizon</term> is found from the gnomon. By "multiplied by twelve" and "multiplied by twelve..." etc., there are also two ways. By "the product of the sun's multiplier..." <note>original: *ghato'rka guna*</note> etc., there are again two ways based on the gnomon as before. By "divided by the sine or the radius multiplied by the midday hypotenuse..." <note>original: *bhakta jyayathavantya dinarddhakarnahata karna*</note> etc., there is one way based on the hypotenuse. There are two ways to find the shadow from the desired radius. Previously, there were four divisions of the desired divisor and two divisions of the desired radius; these together make six divisions, from which thirty-six (36) methods of shadow calculation are derived. ||37||

## Mathematical Rationale
<note>The term 'Upapatti' refers to the geometric proof or demonstration of the rules.</note>

The celestial pole-prolongation circle passing through the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle lies below the eastern point in the Northern Hemisphere and above the eastern point in the Southern Hemisphere. Draw two lines parallel to the East-West line from those two points. The two perpendicular lines drawn from the intersection of the pole-prolongation circle and the equinoctial circle above the planet at the desired position are the "desired radius" <term>Istantya: the distance from the planet to the rising/setting line</term> in both hemispheres. At midday, the planet stays in the meridian circle; therefore, the perpendicular lines from the intersection of the planet's pole-prolongation circle (meridian) and the equinoctial circle (equatorial zenith) to the parallel lines are the "total radius" <term>Antya: the sine of the semi-diurnal arc</term> in both hemispheres. The perpendicular line from the intersection of the pole-prolongation circle and the equinoctial circle to the vertical line of the equator is the sine of the hour angle <note>original: *natakalajya*</note>. From its base to the equatorial zenith is the versed sine <note>original: *utkramajya*</note> of the hour angle. The segment of the equatorial vertical line from the equatorial zenith to the parallel line is the *Antya*. The segment of the equatorial vertical line from the base of the sine of the hour angle to the parallel line is equal to the *Istantya*. If we subtract the versed sine of the hour angle from the *Antya*, we get the segment of the equatorial vertical line from the base of the sine of the hour angle to the parallel line (*Istantya*). All these matters are clearly visible on the armillary sphere. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya says the same in accordance with the ancient teachers in the verse "by the versed sine of the hour angle..." <note>original: *natotkramajya khara ityanena*</note> etc. ||37||

->Now he describes the time since sunrise and the hour angle<-

> The radius multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divided by the shadow hypotenuse,
> Is the vertical sine. In the North and South, subtract or add the earth-sine, ||38||
> Multiply by the radius and divide by the half-diurnal circle; the arc of the result,
> Added in the Northern Hemisphere and subtracted in the Southern, gives the ascensional difference. ||39||

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

-> **Subtract the remaining breaths of the day from the forenoon or afternoon half-day.** <-
-> **The arc of the versed sine of the remainder from the radius is the breaths of the hour angle. (40)** <-

**Vasanabhashya <note>The author's own commentary or "explanation of causes"</note>:** — On a desired day and at a desired time, for whatever shadow one asks about the time, the hypotenuse of the shadow <term>chayakarna: the diagonal of the right-angled triangle formed by the gnomon and its shadow</term> at that time should be calculated. Then, one should divide the radius <term>trijya: the sine of 90 degrees, usually 3438 minutes</term> multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse <term>vishuvatkarna: the shadow hypotenuse at noon on the equinox</term> by that shadow hypotenuse. The result is the "divisor" <term>cheda</term>. In the northern and southern celestial hemispheres respectively, subtract or add the earth-sine <term>kshitijya</term> and multiply by the radius. Then divide by the radius of the diurnal circle <term>svahoratrardha</term>. The result is given a name; by taking its arc and subtracting it from the breaths of the ascensional difference <term>charadala-prana</term>, the remaining breaths are the elapsed or remaining time of the day.

Thus is the calculation of elapsed/remaining day. Now for the calculation of the hour angle <term>nata-kala: the time distance from the meridian</term>: subtract the result from the radius. When the value named "result" is subtracted from the end of the radius, the arc of the remaining versed sine <term>utkramajya</term> should be taken. The minutes of that arc are the breaths of the hour angle. Here too, if the subtraction is reversed, add it to the radius. Its versed sine or sine should be treated as stated. The number of minutes are the breaths of the hour angle.

The underlying logic <term>vasana</term> is as follows: just as the shadow was calculated from the time previously, here the time is established inversely from the shadow. This is demonstrated through the instrument. For example, from the zenith, the equinoctial shadow is the base of a triangle where twelve is the upright and the equinoctial hypotenuse is the hypotenuse. In the case of the desired gnomon-upright, since twelve is the multiplier in the first case and the divisor in the second, they cancel out. The equinoctial hypotenuse multiplied by the shadow hypotenuse and divided by the radius gives the "divisor." When the radius is subtracted in the northern hemisphere or added in the southern, the sine of the distance between the Sun and the equatorial horizon <term>unmandala</term> is produced in the diurnal circle. To transform this into the circle of the radius, a proportion is used: multiplied by the radius and divided by the radius of the diurnal circle. The result is the sine-form of the Sun's distance from the equatorial horizon transformed to the radius-scale. Its arc is the distance on the surface of the diurnal circle.

---

In the northern hemisphere, this is increased by the breaths of the ascensional difference, because it is situated below one's own horizon. In the southern hemisphere, it is subtracted from the sine. Thus, it is said: added in the north and subtracted in the south from the ascensional breaths, it gives the breaths elapsed in the day for the forenoon or afternoon. Where the "divisor" is smaller than the earth-sine, the Sun is between the equatorial horizon and the local horizon. The divisor then represents the Sun's position above the horizon. Therefore, by subtracting from the earth-sine, the remainder is the portion of the earth-sine between the Sun and the equatorial horizon. By transforming that to the radius and taking the arc, those are the breaths of the diurnal circle between the equatorial horizon and the Sun. Subtracting those from the breaths of the ascensional difference gives the elapsed or remaining breaths of the day. Since the distance between the equatorial horizon and the local horizon is the ascensional difference, the calculation of the elapsed day is proven.

Now, the logic for the hour angle: the value that remains equal to the "result" is the cord extending east-west from the diurnal circle marked by the Sun, as before. The logic of the formula "the versed sine from the end of the half-day" means that it is the arrow <term>shara: the versed sine</term> of the arc defined by that cord. By taking the arc of that sine-segment inversely, the breaths of the Sun's distance from the meridian are obtained. This is proven.

The remainder is the versed sine <note>utkramajya</note> of the hour angle. From the segments of the versed sine, its arc represents the hour angle in respiration units <note>asus</note> for the eastern and western hemispheres. (Verses 38-40)

### Mathematical Proof

$\frac{Radius \times 12}{Hypotenuse\ of\ Shadow} = Sine\ of\ Altitude$. By the ratio of the equatorial triangle, the $Corrected\ Radius\ of\ the\ Diurnal\ Circle\ (Ishtahriti) = \frac{Palakarna \times Sine\ of\ Altitude}{12} = \frac{Palakarna}{12}$ <note>Palakarna refers to the hypotenuse of the equatorial shadow</note>.

$\frac{Radius \times 12}{Hypotenuse\ of\ Shadow} = \frac{Palakarna \times Radius}{Hypotenuse\ of\ Shadow}$. In the northern hemisphere, by subtracting the earth-sine <note>kujya</note> from the corrected radius, and in the southern hemisphere by adding it, we obtain the "Kala" <note>a specific chord</note>. Multiplying this by the Radius and dividing by the radius of the diurnal circle <note>dyujya</note> gives the formula. Its arc is the time elapsed since rising relative to the celestial equator <note>unmandal</note>. By applying the ascensional difference <note>chara</note> correction, one finds the time elapsed since sunrise <note>unnatakala</note> at one's local station in the eastern or western hemispheres. By subtracting the previously obtained value (the cosine of the hour angle) from the Radius, one gets the versed sine of the hour angle. From the segments of the versed sine, its arc represents the measure of the hour angle <note>natakala</note> in the eastern and western hemispheres. (Verses 38-40)

### Now, another method for calculating the time elapsed and the hour angle is described:

> Multiply the square of the radius by the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow and divide by the product of the radius of the diurnal circle and the hypotenuse of the current shadow. In the northern hemisphere, subtract the sine of the ascensional difference; in the southern, add it. (Verse 41)
>
> To the resulting arc, add the respiration units of the ascensional difference in the northern hemisphere and subtract them in the southern. This gives the time elapsed since sunrise or remaining until sunset. (Verse 42)
>
> Subtract the result from the "Antya" <note>the total sine-versed chord of the day-half</note>; the arc of the remainder found through versed sines gives the hour angle in the eastern and western sky. (Verse 43)

**Vasanabhashya (Commentary):**—For the shadow from which the time elapsed or remaining is desired, first determine the hypotenuse of that shadow. Multiply the radius of the diurnal circle <note>svahoratrardha</note> by it. Then, divide the square of the radius (multiplied by the equinoctial shadow's hypotenuse) by that product. The result is a sine. In the northern hemisphere, subtract the sine of the ascensional difference <note>kshayavriddhijya</note> from this; in the southern, add it. Find the arc of the result. To this arc, add the respiration units of the ascensional difference in the northern hemisphere and subtract in the southern to find the time elapsed since sunrise or remaining until sunset. If, in the northern hemisphere, the sine of the ascensional difference cannot be subtracted from the result, subtract the result from it instead; subtract that arc from the ascensional difference to find the time. This is the calculation for time elapsed <note>unnatakala</note>. Now for the hour angle <note>natakala</note>: subtract the result from the "Antya." The arc of the remainder is called the versed sine arc; the minutes of that arc are the respiration units of the hour angle. If, after subtracting the result from the Antya, the remainder is greater than the radius, <unclear>then calculate the position using the sine; in the arc of the radius at the number 5400, the sines are the hour angle.</unclear>

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<page-num>323</page-num>

The breaths of time <note>Prāṇas: a unit of time equal to 4 seconds, or the time taken for one respiration</note> are derived here. This rationale <note>Vāsanā: the underlying logic or demonstration of a rule</note> follows a triple rule of three to bring the sine from the center of the earth. It is as follows: If for the hypotenuse of the shadow <note>Chāyā-karṇa</note> the base is twelve <note>the standard 12-digit gnomon</note>, then for the radius-hypotenuse, what is the result? The result is the **Great Sine of Altitude** <note>Bṛhacchanku</note>. Then the second rule: If for a base of twelve digits the hypotenuse is the equinoctial shadow-hypotenuse <note>Viṣuvat-karṇa</note>, then for the base of the Great Sine of Altitude, what is the result? This is the divisor. Then the third rule: If this divisor belongs to the diurnal circle <note>Svāhorātra-vṛtta</note>, then how much is it in the circle of the radius? The result is the sines.

In this state, twelve is the multiplier in the first step and the divisor in the second. The meaning is that the sine situated on the diurnal circle, which is positioned at the horizon, becomes the sine resting on the radius circle. In the Northern Hemisphere <note>Uttara-gola</note>, the **Sine of Earth-Sine** <note>Kṣaya-vṛddhi-jyā; also known as Carajyā</note> is subtracted from it. Because it is located below the horizon in the South, the sine becomes the interval between the horizon and the sub-horizontal circle. Its arc is the segment of the diurnal circle in that interval. In the Northern Hemisphere, this is added to the **Ascensional Difference** <note>Cara-prāṇas</note>. In the South, it is otherwise. By this, the breaths of time elapsed or remaining in the day from the horizon are found; the rest is as before.

In calculating the **Hour Angle** <note>Nata-kāla: time from noon</note>, whatever result is obtained is the sine; subtract that from the **Antyā** <note>the sine of the semi-diurnal arc</note>. The remaining sine-segment is the versed sine <note>Śara: literally 'arrow'</note> of the arc cut by the east-west line shown previously. Therefore, the logic for bringing the versed sine of the arc should be applied as before. When the result cannot be subtracted from the Sine of Earth-Sine, the logic of reverse subtraction etc. is applied as before. In calculating the time, if after subtracting the result from the Antyā, a value greater than the radius remains, the logic for finding the arc is also established as before. One should demonstrate all of this as it stands on the **Armillary Sphere** <note>Gola</note>. Now, having described the calculation of the Antyā-sine from the **Time since Sunrise** <note>Unnata-kāla</note>, the author speaks an Arya verse on the calculation of the Hour Angle by the inverse method. [Verses 41-43]

**V. M. —** One should take the result of the square of the radius multiplied by the equinoctial shadow-hypotenuse <note>Pala-karṇa</note> and divided by the semi-diurnal radius <note>Dyu-jyā</note> and the shadow-hypotenuse. In the Northern Hemisphere, that result is decreased by the **Sine of Ascensional Difference** <note>Carajyā</note>, and in the Southern Hemisphere, it is increased. The arc of that result, when increased by the breaths of the ascensional difference in the North and decreased in the South, gives the breaths of the day elapsed or remaining <note>Unnata-kāla</note> in the eastern or western halves of the sky. Subtract the previously obtained result from the **Antyā**; with the remainder, using the segments of the versed sines, the arc should be made. Then the breaths of the **Hour Angle** <note>Nata-kāla</note> for the eastern and western halves of the sky are found. [Verses 41-43]

->The Proof Here<-

<term>Desired Sine of Altitude</term> <note>Iṣṭa-śaṅku</note> = $\frac{Radius \cdot 12}{Shadow-Hypotenuse}$
Then, by the proportion of the latitude-triangle, the <term>Desired Sine of Amplitude</term> <note>Iṣṭa-hṛti</note> = $\frac{Equinoctial-Hypotenuse \cdot Desired-Altitude}{12}$

= $\frac{Pala-karṇa}{12} \cdot \frac{Radius \cdot 12}{Shadow-Hypotenuse} = \frac{Pala-karṇa \cdot Radius}{Shadow-Hypotenuse}$
Then, if by the <term>Day-Radius</term> <note>Dyu-jyā</note> the Desired Sine of Amplitude is obtained, then by the <term>Radius</term> <note>Tri-jyā</note> what is obtained?
The Desired Antyā = $\frac{Pala-karṇa \cdot Radius \cdot Radius}{Shadow-Hypotenuse \cdot Day-Radius} = \frac{Pala-karṇa \cdot Radius^2}{Shadow-Hypotenuse \cdot Day-Radius} =$ Result.

Then, according to the Northern or Southern Hemisphere:
Desired Antyā $\mp$ <term>Sine of Ascensional Difference</term> <note>Carajyā</note> = Chord-line.
The arc of this = Arc of the chord-line.
In the North/South Hemispheres: Arc of the chord-line $\pm$ <term>Ascensional Difference</term> <note>Carāsu</note> = Time elapsed/remaining in the day = <term>Time since Sunrise</term> <note>Unnata-kāla</note>.

> "Or if the square of the radius <note>original: "trijya"</note> is multiplied by the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "palakarna"</note> and divided by the product of the radius... the result, when increased or decreased by the sine of the ascensional difference <note>original: "charajya"</note> as prescribed..."

> "The square of the radius multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divided by the product of the day-radius and the desired shadow-hypotenuse, etc."

Bhaskaracharya has also stated everything in accordance with the original Teacher's <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> instructions. ||41-42-43||

### Now, the "Elevated Time" and "Hour Angle" are described by another method

**Hindi Commentary:** — Multiply the square of the radius by the square of the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>Note: The text here simplifies the ratio</note> and divide by the product of the day-radius <note>original: "dyujya"</note> and the hypotenuse of the desired shadow <note>original: "ishtachhaya karna"</note>. In the Northern Hemisphere, subtract the sine of the ascensional difference from this result; in the Southern Hemisphere, add it. To the arc of this value, add the ascensional difference breaths in the North and subtract in the South. This gives the elapsed breaths of the day in the morning (Eastern hemisphere) or the remaining breaths in the evening (Western hemisphere)—this is the "Elevated Time" <note>original: "unnata kala"</note>. Subtracting the previously obtained result from the "Final" <note>Antya</note> leaves a remainder; by taking the arc of this remainder using versed sine segments, the measure of the hour angle <note>original: "natasu"</note> is found for the Eastern and Western hemispheres. ||41-42-43||

### Mathematical Proof

Desired Sine-Altitude <note>original: "ishtashanku"</note> = (Radius × 12) / Desired Shadow-Hypotenuse. By the proportion of the latitude-triangle, the Desired Sine-Amplitude <note>original: "ishtahriti"</note> = (Equinoctial Hypotenuse × Sine-Altitude) / 12 = (Equinoctial Hypotenuse / 12) × (Radius × 12 / Desired Shadow-Hypotenuse) = (Equinoctial Hypotenuse × Radius) / Desired Shadow-Hypotenuse.

Now the proportion: If the day-radius gives the Desired Sine-Amplitude, what does the Radius give?

From this proportion, the "Desired Final" <note>Ishtantya</note> is derived: (Equinoctial Hypotenuse × Radius / Desired Shadow-Hypotenuse) × (Radius / Day-radius) = (Equinoctial Hypotenuse × Radius²) / (Desired Shadow-Hypotenuse × Day-radius) = Desired Final = Result. In the Northern and Southern hemispheres respectively: Desired Final ∓ Sine of Ascensional Difference = Chord <note>Sutra</note>. The arc of this = Arc-Chord. In the Northern and Southern hemispheres: Arc-Chord ± Ascensional Difference Breaths = Elevated Time in the Eastern/Western hemispheres. Furthermore, Final — Result = Final — Desired Final = Versed Sine of the hour angle. By taking the arc of this from versed sine segments, the measure of the hour angle is found. Sripati, in the *Siddhanta-shekhara* with the verse "Or if the square of the radius is multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse..." etc., and Bhaskaracharya with "The square of the radius multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse..." etc., have spoken in total agreement with the Teacher. ||41-42-43||

->Now, he speaks again by another method<-

> **The square of the radius multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse, divided by the day-radius and the shadow-hypotenuse, is subtracted from the Final.**
> **The arc of the remaining versed sine gives the breaths of the hour angle; the remainder are the breaths of the elevated time. ||44||**

**Vāsanā Commentary:** If the value is greater than the sine, or if the sine is greater than the value used for calculating the shadow, the time in *ghatikas* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> becomes greater than fifteen. This refers to their R-sine <term>Kramajyā: the standard sine function</term>. When that is added to the radius, it becomes the versine <term>Utkramajyā: the versed sine or versine function</term>. Thus, in calculating the hour angle <note>time from noon</note>, an addition of the arcs must be performed. This is what is meant: if the result subtracted from the *antyā* <note>the sine of the semi-diurnal arc</note> is greater than the radius, then one must add the arc of the excess sine to the arc of the radius to find the arc of the versine. This meaning is explained in the formula along with its underlying rationale. Now, regarding the calculation of the time since sunrise <note>unnatakāla</note> for the Sun at that position, the specific procedure is stated in the latter half of the verse:

->In the case of inverse subtraction, the ascensional difference <term>Carāsavaḥ: the difference in time between equatorial and local rising</term> is subtracted; the rest is as before. In the northern hemisphere, the result is diminished by the earth-sine <term>Kṣitijyā: the sine of the interval between the horizon and the celestial equator</term>—<-

In the case mentioned where the earth-sine is greater, one performs the inverse calculation, multiplies by the radius, and finds the arc from the semi-diurnal circle. Wherever such a procedure is possible, it has been explained by us previously along with the rationale. The procedure for finding the shadow from the time since sunrise in that region was mentioned earlier in the verse beginning "The small, less than the question..." by the Teacher <note>referring to the original author, likely Bhāskara I or Brahmagupta</note>, and I have explained it with the rationale. By "the rest is as before," I have shown only the remainder here. Generally, this is how time is calculated from the shadow. The answer to the question "Who knows how to calculate the shadow at midday for a desired day by taking the Sun's declination and the latitude?" is given in four verses. || 46 ||

**Scientific Commentary:** For however many minutes <note>kalā</note> exceed the 90-degree minutes (5400'), the R-sine of those minutes added to the radius (tri-jyā) becomes the versine of the arc exceeding 90 degrees. Similarly, for a versine greater than the radius, the arc is found by adding the arc of the excess sine to the 90-degree minutes (5400'). In the northern hemisphere, if the time-degrees since sunrise are less than the ascensional difference, then an inverse subtraction occurs. In that case, the ascensional difference is subtracted from the arc (time-degrees), and that sine is designated as the "inverse formula." Therefore, the rest of the division by the divisor etc. should be known as before, but using the logic that the difference between positive and negative values is a sum, a subtraction should be performed where a sum is indicated. || 46 ||

### Rationale here

The rationale here should be understood as being in the form of the explanation itself. It should be observed by the wise that Śrīpati has simply clarified what was stated by the Teacher. || 46 ||

### Proof

The proof should be understood as being contained within the commentary itself. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, through verses such as "greater than the ghatis of the lunar day," Sripati has simply clarified the teachings of the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note>. ||46||

->Now, the calculation of the degrees of altitude at midday, the calculation of the midday shadow, and the calculation of the central shadow<-
->as well as the various methods for calculating the day-radius and other factors:<-

The sum or difference of the degrees of the Sun's declination at midday and the degrees of local latitude—depending on whether they are in the same or opposite directions—results in the <term>zenith distance</term><note>original: "natabhaga"; the angular distance from the zenith</note>. By subtracting these zenith distance degrees from ninety, the remaining degrees are the <term>altitude</term><note>original: "unnatabhaga"</note>. ||47||

The sine of the zenith distance multiplied by twelve and divided by the sine of the altitude degrees yields the result: the desired midday shadow for that day. Or, by the previously mentioned methods, the midday shadow is found. ||48||

The radius multiplied by twelve and divided by the sine of the altitude is the <term>hypotenuse</term><note>of the shadow</note>. Alternatively, the midday shadow is the square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and twelve <note>the height of the gnomon</note>. ||49||

The <term>midday chord</term><note>original: "dyudalantya jya"</note> may be used as the divisor, or the midday shadow can be found by the previously mentioned methods. Or, the midday shadow can be found in many ways using the midday chord as the divisor. ||50||

**Vasanabhashya (Commentary):** Having calculated the sine of the true solar declination for the midday of the desired day, the zenith distance degrees are found. These are the degrees of the Sun's declination at midday; by adding them to one's own latitude if they are in the same direction, or taking the difference if they are in opposite directions, the zenith distance degrees are produced. The direction is known from their sum. In the case of the Sun's position, the direction of the remainder is the direction of the zenith distance. By subtracting those from ninety, the remaining degrees become the altitude degrees. Then, taking the sine of the zenith distance, multiply by twelve and divide by the sine of the altitude. The result is the midday shadow of a twelve-digit gnomon in <term>angulas</term><note>traditional Indian inches</note>. In this way, by whatever proportion the sine of the zenith distance is multiplied and divided by the sine of the altitude, the midday shadow for that midday is produced. "By the previously mentioned methods" means that by assuming the midday measurements and using the formulas for the day-radius etc., the shadow at midday can be found in many ways through the elapsed time. Alternatively, one should divide the radius multiplied by twelve by the sine of the altitude; the result is the midday hypotenuse. The midday shadow is then found by the method of the square root of the difference of the squares of the hypotenuse and twelve. Or, by treating the midday chord as the divisor, the midday shadow is calculated by that method. Or, by assuming the midday sine and using the sine-divisor or other methods mentioned, the midday shadow should be calculated. Its southern or northern direction is determined by the zenith distance...

### Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>original: "Tri-praśna-adhikāra"; the "Three Problems" refer to the fundamental astronomical determinations of direction, place (latitude), and time.</note>

The orientation is north-south, and it becomes south-facing with the northern [planets/points]. That south-facing portion occurs where the latitude is less than twenty-four degrees. Here is the underlying rationale <term>vāsanā</term><note>The geometric or logical explanation behind a mathematical rule.</note>: Midday occurs when the thousand-rayed sun enters the local meridian circle.

The local latitude is the distance between the prime vertical <term>samamaṇḍala</term><note>The east-west vertical circle.</note> and the celestial equator <term>viṣuvanmaṇḍala</term>. When the sun is north of the equator and south of the prime vertical, the degrees of declination <term>krānti</term> are subtracted from the degrees of latitude. When the zenith distance <term>natabhāga</term><note>Literally "degrees of bowing"; the angular distance from the zenith.</note> is less than the local latitude because the sun is attached to the prime vertical, the degrees of distance from the prime vertical are the zenith distance. If the sun is south of the prime vertical, it does not enter the prime vertical, and the latitude degrees are subtracted from the declination degrees. Because the local latitude is less than the northern declination, the zenith distance is measured from the equator. In the southern hemisphere, the distance from the prime vertical is south of the equator by the degrees of local latitude, and then further by the degrees of southern declination. Therefore, their sum always constitutes the zenith distance. Thus it is said: the zenith distance is equal to the sum or difference of the midday sun's declination and the latitude, depending on whether they are in the same or opposite directions.

When the northern declination is equal to the latitude, there is an absence of shadow for the gnomon <term>śaṅku</term> at midday, because the sun is situated exactly in the middle of the prime vertical; at that time, the zenith distance is zero. Subtracting those degrees from ninety, the remainder is the altitude <term>unnatabhāga</term>. Since the distance from the southern or northern horizon to the center of the prime vertical along the meridian is ninety degrees, the altitude degrees are determined accordingly. Thus, the sine of the zenith distance <term>dṛgjya</term> is like the sine of latitude, and the sine of altitude is the gnomon, like the sine of co-latitude. The hypotenuse <term>karṇa</term> is the radius <term>vyāsārddha</term>; all this should be demonstrated on the armillary sphere in the meridian circle.

To find the shadow by the Rule of Three <term>trairāśika</term> when the sun is north or south of the prime vertical: If the sine of altitude is the gnomon and the sine of zenith distance is the shadow, then for a gnomon of twelve digits, what is the result? The result is the midday shadow. Thus it is said: the sine of zenith distance multiplied by twelve and divided by the sine of altitude is the shadow for any desired midday. Even with a gnomon of a desired size, or by calculating the elapsed time from the remainder of the day, one can bring about the shadow as stated; this is consistent because of the nature of time and the specific rationale of the diurnal circle. Alternatively, the shadow can be found by the Rule of Three using the hypotenuse: if the sine of altitude is the gnomon and the radius is the hypotenuse, then for a twelve-digit gnomon, what is the result? The result is the hypotenuse of the shadow <term>vibhā-karṇa</term>. Subtracting the square of the gnomon from the square of that hypotenuse and taking the square root, the shadow is produced. This is also logical. Or, using the formula for the "great last sine" <term>antyājyā</term> shown previously, by assuming midday as the limit, the calculation of the rising-sine <term>udayajyā</term> for the purpose of finding the shadow is also appropriate. Therefore, everything is consistent and should be shown on the sphere as it exists. If one knows the gnomon of the non-equinoctial circle without dispute, he illuminates the northern hemisphere... [Verses 47-50].
