<page-num>330</page-num>

The difference between these two results in the zenith distance <note>the angular distance from the point directly overhead</note> at midday. By subtracting the zenith distance from ninety, the remainder should be understood as the altitude <note>the angular height above the horizon</note>. ||47||

->**Here is the Demonstration**<-

If at the time of midday the Sun is on the meridian circle between the zenith <note>the point directly above the observer</note> and the celestial equatorial zenith <note>the point directly above the equator</note>, then the distance from the Sun to the equatorial zenith is the Sun's declination <note>the Sun's distance north or south of the celestial equator</note>. The distance between the observer's zenith and the equatorial zenith is the latitude. Here, the difference between these two is the zenith distance from the Sun to the zenith. If the Sun is south of the equatorial zenith, then the distance from the Sun to the equatorial zenith is the declination. In this case, because the latitude and the Sun's declination are in the same direction (latitude is always considered south relative to the zenith in this context, and the Sun is south of the celestial equator, so the direction of declination is also south), the sum of the two results in the Sun's midday zenith distance. Since the distance from the zenith to the horizon is ninety degrees, by subtracting the zenith distance, the midday altitude from the Sun to the horizon is obtained. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*:

> "The sum or difference of the arc of declination of the midday sun and the latitude—depending on whether they are in the same or different directions—results in the degrees of the north-south zenith distance of the Sun from the zenith. These subtracted from ninety become the altitude degrees." <note>original Sanskrit: "madhyandinoṣṇakiraṇāpamachāpabhāsvākṣāṃśayogavivaraṃ..."</note>

This was stated by Shripati. In the *Siddhanta-shiromani*:

> "The latitude and its complement, when adjusted by the declination, become the zenith distance and altitude at midday. Or, the zenith distance subtracted from ninety becomes the altitude, and the altitude subtracted from ninety becomes the zenith distance." <note>original Sanskrit: "palāvalambāvapamena saṃskṛtau..."</note>

This statement by Bhaskara is exactly in accordance with what the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> has said. ||47||

->**Now the method for calculating the midday zenith distance and altitude is described**<-

**Hindi Commentary:** By adding the Sun's midday declination and the latitude when they are in the same direction, and taking their difference when they are in different directions, the Sun's midday zenith distance is found. By subtracting the zenith distance from ninety degrees, the remainder is the altitude. ||47||

->**Demonstration**<-

At midday, if the Sun is between the zenith and the equatorial zenith, then the Sun's midday declination from the Sun to the equatorial zenith is toward the north because the Sun is north of the celestial equator; however, the direction of latitude is always south. Therefore, by taking the difference between the Sun's declination and the latitude (which are in different directions), the zenith distance from the Sun to the zenith is found. If the Sun is south of the equatorial zenith, then because the directions of latitude and declination are both south, their sum results in the zenith distance. By subtracting the zenith distance from the ninety degrees between the zenith and the horizon, the midday altitude from the equatorial zenith to the horizon is obtained. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, Shripati—through the verse "The sum or difference of the arc of declination..."—and in the *Siddhanta-shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya—through the verse "The latitude and its complement..."—have said exactly the same as the Teacher. ||47||

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>The "Three Problems" refer to the determination of time, direction, and place using a gnomon's shadow.</note>

**Vāsanā-Bhāṣya (Explanatory Commentary):** — When the northern declination <note>The angular distance of the Sun north of the celestial equator</note> is less than the sine of the local latitude, the Sun enters the **prime vertical** <term>Samamaṇḍala: the vertical circle passing exactly East and West</term> on that day. To calculate the **gnomon** <term>Śaṅku: a vertical pillar used to measure shadows</term> at the moment of entry, the ancient teachers provided a method: the sine of declination multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divided by the equinoctial shadow results in the gnomon at the prime vertical. This is the "Great Gnomon."

In this context, one should demonstrate the Sun’s rising-setting line and the diurnal circle on the armillary sphere. At that moment, the prime vertical itself acts as the observation circle. Where it intersects the diurnal circle, the plumb-line hangs down. This line touches the east-west line on the ground. That length is the gnomon. At the moment of entering the prime vertical, the distance from the base of the gnomon (placed on the local east-west line) to the rising-setting line is the "gnomon-amplitude" <note>Śaṅkutala</note>, which is equal to the **amplitude** <term>Agrā: the distance of the rising Sun from the East point</term>.

Therefore, this calculation of the prime vertical gnomon is derived from two proportions:
1. If the radius (hypotenuse) corresponds to the cosine of latitude (side), what does the sine of declination (side) correspond to? The result is the amplitude, which at the moment of prime vertical entry is equal to the gnomon-amplitude.
2. Then the second proportion: If the sine of latitude (side) gives the cosine of latitude (gnomon), what gnomon does the gnomon-amplitude (equal to the amplitude) give?

In place of the cosine of latitude, we use 12 (the standard gnomon height); in place of the sine of latitude, we use the equinoctial shadow; and in place of the radius, we use the equinoctial hypotenuse. Because the value 12 acts as a divisor in the first proportion and a multiplier in the second, they cancel out. Thus, the sine of declination multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divided by the equinoctial shadow yields the gnomon at the prime vertical.

Now, if the northern declination is greater than the latitude, the Sun reaches midday north of the prime vertical. In that case, there is no entry into the prime vertical, and the midday shadow faces south. If the northern declination equals the latitude, the Sun is seen in the prime vertical exactly at midday; then the gnomon is the radius. If there is southern declination, the rising and setting occur south of the prime vertical. All of this should be demonstrated on the sphere. By marking the Sun's position at the intersections of the diurnal and vertical circles, one sees that at the equator <note>Nirakṣadeśa: the place with no latitude</note>, the Sun never enters the prime vertical except on the equinox, because the celestial sphere does not tilt north or south there.

Alternatively, he provides an *Arya* verse to explain the calculation of the prime vertical gnomon in two ways. ||51||

**Vivarana-mārga (Path of Explanation):** — If the northern declination (sine of declination) is less than the sine of latitude, then the sine of declination multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divided by the equinoctial shadow is the gnomon when the Sun is in the prime vertical (the **Prime Gnomon**). ||51||

->**The Proof**<-

The equinoctial shadow is the base. Twelve is the upright. The equinoctial hypotenuse is the hypotenuse. This is the first "latitude-triangle." The sine of declination is the base. The difference between the diurnal side and the earth-sine is the upright. The prime gnomon is the hypotenuse. This is the second latitude-triangle. Because these two are similar triangles, the proportion is:
$\frac{\text{Equinoctial Hypotenuse} \cdot \text{Sine of Declination}}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}}$ = Prime Gnomon.

Only when the northern declination is less than the latitude does the Sun enter the prime vertical. In the *Siddhānta Śiromaṇi*, **Bhāskara** <note>Bhāskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note> stated: "The Sun enters the prime vertical when the declination is small," following the same sequence described by the ancient teachers. ||51||

The Sun enters the prime vertical only when the northern declination is less than the latitude. ->Now another method for finding the Prime Vertical Gnomon is stated<-

> The sine of the Sun's longitude <note>original: "surya-jya"</note> should be multiplied by the sine of the maximum declination <note>original: "jinabhagajya" - the sine of 24 degrees</note> and divided by the sine of the latitude.

**Sanskrit Commentary** — Multiply the sine of the Sun's longitude by the sine of the maximum declination (meaning by 1397 <note>note: a specific value used in ancient trigonometry</note>) and divide by the sine of the latitude. The result is the Prime Vertical Gnomon. The logic here involves three proportions <note>term: "trairashika" - the rule of three</note>:
1. If for the radius <note>original: "vyasardha"</note> we get the maximum declination, what do we get for the given sine of the Sun? Result: Sine of declination.
2. If for the cosine of latitude <note>original: "lambaka"</note> as the upright we get the radius as the hypotenuse, what do we get for the sine of declination as the upright? Result: Amplitude <note>original: "agra"</note>.
3. If for the sine of latitude as the base we get the cosine of latitude as the gnomon, what do we get for the amplitude as the base?
In this setup, the radius appears as a divisor in the first proportion and a multiplier in the second, so they cancel out. Similarly, the cosine of latitude appears as a divisor in the second and a multiplier in the third, so they cancel. Thus, the sine of the Sun multiplied by the sine of maximum declination and divided by the sine of latitude gives the Prime Vertical Gnomon.
For the second method: If for the equinoctial shadow we have a 12-digit gnomon, then for the amplitude what gnomon do we get? The result is the Prime Vertical Gnomon. The spatial logic should be demonstrated on the armillary sphere as before. This verse answers the question of one who knows the relationship between the latitude and the prime vertical hypotenuse. ||52||

**Scientific Commentary** — The sine of the Sun's longitude multiplied by the sine of 24 degrees and divided by the sine of latitude is the Prime Vertical Gnomon. Alternatively, the amplitude multiplied by twelve and divided by the equinoctial shadow is the Prime Vertical Gnomon. ||52||

## Here is the Proof

If the Sine of the maximum declination <note>original: "jinajya" (24 degrees)</note> is obtained by the Radius <note>original: "trijya"</note>, then what is obtained by the Sine of the Sun's longitude <note>original: "ravibhujajya"</note>?
**Declination Sine = (Max Declination Sine · Longitude Sine) / Radius**. 
The Sine of Latitude <note>original: "akshajya"</note> is the base; the Sine of Co-latitude <note>original: "lambajya"</note> is the upright; the Radius is the hypotenuse. This is the first "Latitude-Triangle" <note>term: Akshakshetra; a right-angled triangle used in Indian astronomy to relate terrestrial latitude to celestial coordinates</note>. 
The Sine of Declination <note>original: "krantijya"</note> is the base; the "Earth-sine-risen-support" <note>original: "kujyonnatadhriti"</note> is the upright; and the Prime Vertical Gnomon <note>original: "samasanku"; the shadow-casting pole's height when the sun is on the prime vertical</note> is the hypotenuse. This is the second Latitude-Triangle. Because these two are similar, the proportion is: if the Sine of Latitude yields the Radius, then what does the Sine of Declination yield?
**Prime Vertical Gnomon = (Radius × Declination Sine) / Sine of Latitude = (Radius / Sine of Latitude) · (Max Declination Sine · Longitude Sine / Radius)**
**= (Max Declination Sine · Longitude Sine) / Sine of Latitude**.
Furthermore, the Equinoctial Shadow <note>original: "palabha"</note> is the base; twelve <note>the standard height of the gnomon in digits</note> is the upright; and the Equinoctial Hypotenuse <note>original: "palakarna"</note> is the hypotenuse. This is the first Latitude-Triangle. The Sine of Amplitude <note>original: "agra"</note> is the base; the Prime Vertical Gnomon is the upright; and the "Support" <note>original: "dhriti"</note> is the hypotenuse. This is the second Latitude-Triangle. Because these are similar, the proportion is: if the Equinoctial Shadow yields an upright of twelve, then what does the Sine of Amplitude yield?
**Prime Vertical Gnomon = (12 · Sine of Amplitude) / Equinoctial Shadow**.
By this, everything stated by the Teacher <note>likely referring to Bhaskara II</note> is proven. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Sripati stated:

> "Multiply the Sine of the Sun's longitude separately by the Sine of the maximum declination <note>original: "jinabhaga-maurvi"</note> and divide by the Sines of the Latitude and Co-latitude. The first result is known as the Prime Vertical Gnomon."

The calculation of the Prime Vertical Gnomon has been described here in accordance with what the Teacher stated. ||52||

---

### Now, another method for determining the Prime Vertical Gnomon is stated:

**Hindi Commentary** — By multiplying the Sine of the Sun's longitude by the Sine of the maximum declination and dividing by the Sine of Latitude, the Prime Vertical Gnomon is found. Or (alternatively), by multiplying the Sine of Amplitude by twelve and dividing by the Equinoctial Shadow, the Prime Vertical Gnomon is found. ||52||

## Proof

If we find the Sine of maximum declination within the Radius, then what do we find in the Sine of the Sun's longitude? From this comes the Sine of Declination:
**(Max Declination Sine · Longitude Sine) / Radius = Declination Sine**.
The Sine of Latitude is the base, the Sine of Co-latitude is the upright, and the Radius is the hypotenuse; this is the first Latitude-Triangle. The Sine of Declination is the base, the "Earth-sine-risen-support" is the upright, and the Prime Vertical Gnomon is the hypotenuse; this is the second Latitude-Triangle. Both are similar, therefore we calculate the proportion: if we find the Radius in the Sine of Latitude, then what do we find in the Sine of Declination? From this comes the Prime Vertical Gnomon:
**(Radius · Declination Sine) / Sine of Latitude = Prime Vertical Gnomon = (Radius / Sine of Latitude) · (Max Declination Sine · Longitude Sine / Radius) = (Max Declination Sine · Longitude Sine) / Sine of Latitude**. Also...

### Now he describes the method for finding the hypotenuse of the shadow in the Prime Vertical

> Multiply the twelve-digit equinoctial shadow by either the sine of the latitude or the sine of the co-latitude separately.
> When divided by the sine of declination, the results are the two hypotenuses of the shadow in the Prime Vertical; the shadows are found as before. || 53 ||

**Vāsanā-bhāṣya <note>Explanatory Commentary</note>:** — One should multiply the sine of latitude by twelve and divide by the sine of declination. The result is the hypotenuse of the shadow at the time of entry into the Prime Vertical. Alternatively, multiply the sine of co-latitude <note>lambajyā</note> by the equinoctial shadow and divide by the sine of declination. The result is the hypotenuse of the shadow at the entry into the Prime Vertical. Then, the calculation of that shadow is as before, and the calculation of the time in *ghatikas* <note>units of 24 minutes</note> is as previously stated. Here, in the absence of the divisor and result, the calculation of the shadow is established through three proportions... <note>The text describes complex geometric derivations involving the celestial sphere</note> ...If the gnomon of the Prime Vertical hypotenuse is twelve, then the Prime Vertical gnomon is the result. Then the second: if the co-latitude is the gnomon, what is the latitude-equivalent gnomon? ... Then the third: if the square of the radius is the co-latitude perpendicular, then having doubled the amplitude-hypotenuse, subtract it from the square of the radius. The square root of the remainder is the corner-gnomon <note>koṇaśaṅku: the gnomon when the sun is in the intermediate directions like NE, SW</note>. For northern declination, in the northern intermediate directions, and for southern, in the southern—having thus brought the gnomon, the shadow should be calculated as before; that is the corner-shadow. Just as with one's own shadow, the calculation of the elapsed or remaining time in *ghatikas* is also as before.

The underlying logic <term>vāsanā: the geometric or physical explanation of a rule</term> is as follows: In the sphere, just as on one's own horizon, a cord extends east-west through the center of the earth, and another extends north-south. (b) One should place another pair of cords at the center of the earth; one extending Northeast to Southwest, and the second extending Southeast to Northwest. Then, having tied cords at all four corners, one should tie four other cords in the form of sines from corner to corner. Thus, a square figure is produced. Including the two diagonals, the intersection of the diagonals is in the middle of the terrestrial globe. Then, from the north-south and east-west cords, one should imagine four square fields... these are connected to all four intermediate directions. They possess diagonal cords for every corner-cord emerging from the center of the earth. Just as the amplitude-cord of that day is tied north-south on one's own horizon at the east and west points according to the method shown in the chapter on the sphere, one <unclear>should tie</unclear> the east-west rising-setting cord at its ends. Then, having placed the diurnal circle <unclear>in its own field</unclear>, the vertical circle from the corner—

Place the points accordingly. Having generated two <term>Svastikas</term><note>A cross-shaped figure used in geometric constructions</note> above and below, one should demonstrate the "dwarf" <note>referring to a specific geometric projection or small-scale model</note> using the known quantities. By the method of "averaging the middle" <note>a technique from the *Kuttaka* or algebra chapters</note>, subtract the remainder and purify the quantity. From this, the square root of the negative unknowns combined with half the square of the unknown, divided by the square of the unknown, results in the unknown value.

Here, one should demonstrate the gnomon <note>the vertical pillar of a sundial</note> in the south-east direction during the southern transit. For instance, where the vertical circle of that corner intersects the diurnal circle, one should suspend a plumb-line. The point where that plumb-line touches the diagonal string is the base of the gnomon. The distance from that gnomon-base to the rising-setting line is the "gnomon-floor" <term>shanku-tala</term>. The distance between the east-west line and the rising-setting line, combined with the gnomon-floor, forms the "arm" <term>bhuja</term>. The distance between the east-west line and the gnomon-base is the "side" <term>bahu</term>. At the time of entering the corner, it forms a square.

Thus, in the first proportion, the radius is the multiplier and in the third, it is the divisor. When these cancel out, in the second, the cosine of latitude <term>lambajya</term> is the divisor and in the third, it is the multiplier. When these also cancel out, the sine of latitude <term>akshajya</term> multiplied by twelve and divided by the hypotenuse of the shadow results in the sine of declination <term>krantijya</term>. It is also proven that the product of the sine of latitude and twelve, divided by the sine of declination, results in the hypotenuse of the shadow. Furthermore, the product of twelve and the sine of latitude is equal to the product of the equinoctial shadow and the cosine of latitude. The divisor remains the same. From this, the rule for the shadow on the prime vertical is established, and the rest should be applied as before. He who understands the positioning and other factors explains the answer to the question regarding the gnomon-shadow at the corners in three verses (Verse 53).

**Scientific Commentary:** The sine of latitude and the cosine of latitude, each multiplied by the twelve digits of the equinoctial shadow and divided by the sine of declination, result in the two hypotenuses of the prime vertical. Then, as before, the two shadows are derived separately. (53)

->**The Derivation**<-

Now, by the proportion of the latitude-triangle:
$\frac{\text{Radius} \cdot \text{Sine of Declination}}{\text{Sine of Latitude}} = \text{Prime Vertical Gnomon}$

Then, if the Prime Vertical Gnomon gives the Radius-hypotenuse, what does a twelve-digit gnomon give?
Prime Vertical Hypotenuse = 
$\frac{\text{Radius} \cdot 12}{\text{Prime Vertical Gnomon}} = \frac{\text{Radius} \cdot 12}{\frac{\text{Radius} \cdot \text{Sine of Declination}}{\text{Sine of Latitude}}} = \frac{12 \cdot \text{Sine of Latitude}}{\text{Sine of Declination}}$

Multiplying both numerator and denominator by the cosine of latitude:
$\frac{12 \cdot \text{Sine of Latitude} \cdot \text{Cosine of Latitude}}{\text{Cosine of Latitude} \cdot \text{Sine of Declination}}$

$= \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Cosine of Latitude}}{\text{Sine of Declination}} = \text{Prime Vertical Hypotenuse}$

By this much, all that was stated by the Teacher is proven. In the *Siddhanta-Shekhara* <note>A major astronomical treatise by Sripati</note>, it is said: "The cosine and sine of latitude multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by the declination respectively... the wise one finds the two hypotenuses of the prime vertical." This confirms the Teacher's statement is appropriate. In the *Surya-Siddhanta* <note>The foundational text of Indian astronomy</note>, the same is stated: "The cosine and sine of latitude multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and twelve... these are the two hypotenuses when the sun is on the prime vertical." (53)

->Now, the calculation of the hypotenuse of the shadow on the Prime Vertical is described<-

<note>The Prime Vertical is the celestial circle passing through the East, West, and Zenith points.</note>

Hindi Commentary: Multiply the sine of latitude <term>Akshajya</term> and the cosine of latitude <term>Lambajya</term> separately by twelve and by the equinoctial shadow <term>Palabha</term>. Dividing these by the sine of declination <term>Krantijya</term> yields two types of hypotenuses for the Prime Vertical. From these, the shadow should be calculated as previously described. ||53||

->Mathematical Proof<-

<margin>By the ratio of the latitude-triangle</margin>
(Radius × Sine of Declination) / Sine of Latitude = Prime Vertical Gnomon <note>Samashanku</note>. From this, we calculate the ratio: if for a Prime Vertical Gnomon we obtain the Radius as the hypotenuse, what will be the hypotenuse for a gnomon of twelve digits? This gives the Prime Vertical hypotenuse:

(Radius × 12) / Prime Vertical Gnomon = (Radius × 12) / [(Radius × Sine of Declination) / Sine of Latitude] = (Sine of Latitude × 12) / Sine of Declination.

By multiplying the divisor and the dividend by the cosine of latitude <term>Lambajya</term>:

(Sine of Latitude × 12 × Cosine of Latitude) / (Cosine of Latitude × Sine of Declination) = (Equinoctial Shadow × Cosine of Latitude) / Sine of Declination = Prime Vertical Hypotenuse.

Thus, the teacher's statement is proven. In the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> <note>A foundational Sanskrit text of Indian astronomy</note>, it is said: "The cosine and sine of latitude multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and twelve, then divided by the sine of declination, are the two hypotenuses when the Sun is on the Prime Vertical." Likewise, in the <term>Siddhanta Shekhara</term>, Shripati says the same as the teacher: "The cosine and sine of latitude multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and twelve, divided by the declination-sine respectively, or else..." ||53||

->Now, the calculation of the Corner Gnomon is stated<-

> Half the square of the Radius, diminished by the square of the Sun's amplitude <term>Arkagra</term>, is multiplied by the square of twelve.
> One part is the 'Eastern' and the other is the 'Other', derived from the product of twelve and the equinoctial shadow. ||54||
> From the square of the equinoctial shadow increased by half the square of the Radius, and added to the square of the 'Other' part,
> the square root, increased or decreased by the 'Other' part in the Northern or Southern hemispheres, is the Gnomon. ||55||
> In the intermediate directions, North or South, in the Northern hemisphere, the 'Other' is subtracted or added.
> The shadow and the time in ghatikas for the Sun when south of the Prime Vertical are as before. ||56||

Vasanabhashya <note>Author's own commentary</note>: Here, the origin of the Corner Gnomons <note>Gnomons for the intermediate directions like NE, NW, SE, SW</note> should be demonstrated. For example, where the equinoctial shadow is seven digits, the latitude is fifty-five degrees. There, the Sun at the end of Gemini rises in the Northeast, and at the end of Sagittarius in the Southeast. In places north of that, Corner Gnomons can occur in all four directions. When the Sun is in the Northern or Southern hemisphere, there is sometimes an absence of the <unclear>gnomon</unclear>. In places south of that, where the latitude is twenty-four degrees...

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>The "Three Problems" in Indian astronomy refer to the determination of direction, place, and time.</note>

Therefore, in the Northern Hemisphere, the corner gnomon <term>Kona-Shanku</term><note>The vertical gnomon's shadow when the sun is exactly in the NE, NW, SE, or SW directions.</note> is possible in the Southeast and Southwest directions. In the Southern Hemisphere, or when the latitude is less than twenty-four degrees, and the sun is in the Northern Hemisphere, the gnomon may sometimes be in the Southeast/Southwest and sometimes in the Northeast/Northwest, depending on whether the sine of the local latitude is less than or greater than the sine of the declination <term>Kranti-jya</term>. For the sun in the Southern Hemisphere, it occurs only in the Southeast and Southwest. These three verses are for the demonstration of those corner gnomons.

On the desired day, having calculated the Sun's amplitude <term>Arkagra</term><note>The distance on the horizon between the east point and the point where the sun rises.</note>, its square should be found. Then, subtract this from half the square of the radius. Multiply the result by the number represented by "Vedas, Eyes, and Moon" (124). The resulting quantity is named the "First" <term>Adya</term>.

Then, take the product of the Sun's amplitude, the number twelve, and the local equinoctial shadow <term>Vishuvat-chhaya</term><note>The shadow of a 12-unit gnomon at noon on the equinox.</note>. This is named the "Other" <term>Anya</term>. Then, divide both of these separately by the square of the local equinoctial shadow increased by two. The two resulting values are the "Corrected First" and "Corrected Other" suitable for the calculation.

Then, squaring the "Other" and adding it to the "First," take the square root; this is named the "Root" <term>Pada</term>. This is the general procedure for all corner gnomons. The specific distinction here is that the "Root" is added to or subtracted from the "Other" respectively, depending on whether the sun is in the Southern or Northern Hemisphere, to find the gnomon in the northern or southern directions.

When the sun moves north of the prime vertical <term>Samamandala</term><note>The great circle passing through the East, West, and Zenith.</note>, the "Root" added to the "Other" gives the gnomon for the Northeast entry. The same applies to the Northwest entry at an equal time before sunset. When the sun rises south of the prime vertical and does not pass north of it, the "Root" subtracted from the "Other" gives the gnomon for the Southeast. The same applies to the Southwest. When the sun enters the Northern Hemisphere and crosses the prime vertical twice (at East and West), the "Root" subtracted from or added to the "Other" gives the position relative to the prime vertical.

---

Now, where the sun rises further north than the Northeast point, the square of the Sun's amplitude will not be subtractable from half the square of the radius. In that case, perform the subtraction in reverse. Multiply the remainder by the square of twelve... <note>The text here describes a mathematical adjustment for high latitudes or high declinations.</note> Having performed the remaining calculation as before and brought out the "Root" and "Other," in one case the "Other" minus the "Root" is the gnomon for the Northeast and Northwest. The "Other" plus the "Root" is the gnomon for the Southeast and Southwest.

Where the sun rises further south than the Southeast point, the square of the amplitude cannot be subtracted from half the square of the radius. In such a case, there is no need for Southeast calculations because a corner gnomon is impossible. This calculation of the corner gnomon is for a place with latitude. For a place on the equator (zero latitude), the square of the sine of declination... the second arm is also the same. Therefore, twice the square of the base is the square of the distance between the foot of the gnomon and the center of the earth. This means it is the square of the sine of the zenith distance <term>Drig-jya</term>. Subtracting that from the square of the radius and taking the root gives the corner gnomon. The corner gnomon is the vertical side <term>Koti</term>, its shadow is the base <term>Bhuja</term>, and the radius is the hypotenuse <term>Karna</term>. From this, it is known... but that is not known. The corner gnomon itself is imagined within the gnomon. Thus, by the rule of three: if for twelve [the height of the gnomon], the shadow is equal to the equinoctial shadow...

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

The <term>gnomon-sine</term> <note>Sanskrit: *shanku-tala*; the distance from the base of the gnomon to the rising-setting line</note> is that which results from the gnomon; what is the result? It is the twelfth part of the square of the <term>equinoctial shadow</term> <note>The shadow cast by a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note>. The measure of the gnomon-sine is such that one should place units equal to the <term>solar amplitude</term> <note>Sanskrit: *arkagra*; the distance of the sun at rising from the East point</note> in front of it; thus, the sum of the gnomon-sine and the amplitude is formed. That itself is the <term>base</term> <note>Sanskrit: *bhuja*</note>. When its square is calculated, in the first place, those squares are equal to the square of the equinoctial shadow. Their divisor is the square of twelve <note>Sanskrit: *arka-kriti*; 12 squared = 144</note>. In the place where the <term>unknowns</term> <note>Sanskrit: *yavaka*; used here like the algebraic 'x'</note> are, they become equal to twice the square of the equinoctial shadow. Their divisor is also the square of twelve. In the second place, there are units equal to the solar amplitude. Thus, the square of the <term>sine of the base</term> is calculated.

Subtracting that from the square of the <term>radius</term> <note>Sanskrit: *trijya*</note>, the remainders are doubled, which gives the square of the gnomon. By this method, the squares of the base are subtracted from the square of the radius. When subtracted, the resulting quantities—both the squared quantity and the quantity of the unknown—become negative. The square of the solar amplitude is a constant unit, so it is subtracted directly from the square of the radius. By doing this, half the square of the gnomon is produced. From the square of the unknown, the negative values are equal to the square of the equinoctial shadow, with a divisor of the square of twelve in the first place. In the second place, from the unknown, by negative movement, they are equal to the product of twice the equinoctial shadow and the solar amplitude, with twelve as the divisor. Then, by multiplying again by twelve, they become <term>homogeneous</term> <note>Sanskrit: *savarna*; having a common denominator</note> with the first quantity. This means the divisor is the square of twelve. This quantity will be useful shortly. The Teacher <note>Likely referring to Brahmagupta</note> has composed only the half-calculation to preserve the <term>rationalization</term> <note>Sanskrit: *vasana*; the underlying logic or proof of the formula</note>. When the half is made, the equinoctial shadow multiplied by the square of twelve is the product. In the third place, the units remaining from the radius-square minus the square of the solar amplitude are complete. These, multiplied by the square of twelve, become homogeneous. After doing the same with the previous quantity, the resulting quantity is named **The First** <note>Sanskrit: *Adya*</note>. Thus it is said: "The square of the amplitude subtracted from the square of the radius and multiplied by the square of twelve is **The First**." For the square, which is half the square of the gnomon, there is a single divisor called the "square-divisor," and that is halved so that it becomes the square of the whole gnomon. When the divisor is moved above, the measure becomes double. That halved value becomes the number "two-go" <note>A chronogram or symbolic number</note>. Thus, one should place the square of the unknown in the first and second sides of the equation. Then the unknown is the gnomon. The second side, by the divisor of the first side, becomes seventy-two when made homogeneous, and the square of the unknown becomes the number "two-go." When situated thus, the known part of the square of the formula should be subtracted. Since the units are from the inverse of that, the square of the unknown in the first side, which is negative and equal to the square of the equinoctial shadow, is subtracted. In the second side, they become those below the unknowns. Therefore, the sum of those two quantities, the entire square of the equinoctial shadow, is combined with that "two-go." In the first side, those of the "Other" designation multiplied by eight are also subtracted from zero in the second side, so they also become positive. In the second side, the constant unit is zero; subtracting that from the units of the first side, only those units named **The First** remain. Even when this is done, there is equality of the two sides. Therefore, for all three quantities, the constant multiplier is the square of the equinoctial shadow; when combined with the square, they are assumed to be equal. By this constant operation, the entire unit remains in the place of the square of the unknown.

---

In this case, in the Southeast, it becomes a positive "Clear Other" in the place of the unknown. And here, the positive—
<note>The following line is struck out in the original manuscript</note>
—becomes the "Clear First" in the place. That too is a positive unit here—
<note>End of strikeout</note>
This being the case, the formula for the square <unclear>...</unclear> half of the middle.

# Chapter on the Three Problems

The square root of the sum of the squares <note>referring to algebraic solutions for unknown quantities</note> is divided by the square of the other... by a single square, the units are divided and always remain so. The clear final values and the half of the unknown... having squared that, the square root of the units combined with it, diminished by the other designated half-unknown, is divided by that square. Always, when the unit is in the place of the square and divided by one, the square root of the quantities from the cubic essence <note>original: "ghanatattvād"</note> is the Corner Gnomon <term>Konashanku: the vertical shadow/altitude of the sun when it is exactly in a corner direction like Northeast or Southwest</term> diminished by the other. By that, it is said, it must be multiplied by the square of the equinoctial shadow... added to the first square, the square root of the first diminished by the final square, diminished by the other, is the gnomon in the southern hemisphere when the sun is in an intermediate direction in the south. This is applicable when the sun rises between the east and the northeast, reaches noon by moving north of the prime vertical, and then sets. There, to calculate the gnomon for the northeast, one subtracts the gnomon-floor <term>Shankutala: the distance from the base of the gnomon to the east-west line</term> from the amplitude <term>Agra: the distance of the sun at sunrise from the east-west line on the horizon</term>; the remainder is the side <term>Bhuja: the north-south distance of the sun from the east-west line</term>. There, as before, the distance between the corner-string and the plumb-line dropped from the intersection of the corner-circle and the diurnal circle—called the Corner Gnomon—is the east-west distance of the base of that gnomon. Its square, subtracted from the square of the radius <unclear>......</unclear> the square root of twice the remainder is the Corner Gnomon for the northeast. By that, as far as the gnomon goes, that same gnomon-floor's amplitude <unclear>......</unclear> should be squared. By doing this, the amplitude diminished by the gnomon-floor becomes the side. In its square <unclear>......</unclear> in the first place, the squares are equal to the square of the equinoctial shadow. The cubic result is a negative square because the cube is half... by the divisor of the sun's square, in the second place, it is equal to the second equinoctial shadow-amplitude, the unknown becomes negative. Since the product of positive and negative is negative. Below that is the divisor of twelve. In the third place is the product of the amplitude and the units; thus is the amplitude.

**V. Bha. <note>Commentary by Vishvanatha Bhaskara</note> —** Half the square of the radius diminished by the square of the amplitude, multiplied by the square of twelve (144), is designated as the **First**. The amplitude multiplied by twelve is the **Final**, designated as the **Other**. These two, the First and the Other, divided by the square of the equinoctial shadow increased by seventy-two (the square of the equinoctial shadow plus 72), become the **Specific First** and **Specific Other**. The square root should be taken from the First added to the square of the Other; then, by adding or subtracting the Other, the Corner Gnomon for the North or South celestial hemispheres is found. The explanation of the remainder is clear. || 54-55-56 ||

->The Proof<-

The plumb-line dropped from the intersection of the corner-circle and the diurnal circle (of the sun situated on the corner-circle) onto the plane of the horizon is the **Corner Gnomon** ($Sh$). The perpendicular from its base to the east-west line is the **Side** ($Bhuja$). The distance from the base of the side to the center, or the perpendicular from the base of the Corner Gnomon to the north-south line, is the **Upright** ($Koti$). The distance from the center of the earth to the base of the Corner Gnomon is the **Sine of Zenith Distance** ($Drigjya$), which is the hypotenuse. In this triangle of Side, Upright, and Hypotenuse, the angle between the hypotenuse and the upright is 45°; therefore, the angle between the hypotenuse and the side is also 45°. Because the Side and Upright are equal, twice the square of the Side equals the square of the Sine of Zenith Distance. Now, it is assumed here:

The measure of the Corner Gnomon = $Sh$. Then, by proportion, the Gnomon-floor = $\frac{Pbha \cdot Sh}{12}$ <note>Pbha: Palabha, the equinoctial midday shadow</note>. By the calculation of the amplitude and gnomon-floor, the measure of the Side in the North and South hemispheres respectively is = $A \mp \frac{Pbha \cdot Sh}{12}$. Now $P$ =

<header>In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta</header>

The amplitude <note>original: "Agra"</note> and the square of the base <note>original: "Bhujavarga"</note> $= \left( \text{Amplitude} \mp \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Sine Altitude}}{12} \right)^2 = \text{Amplitude}^2 \mp \frac{2 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Sine Altitude}}{12} + \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Sine Altitude}^2}{144}$

When doubled, then the square of the Sine of Zenith Distance <note>original: "Drigjyavarga"</note> $= \frac{144 \cdot \text{Amplitude}^2 \mp 24 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Sine Altitude} + \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Sine Altitude}^2}{72} = \text{Radius}^2 - \text{Sine Altitude}^2$

By rearranging and simplifying:
$(72 + \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2) \cdot \text{Sine Altitude}^2 \mp 24 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Sine Altitude} = 72 \cdot \text{Radius}^2 - 144 \cdot \text{Amplitude}^2 = 144 \left( \frac{\text{Radius}^2}{2} - \text{Amplitude}^2 \right)$

Dividing both sides by $(72 + \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2)$, then:
$\text{Sine Altitude}^2 \mp \frac{24 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Sine Altitude}}{72 + \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2} = \frac{144 \left( \frac{\text{Radius}^2}{2} - \text{Amplitude}^2 \right) <gloss>\text{here } 144</gloss>}{72 + \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2}$

Let $\left( \frac{\text{Radius}^2}{2} - \text{Amplitude}^2 \right) = \text{First Term}$ and $12 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow} = \text{Second Term}$.
Then $\text{Sine Altitude}^2 \mp \frac{2 \cdot \text{Second Term}}{72 + \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2} = \frac{\text{First Term}}{72 + \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2}$

Letting these be simplified as $y'^2 \mp 2 \cdot \text{Second}' = \text{First}'$. By adding the square of the Second' to both sides:
$y'^2 \mp 2 \cdot \text{Second}' + \text{Second}'^2 = \text{First}' + \text{Second}'^2$. Taking the square root: $y' \mp \text{Second}' = \sqrt{\text{First}' + \text{Second}'^2}$.
Therefore, Sine Altitude $(y) = \sqrt{\text{First}' + \text{Second}'^2} \pm \text{Second}'$.

By this, the method stated by the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> is proven. When $\frac{\text{Radius}^2}{2} < \text{Amplitude}^2$, then in the Northern Hemisphere <note>original: "Uttara-gola"</note>, because the First Term becomes negative, four "Corner Gnomons" <note>intermediate direction altitudes</note> are produced. However, in the Southern Hemisphere, there is an absence of the Corner Gnomon.

In the **Siddhanta-shekhara**:
> Half the square of the Radius diminished by the square of the Amplitude, multiplied by 144, is the first term.
> The product of the Amplitude and the Equinoctial Shadow is the other. These are divided by the square of the Equinoctial Shadow increased by 72.
> From the first term added to the square of the second, the square root is taken.
> This root, increased or decreased by the second term, gives the Corner Gnomon in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres respectively.
> In the Northern Hemisphere, the result is both the sum and the difference; in the Southern, it is as before from the prime vertical, and the shadow, hypotenuse, and desired ghatikas are calculated as previously.

This method of bringing forth the Corner Gnomon stated by Shripati is exactly in accordance with what the Teacher stated. Also in the **Surya-siddhanta**: "From half the square of the Radius, diminished by the square of the Amplitude, multiplied by twelve..." etc., this same method for calculating the Corner Gnomon is mentioned.

In the **Siddhanta-shiromani**, with the verse "The square of the Amplitude doubled, from the square of the Radius..." etc., Bhaskara has calculated the Corner Gnomon by an iterative method, assuming the Amplitude of the intermediate direction to be equal to the base. That is, twice the square of the Amplitude (twice the square of the base) is equal to the square of the Sine of Zenith Distance. If twice the square of the Amplitude is subtracted from the square of the Radius, an approximate square of the Gnomon is found. Taking its root, and then <term>calculating the base of the gnomon<note>original: "Shankutala" - the distance from the center of the horizon circle to the projection of the gnomon's tip</note></term>, if it is applied to the Amplitude, an approximate base is formed; thus by repeated calculation <note>iteration</note> the result is refined.

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>original: "Tri-prashna-adhikara". This chapter deals with the three fundamental problems of time, space, and direction using a gnomon.</note>

Page 343

The knowledge of the true corner gnomon <term>Kona-shanku; the vertical pillar used for astronomical measurements when the sun is in a specific intermediate direction</term> should be attained. However, if the value of the side <note>the "Bhuja" or base of the triangle</note> is equal to the Sine of 45 degrees <note>Sine 45° = $\sqrt{\frac{Radius^2}{2}}$</note>, then an inconsistency arises in this method. For example: if $Side^2 = Amplitude^2 = Radius^2 = Day-Sine^2$, then $\sqrt{Radius^2 - Amplitude^2} = \sqrt{Radius^2 - Radius^2} = 0$. This results in the corner gnomon being zero. Consequently, the base of the gnomon <note>Shanku-tala</note> becomes zero, and due to the correction of the amplitude, it remains only the previous side; therefore, the iterative process <term>Sakrit-karman; a single-step calculation</term> cannot proceed here.

Furthermore, if the Side is greater than Sine 45°, the measure of the corner gnomon would become a negative value. If one brings forth the measure of the amplitude <term>Agra; the distance of the sun at rising from the east-west line</term> by assuming the Side to be Sine 45°, then for any amplitude smaller than that in the Northern Hemisphere <note>Uttara-gola</note>, the inconsistency mentioned by Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note> would occur.

As per Bhaskara's statement: $\sqrt{Radius^2 - 2 \cdot Side^2} = \text{Corner Gnomon}$.
Then, the Base of the Gnomon = $\frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{12} \sqrt{Radius^2 - 2 \cdot Side^2}$.
Therefore, Side = $\frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{12} \sqrt{Radius^2 - 2 \cdot Side^2} - \text{Amplitude} = \text{Sine } 45^\circ$.

Through transposition and other operations:
$\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \sqrt{Radius^2 - 2 \cdot Side^2} = 12 \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ + \text{Amplitude} \cdot 12 = 12 (\text{Amplitude} + \text{Sine } 45^\circ)$.
By squaring both sides:
$\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot Radius^2 - \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot 2 \cdot Side^2 = 144 (\text{Amplitude}^2 + 2 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ + \text{Sine}^2 45^\circ)$.
Dividing both sides by two:
$\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot \frac{Radius^2}{2} - \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot Side^2 = 72 \cdot \text{Amplitude}^2 + 144 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ + 72 \cdot \text{Sine}^2 45^\circ$.
This equals $\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Sine}^2 45^\circ$.

<margin>By balancing the terms <note>Samashodhana</note> involving $-\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot Side^2$</margin>

$\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Sine}^2 45^\circ - 72 \cdot \text{Sine}^2 45^\circ = \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Amplitude}^2 + 144 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ + 72 \cdot \text{Amplitude}^2$.
By factoring out common terms:
$\text{Sine}^2 45^\circ (\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 - 72) = \text{Amplitude}^2 (\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72) + 144 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ$.
Then:
$\frac{\text{Sine}^2 45^\circ (\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 - 72)}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72} = \text{Amplitude}^2 + \frac{144 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72}$.
By completing the square <term>Varga-purtikarana</term>:

$\frac{\text{Sine}^2 45^\circ (\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 - 72)}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72} + \frac{(72 \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ)^2}{(\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72)^2} = \text{Amplitude}^2 + \frac{144 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72} + \frac{(72 \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ)^2}{(\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72)^2}$.

On the first side, by finding a common denominator:
$\frac{\text{Sine}^2 45^\circ \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^4}{(\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72)^2} = \text{Amplitude}^2 + \frac{2 \cdot 72 \cdot \text{Amplitude} \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72} + \frac{(72 \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ)^2}{(\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72)^2}$.
Taking the square root:
$\frac{\text{Sine } 45^\circ \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72} = \text{Amplitude} + \frac{72 \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72}$.
Therefore, $\text{Amplitude} = \frac{\text{Sine } 45^\circ \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72} - \frac{72 \cdot \text{Sine } 45^\circ}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72} = \frac{\text{Sine } 45^\circ (\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 - 72)}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72}$.
By this, the formula of the Great Scholar Sudhakara Dvivedi <note>A famous 19th-century astronomer and mathematician from Varanasi</note> is proven.

The deviation in the southern hemisphere has been demonstrated by the editor in the commentary on the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A major 12th-century work by Bhaskara II</note> with the verse: **"The calculation made by the shadow of the gnomon, multiplied by the sight and the mountains, divided by the five fires..."** and so forth.

# Now, it is demonstrated where the fourfold corner-gnomons occur

In a place where the maximum amplitude <note>The angular distance of the rising sun from the true east</note> = Sine 45°, the measure of the equinoctial shadow <term>Palabha: the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</term> is derived. Let the measure of the equinoctial shadow = $x$. Then the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow squared = $x^2 + 12^2$. From this, $\frac{(x^2 + 12^2) \cdot \text{Sine}^2(\text{Obliquity})}{12^2}$ = Maximum Amplitude$^2$ = Sine$^2$ 45°. By clearing the denominator: $x^2 \cdot \text{Sine}^2(\text{Obliquity}) + 12^2 \cdot \text{Sine}^2(\text{Obliquity}) = 12^2 \cdot \text{Sine}^2 45^\circ$. By rearranging: $x^2 \cdot \text{Sine}^2(\text{Obliquity}) = 12^2 \cdot \text{Sine}^2 45^\circ - 12^2 \cdot \text{Sine}^2(\text{Obliquity}) = 12^2 (\text{Sine}^2 45^\circ - \text{Sine}^2(\text{Obliquity}))$. Therefore, $x^2 = \frac{12^2 (\text{Sine}^2 45^\circ - \text{Sine}^2(\text{Obliquity}))}{\text{Sine}^2(\text{Obliquity})}$. By taking the square root, $x = \frac{12 \sqrt{\text{Sine}^2 45^\circ - \text{Sine}^2(\text{Obliquity})}}{\text{Sine}(\text{Obliquity})} = 17|5|22$. By this, it is proved that where the equinoctial shadow = 17|5|22, there the maximum amplitude = Sine 45°. In places where the equinoctial shadow is greater than 17|5|22, there is an absence of the corner-gnomon in the southern hemisphere, because there $2x \cdot \text{Amplitude} > \text{Radius}^2$. However, in the northern hemisphere, four corner-gnomons are produced. By this, the commentary stated by Bhaskara is also proven consistent. || 54-55-56 ||

# Now, the method for bringing forth the corner-gnomon is stated

**Hindi Commentary.**—Subtract the square of the Sun's amplitude from half the square of the radius, and multiply the result by the outer square; this is named the "First" (Adya). The product of the amplitude, twelve, and the equinoctial shadow is named the "Other" (Anya). Adding seventy-two (72) to the square of the equinoctial shadow and dividing the "First" and "Other" by this gives the "Specific First" and "Specific Other." Add the square of the "Specific Other" to the "Specific First" and take the square root. Adding and subtracting the "Specific Other" to/from that root gives the corner-gnomon in the northern and southern hemispheres respectively. The explanation of the remainder is clear. || 54-55-56 ||

### Mathematical Proof

The perpendicular dropped from the Sun situated on the corner-circle <note>The vertical circle at 45 degrees from the meridian</note> to the plane of the horizon is called the corner-gnomon. From its base to the east-west line, the perpendicular is designated as the "Base" (Bhuja). From the root of the "Base" to the center of the Earth, or the perpendicular from the base of the corner-gnomon to the north-south line, is designated as the "Upright" (Koti). From the center of the Earth to the base of the corner-gnomon is the hypotenuse of the sine of the zenith distance. In this triangle of Base-Base and Upright-Upright, the angle produced by the hypotenuse and the Upright = 45°. Therefore, the angle produced by the hypotenuse and the Base is also = 45°. Thus, Base = Upright, and therefore $2 \cdot \text{Base}^2 = \text{Sine}^2(\text{Zenith Distance})$. There, we assume the measure of the corner-gnomon = $x$. Then, by proportion, the base of the gnomon = $\frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot x}{12}$. By the refinement of the amplitude and the gnomon-base in the northern hemisphere and...

# Chapter on the Three Problems

->Chapter on the Three Problems<-

In the southern hemisphere, the side <term>Bhuja; the base of a right-angled triangle in spherical astronomy</term> is sequentially calculated as $= \text{Amplitude} \pm \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Gnomon}}{12}$. Here, $\text{A} = \text{Amplitude}$. The square of the side $= (\text{A} \pm \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Gnomon}}{12})^2$

$= \text{A}^2 \pm \frac{2 \text{A} \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Gnomon}}{12} + \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Gnomon}^2}{144}$. By doubling this, $2 \text{Side}^2 = \text{Sine of Zenith Distance}^2 = \text{Radius}^2 - \text{Gnomon}^2$

$= \frac{144 \text{A}^2 \pm 24 \text{A} \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Gnomon} + \text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Gnomon}^2}{72}$. By clearing the denominator and simplifying, we get $(\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72)\text{Gnomon}^2 \mp$

$24\text{A} \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Gnomon} = 72 \text{Radius}^2 - 144 \text{A}^2 = 144 (\frac{\text{Radius}^2}{2} - \text{A}^2)$. Dividing both sides by $(\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72)$

gives $\text{Gnomon}^2 \mp \frac{24\text{A} \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow} \cdot \text{Gnomon}}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72} = \frac{144 (\frac{\text{Radius}^2}{2} - \text{A}^2)}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72}$. Here, $144 (\frac{\text{Radius}^2}{2} - \text{A}^2)$

$= \text{designated as the First Term}$, and $12\text{A} \cdot \text{Equinoctial Shadow} = \text{designated as the Last Term}$. Then, $\text{Gnomon}^2 \mp \frac{2 \text{Last}}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72} = \frac{\text{First}}{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}^2 + 72}$

$= \text{Gnomon}^2 \mp 2 \text{Last}' = \text{First}'$. By adding $\text{Last}'^2$ to both sides, $\text{Gnomon}^2 \mp 2 \text{Last}' + \text{Last}'^2 = \text{First}'$

$+ \text{Last}'^2$. Taking the square root, $\text{Gnomon} \mp \text{Last}' = \sqrt{\text{First}' + \text{Last}'^2} \therefore \text{Gnomon} = \sqrt{\text{First}' + \text{Last}'^2} \pm \text{Last}'$

By this, the statements of the ancient teachers are proven. When $\frac{\text{Radius}^2}{2} < \text{A}^2$, then in the northern hemisphere, because the value of the First Term becomes negative, four "Corner Gnomons" <note>Konashanku: the gnomon's shadow when the sun is in the intermediate directions like NE, NW, etc.</note> are produced, and in the southern hemisphere, there is an absence of the Corner Gnomon. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, the verses written in the Sanskrit proof <note>original: "उपपत्ति" (Upapatti)</note> beginning with "Half the square of the radius diminished by the square of the amplitude..." show that Shripati’s method for the Corner Gnomon is exactly in accordance with the teachers' words. In the *Surya Siddhanta* as well, the calculation of this Corner Gnomon is stated via "From half the square of the radius, subtract the square of the sine of amplitude..." In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya, by assuming the side to be equal to the known amplitude in verses like "The square of the amplitude doubled from the square of its own radius...", has calculated the Corner Gnomon through an iterative process <term>Asakrit-karma; a method of successive approximation</term>. That is, twice the square of the amplitude $= 2 \text{Side}^2 = \text{Sine of Zenith Distance}^2$. Subtracting twice the square of the amplitude from the square of the radius leaves the square of the "unreal" Corner Gnomon. Taking its square root and performing the iterative calculation—by adjusting the amplitude—results in the "unreal" side. By performing the iterative process in this way, the "real" Corner Gnomon is known. However, if the $\text{Side} = \text{Sine of } 45^\circ$

$= \sqrt{\frac{\text{Radius}^2}{2}}$, then a discrepancy occurs such as: $2 \text{Side}^2 = 2 \text{Earth-sine}^2 = \text{Radius}^2 =$ <note>Original likely intended $2\text{Amplitude}^2$ but appears as "dhara" (Earth-sine)</note>

$\text{Sine of Zenith Distance}^2$. Therefore $\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - 2 \text{Amplitude}^2} = 0 = \text{Corner Gnomon}$. From this, the desired time <note>Ishtakala: the specific time of day being calculated</note> also $= 0$. Before adjusting the amplitude, it remains only the side; therefore, the iterative process will not even begin.

# In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta

If the <term>base</term><note>bhuj: the side of a right-angled triangle, here referring to a specific arc or sine value</note> is greater than the <term>sine of 45°</term><note>jya 45</note>, then the value of the <term>corner gnomon</term><note>konashanku: the gnomon's shadow when the sun is in one of the intermediate directions like NE, NW, SE, SW</note> becomes negative. Therefore, by accepting the base as equal to the sine of 45°, if we derive the value of the <term>amplitude</term><note>agra: the distance of the sun at rising from the east-west line</note>, then for an amplitude less than that in the Northern Hemisphere, an error <note>original: "vyabhichara" meaning inconsistency or deviation</note> occurs in the method described by Bhaskara. For instance, according to Bhaskara's statement: $\sqrt{Radius^2 - 2 \cdot Amplitude^2}$ = Corner Gnomon. From this:

<br>
            Equinoctial Shadow     /-----------------
Gnomon Base = ————————————————— \  / Radius^2 - 2 \cdot Amplitude^2  
                   12            \/
<br>
From this, Base = (Equinoctial Shadow / 12) $\cdot \sqrt{Radius^2 - 2 \cdot Amplitude^2}$ - Amplitude = Sine 45°
<br>

By clearing the denominator and further steps:

(Equinoctial Shadow) $\cdot \sqrt{Radius^2 - 2 \cdot Amplitude^2}$ = 12 $\cdot$ Sine 45 + Amplitude $\cdot$ 12 = 12 (Amplitude + Sine 45). By squaring both sides:

(Equinoctial Shadow)$^2 \cdot Radius^2$ - (Equinoctial Shadow)$^2 \cdot 2 \cdot Amplitude^2$ = 144 (Amplitude$^2$ + 2 $\cdot$ Amplitude $\cdot$ Sine 45 + Sine$^2$ 45). Dividing both sides by two:

(Equinoctial Shadow)$^2 \cdot \frac{Radius^2}{2}$ - (Equinoctial Shadow)$^2 \cdot Amplitude^2$ = 72 $\cdot$ Amplitude$^2$ + 144 $\cdot$ Amplitude $\cdot$ Sine 45 + 72 $\cdot$ Sine$^2$ 45 = (Equinoctial Shadow)$^2 \cdot Sine^2$ 45 - (Equinoctial Shadow)$^2 \cdot Amplitude^2$. By simplifying the terms:

(Equinoctial Shadow)$^2 \cdot Sine^2$ 45 - 72 $\cdot$ Sine$^2$ 45 = (Equinoctial Shadow)$^2 \cdot Amplitude^2$ + 12$^2 \cdot$ Amplitude $\cdot$ Sine 45 + 72 $\cdot$ Amplitude$^2$. By isolating the common factors:

<br>
        Sine$^2$ 45 ( (Equinoctial Shadow)$^2$ - 72 ) = Amplitude$^2$ ( (Equinoctial Shadow)$^2$ + 72 ) + 12$^2 \cdot$ Amplitude $\cdot$ Sine 45
<br>
$\therefore \frac{Sine^2 45 ( (Equinoctial Shadow)^2 - 72 )}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72} = Amplitude^2 + \frac{12^2 \cdot Amplitude \cdot Sine 45}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72}$
<br>
By completing the square:
<br>
$\frac{Sine^2 45 ( (Equinoctial Shadow)^2 - 72 )}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72} + (\frac{72 \cdot Sine 45}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72})^2 = Amplitude^2 + \frac{12^2 \cdot Amplitude \cdot Sine 45}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72} + (\frac{72 \cdot Sine 45}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72})^2$
<br>

By finding a common denominator in the first side: $\frac{Sine^2 45 \cdot (Equinoctial Shadow)^4}{((Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72)^2} = Amplitude^2 + \frac{2 \cdot 72 \cdot Amplitude \cdot Sine 45}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72}$

<br>
$+ \frac{(72 \cdot Sine 45)^2}{((Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72)^2}$. Taking the square root: $\frac{Sine 45 \cdot (Equinoctial Shadow)^2}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72} = Amplitude + \frac{72 \cdot Sine 45}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72}$
<br>

$\therefore Amplitude = \frac{Sine 45 \cdot (Equinoctial Shadow)^2}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72} - \frac{72 \cdot Sine 45}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72} = \frac{Sine 45 ((Equinoctial Shadow)^2 - 72)}{(Equinoctial Shadow)^2 + 72}$
<br>

From this, the formula "The square of the equinoctial shadow diminished by..." etc., written in the Sanskrit commentary <note>Sanskrit-upapatti</note> by Mahamahopadhyaya Pandit Sudhakara Dvivedi, is derived. In the Southern Hemisphere, the correction for the error has been made in the commentary of the *Siddhanta Shiromani* using the phrase "devoid of the square of the amplitude and shadow" <note>original: "agra-prabha-kriti-vihin"</note> etc.

->We now consider in which country and in which hemisphere there are four corner gnomons.<-

In a country where the maximum amplitude <note>original: "paramāgrā"</note> = sine 45°, we calculate the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "palabhā"</note> for that location. Let us assume:
The value of the equinoctial shadow = $y$. Then the square of the hypotenuse <note>original: "paka^2"</note> = $y^2 + 12^2$. Therefore, $\frac{(y^2 + 12^2) \cdot \text{sine}^2 \text{ obliquity}}{12^2}$ = maximum amplitude$^2$ = sine$^2$ 45°.
By clearing the denominator: $y^2 \cdot \text{sine}^2 \text{ obliquity} + 12^2 \cdot \text{sine}^2 \text{ obliquity} = 12^2 \cdot \text{sine}^2 45^\circ$. By simplification: $y^2 \cdot \text{sine}^2 \text{ obliquity} = 12^2 \cdot \text{sine}^2 45^\circ - 12^2 \cdot \text{sine}^2 \text{ obliquity} = 12^2 (\text{sine}^2 45^\circ - \text{sine}^2 \text{ obliquity})$. Therefore, $y^2 = 12^2 \frac{(\text{sine}^2 45^\circ - \text{sine}^2 \text{ obliquity})}{\text{sine}^2 \text{ obliquity}}$.
Taking the square root: $y = \frac{12 \sqrt{\text{sine}^2 45^\circ - \text{sine}^2 \text{ obliquity}}}{\text{sine } \text{obliquity}}$ = 17;51,22. This proves that in a country where the equinoctial shadow is 17;51,22, the maximum amplitude will be sine 45°. In a country where the equinoctial shadow is greater than 17;51,22, there will be an absence of the corner-gnomon <note>term: "koṇāśaṅku" - the gnomon shadow when the sun is at the intermediate directions like NE, SE, etc.</note> in the southern hemisphere <note>original: "dakṣiṇagola"</note>. Because there, $2 \times \text{amplitude} > \text{radius}$, while in the northern hemisphere <note>original: "uttaragola"</note>, four corner-gnomons are produced. From this, the commentary stated by Bhāskara arises. ||54-55-56||

->Now he describes the knowledge of the equinoctial shadow from the knowledge of two base-shadows<-

> The difference between the products of the two base-shadows and their cross-hypotenuses, if in the same direction, or their sum if in different directions, divided by the difference of the hypotenuses, is the equinoctial shadow. ||57||

**Sudhākara Bhāṣya:** The "distance between the base of the gnomon and the east-west line" refers to the distance of the gnomon's foot from the east-west line. In other words, it is the base-shadow <note>term: "bhuja" - the north-south component of the gnomon's shadow</note> of a twelve-finger gnomon. Thus, for two base-shadows, the difference of the products of the cross-hypotenuses <note>note: multiplying the first base by the second hypotenuse and vice versa</note> in the same direction, or the sum in different directions, divided by the difference of the two hypotenuses, becomes the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "viṣuvacchāyā"</note>.

<margin>1</margin>
The proof here is clear from the method of Bhāskara: "The difference of the products of two shadows' bases and their cross-hypotenuses when in the same direction," etc. ||57||

**Vimalā Mārgadarśinī:** The "distance between the base of the gnomon and the east-west line" means the east-west distance of the gnomon's foot, which is the base-shadow. Thus, for two base-shadows, the difference (subtraction) of the cross-hypotenuse products in the same direction, or the sum (addition) in a different direction, divided by the difference of the hypotenuses, results in the equinoctial shadow (latitude shadow). ||57||

->Here is the proof<-

Now, let the value of the equinoctial shadow = $y$. The base-shadow in the circle of the first shadow-hypotenuse = $b$. Likewise, the second base-shadow in the circle of the second shadow-hypotenuse = $b'$. Let the shadow-hypotenuses be $h, h'$. Then the amplitude on the hypotenuse-circle = $y \pm b$. Also, $y \pm b'$ = amplitude on the hypotenuse-circle. Then the amplitude in the radius-circle <note>original: "trijyāgola"</note> = $\frac{(y \pm b) \cdot \text{radius}}{h} = A$. Thus, $\frac{(y \pm b') \cdot \text{radius}}{h'} = \frac{y \cdot \text{radius} \pm b \cdot \text{radius}}{h} =$

<meta>This page continues the mathematical derivation of the Palabha (equinoctial shadow) using the relationship between shadows and the celestial sphere, specifically referencing the works of Brahmagupta, Shripati, and Bhaskaracharya.</meta>

<page-num>348</page-num>
<header>In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta</header>

In the sphere of the radius, the <term>Agra</term><note>The amplitude or the distance of the sun from the east-west line at rising</note> $=$ $\frac{y \cdot R \pm R \cdot B}{K}$. By clearing the denominators: $y \cdot R \cdot K' \pm B' \cdot R \cdot K = y \cdot R \cdot K \pm R \cdot B \cdot K'$ or $y \cdot K' \pm B' \cdot K = y \cdot K \pm B \cdot K'$. By simplification: $B \cdot K' \mp B' \cdot K = y \cdot K' - y \cdot K = y (K' - K)$.

$y \cdot K = y (K' - K) \therefore \frac{B \cdot K' \mp B' \cdot K}{K' - K} = y$. Thus, what was stated by the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> is proven. In the *Siddhanta-Shekhara*:

>"The difference between the products of the two distances from the east-west line and their respective inverse hypotenuses, when the directions are the same, or their sum when the directions are different; that result divided by the difference of the hypotenuses, yields the clear equinoctial shadow."<

This is the method of Shripati. In the *Siddhanta-Shiromani*:

>"The difference between the two arms (base shadows) of the two shadows, multiplied by the opposite hypotenuses when in the same direction, or their sum when in different directions, divided by the difference of the hypotenuses, is the equinoctial shadow."< 

The method of Bhaskaracharya is also exactly in accordance with what the Teacher stated. ||57||

->Now, the knowledge of the Equinoctial Shadow (Palabha) is explained through the knowledge of two base shadows (Bhujas)<-

<margin>Hindi Commentary</margin> — The <term>Bhuja</term><note>The "arm" or base of the shadow triangle</note> is the distance between the <term>Shankumula</term><note>The base of the gnomon</note> and the <term>East-West line</term>. In this way, the product of the two base shadows and the <term>inverse hypotenuses</term> (<term>desired hypotenuses</term>)—meaning the product of the first base shadow and the second shadow-hypotenuse, and the product of the second base shadow and the first shadow-hypotenuse—their difference if in the same direction, or their sum if in different directions, divided by the difference of the shadow-hypotenuses, results in the <term>Palabha</term><note>The length of the shadow cast by a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note>. ||57||

---

### Proof (Upapatti)

Let us assume the <term>Palabha</term> $= y$. In the sphere of the shadow-hypotenuse, the <term>Bhuja</term> $= B$. In the same sphere, the second base shadow $= B'$. The two shadow-hypotenuses $= K$ and $K'$. Then the <term>Karnavrttagra</term><note>The amplitude on the hypotenuse circle</note> $= y \pm B$. The second amplitude $= y \pm B'$. From this, in the sphere of the radius, the <term>Agra</term> $= \frac{(y \pm B) R}{K}$. Also, $\frac{(y \pm B') R}{K'} = \frac{y \cdot R \pm B' \cdot R}{K'} = \text{Agra in the radius sphere} = \frac{y \cdot R \pm B \cdot R}{K}$. By clearing the denominators, $y \cdot K \pm B \cdot K = y \cdot K' \pm B' \cdot K$. By simplification, $B \cdot K' \mp B' \cdot K = y \cdot K' - y \cdot K = y (K' - K)$.

$\therefore y = \frac{B \cdot K' \mp B' \cdot K}{K' - K}$. Thus, the Teacher's statement is proven. The method of Shripati written in the Sanskrit proof in the *Siddhanta-Shekhara* as "The difference between the products of the two distances..." etc., and the method stated by Bhaskara in the *Siddhanta-Shiromani* as "Of the two arms of the two shadows..." etc., are both exactly in accordance with the Teacher's words. ||57||

## Now, he describes another method for knowing the equinoctial shadow:

-> The shadow's amplitude <note>original: "chāyāvṛttāgrā"</note> decreased by the northern difference, or increased by the southern difference, <-
-> is the equinoctial shadow during the signs beginning with Aries; in those beginning with Libra, the difference is likewise subtracted. ||58|| <-

**Sudhakara Bhashya:** The shadow's amplitude, taken according to its direction, is the amplitude on the circle of the shadow's hypotenuse. It is decreased by the northern difference—meaning the distance between the east-west line and the base of a twelve-digit gnomon, which is the "arm" <term>bhuja: the side of a right-angled triangle representing the north-south distance</term>—and increased by the southern arm. This applies to the signs beginning with Aries, meaning in the Northern Hemisphere <note>original: "uttaragola"</note>. In the signs beginning with Libra, meaning in the Southern Hemisphere, that same difference (the measure of the arm) subtracted from the shadow's amplitude results in the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "viṣuvacchāyā" or "palabhā": the shadow cast by a vertical gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox</term>.

### Here is the proof:

The "arm" is produced by the calculation of the gnomon's base <note>original: "śaṅkutala"</note> and the amplitude. In the case of the "small gnomon" <note>referring to the twelve-digit standard</term>, the gnomon's base is the equinoctial shadow. The amplitude is the shadow's amplitude on the circle of the hypotenuse, taken according to its direction. In the Northern Hemisphere, before the sun enters the prime vertical <note>the east-west vertical circle</note>, the shadow's amplitude is greater than the equinoctial shadow, and the arm is northern; therefore, the shadow's amplitude decreased by the northern arm is the equinoctial shadow. After it passes the prime vertical, the shadow's amplitude is subtracted from the equinoctial shadow, and the remainder is the southern arm; therefore, the amplitude increased by that arm becomes the equinoctial shadow. In the Southern Hemisphere, the measure of the arm is always the sum of the equinoctial shadow and the shadow's amplitude; therefore, it is clear that the arm subtracted from the shadow's amplitude results in the equinoctial shadow. ||58||

**Vivarana Bhashya:** The shadow's amplitude (amplitude on the hypotenuse circle), taken according to its direction, in the signs beginning with Aries <gloss>Aries, etc.</gloss>—meaning in the Northern Hemisphere—is decreased <gloss>lessened</gloss> by the northern <gloss>northward</gloss> difference <gloss>the arm, which is the east-west distance from the base of the twelve-digit gnomon</gloss>, and increased by the southern <gloss>southward</gloss> arm; then it becomes the equinoctial shadow <gloss>palabhā</gloss>. Likewise, in the signs beginning with Libra, meaning in the Southern Hemisphere, that difference <gloss>the measure of the arm</gloss> subtracted from the shadow's amplitude results in the equinoctial shadow. ||58||

### Here is the proof:

It is shown how the gnomon's base is equal to the equinoctial shadow in the sphere of the shadow's hypotenuse:

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| (Palabhā × Drig) / 12 = Gnomon's Base | 12 × Tri / Drig = Hypotenuse | Therefore, by substitution: (Palabhā × 12 × Tri) / (12 × Drig) = Gnomon's Base |

In the sphere of the shadow's hypotenuse, the Gnomon's Base = (Palabhā × 12 × Tri × Drig) / (12 × Drig × Tri) = Palabhā. <note>The formula demonstrates that through geometric substitution, the base of the gnomon on the shadow's path is equivalent to the equinoctial shadow.</note>

The arm is produced by the calculation of the gnomon's base and the amplitude. The shadow's amplitude is taken according to its direction. In the Northern Hemisphere, before the Sun's entry into the prime vertical, the shadow's amplitude is decreased by the equinoctial shadow (which is equal to the gnomon's base), and that becomes the northern arm; therefore, the shadow's amplitude decreased by the northern arm is the equinoctial shadow. After the entry, the shadow's amplitude is subtracted from the equinoctial shadow, and the remainder is the southern arm; therefore, the amplitude increased by that arm is the equinoctial shadow. In the Southern Hemisphere, the arm is always the sum of the shadow's amplitude and the equinoctial shadow; therefore, the shadow's amplitude decreased by the arm's measure is the equinoctial shadow. As stated in the *Siddhanta Shekhara*: **"The shadow's amplitude, when adjusted by the northern difference..."**

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

<page-num>350</page-num>
<header>In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta</header>

"When the sun is in the six signs beginning with Aries <note>the northern hemisphere</note>, the equinoctial shadow is determined by subtracting the northern difference or adding the southern difference. Likewise, when the luminous sun is in the six signs beginning with Libra <note>the southern hemisphere</note>, the difference is subtracted in the same manner." This statement by Shripati <note>an 11th-century Indian mathematician</note> is merely a variation of the verse spoken by the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note>. || 58 ||

->Now, another method for knowing the Equinoctial Shadow is described<-

**Hindi Commentary —** In the six signs starting with Aries—that is, in the Northern Hemisphere—the Equinoctial Shadow <term>Palabha: the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</term> is found by subtracting the northern difference (the distance between the 12-digit gnomon's base and the east-west line) from the shadow-radius amplitude <note>the distance of the sun's shadow from the east-west line</note>, or by adding the southern difference. In the six signs starting with Libra—that is, in the Southern Hemisphere—the Equinoctial Shadow is found by subtracting the shadow-radius amplitude from that difference (the value of the side/base). || 58 ||

->Mathematical Proof<-

In the sphere of the shadow-radius, the base of the gnomon <term>Shankutala: the distance from the rising-setting line to the foot of the gnomon</term> is equal to the Equinoctial Shadow. For example: $\frac{\text{Palabha} \times \text{Sine Altitude}}{12}$ = Shankutala. Since $\frac{\text{Radius} \times 12}{\text{Shadow-Radius}}$ = Sine Altitude, by substitution we get $\frac{\text{Palabha} \times \text{Radius} \times 12}{12 \times \text{Shadow-Radius}}$ = Shankutala. Converting this into the sphere of the shadow-radius: $\frac{\text{Palabha} \times \text{Radius} \times 12 \times \text{Shadow-Radius}}{12 \times \text{Shadow-Radius} \times \text{Radius}}$ = Palabha = the Shankutala in the shadow-radius sphere. 

In the Northern Hemisphere, before the sun enters the prime vertical, the northern side is found by subtracting the Equinoctial Shadow (which is equal to the Shankutala) from the shadow-amplitude. Therefore, subtracting the northern side from the shadow-amplitude gives the Equinoctial Shadow. After the sun passes the prime vertical, the remaining southern side is found by subtracting the shadow-radius amplitude from the Equinoctial Shadow; thus, adding this side to that amplitude gives the Equinoctial Shadow. In the Southern Hemisphere, the side is always the sum of the shadow-radius amplitude and the Equinoctial Shadow; therefore, subtracting the shadow-radius amplitude from the side gives the Equinoctial Shadow. The method described by Shripati in the *Siddhanta-Shekhara*—written in the Sanskrit proof as "The amplitude determined by the shadow-circle is the same as the northern difference," etc.—is consistent with what the Teacher has stated. || 58 ||

->Now he describes the arrangement of the Equinoctial Shadow and Amplitude in the desired shadow-circle<-

> In the desired shadow-circle, the line connecting the two points of rising and setting is the rising-setting line.
> From the base of that gnomon, the distance to the rising-setting line is the Equinoctial Shadow; here, the amplitude is also found. || 59 ||

**Sanskrit Commentary —** In the desired shadow-circle, the line passing through the two points of the east and west directions—specifically, the points transformed into the shadow-circle—is the rising-setting line. "From that gnomon" means from the base or root of the sun's gnomon to the rising-setting line, the distance is the Equinoctial Shadow. Thus, the result to be understood is that in this shadow-circle, the amplitude is known through the side and the equinox.
