The rationale here is as follows: Just as in the case of the Great Sine-Gnomon <note>original: *mahashanku*; the vertical line from the planet to the horizon</note>, the distance from the rising-setting line to the end of the gnomon's base is the "gnomon-base" <note>original: *shankutala*</note>. Due to the similarity of the latitude-triangles <note>original: *akshakshetra*</note> of the small twelve-digit gnomon, the distance from the rising-setting line of the shadow-circle to the base of the small gnomon is the equinoctial shadow <note>original: *palabha*; the shadow cast at noon on the day of the equinox</note>. This is perfectly clear to all experts in spherical astronomy. ||56||

**Vijnana Bhashya commentary:** In the desired shadow-circle, the line used for calculating the two tips—meaning the east and west directions—is called the rising-setting line. By proportion from the gnomon, the distance from the gnomon's base to that line (the distance up to the rising-setting line) is the equinoctial shadow. Here (in this shadow-circle), the amplitude <note>original: *agra*; the distance of the sun from the east-west line at rising</note> should be understood through the base <note>original: *bhuja*</note> and the equinoctial shadow. ||56||

### The Rationale

->The line produced by the two tips of the east and west directions transformed into the shadow-radius-circle is<-
->designated as the rising-setting line. There, the distance between the rising-setting line and the gnomon's base is the gnomon-base.<-
->In the shadow-circle, the gnomon-base is exactly equal to the equinoctial shadow. Therefore, when the rising-setting line<-
->is drawn in the shadow-circle and a twelve-digit gnomon is placed according to the rules, the distance between them<-
->calculated by mathematics is equal to the equinoctial shadow; and when measured physically in digits, it is<-
->perceptibly equal to the equinoctial shadow. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, it is said: "In the circle of the desired shadow,<-
->the line of its tips is indeed called the rising-setting line. By the rule of three, the distance of this gnomon is<-
->clearly seen as the equinoctial shadow." This statement by Shripati <note>An 11th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> is exactly in accordance with the teacher's teaching. ||56||<-

Its distance from the gnomon's base is the equinoctial shadow. In this shadow-circle, the amplitude should be understood from the base and the equinoctial shadow. ||56||

### Now, the method for bringing forth the Sine of Declination from the base and the shadow:

->**The distance between the gnomon and the east-west line, or the difference between the equinoctial shadow and the gnomon,**<-
->**is the northward or southward movement in digits. This, divided by the shadow-hypotenuse, is the Sine of Declination. ||60||**<-

**Sudhakara Bhashya commentary:** The distance between the gnomon and the east-west line is the "base" <note>original: *bhuja*</note> related to the small gnomon. The equinoctial shadow is the *palabha*...

# Chapter on the Three Problems

...and in the case of the northern side <note>the "bhujā" or side of the shadow</note>, by multiplying the sum of these two by the cosine of latitude <term>lambajyā: the sine of the co-latitude</term> and dividing by the hypotenuse of the shadow <term>chāyākarṇa</term>, the sine of declination <term>krāntijyā</term> is obtained. ## Mathematical Proof

In the Northern Hemisphere (as stated in verse 58), the Southern Side = Equinoctial Shadow - Distance between the tip of the shadow and the amplitude line = *bhu*. Therefore, the distance between the tip of the shadow and the amplitude line = Equinoctial Shadow - *bhu*. Thus, in the Southern Side, the difference between the side and the equinoctial shadow is proven to be the distance to the amplitude line. In the Northern Hemisphere, the Northern Side = Distance to the amplitude line - Equinoctial Shadow = *bhu*. Therefore, the distance to the amplitude line = Equinoctial Shadow + *bhu*.

Now we apply the rule of proportion: If for the hypotenuse of the shadow we get the distance to the amplitude line, then for the radius <term>trijyā</term>, what do we get? This yields the amplitude <term>agrā</term>.
<gloss>(Distance to amplitude line × Radius) / Hypotenuse of shadow = Amplitude</gloss>
From this, we calculate another proportion: If for the radius we get the cosine of latitude, then for the amplitude, what do we get? This yields the sine of declination.
<gloss>(Cosine of latitude × Amplitude) / Radius = (Cosine of latitude × Distance to amplitude line × Radius) / (Hypotenuse of shadow × Radius) = (Cosine of latitude × Distance to amplitude line) / Hypotenuse of shadow = Sine of declination.</gloss>
Thus, the teacher's statement is proven. In the *Siddhānta Śekhara* <note>A major astronomical treatise by Śrīpati</note>, the verse beginning with "The line between the shadow and the equinoctial shadow..." expresses the same logic as Śrīpati Ācārya. In the *Sūrya Siddhānta* <note>The foundational text of Indian astronomy</note>, the statement "The desired amplitude multiplied by the cosine of latitude and divided by its own shadow-hypotenuse..." is also identical to the teacher's rule. This concludes verse 60.

## Now, the method for bringing forth the Sun's position from the sine of declination:

> The declination multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of 24 degrees <note>original: "jinabhāga" referring to the maximum declination or obliquity of the ecliptic</note> gives the sine of the longitude. In the first quadrant beginning with Cancer <note>Aries</note>, this is the arc itself. In the second beginning with Cancer, subtract the arc from a half-circle <note>180 degrees</note>. In the third beginning with Libra, add it to a half-circle. In the fourth beginning with Capricorn, subtract the arc from a full circle <note>360 degrees</note> to find the true Sun. This must be done repeatedly, reversing the sign of the equation of center <term>mandaphala</term> (adding if it was subtracted, subtracting if it was added). From this, by applying the terrestrial longitude correction <term>deśāntara</term> as before, the mean Sun is found. ||61-62||

**Commentary by Sudhākara Dvivedī:** The declination (sine of declination) multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the maximum declination <note>24 degrees</note> becomes the sine of the Sun's longitude. The arc of that sine in the first three signs starting from Aries is the true Sun. In the three signs starting from Cancer, subtract that arc from a half-circle; the remainder is the true Sun. Similarly, in the three signs starting from Libra, the true Sun is equal to the arc plus a half-circle. In the three signs starting from Capricorn, subtract that arc from a full circle (twelve signs); the remainder should be known as the true Sun. In that process of iterative calculation, the equation of center <term>mandaphala</term> should be applied inversely—positive if it was negative and negative if it was positive—to find the mean Sun at one's own location. Then, by applying the terrestrial longitude correction—adding the correction for western longitude and subtracting for eastern—the mean Sun is established as previously described.

The proof here is clear through inverse operation. By the method of Bhāskara <note>Bhāskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note>—"That arc in the first quadrant becomes the Sun of the year; in others..." and so on—knowledge of the quadrant is easily understood. || 61-62 ||

**V. Mā. <note>Commentary by Viṣṇu Śarmā or similar</note>—** The declination (sine of declination) multiplied by the radius (tri-radius) and divided by the sine of the maximum declination <note>original: "jinajyā", referring to the sine of 24 degrees</note> gives the sine of the Sun's longitude. Its arc (the angle) in the first quadrant (the three signs starting with Aries) is known as the true Sun. In the second quadrant (the three signs starting with Cancer), subtract that arc from half a circle (six signs); the remainder is the true Sun. In the third quadrant (the three signs starting with Libra), the true Sun is equal to that arc plus half a circle (six signs). In the fourth quadrant (the three signs starting with Capricorn), subtract that arc from the full circle (twelve signs); the remainder shall be the true Sun. In that calculation, if the correction for the equation of center <note>term: mandaphala - the correction for the Sun's elliptical orbit</note> was additive, it should be made subtractive, and if subtractive, it should be made additive to find the mean Sun at one's own location. From this, by accounting for the terrestrial longitude <note>term: deśāntara - the distance from the prime meridian</note>—that is, adding the longitude correction for eastern locations and subtracting it for western locations—the mean Sun is calculated as before. || 61-62 ||

### The Proof Here

If the radius is obtained from the sine of maximum declination, then what is obtained from the sine of the Sun's declination? By the proportion of the declination field, the sine of the Sun's longitude arrives. Its form is:
<note>Mathematical fraction</note>
(Radius × Sine of Declination) / Sine of Max Declination
The arc of this would be the degrees of the Sun's longitude. In the first quadrant, this itself is the true Sun. In the second quadrant, by subtracting from half a circle; in the third quadrant, by adding to half a circle; and in the fourth quadrant, by subtracting from a full circle, the true Sun is found—this is directly visible on the armillary sphere. In the *Siddhānta Śiromaṇi*, Bhāskara says exactly what the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> stated: "That arc in the first quadrant becomes the Sun of the year; in others..." and so on. However, the method shown by Bhāskara and other teachers to identify the quadrant through descriptions of the seasons is not entirely accurate. For this reason, Kamalākara, in the *Siddhānta-tattva-viveka*, rejected it with mockery, saying: "This sign of the seasons mentioned previously is not found everywhere. It is only for the pleasure of bad poets, not for the determination of the planets' quadrants."

Thus, to know this, he showed his own method: "In the first quadrant, the equinoctial shadow <note>term: palabha - the shadow of a vertical gnomon at noon on the equinox</note> decreases and is less than the midday shadow; in the second, the shadow is small but increasing. In the third, the shadow is greater and increasing; in the fourth, it decreases again and is smaller." The logic for this is: When the Sun (with its precession) is at the beginning of Aries, the midday shadow is the equinoctial shadow, as stated by Bhāskara. From that day onward, in a country north of the equator:
<note>Mathematical formula</note>
"Sine of Zenith Distance × 12 / Cosine of Zenith Distance = 12 / Gnomon = Shadow"
According to this definition of the shadow, as the midday zenith distance decreases and the midday gnomon <note>term: śaṅku - the vertical pillar used for shadows</note> increases, the midday shadow will successively decrease. Therefore, when the midday shadow is less than the equinoctial shadow and decreasing, it must be the Sun's first quadrant. In the second quadrant, the midday zenith distance increases successively, so the midday shadow increases; when it is less than the equinoctial shadow but increasing, it must be the Sun's second quadrant. In the third quadrant, the midday shadow is greater than the equinoctial shadow...

The north-pointing shadow increases (due to the Sun's movement toward the south). In a place located on the terrestrial equator, in the first quadrant, the decrease in the central shadow occurs due to the increase in the central zenith distance. There, the shadow must be southerly (because the Sun is positioned north of one's own zenith). In the second quadrant, the decrease in the central shadow occurs due to the decrease in the central zenith distance (due to the Sun's movement from north to south). In the third and fourth quadrants, there is no fixed rule for the increase or decrease of the zenith distance; therefore, the knowledge of the quadrant cannot be determined by a single rule regarding the central shadow. For this reason, it is said: "If the shadow is southerly and increasing, it is the first quadrant. Observing it decreasing while remaining southerly, know it to be the Sun's second quadrant." Since this wonderful method is seen mentioned in the *Siddhānta Śekhara* <note>A major astronomical work by Śrīpati, c. 1039 CE</note>, the method starting with "In the first quadrant, the shadow is decreasing and less than the equinoctial shadow, etc." does not belong to Kamalākara; in reality, this method belongs to Śrīpati. ||61-62||

Its arc is the true Sun in the first quadrant. This is directly observed on the armillary sphere. In the *Siddhānta Śiromaṇi*, Bhāskarācārya speaks in accordance with the teachings of the ancient masters, saying "That arc is in the first quadrant, in the second..." etc. However, Bhāskara and other masters determined the Sun's quadrant through the description of the seasons, which is not precise. For this reason, in the *Siddhānta Tattva Viveka*, Kamalākara refuted this using the verse "By the seasons, etc." written in the Sanskrit proof. <header>In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta</header>

By observation, the progressive decrease in the central zenith distance <note>original: "madhyanatansha"</note> and the increase in the central gnomon-shadow <note>original: "madhyashanku"</note> leads to a gradual decrease in the central shadow. Therefore, when the central shadow is less than the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "palabha"</note> and is progressively decreasing, it is the Sun's first quadrant. In the second quadrant, the central zenith distance increases progressively until the Sun reaches the autumnal equinox <note>original: "tuladi sampat"</note>; thus, when the shadow is less than the equinoctial shadow but increasing, it is the second quadrant. In the third quadrant, the central shadow becomes greater than the equinoctial shadow and increases progressively (due to the Sun's southward movement). In the fourth quadrant, due to the tendency to move northward again, the zenith distance progressively decreases; therefore, the shadow is greater than the equinoctial shadow but decreasing. Thus, the statement **"In the first quadrant, it is decreasing..."** <note>original: "Adye pade'pachayino"</note> is logically sound. 

In regions south of the equator <note>original: "niraksha desh"</note>, in the first quadrant, the central shadow increases due to the increase in the central zenith distance, but because the Sun remains north of the local zenith <note>original: "svasvastika"</note>, the tip of the shadow falls toward the south. Therefore, the verse written in the Sanskrit commentary, **"If the southern tip is increasing..."** <note>original: "Vriddhi prayanti yadi dakshinagra"</note>, is logically consistent. In the second quadrant, due to the Sun's progressive southward movement, the central shadow decreases as the central zenith distance decreases. In the third and fourth quadrants, because of the irregularity in the increase and decrease of the zenith distance, the knowledge of the quadrant cannot be determined by a single rule through the central shadow. All these matters are clear from observing the armillary sphere <note>original: "gola"</note>. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, this marvelous method starting with **"In the first quadrant, it is decreasing..."** is seen. This proves that this method of determining the Sun's quadrant actually belongs to Shripati <note>An 11th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>, and not to Kamalakar <note>A 17th-century astronomer; the author is clarifying a historical attribution</note>. || 61-62 ||

### Now, he describes a special rule for the Sun's gnomon-shadow in the elevation of the Moon's horns:

> For the sake of the elevation of the Moon's horns, the gnomon-shadow is calculated from the elapsed or remaining ghatikas <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> of the night.
> Using the method of the opposite hemisphere <note>original: "viparita-gola-vidhina"</note>, it is like the declination at midnight. || 63 ||

**Sudhakara Bhashya (Commentary):**—To find the elevation of the horns in the western direction, one should use the elapsed ghatikas of the night (as altitude), and in the eastern direction, the remaining ghatikas of the night (as altitude). Using the rule **"From the elapsed and remaining [time] of the day..."** and the method of the opposite hemisphere, the Sun's gnomon-shadow <note>original: "shanku"</note> should be calculated. If the Sun's gnomon-shadow is desired through the hour angle <note>original: "nata-nadika"</note>, then that shadow should be brought forth using the declination at midnight and the hour angle.

**Rationale here:** This is clear from Bhaskara's method for the elevation of the horns, starting with **"By the remaining or elapsed breaths of the night..."** <note>original: "nishavasheshairusubhirgatairva"</note>. Since the Sun is below the horizon during the visible elevation of the [Moon's] horns, the time interval within the lower meridian is required; therefore, the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> has given the instruction to calculate it from the midnight declination and the hour angle. || 63 ||

**Vijnana Bhashya (Explanatory Commentary):**—In the western direction, for the sake of the elevation of the Moon's horns, using the elapsed ghatikas of the night (as altitude), and in the eastern direction, using the remaining ghatikas of the night (as altitude), the Sun's gnomon-shadow is to be calculated by the method of the opposite hemisphere...

When the Sun's gnomon <note>The *shanku* or gnomon refers here to the sine of the altitude of the sun</note> is required, it should be calculated using the time intervals relative to midnight. || 63 ||

->**The Rationale**<-

The elevation of the Moon's horns <note>The "horns" refer to the tips of the lunar crescent</note> is only visible when the Sun is positioned below the horizon. Therefore, to determine the hour angle from the lower meridian, the Teacher <note>Referring to the original author of the text being commented upon</note> has prescribed the calculation of the hour angle based on the difference from midnight. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati stated: "For the elevation of the Moon's horns, one should calculate the gnomon using the elapsed or remaining breaths of the night, applying the methods in reverse according to the celestial sphere." Similarly, Bhaskara in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* stated: "The Sun's gnomon below the horizon is found via the remaining or elapsed time of night, reversing the hemispheric rules." This aligns perfectly with the Teacher's instructions. || 63 ||

Now, a specific rule is given regarding the **Sun's gnomon** <term>Ravi-shanku: the vertical shadow-casting pole, used here to represent the sine of the Sun's altitude</term> in the context of the **elevation of the Moon's horns** <term>Chandra-shringonnati: the visual orientation and "pointedness" of the lunar crescent</term>.

**Hindi Commentary:** To find the elevation of the Moon's horns in the western direction, use the elapsed time of the night; for the eastern direction, use the remaining time of the night. Using the rule "from the lesser of the elapsed or remaining time of day," etc., one should calculate the Sun's downward **gnomon calculation** <term>Shanku-sadhana</term> by reversing the standard hemispheric rules. The gnomon should also be calculated from the hour angle using the method described by the Teacher. || 63 ||

->**Rationale**<-

The elevation of the Moon's horns is visible only when the Sun is below the horizon. Therefore, to know the hour angle from the lower meridian, the Teacher has described the calculation of the hour angle through the difference between the Sun and the midnight point. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati (in the verse cited in the Sanskrit rationale) and Bhaskara in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* (in the verse "By the breaths of the night...") have spoken in total agreement with the Teacher's words. || 63 ||

### Now, the formula for the Rising-Setting Line is stated:

> The amplitude <note>The distance on the horizon between the East point and the point where a celestial body rises</note> on the horizon is the sine of declination multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of colatitude. Twice the square root of the difference between the square of the radius and the square of that amplitude is the Rising-Setting Line. || 64 ||

**Sudhakara's Commentary:** When the **declination** <term>Kranti: the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</term>—specifically the **sine of declination** <term>Kranti-jya</term>—is multiplied by the **radius** <term>Trijya: the standard radius used in Indian trigonometry, often 3438 minutes</term> and divided by the **sine of colatitude** <term>Lamba-jya</term>, the result is the amplitude. This amplitude exists on the horizon in the East and West. That is, it represents the distance from the East and West cardinal points on the horizon. Twice the square root of the radius squared minus that amplitude squared becomes the "Rising-Setting Line" <note>The chord of the diurnal arc on the horizon plane</note>.

<header>In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta</header>

Here is the proof. The <term>Kujya</term> <note>the sine of the terrestrial latitude or earth-sine</note> is the base. The <term>Krantijya</term> <note>sine of declination</note> is the perpendicular. The <term>Agra</term> <note>amplitude at the horizon</note> is the hypotenuse. This is the well-known "figure of the latitude" <note>Akshakshetra: a right-angled triangle used in Indian astronomy to relate celestial coordinates</note>. Therefore, if the radius is the hypotenuse for a perpendicular equal to the sine of the colatitude <note>Lambajya</note>, then what will it be for a perpendicular equal to the sine of declination? The result is the Amplitude (Agra) = (Sine of Declination × Radius) / Sine of Colatitude. The square root of the difference between the square of the radius and the square of the amplitude is the "cosine of the amplitude"; twice that value is known as the "Rising-Setting Line" <note>Udayastasutra: the chord connecting the rising and setting points of a planet on the horizon</note>. ||64||

**Scientific Commentary**—The declination (sine of declination) multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the colatitude results in the amplitude. This represents the distance on the horizon from the east and west points (the celestial equinoctial points) according to the direction of the planet. The square root of the difference between the squares of the radius and this amplitude, when doubled, becomes the Rising-Setting Line. ||64||

->Here is the Proof<-

If the radius is obtained from the sine of the colatitude, then what is obtained from the sine of declination? By the proportion of the "figure of the latitude," the Amplitude (Agra) = (Radius × Sine of Declination) / Sine of Colatitude. When the square of the amplitude is subtracted from the square of the radius and the square root is taken, we get the "cosine of the amplitude" = √(Radius² — Amplitude²). Twice this value is the Rising-Setting Line. In the <term>Siddhanta Shekhara</term> <note>An astronomical treatise by Shripati, c. 1039 CE</note>, it is said: "The amplitude is formed on the horizon from the east-west line; the square root of the difference between the squares of the radius and that amplitude, multiplied by two, is called the north-south Rising-Setting Line by those proficient in the celestial sphere." This statement by Shripati and the statement in the <term>Siddhanta Shiromani</term> <note>The major work of Bhaskara II, c. 1150 CE</note>—"The sine of the portion of the diurnal circle intercepted between the horizon and the prime vertical is the amplitude at the east and west"—by Bhaskara are exactly in accordance with the Teacher's <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> instruction. ||64||

->Now the Rising-Setting Line is described<-

**Hindi Commentary**—Multiplying the <term>Krantijya</term> <note>sine of declination</note> by the radius and dividing by the <term>Lambajya</term> <note>sine of colatitude</note> gives the <term>Agra</term> <note>amplitude</note>. This amplitude is measured in the east and west directions from the east-point and west-point respectively. Doubling the square root of the difference of the squares of this and the radius results in the <term>Udayastasutra</term> <note>Rising-Setting Line</note>. ||64||

->Proof<-

If we find the radius within the sine of colatitude, then what do we find in the sine of declination? From this proportion of the "figure of the latitude" comes the amplitude: (Radius × Sine of Declination) / Sine of Colatitude = Amplitude. Subtracting the square of the amplitude from the square of the radius and taking the root gives the cosine of the amplitude. Doubling this gives the Rising-Setting Line. As stated in the Siddhanta Shekhara, "That which is east-west..."

<header>Chapter on the Three Problems</header>

Regarding the verse beginning with "On the horizon, the earth-shadow..." <note>original: "क्षितिजे कुताप्रा"</note> written in the commentary, Sripati, as well as Bhaskaracharya in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* with the verse "The sine of the amplitude at the middle of the diurnal circle..." <note>original: "स्वरात्रमममण्डलमध्यभागजीवाग्रका"</note>, both speak in accordance with the ancient teachers. ||64||

## Now, the calculation of the base of the gnomon is described:

> From the product of the sine of latitude and the gnomon, divided by the cosine of latitude, the result is the base of the gnomon.
> Measured from the rising-setting line, it is to the south during the day and to the north during the night. ||65||

**Sudhakara Dvivedi's Commentary:** — The meaning is clear.

**The Rationale here:** Due to the influence of the latitude <term>Aksha: the terrestrial latitude or the angle of the pole</term>, the diurnal circles are inclined to the south during the day and to the north during the night. Therefore, the base of the gnomon is southern during the day and northern at night. The calculation of the base of the gnomon through the proportion of the latitude-triangle is evident. ||65||

**Vishnu Kant Jha's Commentary:** — From the product of the sine of latitude <note>Akshajya</note> and the gnomon <note>Shanku</note>, divided by the cosine of latitude <note>Lambajya</note>, the result is the base of the gnomon <note>Shankutala</note>. This is measured from the rising-setting line <note>Udayastasutra</note> towards the south during the day and towards the north during the night. ||65||

### The Rationale

The perpendicular dropped from a planet onto the plane of the horizon is the gnomon <term>Shanku: the vertical pillar or the sine of altitude</term>. The distance from the foot of this gnomon to the rising-setting line is the base of the gnomon <note>Shankutala</note>. Since the diurnal circle above the horizon moves toward the south, the base of the gnomon during the day is south of the rising-setting line. Because the diurnal circle below the horizon moves toward the north, the base of the gnomon at night is north of the rising-setting line; this is clearly visible on the armillary sphere. By the proportion of the latitude-triangle: "If the sine of latitude is obtained for the cosine of latitude, then what is obtained for the gnomon?" By this:
Base of the Gnomon = (Sine of Latitude × Gnomon) / Cosine of Latitude.

In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Sripati says: "The gnomon multiplied by the sine of latitude and divided by the cosine gives the result. That is the north-south base of the gnomon from the rising-setting line during the day and night." In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskara says: "Because the diurnal circle above the horizon moves south during the day, the base of the gnomon is southern; because it moves north below the horizon at night, it is northern. This explanation of the gnomon's base is logically sound." These statements are entirely in agreement with the ancient teachers. ||65||

---

->Now the calculation of the base of the gnomon is explained in Hindi<-

**Hindi Commentary:** — Dividing the product of the sine of latitude and the gnomon by the cosine of latitude results in the base of the gnomon. It is south of the rising-setting line during the day and north during the night. ||65||

### Rationale

If we find the sine of latitude within the cosine of latitude, then what do we find in the gnomon? From this latitude-triangle proportion, the base of the gnomon is derived.

# The Corrected Treatise of Brahma

## Chapter on Lunar Eclipses

->Now the chapter on lunar eclipses is explained; first, the author states the purpose for beginning this section:<-

> Knowledge of time is generally sought by the virtuous for the sake of knowing the parvan <note>The 'parvan' refers to the precise moment of the new or full moon, essential for Vedic rituals.</note>.
> The true differences between the eclipses of the Moon and the Sun are made clear by the learned. ||1||
> Direction, color, deflection, time, immersion, emergence, duration, and total obscuration; ||2||
> The contact, the shadow, the clearance, the attainment of the desired eclipse, and the graphical representation—
> Because there are fourteen such differences in the knowledge of those two, the lunar and solar eclipses, I shall therefore speak on the subject of eclipses. ||3||

**Sudhakara's Commentary:**—By the "virtuous," meaning virtuous mathematicians, knowledge of time is sought mostly for the sake of knowing the *parvan*. Conversely, it follows that from the knowledge of the *parvan*, the knowledge of time becomes clear. The implied meaning is that through the knowledge of time, the performance of sacrifices and other rituals becomes accurate. For the sake of understanding the eclipses of the Moon and the Sun, the "true differences"—such as direction, place, time, and color—are clarified by the distinctions to be described.

The fourteen differences, such as direction, color, and deflection, are clarified as follows:
1. **Direction**: For the Moon, the first contact is in the East; for the Sun, it is in the West.
2. **Color**: In a lunar eclipse, when less than half is eclipsed, the colors are smoky and so on; for the Sun, it is always black.
3. **Deflection** <term>Valana: the variation of the ecliptic from the prime vertical</term>: In a lunar eclipse, the deflections arising at contact and clearance are applied from East to West; in a solar eclipse, from West to East.
4. **Time**: In a lunar eclipse, the middle of the eclipse is always at the end of the *tithi* <note>The lunar day</note>; in a solar eclipse, that rule does not hold.
5. & 6. **Immersion and Emergence**: These two are mutually reversed in lunar and solar eclipses; thus, there is a difference there too.
7. **Duration**: The duration is great in a lunar eclipse and small in a solar eclipse.
8. **Total Obscuration**: Similarly, the time of total darkness is great in a lunar eclipse and small in a solar eclipse.
9. **Contact**: The determination of the time of contact in a lunar eclipse is from half the duration; in a solar eclipse, it is from half the duration adjusted by parallax.
10. **Shadow**: The difference in shadow during contact etc., is well known due to the difference in their respective distances.
11. **Clearance**: In a lunar eclipse, clearance is in the West; in a solar eclipse, it is in the East.
12. **Magnitude of Eclipse**: In a lunar eclipse, it is from the latitude; in a solar eclipse, it is from the latitude adjusted by parallax.
13. **Desired Eclipse**: In a lunar eclipse, it is from the latitude of that time and the calculated half-duration; in a solar eclipse, it is from the latitude adjusted by parallax and the corrected half-duration.
14. **Graphical Representation**: In a lunar eclipse, it is from the calculated latitude; in a solar eclipse, it is from the latitude adjusted by parallax.

Thus, here we have: 1. Direction, 2. Color, 3. Deflection, 4. Time, 5. Immersion, 6. Emergence, 7. Duration, 8. Total Obscuration, 9. Contact, 10. Shadow, 11. Clearance, 12. Magnitude, 13. Desired Eclipse, 14. Graphical Representation.

### The Fourteen Distinctions. Since the knowledge of these fourteen distinctions arises from the understanding of lunar and solar eclipses, I shall therefore explain the eclipses of the Moon and the Sun. || 1-2-3 ||

> **Sanskrit Commentary:**—Virtuous people (**either those learned in the Vedas or skilled astronomers**) generally (**mostly**) desire the knowledge of time for the sake of knowing the *parvan* <note>A 'parvan' refers to the transition days of the moon, specifically the New Moon and Full Moon</note> (**the start and end times of the New Moon and Full Moon festivals are primarily necessary for those who know how to perform the rituals prescribed by the Vedas; therefore, in the science of astronomy (Jyotisha) as well, the primary goal is to understand at what time these festivals begin and end**). For the understanding of lunar and solar eclipses, the actual differences (**such as direction, location, and time**) become clear through the following distinctions:
> 
> 1. **Directional difference** (**in a lunar eclipse, the first contact is on the east; in a solar eclipse, it is on the west**).
> 2. **Color difference** (**in a lunar eclipse—during partial, more than half, or total obscuration—the Moon takes on colors such as black, dark red, or tawny. In a solar eclipse, the color of the Sun is always black**).
> 3. **Deflection difference** (**the deflection at contact and separation is from the east and west in a lunar eclipse, but from the west and east in a solar eclipse**).
> 4. **Time difference** (**in a lunar eclipse, the first contact always occurs exactly at the end of the lunar day (Tithi); in a solar eclipse, there is no such fixed rule**).
> 5. **Immersion and Emergence** (**these occur in opposite ways in lunar and solar eclipses, which is also a distinction**).
> 6. **Duration difference** (**the duration is long in a lunar eclipse and short in a solar eclipse**).
> 7. **Total darkness difference** (**the period of total obscuration is great in a lunar eclipse and small in a solar eclipse**).
> 8. **First Contact** (**the determination of the time of contact**): in a lunar eclipse, it is calculated from half the duration; in a solar eclipse, it is from half the duration adjusted by parallax <term>parallax: the displacement in the apparent position of a celestial body</term>.
> 9. **Shadow difference** (**this occurs due to the difference in their respective gnomon shadows at the time of contact, etc.**).
> 10. **Release difference** (**release/end of eclipse is in the west for the Moon and in the east for the Sun**).
> 11. **Magnitude difference** (**in a lunar eclipse, it is calculated from the latitude; in a solar eclipse, from the latitude adjusted by parallax in latitude**).
> 12. **Specific Magnitude difference** (**in a lunar eclipse, from the latitude of that moment and the calculated half-duration; in a solar eclipse, from the latitude adjusted by parallax and the corrected half-duration**).
> 13. **Projection difference** (**in a lunar eclipse, from the calculated latitude; in a solar eclipse, from the latitude adjusted by parallax**).
> 
> Thus, there are fourteen distinctions here. Since the knowledge of these fourteen distinctions arises from the understanding of the eclipses of the Sun and Moon, I shall explain the lunar and solar eclipses. || 1-2-3 ||

> **Hindi Commentary:**—Good astronomers generally speak of the knowledge of time for the sake of knowing the *parvan*; that is, the start and end times of festivals like the New Moon and Full Moon are primarily useful to good astronomers or Vedic scholars for performing Vedic rituals. Therefore, in the science of astronomy, the primary knowledge sought is when these festivals begin and end. The actual differences for the knowledge of lunar and solar eclipses (**direction, place, time, etc.**) are made clear by the following distinctions:

# Now, the method for calculating instantaneous positions is stated:

**Multiply the elapsed or remaining portions of the lunar day by the daily motion, and divide by the difference in daily motions. Subtract the result if elapsed, or add if remaining.**
**The Sun and Moon then become equal in minutes of arc; the Node also becomes instantaneous through this.** **(4)**

**Sudhakara Bhashya (Commentary):** The elapsed or remaining minutes of the lunar day <term>Tithigatagamya: the portion of the Tithi that has passed or is yet to come</term> are multiplied by the daily motion of the Sun and the Moon. In both cases, divide by the difference between the Sun's and Moon's daily motions. If the time is elapsed, subtract the result; if it is remaining, add the result to the Sun and Moon. Thus, they become instantaneous and equal in minutes of arc at the end of the lunar day. Similarly, the Node <note>Rahu, the ascending node of the Moon</note> also becomes instantaneous based on its own motion.

->**The Rationale:** To find the elapsed or remaining minutes of the lunar day, one would multiply by sixty and divide by the difference in motion of the Sun and Moon to get the ghatikas (units of time). Those ghatikas, multiplied by the daily motion and divided by sixty, would yield the motion-adjustment in minutes of arc. Here, since the multiplier and divisor of sixty are equal, they cancel each other out, resulting in the procedure as stated. (4)<-

**Vijnana Bhashya (Explanatory Commentary):** Multiply the elapsed or remaining minutes of the lunar day by the daily motion of the Moon and the Sun. Divide by the difference in the daily motions of the Sun and Moon. Subtract the result from the Moon and Sun if calculating from elapsed time, or add if calculating for remaining time. At the end of the lunar day, the Sun and Moon become instantaneous and equal in their minutes of arc. Similarly, the Node becomes instantaneous according to its own motion. (4)

->**The Rationale**<-

If sixty ghatikas are obtained for the difference in the daily motions of the Sun and Moon in minutes, then by proportion, how many ghatikas are obtained for the elapsed or remaining minutes of the lunar day? Since the specific daily motion in minutes is obtained for sixty ghatikas, then for the elapsed or remaining ghatikas of the lunar day...

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
<note>The Brahmasphuta-siddhanta is a seminal 7th-century astronomical treatise by Brahmagupta.</note>

And why did these occur? The Moon's motion minutes (past) = $\frac{60 \times \text{elapsed tithi minutes}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}} \times \frac{\text{Moon's daily motion minutes}}{60} =$

$\frac{\text{elapsed tithi minutes} \times \text{Moon's daily motion minutes}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}}$, similarly, the Moon's motion minutes to be traversed = $\frac{60 \times \text{remaining tithi minutes}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}} \times \frac{\text{Moon's daily motion minutes}}{60}$

$= \frac{\text{remaining tithi minutes} \times \text{Moon's daily motion}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}}$, in the same way, the Sun's elapsed motion minutes = $\frac{60 \times \text{elapsed tithi minutes}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}} \times$

$\frac{\text{Sun's daily motion}}{60} = \frac{\text{elapsed tithi minutes} \times \text{Sun's daily motion}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}}$,

The Sun's motion minutes to be traversed = $\frac{60 \times \text{remaining tithi minutes}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}} \times \frac{\text{Sun's daily motion}}{60} = \frac{\text{remaining tithi minutes} \times \text{Sun's daily motion}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}}$

By this, what the Teacher <note>Referring to Brahmagupta</note> has stated is proven. ||4||

->Now the method for instantaneous correction is described<-

**Hindi Commentary** — Multiply the elapsed minutes of the lunar day (*tithi*) and the remaining minutes of the lunar day separately by the Moon's motion and the Sun's motion. Divide these by the difference between the motions of the Sun and Moon. In the case of elapsed motion, subtract these results from the Moon and Sun; in the case of remaining motion, add them. Then, at the end of the *tithi*, the instantaneous Sun and Moon become equal in minutes (*samaliptika*). In this same way, the Node <note>The lunar node or Rahu</note> also becomes instantaneous based on its own motion. ||4||

->Mathematical Proof<-

If 60 *ghatis* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 ghatis make one day</note> are obtained in the difference of the Sun and Moon's motion minutes, then what is obtained in the elapsed and remaining minutes of the *tithi*? By this proportion, the elapsed *ghatis* and remaining *ghatis* of the *tithi* are found:

$\frac{60 \times \text{elapsed tithi minutes}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}} =$ elapsed *tithi ghatis*, $\frac{60 \times \text{remaining tithi minutes}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}} =$ remaining *tithi ghatis*. Again, we calculate the proportion: if the respective motion minutes are obtained in 60 *ghatis*, then what is obtained in the elapsed and remaining *ghatis*? By this proportion, the Moon's elapsed motion minutes = $\frac{60 \times \text{elapsed tithi minutes}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}}$

$\times \frac{\text{Moon's daily motion}}{60} = \frac{\text{elapsed tithi minutes} \times \text{Moon's daily motion}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}}$

Similarly, the Moon's remaining motion minutes = $\frac{60 \times \text{remaining tithi minutes}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}} \times \frac{\text{Moon's daily motion}}{60} = \frac{\text{remaining tithi minutes} \times \text{Moon's daily motion}}{\text{difference between Sun and Moon's motion}}$, and in the same way...

### Now, he describes the calculation of the latitude minutes at the end of the lunar day <note>Tithi</note>

> The sine of the sum of the Moon and its node <note>Rahu</note> multiplied by 270 <note>the cube of three, 3³ = 27, times ten</note> and divided by the radius <note>Trijya</note> results in the latitude minutes. These are North if the sum is less than six signs, and South if it is greater. ||55||

**Sudhakara Bhashya <note>Commentary by Sudhakara Dvivedi</note>:** — When the sum of the Moon and its node is less than six signs <note>180 degrees</note>, the latitude minutes are North; when greater, they are South. The rest is clear.

->The proof here: It is clear through the method of Bhaskara, starting with "The sine of the Moon's longitude including the node multiplied by its own..." etc. ||55||<-

**Vijnana Bhashya <note>Scientific/Explanatory Commentary</note>:** — The sine of the sum of the Moon and its node (the sine of the Moon's longitude corrected for the node) multiplied by 270 and divided by the radius results in the latitude <term>Vikshepa</term> <note>celestial latitude or 'deflection'</note> minutes. These are North (positive) if the sum of the Moon and node is less than six signs, and South (negative) if the sum is greater than six signs. ||55||

### The Proof here

The intersection of the ecliptic and the Moon's orbit is the Node <term>Pata</term>. A circle should be drawn ninety degrees from the position of the Node; in that circle, the arc between the ecliptic and the Moon's orbit is the Moon's maximum latitude. Where the center of the Moon's disk lies on its orbit, the secondary circle to the ecliptic <term>Kadamba-prota-vritta</term> <note>a circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic</note> passing through it meets the ecliptic at the Moon's position. The distance from the center of the Moon's disk to the Moon's position on this secondary circle is the Moon's mean latitude. The arc on the Moon's orbit from the Node to the center of the Moon's disk is the argument of latitude. The arc on the ecliptic from the Node to the Moon's position is the longitude from the node. The circle ninety degrees from the Node is the circle of maximum difference. From the Node to the intersection of this maximum difference circle and the Moon's orbit is ninety degrees. Similarly, from the Node to the intersection of the maximum difference circle and the ecliptic is ninety degrees. In the circle of maximum difference, the interval between the ecliptic and the Moon's orbit is the Moon's maximum latitude in degrees; thus, one triangle is established. From the Node to the center of the Moon's disk on the Moon's orbit is the hypotenuse; the longitude from the node on the ecliptic is the base. The Moon's mean latitude on the secondary circle between the Moon's center and its position is the perpendicular side. Thus, a second spherical right-angled triangle is established. A proportion is made using the sine-fields of these two spherical right-angled triangles: If by the radius...

### Mathematical Proof (Upapatti)

The intersection of the <term>ecliptic</term><note>the Sun's apparent path</note> and the <term>lunar orbit</term><note>Vimandala</note> is known as the <term>Node</term><note>Pata</note>. A circle drawn ninety degrees from the Node represents the maximum distance between these two circles. The arc of this maximum distance circle contained between the ecliptic and the lunar orbit is the <term>maximum latitude</term><note>Paramashara</note>. Where the center of the Moon's disk lies on the lunar orbit, a circle drawn through the <term>poles of the ecliptic</term><note>Kadamba-prota-vritta</note> marks the Moon's position on the ecliptic. The distance from the center of the Moon's disk to this ecliptic position along that polar circle is the Moon's mean latitude. 

A spherical right-angled triangle is formed by three arcs: the hypotenuse (the arc on the lunar orbit from the Node to the Moon's center), the base (the arc on the ecliptic from the Node to the Moon's longitude), and the perpendicular (the Moon's mean latitude). A second spherical right-angled triangle is formed from the Node to the intersection of the maximum distance circle: ninety degrees on the lunar orbit, ninety degrees on the ecliptic, and the maximum latitude. Since these two spherical triangles are similar in their sine-proportions, we calculate the ratio: if for the full radius we obtain the sine of the maximum latitude, then for the sine of the Moon's longitude on its orbit, what shall we get? By this proportion, the sine of the Moon's mean latitude is derived:

-> (Sine of Max Latitude × Sine of Moon's Orbital Longitude) <-
-> ------------------------------------------------------- = Sine of Mean Latitude <-
->                         Radius                          <-

However, the Moon's exact longitude on its own orbit is not directly known here; through calculation, the longitude relative to the node on the ecliptic is known. Therefore, the Teacher <note>the author of the original Sanskrit text</note> has accepted the ecliptic longitude as equivalent to the orbital longitude. Thus:

-> (Sine of Max Latitude × Sine of Moon's Longitude) <-
-> ------------------------------------------------- = Sine of Mean Latitude <-
->                      Radius                       <-

Furthermore, the identity between the sine and the arc itself is accepted here <note>a common simplification in ancient trigonometry for small angles</note>. Thus:

-> (Max Latitude × Sine of Moon's Longitude) <-
-> ----------------------------------------- = Mean Latitude <-
->                  Radius                   <-

-> 270 × Sine of Moon's Longitude <-
-> ------------------------------ This latitude follows the direction of the Moon's <-
->             Radius             <-

hemisphere; that is, it belongs to whichever celestial hemisphere the Moon is currently occupying. Thus, the Teacher's statement is proven. However, this calculation is not perfectly precise because the orbital longitude is the hypotenuse while the ecliptic longitude is the base arc...

<meta>This page continues the mathematical derivation of planetary latitudes and diameters, specifically focusing on the Moon's position relative to its node and the calculation of solar and lunar disks.</meta>

<header>In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta</header>

The Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> has assumed these two to be equal; he has accepted the Sine of the Moon's maximum latitude as equal to the maximum latitude itself, and the Sine of the Moon's mean latitude as the mean latitude. This is technically inaccurate, therefore we shall now perform the true calculation. In a spherical right-angled triangle formed by three components—the Moon's ecliptic longitude, the Moon's longitude from the node <note>Sapaata-chandra-bhujansha</note>, and the Moon's mean latitude—the angle produced is the Moon's maximum latitude. In said triangle, according to the rule "The sine of the middle part multiplied by the radius equals the product of the tangents of the adjacent parts" and "Take the cosine in place of the hypotenuse and angles," we have: 

Cosine of Moon's Max Latitude × Radius = Tangent of Moon's Ecliptic Longitude × Tangent of Moon's Longitude from Node.

Therefore: $\frac{\text{Cosine of Moon's Max Latitude} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Tangent of Moon's Longitude from Node}} = \text{Tangent of Moon's Ecliptic Longitude}$.

By taking the arc of this tangent value and subtracting it from 90 degrees, the Moon's ecliptic longitude is known. Then, in the previously mentioned spherical right triangle, the product of the cosines of the sides is equal to the product of the radius and the cosine of the hypotenuse. By this rule:

Radius × Cosine of Moon's Ecliptic Longitude = Cosine of Moon's Latitude × Cosine of Moon's Longitude from Node.

Therefore: $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Cosine of Moon's Ecliptic Longitude}}{\text{Cosine of Moon's Longitude from Node}} = \text{Cosine of Moon's Latitude}$.

By subtracting the arc of this value from 90 degrees, the Moon's mean latitude is found. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya <note>a 12th-century mathematician</note> has stated the same in accordance with the Teacher's words in the verse beginning with "The sine of the instantaneous Moon from the node..." etc. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati has calculated the Moon's latitude in the verse beginning "Of the cold-rayed one <note>the Moon</note> subtracted from the node..." which also aligns with the Teacher's method. Shripati merely used the "Moon minus the node" <note>Vipata-chandra</note> because the node is subtracted from the signs of the zodiac. By reducing the multiplier of the Moon's maximum latitude (270) and Shripati's radius (3438) by a factor of five, Shripati's verse is proven. || 5 ||

$\frac{8 \text{ Moon-motion} - 25 \text{ Sun-motion}}{60}$. By this, everything stated by the Teacher <note>Referring to Brahmagupta</note> is proved. (1) By this also, the calculation of the Earth's shadow diameter stated by Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, a 12th-century mathematician</note>—"The motion of the Sun divided by five and then by twelve, and the motion of the Moon multiplied by two and divided by fifteen, etc."—is justified. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*: "The motions of the Sun and Moon multiplied by eleven (11) and ten (10) respectively, or divided by twenty (20) and two hundred forty-seven (247), are the minutes of their diameters. The Sun's motion multiplied by five and divided by twelve, and the Moon's motion multiplied by two and divided by fifteen; half the difference of these results is the diameter of the Shadow <note>literally 'the diameter of the son of Sinhika,' a poetic name for Rahu/the shadow</note>." This statement by Shripati is exactly in accordance with the Teacher's statement. The Teacher's Earth-shadow diameter $=$

$\frac{8 \text{ Moon-motion}}{60} - \frac{25 \text{ Sun-motion}}{60} = \frac{2 \text{ Moon-motion}}{15} - \frac{5 \text{ Sun-motion}}{12} =$ Shripati's Earth-shadow diameter. "The motion of the Sun increased by its tenth part and halved, is the Sun's diameter; the Moon's diameter is its motion multiplied by three and divided by seventy-four (74)."
This calculation of the angular diameters of the Sun and Moon by Bhaskaracharya, as well as: "The motion of the Sun divided by five (5) and then by twelve (12), and the motion of the Moon multiplied by two (2) and divided by fifteen (15); the difference of the results is the measure of the Earth's shadow," is also exactly in accordance with Shripati. || 6 ||

### Now the calculation of the diameters of the Sun, Moon, and Earth's shadow is described.

**Hindi Commentary.**—Multiplying the Sun's motion by eleven and dividing by twenty (20) gives the value of the Sun's diameter <term>Bimba: the apparent angular diameter of a celestial body</term>. Multiplying the Moon's motion by ten and dividing by two hundred forty-seven (247) gives the value of the Moon's diameter. Dividing the difference between twenty-five times the Sun's motion and eight times the Moon's motion by sixty (60) gives the diameter of the Earth's shadow <term>Bhubha: the Earth's shadow or umbra at the Moon's distance</term>. || 6 ||

---

### Proof

By the method stated by Bhaskara, "The motion of the Sun increased by its tenth part and halved," the Sun's diameter $=$

$$\frac{\text{Sun-motion} + \frac{\text{Sun-motion}}{10}}{2} = \frac{10 \text{ Sun-motion} + \text{ Sun-motion}}{20} = \frac{11 \text{ Sun-motion}}{20}$$

From the statement "the Moon's diameter is its motion multiplied by three and divided by seventy-four," the Moon's diameter $=$ $\frac{3 \text{ Moon-motion}}{74} = \frac{3 \text{ Moon-motion} \times 10}{74 \times 10} = \frac{3 \text{ Moon-motion} \times 10}{740} = \frac{\text{ Moon-motion} \times 10}{\frac{740}{3}} = \frac{\text{ Moon-motion} \times 10}{247}$

With a slight difference. For the calculation of the Earth's shadow diameter, by the method of the reviser: "The sum of the horizontal parallaxes of the Sun and Moon, minus half the Sun's diameter, equals half the Earth's shadow diameter." <note>original: "रपलं + चंपलं - रविर्द्ध = भूभाविर्द्ध"</note>

# Chapter on Lunar Eclipses

However, the Sun's motion in minutes = $\frac{\text{Sun's daily motion}}{15}$, the Moon's motion in minutes = $\frac{\text{Moon's daily motion}}{15}$, and the Sun's diameter = $\frac{<unclear>?</unclear>}{20} = \frac{11 \times \text{Sun's daily motion}}{20 \times 2} = \frac{11 \times \text{Sun's daily motion}}{40}$

By substituting these values = $\frac{\text{Sun's motion}}{15} + \frac{\text{Moon's motion}}{15} - \frac{11 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{40} - \frac{\text{Sun's motion}}{15} - \frac{11 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{40} + \frac{\text{Moon's motion}}{15} =$

$\frac{8 \times \text{Sun's motion} - 33 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{120} + \frac{\text{Moon's motion}}{15} = \frac{-25 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{120} + \frac{\text{Moon's motion}}{15} = - \frac{5 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{24} + \frac{\text{Moon's motion}}{15} = \frac{\text{Moon's motion}}{15} - \frac{5 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{24}$

= <term>Earth's Shadow Diameter</term> <note>original: bhūbhāvi</note> - $\frac{1}{2}$, and by doubling it: $\frac{2 \times \text{Moon's motion}}{15} - \frac{5 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{12}$ = <term>Earth's Shadow Diameter</term> $\dots$ (1) Here, by multiplying the denominator and numerator of the first part by four, and the denominator and numerator of the second part by five, we get $\frac{8 \times \text{Moon's motion}}{60} - \frac{25 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{60} = \frac{8 \times \text{Moon's motion} - 25 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{60} =$ <term>Earth's Shadow Diameter</term>. Through this, all the statements of the ancient teachers are proven. (1) In this, the method for calculating the <term>diameter of the Earth's shadow</term> <note>original: bimbānayana</note> stated by Bhāskara, such as "the difference in motions multiplied by five and divided by the Sun's diameter," is proven; in the <term>Siddhānta Śekhara</term>, the method of <term>Śrīpati</term> written in the Sanskrit commentary as "multiplied by eleven and ten for the Sun and Moon respectively" is consistent with the teachers' methods. The <term>Earth's Shadow Diameter</term> according to the teachers = $\frac{8 \times \text{Moon's motion}}{60} - \frac{25 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{60} = \frac{2 \times \text{Moon's motion}}{15} - \frac{5 \times \text{Sun's motion}}{12}$. The <term>Earth's Shadow Diameter</term> mentioned by <term>Śrīpati</term> in the Sanskrit commentary as "the motion of the Sun increased by its tenth part and halved," and the calculation of the diameters of the Sun and Moon by <term>Bhāskarācārya</term>, as well as the calculation of the Earth's shadow diameter in the Sanskrit commentary, are consistent with <term>Śrīpati's</term> method. || 6 ||

->Now he describes the <term>magnitude of the eclipse</term> <note>original: grāsamāna</note><-

> **Half the sum of the diameters of the eclipsed and eclipsing bodies, diminished by the latitude, is the portion eclipsed.**
> **If this is greater than the eclipsed body, it is a total eclipse; if less, it is a partial eclipse. || 7 ||**

->Sudhākara Bhāṣya: The meaning of this verse is clear.<-

The mathematical proof here is evident through <term>Bhāskara's method</term>, which states: "Half the sum of the diameters of the eclipsed and eclipsing circles, minus the latitude, is the measure of the obscured portion." || 7 ||

Vijaya Mārga: **Half the sum of the diameters of the eclipsed and eclipsing bodies** (meaning half the sum of the diameters of the Moon and the Earth's shadow in a lunar eclipse, or the Sun and Moon in a solar eclipse) **diminished by the latitude** (subtracted by the Moon's celestial latitude) **is then the magnitude of the eclipse.** **If the magnitude of the eclipse is greater than the eclipsed body** (the body being covered), **a total eclipse occurs; if the magnitude of the eclipse is less than the eclipsed body, a partial eclipse occurs.** || 7 ||

### Here is the Proof:

<margin>(a)</margin>
Bhu = Center of the Earth's shadow disk. Cha = Center of the Moon's disk. Bhu-Cha = Lunar latitude <note>The angular distance of the Moon from the ecliptic</note>.
Bhu-Ra = Radius of the Earth's shadow disk. Cha-Na = Radius of the Moon's disk. Na-Ra = Magnitude of the eclipse <term>Grasamana: the portion of the celestial body covered during an eclipse</term>.
Bhu-Ra + Cha-Na = Bhu-Ra + Ra-Cha + Na-Ra = Bhu-Cha + Na-Ra = Lunar latitude + Magnitude of eclipse + Radius of Earth's shadow + Radius of Moon's disk = Half the sum of the diameters <term>Manaikyardha: the sum of the radii of the obscuring and obscured bodies</term>.

Therefore: Half the sum of the diameters — Lunar latitude = Magnitude of the eclipse. If this magnitude is greater than the Moon's disk, a total eclipse occurs. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, a 12th-century Indian mathematician</note> stated: "Half the sum of the circles of the obscured and the obscurer, diminished by the latitude..." and Shripati in the *Siddhanta Shekhara* likewise said: "The latitude subtracted from half the sum of the diameters of the covering and covered bodies..." following the same method as the Teacher <note>Referring to Brahmagupta, the original author</note>. || 7 ||

#### Now the calculation for the magnitude of the eclipse is described.

**Hindi Commentary** — By subtracting the lunar latitude from the half-sum of the diameters of the obscured and obscuring bodies (in a lunar eclipse, the Moon and Earth's shadow; in a solar eclipse, the Sun and the Moon), the remainder is the magnitude of the eclipse. If the magnitude is greater than the diameter of the body being eclipsed, it is a total eclipse; if the magnitude is less, it is a partial eclipse. || 7 ||

### Proof

Refer to diagram (a) in the Sanskrit proof. Bhu = Center of the Earth's shadow, Cha = Center of the Moon, Bhu-Cha = Lunar latitude, Bhu-Ra = Radius of Earth's shadow, Cha-Na = Radius of the Moon, Na-Ra = Magnitude of eclipse. Bhu-Ra + Cha-Na = Bhu-Ra + Ra-Cha + Na-Ra = Bhu-Cha + Na-Ra = Lunar latitude + Magnitude of eclipse = Radius of Earth's shadow + Radius of Moon = Half the sum of the diameters. Therefore: Half the sum of the diameters — Lunar latitude = Magnitude of eclipse. It is clear from looking at the geometry of the diagram that if the magnitude is greater than the Moon's disk (the obscured body), a total eclipse must occur. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya says "Half the sum of the circles of the obscured and obscurer..." <note>original: "yacchadya sanchadakamandalaikyakhandam"</note> and in the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati says "The latitude is subtracted from half the sum of the diameters of the covering and covered bodies, they call this the obscured portion" <note>original: "ksepo bhavatyatha pidhanapidheyabimbayogardhamunamamuna sthagitam vadanti"</note>, which aligns exactly with the Teacher's words. || 7 ||

#### Now he describes the calculation for the half-duration and half-totality.

> **From the square of the sum and difference of the obscured and obscurer,**
> **subtract the square of the latitude; the square roots of these, treated like the lunar day,**
> **are the half-duration and half-totality.** || 8 ||

# Chapter on the Authority of Lunar Eclipses
Page 35

**Sudhakara Dvivedi's Commentary:** The square root is treated like the calculation of a lunar day <note>tithi</note>. That is to say, the square root is multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference between the velocities of the Sun and the Moon to find the half-duration of the eclipse <term>Sthityardha: half the total duration from first to last contact</term> and the half-duration of totality <term>Vimardhardha: half the duration of the total phase</term>. The remainder is clear.

The derivation here is evident through the method of Bhaskara <note>referring to the 12th-century astronomer Bhaskara II</note> using "the squares of the sum and difference of the semi-diameters," etc. || 8 ||

**Visvanatha's Commentary:** From the half-sum and half-difference of the diameters of the obscured body <note>the Moon</note> and the obscurer <note>the Earth's shadow</note>—meaning the squares of the sum of the semi-diameters and the difference of the semi-diameters—subtract the square of the latitude <term>Vikshepa: the angular distance of the Moon north or south of the ecliptic</term>. Taking the square root of that and treating it like a lunar day—meaning multiplying by sixty and dividing by the difference in the daily motions of the Sun and Moon—the results are the half-duration of the eclipse and the half-duration of totality respectively. || 8 ||

->**The Derivation**<-

When the external contact between the Earth's shadow <term>Bhubha</term> and the Moon's disk occurs, the distance on the ecliptic <term>Kranti-vritta</term> from the point where the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the Moon's center meets the ecliptic, to the center of the Earth's shadow, is the "half-duration arc" in minutes. The distance from the intersection of that secondary circle with the ecliptic to the Moon's center is the latitude at the moment of contact. Similarly, when internal contact <note>the start of totality</note> occurs, the distance on the ecliptic from the intersection point to the center of the Earth's shadow is the "half-totality arc," and the distance from the Moon's center to the ecliptic is the latitude at the moment of immersion <note>Sammilana</note>. A circle should be drawn passing through the center of the Moon and the center of the Earth's shadow.

**Bhu** = Center of the Earth's shadow disk.
**Cha1** = Center of the Moon's disk at the moment of external contact.
**Cha1-Ra** = Latitude at contact.
**Ra-Bhu** = Half-duration arc.
**Cha2** = Center of the Moon's disk at the moment of internal contact (immersion).
**Cha2-Sha** = Latitude at immersion.
**Sha-Bhu** = Half-totality arc.
**Na** = Point of contact.
**Bhu-Cha** = Distance between centers on the circle passing through the Moon and Earth's shadow.
**Cha-Na** = Radius of the Moon's disk.
**Bhu-Ta** = Radius of the Earth's shadow.
**Bhu-Cha (at contact)** = Sum of the semi-diameters of the Moon and Earth's shadow.
**Bhu-Cha (at immersion)** = Difference of the semi-diameters of the Moon and Earth's shadow.

Here, the Teacher <note>the author of the original verses</note>, by treating the triangles **Bhu-Cha-Ra** and **Bhu-Cha-Sha** as plane right-angled triangles, has provided the clear calculation for the half-duration and half-totality as follows:

<vocab>
**Lunar Eclipse (Chandra-grahana):** The passage of the Moon through Earth's shadow.
**Half-totality (Vimardhardha):** Half the time the Moon spends completely inside the shadow.
**Half-duration (Sthityardha):** Half the time from the first moment the Moon touches the shadow until it leaves it.
**Earth's Shadow (Bhubha):** Literally "Earth-shadow," the dark cone cast by Earth into space.
**Secondary to the Ecliptic (Kadamba-prota-vritta):** A great circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic.
**Ecliptic (Kranti-vritta):** The apparent path of the Sun.
**Latitude at Contact (Spashika-shara):** The Moon's celestial latitude at the moment the eclipse begins.
**Immersion (Sammilana):** The moment the Moon is fully engulfed in the shadow.
</vocab>

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

$\sqrt{\text{Earth-Moon}^2 - \text{Moon-Projection}^2} = \text{Earth-Radius} = \sqrt{\text{Sum of Radii}^2 - \text{Latitude at Contact}^2} = \text{Half-duration minutes}$, then by proportion: "If sixty ghatikas <note>A ghatika is a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> are obtained by the difference in the motions of the Sun and Moon, then what is obtained for the minutes of the half-duration?" By this, the ghatikas of the half-duration are arrived at = $\frac{60 \times \text{Half-duration minutes}}{\text{Difference in motion}}$, similarly in the Earth-Moon-Projection triangle:

$\sqrt{\text{Earth-Moon}^2 - \text{Moon-Projection}^2} = \text{Earth-Radius} = \sqrt{\text{Difference of Radii}^2 - \text{Latitude at Totality}^2} = \text{Half-totality minutes}$, then as before by proportion, the ghatikas of the half-totality = $\frac{60 \times \text{Half-totality minutes}}{\text{Difference in motion}}$. However, here, due to the ignorance of the specific latitudes at the moments of contact and totality, the calculation of the half-duration and half-totality is performed using the latitude at the time of the middle of the eclipse; this is not strictly accurate. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara*: "Having squared the sum and difference of the semi-diameters and subtracted the square of the latitude, the square roots of the remainders, when treated like the lunar day, shall be respectively the half-duration and the half-totality." This is the verse of Shripati. In the *Siddhanta-shiromani*: "From the squares of the sum and difference of the semi-diameters, subtracted by the square of the latitude, the square roots multiplied by sixty (60) and divided by the difference in daily motion, result in the half-duration and half-totality." This verse by Bhaskaracharya is exactly in accordance with what the Teacher <note>Referring to Brahmagupta</note> has stated. || 7 ||

Then, multiplying both by sixty and dividing by the difference in the motions of the Sun and Moon gives the half-duration and the half-totality. || 7 ||

->### Rationale (Upapatti)<-

Look at diagram (A) written in the Sanskrit rationale here. At the time of the external contact of the Earth's shadow-disk and the Moon's disk, the distance on the ecliptic from the intersection of the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the Moon's center to the center of the Earth's shadow is the **half-duration minutes**. The distance on the secondary to the ecliptic from the intersection point to the Moon's center is the **latitude at contact**. Similarly, at the time of internal contact (totality) of the Earth's shadow-disk and the Moon's disk, the distance on the ecliptic from the intersection of the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the Moon's center to the center of the Earth's shadow-disk is the **half-totality minutes**. On the secondary to the ecliptic, from the Moon's center to the ecliptic, is the **latitude at internal contact (totality)**. Let a circle be drawn through the Moon's center and the Earth's shadow center: <term>Bhu (Earth)</term> = Center of the Earth's shadow-disk, <term>Cha (Moon)</term> = Moon's center at the time of external contact, <term>Cha-Sha (Moon-Lat)</term> = Latitude at contact, <term>Ra-Bhu</term> = Half-duration minutes, <term>Cha</term> = Moon's center at the time of internal contact (totality), <term>Cha-Sha (Moon-Lat)</term> = Latitude at totality, <term>Ra-Bhu</term> = Half-totality minutes, <term>Na</term> = Point of contact, <term>Bhu-Cha</term> = Distance between centers in the circle passing through the centers of the Moon and the Earth's shadow, <term>Cha-Na</term> = Moon's disk...

Radius, Earth's Shadow = Radius of the Earth's shadow disk, Earth-Moon$^1$ = Half the sum of the diameters <note>Sanskrit: *mānaikyārdha*</note> of the Moon's disk and the Earth's shadow disk, Earth-Moon$^1$ = Half the difference of the diameters <note>Sanskrit: *mānāntarārdha*</note> of the Moon's disk and the Earth's shadow disk. Here the Teacher <note>Referring to the author of the original astronomical treatise</note> has calculated the half-duration of the eclipse <note>Sanskrit: *sthityardha*</note> and the half-duration of totality <note>Sanskrit: *vimardārdha*</note> by assuming the Earth-Moon-Vertex triangle to be a plane right-angled triangle. For instance, in the right-angled triangle Earth-Moon-Vertex: $\sqrt{\text{Earth-Moon}^2 - \text{Moon's Latitude}^2} = \text{Earth-Radius}^1 = \sqrt{\text{Half-Sum}^2 - \text{Latitude at Contact}^2} = \text{Half-duration in minutes of arc}$. Then the proportion is made: if sixty *ghatis* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> are obtained in the difference of the velocities of the Sun and Moon, then what is obtained in the half-duration minutes of arc? From this, the half-duration in *ghatis* is derived: $\frac{60 \times \text{Half-duration arc}}{\text{Difference in velocity}} = \text{Half-duration in ghatis}^1$. Similarly, in the right-angled triangle Earth-Moon-Vertex$^1$: $\sqrt{\text{Earth-Moon}^2 - \text{Moon's Latitude}^2} = \text{Earth-Vertex}^1 = \sqrt{\text{Half-Difference}^2 - \text{Latitude at Immersion}^2} = \text{Half-duration of totality in minutes of arc}$. By the same proportion as before, the Half-duration of totality in *ghatis* $= \frac{60 \times \text{Half-duration of totality arc}}{\text{Difference in velocity}}$. However, here the latitude at contact and the latitude at immersion are not known; what is known is the latitude at the middle of the eclipse. Therefore, the half-duration and half-duration of totality have been calculated by assuming the latitude at contact and immersion to be equal to the latitude at the middle of the eclipse. This is not strictly accurate. The verse by Sripati in the *Siddhanta Shekhara* beginning with "The squares of the sum and difference of the half-diameters..." and the verse by Bhaskaracharya in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* beginning with "From the squares of the sum and difference of the half-diameters..." are in accordance with the Teacher's statement. || 7 ||

## Now he describes the correction of the half-duration and the half-duration of totality.

> The individual motions multiplied by the half-duration of the eclipse or totality and divided by sixty;
> In the beginning, these are subtracted from the Sun, Moon, and Node, and at the end, they are added, repeatedly. || 9 ||

**Sudhakara Bhashya:**—The meaning is clear. The derivation here is clarified by the method of Bhaskara in the verses beginning with "The individual motion multiplied by the half-duration *ghatis*..." and "Thus, by subtracting and adding the result of the half-duration of totality..." || 9 ||

**Vijnana Bhashya:**—The individual motion (velocity of the Sun, velocity of the Moon, and velocity of the Node) multiplied by the half-duration of the eclipse or totality (multiplied separately by the half-duration *ghatis* and the half-duration of totality *ghatis*) and divided by 60—this should be subtracted from the Sun, Moon, and Node at the beginning <note>The start of the eclipse</note>, and added to them at the end. That is, add to the first half-duration and subtract from the last half-duration; similarly, add to the first half-duration of totality and subtract from the last half-duration of totality. By performing this operation repeatedly <note>Sanskrit: *asakrit*, an iterative process</note>, the corrected half-duration and half-duration of totality are obtained. || 9 ||

---

### Here is the derivation:

If the minutes of the Moon's motion are obtained in sixty *ghatis*, then what is obtained in the half-duration *ghatis*—

By this proportion, the arc of the Moon's motion corresponding to the half-duration of the eclipse is obtained. Similarly, the motion of the <term>Node</term><note>The lunar node, Rahu, where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic.</note> corresponding to the half-duration should also be calculated. By subtracting or adding these two results to the Moon and its Node respectively, they become more precise than before. Then, using the rule "the sine of the sum of the Moon and Node multiplied by the cube of three and divided by the radius," one should calculate the <term>Lunar Latitude</term><note>original: "Chandra-shara"; the angular distance of the Moon north or south of the ecliptic.</note>. Following this, using the rule "of the diameter of the obscured body increased or decreased by the obscurer," the half-duration and half-totality should be calculated. Then, by the rule "the minutes of the half-duration and half-totality divided by sixty and multiplied by their own motions," one calculates the Moon's motion and the Node's motion for that half-duration. By subtracting or adding these, the Moon and Node become even more precise. By repeating this process <term>iteratively</term><note>original: "asakrit-karma"; a method of successive approximation to reach a precise value.</note>, the true <term>Half-Duration</term><note>original: "Sthityardha"; half the time from first contact to last contact.</note> is found. In the same way, through iterative calculation, the true <term>Half-Totality</term><note>original: "Vimardardha"; half the duration of the total phase of the eclipse.</note> is found.

In the <term>Siddhanta-Shekhara</term>, Shripati stated: "The motions of the Sun, Moon, and the Darkness <insert>the Node</insert> are multiplied by the ghatis of the half-duration or half-totality and divided by sixty. These are subtracted or added to the first and last positions iteratively." 

In the <term>Siddhanta-Shiromani</term>, Bhaskaracharya stated: "The motion of the body multiplied by the ghatis of the half-duration and divided by sixty is subtracted from or added to the positions. Having thus adjusted the Moon and the Node, the first and last half-durations are made precise through the resulting latitudes. Similarly, using the latitudes derived from the Moon and Node adjusted by the results of the half-totality, the first and last segments of the half-totality are refined as before." This confirms that they have followed the same method taught by the ancient Teacher <insert>Brahmagupta</insert>. || 9 ||

# Chapter on Lunar Eclipses

The half-duration of totality is given; in the *Siddhanta Shekhara* <note>A major 11th-century astronomical treatise by Sripati</note>, the half-duration of the eclipse and the half-duration of totality are clearly <unclear>shown</unclear>. However, in the verses written in the *Saurapati*, Sripati—and likewise Bhaskaracharya in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>The 12th-century masterpiece of Indian mathematics and astronomy</note> through verses such as "The planet's own motion multiplied by its own half-duration and divided by sixty, subtracted or added..."—speaks in agreement with the Teacher <note>Referring to the primary authority being commented upon</note>. || 9 ||

->Now the calculation for the times of immersion and emersion is stated.<-

### Immersion occurs after the start of the eclipse by the half-duration of the eclipse minus the half-duration of totality.
### Emersion occurs before the end of the eclipse by the same amount; the duration of totality is half the interval between them. || 10 ||

**Sudhakara's Commentary:** When the half-duration of totality is subtracted from the half-duration of the eclipse's beginning, the time of **immersion** <term>nimilana: the moment the moon is completely covered by the shadow</term> occurs after the initial contact. Similarly, when the half-duration of totality is subtracted from the half-duration of the eclipse's end, the time of **emersion** <term>unmilana: the moment the moon begins to emerge from the shadow</term> occurs prior to the final contact. Half the sum of these two times (immersion and emersion) constitutes the total duration of totality. This means that the eclipsed body remains submerged within the obscuring body <note>the Earth's shadow</note> for that specific duration.

When the half-duration of totality is subtracted from the half-duration of the final contact, emersion occurs before the end. Half of their sum (the average of the immersion and emersion times) represents the period during which the eclipsed disk remains submerged within the obscuring disk. || 10 ||
