# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

Thereafter, using the ascensional difference <note>original: "charasu"</note> of the nonagesimal <term>Vintribha: the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point (ascendant)</term>, one should calculate the sine of the altitude of the nonagesimal <note>original: "vintribhashanku"</note> using the method "of the remainder of the day passed," etc. ||2-3||

### **Mathematical Rationale**

The point where the vertical circle of the ninety-degree point (the nonagesimal circle) meets the ecliptic is the nonagesimal point. When the Sun is exactly at this nonagesimal point, there is an absence of apparent parallax. The arc of the ecliptic between the two circles passing through the poles of the ecliptic <note>original: "kadambaprotavritta"</note>—one passing through the true Sun and the other through the depressed (parallax-shifted) Sun—represents the Sun's apparent parallax. However, when the Sun is at the nonagesimal position, the vertical circle passing through it and the circle passing through the depressed Sun coincide with the nonagesimal circle itself. Therefore, there is no apparent parallax at that position. Thus, the teacher's statement, "There is no parallax when the Sun is equal to the nonagesimal," is logically sound.

At the moment of the geocentric conjunction <term>Garbhiya-manthakala: the time when the centers of the Sun and Moon are aligned as seen from the Earth's center</term>, the Sun and Moon are at the same point. Therefore, the depressed Sun and depressed Moon lie on the same vertical circle. The depressed Moon is shifted further down from the depressed Sun. Consequently, if the Sun is less than the nonagesimal (to the east), the point where the circle through the depressed Moon meets the ecliptic will be below (behind) where the circle through the depressed Sun meets it. In this case, because the slow-moving planet (the depressed Sun's position) is ahead of the fast-moving planet (the depressed Moon's position), the conjunction is yet to come <note>original: "gamya"</note>. Therefore, the topocentric conjunction <term>Prishthiya-manthakala: conjunction as seen from the Earth's surface</term> occurs after the geocentric one. Thus, by adding the difference of apparent parallax to the geocentric time, the topocentric time is found.

If the Sun is greater than the nonagesimal (to the west), the depressed Moon is below the depressed Sun, but the intersection of the Moon's circle with the ecliptic occurs "above" (ahead of) the Sun's intersection. Thus, because the fast-moving planet is ahead of the slow-moving planet, the conjunction has already passed <note>original: "gata"</note>. Therefore, by subtracting the parallax difference from the geocentric time, the topocentric time is found. Thus, the teacher's statement "it occurs when it is more or less" is logically sound. See diagram (A) in the Sanskrit commentary here. ||2-3||

### **Now, considering the Parallax in Latitude (Nati)**

See diagram (B) in the Sanskrit commentary here.
Kha = Zenith <note>original: "Khasvastika"</note>
Vi = Nonagesimal
Ra = Sun on the ecliptic
Lam-Ra = Depressed Sun
Sam-Ra-Stha = Position of the depressed Sun on the ecliptic

The arc from the Sun to the depressed Sun is the total parallax <note>original: "drig-lamban"</note>. The arc from the depressed Sun to its position on the ecliptic is the parallax in latitude <note>original: "nati"</note>. The arc from the Sun to the intersection point on the ecliptic is the apparent parallax in longitude.
Kha-Ra = Zenith distance of the Sun.
Kha-Vi = The arc of the ecliptic's zenith distance (Drigkshepa).
The spherical right-angled triangle formed by the Zenith, Nonagesimal, and Sun, and the triangle formed by total parallax, parallax in latitude, and parallax in longitude are similar. Therefore, we calculate the proportion: if in the sine of the zenith distance we find the field of view, then in the sine of total parallax...

<header>In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta</header>

...From this, the sine of the solar parallax in latitude <note>original: "natijya"</note> is derived. Since the calculation of this parallax depends upon the sine of the ecliptic zenith distance <note>original: "drk-kshepa"</note>, it is certain that in the absence of **ecliptic zenith distance**, there is also an absence of parallax in latitude. In regions with low latitude, the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> assumed the position of celestial latitude to be on the meridian circle <note>original: "yamyottara vrtta"</note> with very little difference. By adjusting for declination <note>original: "kranti"</note> and terrestrial latitude <note>original: "akshansha"</note>—similar to the calculation for midday—he established the position of zero zenith distance when the terrestrial latitude equals the northern declination. Therefore, the Teacher’s statement, "**When the sine of declination is northern and equal to the sine of latitude, there is no zenith distance**" <note>original: "tasya krantijyodak yadakshajiva sama na tada"</note>, is entirely logical. In the *Surya-Siddhanta-Shiromani*, the mathematician Bhaskaracharya has said something similar to the Teacher’s words with the phrase "**Parallax does not occur when the longitude of the nonagesimal is equal...**" <note>original: "na lambanam vighribhasammatulye"</note> and so on.

->Now, by way of context, we shall consider where the maximum value of the parallax in altitude occurs.<-

The arc of the vertical circle on the lunar sphere, contained between two lines—one from the Earth's center <note>geocentric</note> and one from the Earth's surface <note>topocentric</note> passing through the center of the Sun in its own orbit—is the solar parallax. Similarly, the arc of the vertical circle on the solar sphere, contained between two lines from the Earth's center and surface passing through the center of the Moon in its orbit, is the lunar parallax. In this way, a triangle is formed. One side is the planet's hypotenuse <note>distance</note> from the Earth's center to the planet's center (Sun or Moon); the second side is the surface-hypotenuse from the Earth's surface to the planet's center; and the third side is the Earth's radius <note>original: "bhuvyasardha"</note>. In the triangle generated by these sides, the angle formed by the surface-hypotenuse and the Earth's radius equals 180° minus the surface zenith distance. Since the sine of an angle and the sine of its supplement are equal, the sine of (180° — surface zenith distance) = the surface sine of altitude <note>original: "prsthiya drgjya"</note>. Then we apply the proportion: if for the planet's hypotenuse we obtain the surface sine of altitude, what would we obtain for the Earth's radius? From this, the sine of the planet's parallax in altitude (**drglambanajya**) is derived. Its form is as follows:

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| (Surface Sine of Altitude $\cdot$ Earth's Radius) | |
| ------------------------------------------------- | = Sine of Parallax in Altitude. In this, the planet's distance and Earth's radius are constants; |
| Planet's Hypotenuse | |

Therefore, it is proven that wherever the surface sine of altitude is at its maximum, the sine of parallax in altitude will also be at its maximum. However, the maximum value of the surface sine of altitude occurs when the planet is on the surface horizon; thus, it is proven that the maximum parallax in altitude occurs exactly at the surface horizon.

->Now we consider where the maximum parallax in latitude occurs.<-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| (Ecliptic Zenith Distance $\times$ Sine of Parallax in Altitude) | |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | = Parallax in Latitude (with slight difference). Also, from the proportion: |
| Radius | |

"If for the Radius <note>total sine</note> we obtain the maximum sine of parallax, what do we obtain for the desired surface sine of altitude?" From this, the desired sine of parallax in altitude is derived:

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| (Max Parallax $\cdot$ Surface Sine of Altitude) | |
| ----------------------------------------------- | = Sine of Parallax in Altitude. By substituting this into the formula for parallax in latitude: |
| Radius | |

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| (Ecliptic Zenith Distance $\cdot$ Max Parallax $\cdot$ Surface Sine of Altitude) | |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | If Surface Sine of Altitude = Sine of Altitude, then: "**The difference between the two orbits at the nonagesimal...**" |
| (Sine of Altitude $\cdot$ Radius) | |

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

"It is that from all sides" <note>original: "सर्वतोऽपि तत्"</note>—this statement by Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note> might be considered correct, but the <term>surface sine of zenith distance (prihajya)</term> is not always equal to the <term>geocentric sine of zenith distance (drijya)</term>; therefore, Bhaskara's statement is not entirely accurate. In the previously mentioned <term>nature of parallax in latitude (nati-svarupa)</term>, if the <term>sine of the ecliptic zenith distance (drikkshepa)</term> is considered constant, then the <term>parallax in latitude (nati)</term> will be at its maximum where the ratio $\frac{surface\ sine}{geocentric\ sine}$ is at its maximum. However, let us consider where this ratio $\frac{surface\ sine}{geocentric\ sine}$ reaches its maximum. Let <term>surface zenith distance (prinatansha)</term> $=$ <term>prina</term>, <term>geocentric zenith distance (garbhiya-natansha)</term> $=$ <term>na</term>, and <term>parallax in altitude (drilambana)</term> $=$ <term>lam</term>. Then, <term>prina</term> $=$ <term>na</term> $+$ <term>lam</term>. According to the rule "of two desired arcs" etc., the sine (<term>na</term> $+$ <term>lam</term>) $=$ <term>surface sine (prihajya)</term> $=$ $\frac{geocentric\ sine \cdot cosine\ of\ parallax + gnomon \cdot sine\ of\ parallax}{radius}$. By clearing the denominator, <term>surface sine</term> $\cdot$ <term>radius</term> $=$ <term>geocentric sine</term>.

<term>Cosine of parallax</term> $+$ <term>gnomon</term> $\cdot$ <term>sine of parallax</term>. But since $\frac{maximum\ parallax\ sine \cdot surface\ sine}{radius} = sine\ of\ parallax$, by substitution: <term>surface sine</term> $\cdot$ <term>radius</term> $=$ <term>geocentric sine</term> $\cdot$ <term>cosine of parallax</term> $+$ $\frac{gnomon \cdot maximum\ parallax\ sine \cdot surface\ sine}{radius}$. Therefore, <term>surface sine</term> $\cdot$ $radius^2$ $=$ <term>geocentric sine</term> $\cdot$ <term>cosine of parallax</term> $\cdot$ <term>radius</term> $+$ <term>gnomon</term> $\cdot$ <term>maximum parallax sine</term> $\cdot$ <term>surface sine</term>.

By isolating the <term>surface sine (prihajya)</term>: <term>surface sine</term> $\cdot$ $radius^2$ $-$ <term>gnomon</term> $\cdot$ <term>maximum parallax sine</term> $\cdot$ <term>surface sine</term> $=$ <term>surface sine</term> ($radius^2$ $-$ <term>gnomon</term> $\cdot$ <term>maximum parallax sine</term>) $=$ <term>geocentric sine</term> $\cdot$ <term>cosine of parallax</term> $\cdot$ <term>radius</term>. Consequently, $\frac{surface\ sine}{geocentric\ sine} = \frac{cosine\ of\ parallax \cdot radius}{radius^2 - gnomon \cdot maximum\ parallax\ sine}$. Looking at this form, it is proven that where the <term>gnomon (shanku)</term> and the <term>cosine of parallax (lambana-kotijya)</term> are at their maximum, the ratio $\frac{surface\ sine}{geocentric\ sine}$ will also be at its maximum. However, the <term>gnomon</term> and the <term>cosine of parallax</term> reach their maximum only at the <term>nonagesimal (vitribha)</term> point <note>the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the rising point</note>. Thus, the maximum <term>parallax in latitude (nati)</term> is proven to occur at the <term>nonagesimal</term> point. This validates the formula of the Great Teacher Pandit Shri Sudhakara Dvivedi <note>a prominent 19th-century astronomer</note>; see the formula in the Sanskrit commentary beginning with "Divided by the sine of the geocentric zenith distance" <note>original: "कुगर्भनतांशगुणेन भक्त"</note> etc.

---

<term>Gnomon (shan)</term> $=$ <term>radius (tri)</term>, <term>cosine of parallax (lankojya)</term> $=$ <term>radius (tri)</term>, therefore at the <term>zenith (khasvastika)</term> $\frac{surface\ sine}{geocentric\ sine} = \frac{radius \cdot radius}{radius^2 - radius \cdot maximum\ parallax\ sine}$

$=$ $\frac{radius^2}{radius(radius - maximum\ parallax\ sine)} = \frac{radius}{versed\ cosine\ of\ maximum\ parallax}$. But when the Sun is at the <term>zenith</term>:

<term>surface sine</term> $=$ 0 and <term>geocentric sine</term> $=$ 0, $\therefore$ $\frac{surface\ sine}{geocentric\ sine} = \frac{0}{0} = \frac{radius}{cosine\ of\ maximum\ parallax}$. But the <term>maximum parallax</term>—

# In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta
<note>This is a foundational 7th-century Sanskrit astronomical text by Brahmagupta.</note>

The cosine of the zenith distance <note>original: "kotijya"</note> multiplied by the radius <note>original: "tri"</note> divided by the cosine of the horizontal parallax is greater than 1, or the ratio of the earth's sine to the apparent sine <note>original: "drgjya"</note> equals 0/0, which is greater than 1. This mathematical peculiarity should be understood. ||2-3||

->Now he describes the calculation of parallax<-

> Divide the square of the radius by four times the gnomon-shadow <note>term: "shanku" (the vertical pillar used to measure shadows and determine celestial altitude)</note>. Divide the result by the sine of the difference between the sun's position and the nonagesimal <note>term: "vitribha-lagna" (the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point)</note> at that time. ||4||
> The result is the parallax in ghatikas <note>term: "ghatika" (a unit of time equal to 24 minutes)</note>. If the sun is greater than the nonagesimal, subtract it; if the sun is less, add it. This process is repeated at the end of the fifteenth lunar day <note>the full moon or new moon conjunction</note> to find the true time. ||5||

**Sudhakara Dvivedi's Commentary:** The meaning of these two verses is clear.

The proof here is evident from Bhaskara's method, such as "considering the nonagesimal as the sun," etc. To understand the true parallax, my own work on eclipses <note>original: "Grahana-karana"</note> should be consulted. ||4-5||

**Vishnukantha Jha's Commentary:** From the square of the radius, divided by four times the sine-altitude of the nonagesimal, and further divided by the sine of the difference between the sun and the nonagesimal at that time, the resulting value is the parallax in ghatikas (the clear time-parallax). If the sun is greater than the nonagesimal (the rising sign minus three signs), then at the end of the fifteenth tithi <note>the moment of conjunction</note>, it is negative (subtracted). If the sun is less than the nonagesimal, it is positive (added). This should be done repeatedly until the true time of the conjunction is established. ||4-5||

->Here is the Proof<-

Kha = Zenith <note>original: "Khasvastika"</note>. Vi = Nonagesimal <note>original: "Vitribha"</note>. Kha-Vi = Zenith distance of the nonagesimal. Stha-Vi = Distance between the planet and the nonagesimal. Stha = Position of the planet. Stha' = Parallax-shifted position of the planet. Ka =

<column-break/>

Pole of the ecliptic <note>original: "Kadamba"</note>. On the circle Ka-Stha', the arc dropped from the zenith is Kha-Pa. From the point of the planet to Ka-Stha'...

-> (1) <-

Therefore, whatever the degrees of latitude are, the formula stated by the Great Teacher <note>M.M. stands for Mahamahopadhyaya, a title for a great scholar.</note> Pandit Sri Sudhakara <note>Refers to Sudhakara Dvivedi, a renowned 19th-century mathematician.</note> regarding the parallax in altitude emerges:

# Chapter on the Authority of Solar Eclipses
417

When the minutes of arc—obtained by multiplying the velocities by the hours of parallax and dividing by sixty—are found, if the parallax is negative <note>subtractive</note>, then the positions of the Sun, Moon, and the Node <note>Rahu, the lunar node</note> calculated for the end of the lunar month should be decreased. If the parallax is positive <note>additive</note>, then the positions of the Sun, Moon, and the Node calculated for the end of the lunar month should be increased by those obtained minutes. Then, the true positions of the Sun, Moon, and the Node at the moment of the true conjunction are established. || 7 ||

### Here is the Proof

All values such as the latitude <term>Shara: the celestial latitude or angular distance from the ecliptic</term> must be derived from the positions of the Sun, Moon, and the Node at the calculated end of the lunar month. In the case of negative parallax, the rule of proportion is applied: "If in sixty hours the minutes of motion for the Sun, Moon, and Node are obtained separately, then what would they be in the hours of parallax?" The resulting minutes should be subtracted from the positions calculated for the end of the lunar month. In the case of positive parallax, they should be added. Thus, they become the true positions at the end of the conjunction. In the *Crest-Jewel of Siddhantas* <note>original: "Siddhanta Shekhara", a major astronomical treatise by Sripati</note>, it is said: "Multiply the motion by the hours of parallax and divide by sixty; with the resulting minutes, the Sun, Moon, and Nodes are increased if the parallax is positive and decreased if it is negative." By this, Sripati has stated exactly what was taught by the Master <note>referring to the original author of the primary text being commented upon</note>. || 7 ||

<header>Chapter on Solar Eclipses</header>

### Chapter on Solar Eclipses

->The sine of that is the first gnomon-shadow of the Moon, joined in the Sun's orbit of visibility.<-
->Joined with the ecliptic for the Sun, and with the secondary circle for the Moon. || 10 ||<-

**Sudhakara Bhashya (Commentary):** — When the zenith distance of the <term>Vitribha-lagna</term> <note>The nonagesimal, or the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</note> is northerly, the sine of the altitude (the arc of the gnomon) should be decreased or increased respectively by the northern or southern <term>Vikshepa</term> <note>Celestial latitude or deviation from the ecliptic</note>. When the zenith distance is southerly, that same arc of the gnomon should be increased by a northern latitude and decreased by a southern one. The sine of the arc thus adjusted is the "Gnomon of the Moon," which effectively means the <term>Driggati</term> <note>The sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal, used to calculate parallax</note> of the Moon. For the Sun, the "first" previously calculated gnomon of the nonagesimal is itself the <term>Driggati</term>.

In the circle of visibility (<term>Drikkshepa-mandala</term>), the <term>Driggati</term> of the Sun is joined with the ecliptic, and the <term>Driggati</term> of the Moon is joined with its own secondary orbit (<term>Vimandala</term>). The meaning is this: the gnomon of the nonagesimal point where the circle of visibility meets the ecliptic is the <term>Driggati</term> of the Sun.

**The mathematical proof:** The arc-degrees in the circle of visibility from the ecliptic to the secondary lunar orbit are, due to the small difference, equal to the latitude of the nonagesimal. Therefore, when the zenith distance of the nonagesimal is northerly and the latitude is northern, the sum of the two gives the arc-degrees from the zenith to the secondary orbit in the circle of visibility: Lunar Zenith Distance = Zenith Distance of Ecliptic + Latitude. Subtracting this from 90 degrees gives the Moon's <term>Driggati</term> arc. <note>The text provides the formula: 90 - (Zenith Distance + Latitude)</note>. Similarly, for a southern latitude, the Lunar Zenith Distance = Zenith Distance - Latitude. In the case of a southern zenith distance of the nonagesimal, the calculation is reversed. Thus, the method for finding the Moon's motion is established. However, the circle of visibility is perpendicular to the ecliptic, not to the secondary lunar orbit. Therefore, the lunar parallax derived from this is not perfectly accurate according to the experts of the <term>Siddhantas</term> <note>Scientific treatises</note>, as it is not measured along the secondary poles. Even **Bhaskara** <note>The famous 12th-century mathematician Bhaskara II</note> first followed this method—calculating the lunar parallax via the gnomon of the nonagesimal—but later, at the end of his chapter on solar eclipses, he refuted this calculation with the statement: "For the sake of the Moon's parallax, this adjustment by the latitude of the nonagesimal..." etc. || 9-10 ||

**Vijnana Bhashya (Technical Commentary):** — When the zenith distance of the nonagesimal is northerly, the arc of the gnomon is decreased or increased by the northern or southern latitude (<term>Shara</term>). When the zenith distance is southerly, it is increased or decreased (increased by northern, decreased by southern). The sine of that adjusted arc is the "Moon-Gnomon" (the <term>Driggati</term> of the Moon). For the Sun, the "first" (previously calculated) gnomon of the nonagesimal is the actual <term>Driggati</term>. In the circle of visibility, the Sun's <term>Driggati</term> is associated with the ecliptic (<term>Apamandala</term>). When associated with the secondary orbit (<term>Vimandala</term>), it is the Moon's <term>Driggati</term>. This means: the gnomon of the point where the circle of visibility meets the ecliptic is the Sun's <term>Driggati</term>, and the gnomon of the point where that same circle meets the lunar orbit is the Moon's <term>Driggati</term>. || 9-10 ||

It includes a scholarly critique of this method, noting that Bhaskara II eventually refined these calculations to account for the tilt of the lunar orbit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of lunar parallax and the geometry of the ecliptic from the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta, specifically focusing on the "Drig-kshepa" (ecliptic zenith distance).</meta>

<page-num>420</page-num>
<header>In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta</header>

## Here is the Proof:

The secondary ecliptic circle <note>original: "Drig-kshepa-vritta"; the vertical circle passing through the zenith and the pole of the ecliptic</note> meets the ecliptic at a certain point. From that point to the orbit of the Moon <note>original: "Vimandala"</note>, along the secondary ecliptic circle, lies the latitude of the nonagesimal <note>original: "Vitribha-lagna-shara"; the latitude of the point 90 degrees behind the rising point</note>, with a small margin of error. Therefore, when the zenith distance of the nonagesimal is toward the north—and the latitude of the nonagesimal is also north—the sum of the two gives the arc of the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance <note>original: "Chandra-drig-kshepa"</note> from the zenith to the Moon's orbit.

Thus: **Moon's ecliptic zenith distance = Zenith distance of the nonagesimal + Latitude of the nonagesimal.**

If these degrees are subtracted from ninety, we get the degrees of the Moon's "Drig-gati" <note>the sine of the arc between the zenith and the ecliptic pole</note>.
**Moon's Drig-gati arc = 90 - (Zenith distance of the nonagesimal + Latitude of the nonagesimal).**

When the latitude of the nonagesimal is south, the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance is the difference: **Zenith distance of the nonagesimal - Latitude of the nonagesimal.**
Consequently, the gnomon arc <note>original: "Shanku-chapa"</note> is **90 - (Zenith distance of the nonagesimal - Latitude of the nonagesimal).**

In the case of a southern zenith distance, the calculation is reversed, which is self-evident. By this method, the calculation of the Moon's motion is established. The secondary ecliptic circle is perpendicular to the ecliptic; however, it is not perpendicular to the Moon's inclined orbit. Therefore, the motion derived from the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance does not lie on the circle passing through the poles of the Moon's orbit <note>original: "Kadamba-prota-vritta"</note>. Consequently, the parallax in latitude <note>term: Nati (parallax in latitude)</note> is not rendered "clear" or "corrected" <note>term: Sphuta (corrected/accurate)</note> simply by this adjustment.

Even Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, 12th-century mathematician</note> previously followed this school of thought, calculating the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance using the phrase "That which is the gnomon of the nonagesimal," etc. However, later in the chapter on Solar Eclipses, he refuted this method, stating: "For the sake of the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance, the correction of the latitude of the nonagesimal is [incorrectly] applied here," etc.

---

(1) In a place where the latitude is twenty-four degrees, when the Sun and Moon are at the beginning of Libra, the Sun itself is at the rising point <note>term: Lagna (the ascending point of the ecliptic)</note> at dawn. When they are at the zenith, the ecliptic and the horizon circle coincide with the East-West circle. Because the horizon circle takes the form of the ecliptic, the Moon would be suspended exactly within that ecliptic-shaped horizon circle.

In such a case:
- Moon's parallax in latitude <note>Nati</note> = 0
- Moon's latitude <note>Shara</note> = 0
- Sun's parallax in latitude = 0

Therefore, according to the rule "The latitude here is not corrected by parallax," the corrected latitude is zero, and the corrected parallax in latitude is also zero. The Sun's parallax in latitude, corrected by the latitude arising from the nonagesimal, becomes the arc of the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance.
**Sun's parallax $\pm$ Latitude of the nonagesimal = 0 $\pm$ Latitude of the nonagesimal = Latitude of the nonagesimal.**

However, this Moon's ecliptic zenith distance arc is useless here, because the purpose of the ecliptic zenith distance is specifically to find the corrected parallax in latitude. But here, the corrected parallax is already zero. Therefore, what purpose does the ecliptic zenith distance serve? Thus, Bhaskara’s refutation is logical.

->The following explains Bhaskara's refutation of Brahmagupta's Moon-ecliptic zenith distance calculation.<-

In a region at 24 degrees latitude, when the Sun and Moon are in Libra at sunrise, the Sun is the rising point. Being at the zenith, the ecliptic and horizon circles align with the East-West circle. Since the horizon circle is ecliptic-shaped, the Moon resides within it. Thus, Moon's parallax = 0, Moon's latitude = 0, and Sun's parallax = 0. Following the principle "The latitude is not corrected by parallax," the corrected latitude and parallax are both zero. The Moon's ecliptic zenith distance arc becomes simply the latitude of the nonagesimal. But this arc is pointless because the only reason we calculate it is to find the corrected parallax, which we already know is zero. Therefore, Bhaskara's critique is correct.

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses
<page-num>421</page-num>

In this context, the statement by Shripati <note>An 11th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>—"with the northern or southern latitude, subtract or add when the zenith distance is northern"—was modified by Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century author of the Siddhanta Shiromani</note> by stating "addition for the same direction and difference for opposite directions." || 9-10 ||

->Now the method for calculating the *Driggati* <term>Driggati: The sine of the zenith distance of the secondary to the ecliptic; essentially the "motion of visibility"</term> of the Sun and the Moon is described.<-

**Hindi Commentary—** When there is northern parallax of the nonagesimal <term>Vitribhalagna: The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant; the nonagesimal</term>, the northern or southern latitude of the Moon at that nonagesimal point should be respectively subtracted from or added to the arc of the sine-altitude <term>Shanku-chapa: The arc corresponding to the gnomon's shadow/altitude</term> of the nonagesimal. In the case of southern parallax, add the northern latitude arc and subtract the southern latitude arc to that same sine-altitude arc. The resulting sine is the Moon's *Vitribhashanku* (Driggati). The previously calculated *Vitribhashanku* of the Sun is its true Driggati. The Sun's Driggati occurs at the intersection of the nonagesimal, the vertical circle, and the ecliptic. The Moon's Driggati occurs at the intersection of the ecliptic's secondary circle and the Moon's orbit <term>Vimandala: The secondary or celestial orbit of the Moon</term>. That is to say, the sine-altitude of the nonagesimal point where the ecliptic's secondary circle meets the ecliptic is the Sun's Driggati; the sine-altitude of the point where that same secondary circle meets the Moon's orbit is the Moon's Driggati. || 6-10 ||

### Mathematical Proof (Upapatti)

From the point where the ecliptic's secondary circle meets the ecliptic, the Moon's latitude at the nonagesimal lies along that same secondary circle with a slight difference. Therefore, when both the northern parallax of the nonagesimal and the northern latitude of the nonagesimal are present, their sum gives the Moon's zenith distance arc in the secondary circle from the zenith to the Moon's orbit = (Zenith distance of the nonagesimal + Latitude at the nonagesimal). Subtracting this from 90 degrees gives the Moon's Driggati arc = 90 - (Zenith distance + Latitude) = (Altitude arc of nonagesimal - Latitude). In the case of southern latitude at the nonagesimal, the Moon's zenith distance arc = (Zenith distance - Latitude); therefore, the sine-altitude arc = 90 - (Zenith distance - Latitude) = (Altitude arc of nonagesimal + Latitude). For southern parallax, the operations should be reversed. Thus, the calculation for the Moon's Driggati is proven.

The secondary circle of the ecliptic is perpendicular to the ecliptic, but not to the Moon's orbit; therefore, the Driggati resulting from the Moon's zenith distance does not lie in the circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic <term>Kadamba-prota-vritta: A circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic</term>. Consequently, correcting it does not yield the "clear" or true parallax <term>Sphuta Nati: Corrected latitude-parallax</term>. Bhaskaracharya also previously followed this view in verses such as "The Drigjya of the nonagesimal sine-altitude..." to calculate the Moon's zenith distance and determine the true parallax. However, at the end of the Chapter on Solar Eclipses, he refuted this method with the statement, "For the sake of the Moon's zenith distance, the correction of the latitude at the nonagesimal here...", etc. Here, Bhaskaracharya has replaced Shripati's rule—"with northern/southern latitude subtract/add in the north"—with "addition for the same direction, difference for opposite directions." || 6-10 ||

### Now he describes the True Parallax (Sphuta Nati).

> Subtract the square of the respective sine-altitude from the square of the radius; the square roots of those are the two *Drigjyas* <note>Sines of zenith distance</note>.
> Multiply these by the mean motion of the Sun and Moon and divide by the radius multiplied by fifteen. || 11 ||

<page-num>424</page-num>
->### In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta<-

By multiplying the solar and lunar <term>Drigkshepa</term><note>The sine of the zenith distance of the ecliptic's highest point</note> by their respective mean motions and dividing by fifteen times the radius, the <term>Nati</term><note>Parallax in latitude</note> of the Sun and Moon is obtained. Alternatively, the <term>Nati</term> of both (Sun and Moon) is found by multiplying the mean motion of the Sun and the mean motion of the Moon by the shadow of the <term>Drigjya</term><note>Sine of the zenith distance</note> equal to their respective <term>Drigkshepa</term>, and dividing by fifteen times their respective shadow-hypotenuse. The meaning of the remainder is clear. || 11-12 ||

---

### Proof

Refer here to the diagram (A) in the Sanskrit commentary. Let:
*   **Kha** = Zenith
*   **Vi** = The <term>Vitribha</term><note>The nonagesimal point; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon</note>
*   **Ra** = The Sun on the ecliptic
*   **Kha-Ra** = Zenith distance of the Sun
*   **Lam-Ra** = The depressed Sun <note>The position of the Sun shifted by parallax</note>
*   **Kha-Vi** = The arc of the <term>Drigkshepa</term>
*   **Kha-Lam** = The surface zenith distance
*   **Ra-Lam** = The <term>Driglambana</term><note>Parallax in altitude</note>
*   **Lam-Stha** = The <term>Ravinati</term><note>Solar parallax in latitude</note>
*   **Stha-Ra** = The <term>Ravispashtalambana</term><note>True solar parallax in longitude</note>

Then, because the sine-fields of the two spherical right-angled triangles **Kha-Ra-Vi** and **Ra-Lam-Stha** are similar, by proportion:

(Solar Drigkshepa × Sine of Solar Parallax in Altitude) / Sine of Solar Zenith Distance = Sine of Solar Nati = Solar Nati (with slight difference).

However, (Maximum Solar Parallax × Sine of Surface Zenith Distance) / Radius = Sine of Solar Parallax in Altitude.

By substitution: (Solar Drigkshepa × Maximum Solar Parallax × Sine of Surface Zenith Distance) / (Sine of Solar Zenith Distance × Radius) = Solar Nati.

Here, for a small difference, Sine of Surface Zenith Distance ≈ Sine of Solar Zenith Distance, and Sine of Maximum Solar Parallax ≈ Maximum Solar Parallax.

Then: (Drigkshepa × Maximum Solar Parallax) / Radius = Solar Nati.

Similarly: (Lunar Drigkshepa × Maximum Lunar Parallax) / Radius = Lunar Nati.

But, (Solar Mean Motion / 15) = Maximum Solar Parallax, and (Lunar Mean Motion / 15) = Maximum Lunar Parallax.

Therefore: (Solar Drigkshepa × Solar Mean Motion) / (Radius × 15) = Solar Nati.
(Lunar Drigkshepa × Lunar Mean Motion) / (Radius × 15) = Lunar Nati.

Thus, the first method is proven. Although for the calculation of Lunar Nati, a diagram exactly like the Solar Nati calculation cannot be formed <note>due to the Moon's own latitude</note>, the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> has calculated the Lunar Nati in the same manner as the Solar Nati.

Solar Nati = (Solar Drigkshepa × Solar Mean Motion) / (Radius × 15) = [(12 × Solar Drigkshepa) / Equinoctial Shadow] × Solar Mean Motion / [15 × (12 × Radius / Equinoctial Shadow)]

= (Vitribha-Shadow × Solar Mean Motion) / (15 × Vitribha-Shadow-Hypotenuse).

Similarly, Lunar Nati = (Lunar Drigkshepa × Lunar Mean Motion) / (Radius × 15) = [(12 × Lunar Drigkshepa) / Equinoctial Shadow] × Lunar Mean Motion / [15 × (12 × Radius / Equinoctial Shadow)]

= (Vitribha-Shadow × Lunar Mean Motion) / (15 × Vitribha-Shadow-Hypotenuse).

By the adjustment of these two, the Solar Nati and Lunar Nati, the <term>Spashta-nati</term><note>True resultant parallax in latitude</note> is obtained.

In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati <note>A prominent 11th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> states, "Then the sine of the zenith distance multiplied by the mean motion divided by 15," and so on. Similarly, in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya <note>Bhaskara II, the famous 12th-century astronomer</note> also says, "The parallax in latitude and the Moon's own mean motion multiplied by the fifteenth part," etc., following the teachings of the ancient masters. || 11-12 ||

->Now, the method for calculating the corrected latitude and the half-duration is described.<-

->**The sum or difference of the parallax in latitude and the Moon’s latitude, depending on whether they are in the same or opposite directions,**<-
->**is the corrected latitude. From this, the half-durations of the eclipse and the totality are found as in a lunar eclipse. || 13 ||**<-

**Sudhakara Bhashya:** The meaning is clear, and the mathematical proof is evident through the method of Bhaskara, starting with "The latitude here is corrected by the parallax in latitude," etc. || 13 ||

**Vishvanatha Bhashya:** When the parallax in latitude <term>avanati: the vertical displacement of the Moon due to the observer's position</term> and the Moon's celestial latitude <term>shashanka-vikshepa: the Moon's distance north or south of the ecliptic</term> are in the same direction, they are added; when in different directions, their difference is taken. This result is the corrected latitude <term>sphuta-vikshepa</term>. From this, the half-duration of the eclipse <term>sthityardha</term> and the half-duration of totality <term>vimardardha</term> should be calculated just as they are in a lunar eclipse. || 13 ||

### The Mathematical Proof

Now, the parallax in latitude of the Sun occurs from the point where the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the eclipsed Sun meets the ecliptic, up to the eclipsed Sun itself. The Moon's latitude is the distance from the point where the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the Moon meets the ecliptic, up to the Moon. By processing these two, we find the distance to the Moon from the intersection of the circle of latitude passing through the eclipsed Sun and the secondary circle passing through the Moon; this is what is called the "corrected latitude" in a solar eclipse. From this corrected latitude, the knowledge of the corrected half-duration and half-totality is easily obtained using the rule: "From the square of the sum or difference of the radii of the eclipsing and eclipsed bodies..." In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati says: "If the directions are the same, the sum; if different, the difference of the parallax and the Moon's latitude is the corrected latitude." In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya also said the same as the ancient masters: "The latitude here is corrected by the parallax; from this, the durations of the eclipse and totality are calculated as before." || 13 ||

->Now the calculation of the corrected latitude and the calculation of the corrected half-duration and half-totality are explained in Hindi.<-

**Hindi Commentary:** By adding the Moon's latitude and the parallax in latitude if they are in the same direction, and taking their difference if they are in different directions, the corrected latitude is obtained. From this, the half-duration of the eclipse and the half-duration of totality are calculated in *ghatis* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> just as in a lunar eclipse. || 13 ||

### Rationale

The solar parallax in latitude <note>original: "ravinati"</note> is measured from the point where the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the eclipsed Sun meets the ecliptic, up to the eclipsed Sun itself. The lunar latitude <note>original: "candrashara"</note> is measured from the point where the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the Moon meets the ecliptic, up to the Moon itself. By refining these two values—specifically from the intersection of the circle of the radius of the cosine of parallax passing through the eclipsed Sun and the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the Moon—one obtains the "clear latitude" <term>spashta-shara; the corrected celestial latitude of the Moon used specifically for solar eclipses</term>. From this corrected latitude, using the rule "from the squares of half the sum and half the difference of the diameters of the obscurer and the obscured," the corrected half-duration <note>original: "spashta-sthityardha"</note> and the corrected half-duration of total obscuration <note>original: "spashta-vimardardha"</note> can be easily understood. 

In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Sripati says: "If the directions are the same or different, the parallax in latitude and the lunar latitude are added or subtracted; if they are in the same direction, the difference or sum results in the corrected latitude." Similarly, in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya has stated in accordance with the ancient teachers: "The latitude here is corrected by the parallax in latitude; from this, the half-duration and half-totality should be calculated as before." ॥ 13 ॥

---

->Now he describes the calculation of the corrected half-duration and half-totality:<-

->Calculate the parallax repeatedly from the end of the lunar day <note>the moment of conjunction</note> as before, subtracted from and added to the half-duration.<-
->If that parallax is greater or less than the parallax at the middle of the eclipse, the half-duration is increased or decreased accordingly.<- ॥ 14 ॥

->If the parallax values are of the same sign, use their difference; otherwise, if one is negative and the other positive, use their sum to increase the half-duration. The same applies to the half-totality.<- ॥ 15 ॥

---

<margin>Sudhakara Dvivedi's Commentary</margin>—From the end of the lunar day <note>the moment of true conjunction</note>, one should calculate the parallax repeatedly <note>an iterative process</note> using the half-duration obtained as in a lunar eclipse, both by subtracting it (for the start) and adding it (for the end), until the values stabilize. The meaning is this: to find the time of first contact, calculate the fixed parallax from the end of the lunar day minus the half-duration; to find the time of separation, calculate it from the end of the lunar day plus the half-duration. 

If that parallax is greater or less than the parallax at the middle of the eclipse—meaning if the parallax at contact is greater than at the middle, and at separation it is less—and if both parallaxes are negative, then the previously calculated half-duration should be increased by the difference between them. If the parallax at contact is less than the middle parallax and the parallax at separation is greater, and both are positive, the half-duration is also increased by their difference. If the situation is reversed for negative or positive values (i.e., if the contact/separation parallaxes are less/greater than the middle for negative, or greater/less for positive), then the half-duration should be decreased by the difference. However, if one parallax is negative and the other is positive, the half-duration should be increased by their sum. In this way, the half-durations for contact and separation are determined. Similarly, the two half-durations for the beginning and end of totality are corrected. That is, having taken the half-duration like a lunar eclipse, one calculates the corrected half-duration...

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses
Page 427

In the place of the half-duration, one should take the half-duration of the moon's obscuration to calculate the two corrected half-durations.

Here is the proof <note>Sanskrit: upapatti; a formal mathematical demonstration</note>. Let the fixed values of parallax at the moments of contact, middle, and separation be $L_1, L_2, L_3$ respectively, and let them be negative. Let the mean half-duration be $S$. Let the calculated time of the end of the New Moon <note>Sanskrit: darśānta; the moment of conjunction</note> be $D$. Then:

->Corrected time of contact = $D - S - L_1 = C$<-
->Corrected time of the middle = $D - L_2 = M$<-
->Corrected time of separation = $D + S - L_3 = S_e$<-

Therefore, the corrected half-duration for the first contact = $M - C = S + L_2 - L_1$.
The corrected half-duration for the separation = $S_e - M = S + L_2 - L_3$.

Thus, if $L_1 > L_2$ and $L_2 > L_3$, then both $(L_1 - L_2)$ and $(L_2 - L_3)$ are positive. If those parallaxes are positive, then by the previous method, the values of $(L_1 - L_2)$ and $(L_2 - L_3)$ will become $(L_2 - L_1)$ and $(L_3 - L_2)$. Therefore, it is clear that if $L_2 > L_1$ and $L_3 > L_2$, then these two are positive; otherwise, they are negative.

Now, if the contact occurs before the nonagesimal <note>term: Vitribha; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the zenith, crucial for parallax calculations</note> and the middle time occurs after it, then $L_1$ is negative and $L_2$ is positive. In that case, the value of $(L_1 - L_2)$ will be $(L_1 + L_2)$, which will be positive. When the sun is west of the nonagesimal and the parallax at contact is positive, the parallax at the middle time—which occurs even further along—will always be positive; thus, there is no confusion regarding positive or negative signs there. Similarly, if the middle time is before the nonagesimal and the separation is after it, then $L_2$ is negative and $L_3$ is positive. By the previous rule, the state of $(L_2 - L_3)$ as $(L_2 + L_3)$ will always be positive. Therefore, it is my view—which the wise should contemplate deeply—that if one is negative and the other positive, the corrected half-duration is always the sum of the two. This makes the teacher's <note>Referring to the original author of the astronomical treatise, likely Bhāskara or similar</note> statement logically sound. 

Because the corrected times of contact and separation are initially unknown, the gross value $L_2$ is first taken in place of $L_1$ and $L_3$. By this: $C = D - S - L_2 = (D - L_2) - S = \text{Corrected New Moon} - S$. Similarly, the gross time of separation = $\text{Corrected New Moon} + S$. Therefore, it is proper to first calculate the parallax from the corrected end of the lunar day <note>tithi</note> as increased or decreased by the half-duration. Furthermore, the half-duration should ideally be calculated using the instantaneous latitude <note>śara</note> at the times of contact and separation. However, here the calculation is done by taking a fixed half-duration based on the corrected latitude at the middle of the eclipse. Therefore, this is a gross <note>approximate</note> method; the teacher will describe another method for the sake of precision later on. ||14-15||

If the parallax at the time of contact is greater than the parallax at the middle of the eclipse, and the parallax at the time of separation is less, then the result is as follows: when the parallaxes calculated for the middle, contact, and separation are negative <note>original: "ऋण" (ṛṇa) - subtractive or negative value</note>, the previously calculated half-duration <term>sthityardha: half the total duration of the eclipse from contact to middle, or middle to separation</term> should be increased by the difference between those two negative values. Similarly, if the parallax at contact is less than at the middle, and at separation it is greater, and both parallaxes calculated for the middle and the respective ends are positive <note>original: "धन" (dhana) - additive or positive value</note>, then the half-duration should also be adjusted by the difference of those positive values. If the situation is reversed—meaning among the negative values, the contact/separation parallax is less or more than the middle, or among the positive values, it is more or less than the middle—then the half-duration should be decreased by that difference. Furthermore, if one parallax is negative and the other is positive, the half-duration should be increased by their sum. In this way, the corrected half-durations for contact and separation are determined. Likewise, the two half-durations of total darkness <term>vimardārdha: the half-duration of the total phase of an eclipse</term> at the moments of immersion and emersion are also corrected. This means that just as the corrected half-duration was calculated for the Moon, the two corrected half-durations of total darkness should be calculated by substituting the "half-duration of total darkness" in place of the "half-duration" in the same procedure. || 14-15 ||

->Here is the Proof<-

Let the fixed parallaxes for the times of contact, middle, and separation be $L_1, L_2, L_3$ respectively, and let them be negative. Let the mean half-duration = $H$, and the calculated time of the new moon <note>conjunction</note> = $N$.
Then:
The corrected time of contact: $C = N - H - L_1$
The corrected middle time: $M = N - L_2$
The corrected time of separation: $S = N + H - L_3$
Therefore, the corrected half-duration of contact = $M - C = H + L_1 - L_2$.
The corrected half-duration of separation = $S - M = H + L_2 - L_3$.
Thus, if $L_1 > L_2$ and $L_3 > L_2$, then both $(L_1 - L_2)$ and $(L_3 - L_2)$ are positive.
If those parallaxes are positive, then the values will be $(L_2 - L_1)$ and $(L_2 - L_3)$.
If $L_1 > L_2$ and $L_3 > L_2$, then these two are positive, otherwise they are negative.

Now, if contact occurs before the nonagesimal <term>vitribha: the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the zenith</term> and the middle time occurs after, then $L_1$ is negative and $L_2$ is positive. In that case, the value of $L_1 - L_2$ will become $(L_1 + L_2)$ as a positive addition. When the Sun is to the west of the nonagesimal, the parallax at contact is positive; since the middle time occurs even further ahead, the parallax for the middle time is always positive, so there is no ambiguity of positive/negative signs there. Furthermore, if the middle time is to the east of the nonagesimal and separation is after it, then $L_2$ is negative and $L_3$ is positive. Then, by the previous rule, the state of $L_2 - L_3$ will always be positive like $(L_2 + L_3)$. Therefore, if one is negative and the other is positive, the corrected half-duration is always found by adding their sum. Because the exact times of contact and separation are initially unknown, the approximate value $L_2$ is first used in place of $L_1$ and $L_3$. By this: $C = N - H - L_2 = (N - L_2) - H = \text{Corrected New Moon} - H$. Similarly, the approximate time of separation = Corrected New Moon + $H$. Therefore, it is proper to first calculate the parallax from the corrected end of the lunar day <note>tithi</note> by adding or subtracting the half-duration. The half-duration is corrected based on the instantaneous latitude <note>śara</note> at the time of contact and separation...

...is appropriate. However, here the calculation was performed by taking a fixed half-duration based on the clear latitude at the middle of the eclipse; therefore, the Teacher <note>Referring to the original author of the astronomical treatise being commented upon</note> describes another method further on for the sake of precision. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A major 12th-century astronomical work by Bhaskara II</note>: **"One should calculate the parallax at the beginning and end of the eclipse from the end of the lunar day, subtracted or added by the half-duration, as previously described. By adding the difference between that and the parallax arising at the middle of the eclipse to the half-duration, the times of contact and separation are found; similarly for the total immersion and emergence using the half-duration of totality. If the first parallax is greater than the middle in negative values, or the last is smaller, or in positive values if the first is less and the last is more... if the signs differ, the sum of the parallaxes is used."** Similarly, Shripati has stated: **"From the end of the lunar day, decreased or increased by the half-duration, the parallax for the start and end should be calculated. The difference between these and the parallax at the middle is found. In the eastern hemisphere, if the parallax at contact is greater than at the middle, and at the end it is less—or the reverse in the western hemisphere—then that difference should be added to the half-duration of the end and contact respectively. This applies when they are in the same hemisphere; if in different hemispheres, the sum of the parallaxes is added to their respective half-durations, as was also said for the half-duration of totality."** This is entirely consistent with what is stated in the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>The "Sun Treatise," one of the oldest fundamental texts of Indian astronomy</note> and by the Teacher. — 14-15

### Now, the means for calculating the refined half-duration and refined half-duration of totality are described.

**Hindi Commentary—** Just as in a lunar eclipse, one should calculate the parallax <term>parallax (lambana): the apparent displacement of a celestial object when viewed from different positions</term> using the iterative method from the end of the lunar day (the moment of conjunction) decreased and increased by the calculated half-duration until the value becomes consistent. It is said here that to know the time of first contact, the parallax should be fixed from the end of the lunar day minus the half-duration; to know the time of separation (end), it should be fixed from the end of the lunar day plus the half-duration. 

If this parallax is greater or less than the parallax at the middle of the conjunction—that is, if the contact parallax is greater than the middle parallax and the end parallax is less, and both the middle and contact parallaxes are negative—then the difference between those two negative values should be added to the previously calculated half-duration. If the contact parallax is less than the middle and the end parallax is greater, and both are positive, then the difference between those two positive values should also be added to the half-duration. If one parallax is negative and the other is positive, then their sum should be added to the half-duration. In this way, the half-durations for contact and separation become "refined" <note>meaning corrected for the observer's specific location on Earth</note>. Similarly, the half-durations for the beginning and end of totality are refined. This means that just as the refined half-duration is calculated for a lunar eclipse, here one takes the half-duration of totality and calculates its refined version in the same manner. — 14-15

->**Mathematical Proof**<-

Let the stabilized parallaxes for the time of contact, middle, and separation be $P_1$, $P_2$, and $P_3$ respectively (assuming they are negative). 
Let the mean half-duration = $D_{half}$
Let the calculated time of the end of the lunar day = $T$
Then:
Refined time of contact = $T - D_{half} - P_1$
Refined middle time = $T - P_2$
Refined time of separation = $T + D_{half} - P_3$

# On the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

Page 430

Therefore, for the purpose of the corrected duration of the first contact <note>spārśika sphuta sthityartha</note>:
Corrected Duration = (Middle - Contact) = Duration + (Parallax₁ - Parallax₂)
For the purpose of the corrected duration of the separation <note>mauksika sphuta sthityartha</note>:
Corrected Duration = (Separation - Middle) = Duration + (Parallax₃ - Parallax₂)

Therefore, if Parallax₁ > Parallax₂ and Parallax₂ > Parallax₃, then both (Parallax₁ - Parallax₂) and (Parallax₂ - Parallax₃) are positive. If those parallaxes are positive, then the values will be (Parallax₁ - Parallax₂) and (Parallax₂ - Parallax₃). If Parallax₂ > Parallax₁ and Parallax₃ > Parallax₂, then (Parallax₂ - Parallax₁) and (Parallax₃ - Parallax₂) will be positive, otherwise they will be negative.

If the first contact occurs before the nonagesimal <note>vitribha; the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon</note> and the middle of the eclipse occurs after it, then Parallax₁ will be negative and Parallax₂ will be positive. Then the value (Parallax₁ - Parallax₂) becomes (Parallax₁ + Parallax₂), which will be positive. Because the sun is to the west of the nonagesimal at the time of contact, and the middle of the eclipse occurs even further along, the parallax at the middle time is always positive; therefore, there is no ambiguity of positive or negative status there. Similarly, if the middle time is to the east of the nonagesimal and the separation <note>mokṣakāla</note> is to the west, then Parallax₂ is negative and Parallax₃ is positive. Then, by the previous method, (Parallax₂ - Parallax₃) becomes (Parallax₂ + Parallax₃), which is always positive.

Therefore, if one is negative and the other is positive, adding their sum to the duration results in the corrected duration <note>sphuta sthityartha</note>. Because the corrected contact time and corrected separation time are unknown, the approximate Parallax₂ was first taken in place of Parallax₁ and Parallax₃.
Then: Contact = (True New Moon - Duration - Parallax₂) = (True New Moon - Parallax₂) - Duration = (Corrected New Moon) - Duration.
And: Approximate Separation = Corrected New Moon + Duration.

Therefore, it is proper to first calculate the parallax from the corrected end of the lunar day <note>tithyanta</note> decreased or increased by the duration. The instantaneous corrected duration is properly derived from the latitude <note>śara</note> at the time of contact and separation, but here the calculation is done using a fixed duration based on the latitude at the middle of the eclipse. Therefore, this is an approximation <note>sthūla</note>. For the sake of precision <note>sūkṣmārtha</note>, the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> describes another method hereafter. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, Shripati says: "From the end of the lunar day, decreased or increased by the half-duration..." and the author of the *Surya Siddhanta* has said similarly to the Teacher: "From the half-duration, decreased or increased as before..." etc. || 14-15 ||

Again, one should calculate the parallax from the end of the lunar day decreased and increased by the half-duration produced by that corrected latitude, doing so repeatedly. Here, this is what is said: Just as for the knowledge of the time of contact, first the corrected latitude at the middle time...

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

## Calculation of Contact and Duration

Based on the <term>half-duration</term><note>Sanskrit: *sthityardha*; the time from the first contact to the maximum eclipse</note>, one should calculate the <term>parallax in longitude</term><note>Sanskrit: *lambana*; the apparent shift in the moon's position due to the observer's location on Earth</note> and the conjunction from the calculated end of the <term>true lunar day</term><note>Sanskrit: *sphuta-tithyanta*; the moment of the New Moon</note>. The <term>latitude</term><note>Sanskrit: *shara*; the celestial latitude of the moon</note> is determined from the position of the moon and its node at that specific time. By applying the correction for <term>parallax in latitude</term><note>Sanskrit: *nati*</note> to the moon's latitude, the <term>clear latitude</term><note>Sanskrit: *spashta-vikshepa*</note> is obtained. From this, the half-duration is calculated just as in a lunar eclipse. 

From the calculated end of the lunar day minus that half-duration, the parallax, the parallax in latitude, the clear latitude, and the true half-duration must be calculated repeatedly until the values no longer change <note>This refers to the mathematical method of successive approximation or iteration to reach a precise result</note>. When the values stabilize, that parallax should be added or subtracted as appropriate to the calculated end of the New Moon (which was already reduced by the half-duration generated by the clear latitude of that moment). This results in the **true time of first contact** <note>Sanskrit: *sparsha-kala*</note>. Similarly, by adding the half-duration to the end of the lunar day, the **true time of separation** <note>Sanskrit: *moksha-kala*</note> is found. 

The difference between these and the end of the true lunar day results in the two true half-durations. That is to say, the difference between the true time of contact (or separation) and the true moment of the New Moon provides the two distinct segments of the eclipse duration. Just as the true segments of duration are calculated using the half-duration, the **half-duration of total obscuration** <note>Sanskrit: *vimardardha*; the time the sun is completely covered in a total eclipse</note> should be calculated through the same iterative process. By perfecting the times of immersion and emersion through this repeated method, the two segments of total obscuration are known. This is consistent with the teachings of Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note> who stated: "From the calculated end of the lunar day, increased or decreased by the half-duration, the parallax is found," and so on. Here, the Teacher <note>Referring to the author of the primary text being commented upon</note> has first assumed the parallax of the middle of the eclipse for both contact and separation as a rough approximation; astronomers know that this does not harm the accuracy of the final result when using the iterative method.

### Geometric Proof

The objective here is to determine the time of contact from the perspective of the observer on the Earth's surface, relative to the number of hours <note>Sanskrit: *ghatika*; a unit of 24 minutes</note> from the Earth's center. 

Let us assume that when the contact occurs from the surface perspective:
* **Su** = Center of the Sun = Solar position.
* **M$_1$** = Center of the Moon's disk.
* **M** = Position of the Moon.
* **MM'** = A segment of the ecliptic.
* **Z** = The Zenith.
* **Z-Su, M$_1$** = The Moon's vertical circle.
* **Z-Su-Su'** = The Sun's vertical circle.
* **M'$_1$** = The center of the Moon's disk shifted by parallax.
* **Su'** = The center of the Sun's disk shifted by parallax.
* **M'$_1$ M''** = The Moon's true latitude.
* **Su' R''** = The Sun's clear latitude, equal to the Sun's parallax in latitude.

**Su' S** = A circle parallel to the ecliptic.
**M'$_1$ S** = The clear latitude at the true time of contact.
**Su' K$_1$** = The sum of the semi-diameters <note>Sanskrit: *manaika-ardha*; the combined radii of the Sun and Moon, which determines when they appear to touch</note>.

Because these arcs are small, the Teachers have treated them as straight lines. Therefore, in the triangle **Su' M'$_1$**, the minutes of the true half-duration are equal to the square root of the difference of the squares of the sides = **Su' S** = **R' M** = True Half-Duration. 
**MM'** = Minutes of the Moon's parallax.
**Su** = **R'** Minutes of the Sun's parallax.
The difference between these two parallaxes = (Parallax Minutes) multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference in the velocities of the Sun and Moon gives what the Teacher calls the "Parallax Hours of Contact" = **P**. 

Similarly, the minutes of the true half-duration multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference in velocity gives the true half-duration in hours as taught by the Teacher. Now, at this time of contact, from the perspective of the Earth's center...

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
<page-num>432</page-num>

The minutes of the difference between the Sun and Moon = $Sun_{diff} = Ch_{v} - Vi_{r} = Ch_{r} + Ch_{ch} - Vi_{r} = Sphu_{sthi} + Chala_{k} - Ra_{lak} = Sphu_{sthik} + L_{1}k$. These in ghatikas <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> = $Sphu_{sthi} + L_{1}$. At the end of the calculated new moon (*amavasya*), from the perspective of the Earth's center, there is no difference between the Sun and the Moon. At the time of contact (*sparsha*), the difference calculated previously between them is $Sphu_{sthi} + L_{1}$ ghatikas. Therefore, by subtracting these desired ghatikas from the calculated end of the new moon, the true time of contact is found.

= $D - Sphu_{sthi} - L_{1}$. Since the true half-duration (*sthiyardha*) and parallax (*lambana*) are unknown at the true time of contact, an iterative process <term>asakrit-karma</term> <note>A repetitive calculation used to converge on a precise value</note> is appropriate. Similarly, for the end of the eclipse (*moksha*), and the beginning and end of totality (*sammilana* and *unmilana*), the true rationale is established by the geometry of the spheres. By this geometric method of mine, everything stated by Bhaskara <note>Referring to Bhaskara I, an earlier mathematician-astronomer</note> is proven true; the remaining rationale is clear. **16-17**

**Vimalabhāṣya (Commentary):** — Parallax should be calculated from the true end of the lunar day (*tithi*) <note>The moment of the new moon</note> as increased or decreased by the half-duration. Again, the parallax must be calculated from the end of the lunar day joined with the half-duration produced by the true latitude (*vikshepa*); this is done iteratively. What is said here is this: to find the time of contact, first the half-duration should be calculated based on the mean true latitude. From the end of the true lunar day diminished by that, the parallax (*lambana*) and the deflection (*nati*) <note>Latitudinal parallax</note> should be calculated. The latitude should then be calculated based on the position of the Moon with its node at that time. By adjusting the latitude with the deflection, the true latitude is found. From that, the half-duration is calculated as in a lunar eclipse. From the end of the lunar day diminished by that, the parallax, deflection, true latitude, and true half-duration must all be calculated again until there is no difference (*avishesha*). When there is no difference, the resulting parallax should be added or subtracted as appropriate to the calculated end of the new moon, diminished by the half-duration produced by the true latitude of that time. That is the true time of contact.

Similarly, from the end of the lunar day increased by the half-duration, the true time of separation (*moksha*) is found. The two true half-durations are the intervals between those and the end of the true lunar day. That is, the intervals between the true time of contact or the true time of separation and the end of the true lunar day are the true contact and separation half-durations. Just as the true half-durations were calculated using the half-duration, the true half-durations of totality (*vimardardha*) should be calculated through the same iterative process using the half-duration of totality. That is, by the same iterative method as before, having determined the true times of the start and end of totality, the true half-durations of totality are known as the differences between those and the middle of the eclipse. Here, the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> has first assumed the parallax of the middle of the eclipse for both contact and separation as a rough approximation; there is no harm in this for the iterative process. **16-17**

<header>Chapter on Solar Eclipses</header>

The minutes of the half-duration <note>term: sthityardha; the time from the first contact of an eclipse to its maximum phase</note> as observed from the surface are equal to the sum of the minutes of the half-duration and the difference in parallax. If one asks how this is so: at the time of first contact, the Moon's position is to the west of the Sun's position. From the perspective of the Earth's center <note>term: garbhābhiprāyika; geocentric</note>, the Sun's position as seen from the surface <note>term: pṛṣṭhābhiprāyika; topocentric</note> would be toward the east. The same applies to the Moon. The minutes of the interval on the ecliptic between the secondary circle passing through the Sun's center (as seen from the surface) and the secondary circle passing through the Moon's center are the minutes of the half-duration. Therefore, the minutes of the Moon's parallax should be added to the minutes of the half-duration; then, the minutes on the ecliptic from the geocentric Moon's position to the topocentric Sun's position $=$ half-duration minutes <gloss>half-duration</gloss> $+$ Moon's parallax. Here, the Sun's parallax minutes must be subtracted; then, the geocentric Sun-Moon interval minutes $=$ half-duration minutes <gloss>half-duration</gloss> $+$ Moon's parallax $-$ Sun's parallax. When the half-duration minutes are less than the Sun's parallax minutes, then the half-duration minutes should be subtracted from the Sun's parallax minutes; that would be the distance from the topocentric Moon's position to the geocentric Sun's position, expressed as $=$ Sun's parallax $-$ half-duration minutes <gloss>half-duration</gloss>. These minutes should be subtracted from the Moon's parallax minutes; then, the geocentric Sun-Moon interval minutes $=$ Moon's parallax $-$ (Sun's parallax $-$ half-duration minutes) $=$ Moon's parallax $-$ Sun's parallax $+$ half-duration minutes $=$ half-duration minutes $+$ difference in parallax. Now, for the purpose of calculating this in ghatis <note>term: ghaṭī; a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>, the proportion is:

60 $\times$ geocentric Sun-Moon interval minutes &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 60 $\times$ (half-duration minutes <gloss>half-duration</gloss> $+$ parallax difference)
---------------------------------------------------------- $=$ ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- $=$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;difference in Sun-Moon velocity &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;difference in Sun-Moon velocity

&nbsp;&nbsp;60 $\times$ half-duration minutes <gloss>half-duration</gloss> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 60 $\times$ parallax difference minutes
------------------------------------------------------- $+$ ----------------------------------------------------------
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;difference in Sun-Moon velocity &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;difference in Sun-Moon velocity

$=$ half-duration ghatis $+$ parallax difference ghatis. It is proven that by this many ghatis before the geocentric conjunction <note>term: darśānta; the end of the new moon tithi</note>, the contact time occurs according to the surface perspective. By subtracting this from the geocentric conjunction time, the ghatis of the contact time from the surface perspective are found.

Geocentric conjunction ghatis $-$ (half-duration ghatis $+$ parallax difference ghatis) $=$ Geocentric conjunction ghatis $-$ half-duration ghatis $-$ parallax difference ghatis.

Therefore, it is proven that in the eastern hemisphere <note>term: pūrvakapāla; the half of the sky from the meridian to the eastern horizon</note>, to find the contact time from the surface perspective, one must subtract the topocentric half-duration ghatis and the parallax difference ghatis from the geocentric conjunction ghatis. Here, half-duration minutes <gloss>half-duration</gloss> $=$ topocentric half-duration minutes should be understood everywhere. Half-duration ghatis <gloss>half-duration</gloss> $=$ topocentric half-duration ghatis.

### Investigation of the Western Hemisphere
<note>original: "paścimakapāle vicāryate" - referring to the western half of the sky from the observer's meridian.</note>

In the western hemisphere, the topocentric end of the conjunction <note>the moment the Sun and Moon appear aligned from the Earth's surface</note> occurs after the geocentric end of the conjunction <note>the alignment as calculated from the Earth's center</note>. The time of contact according to the surface observer occurs before the topocentric end of the conjunction. Therefore, because both the surface-based contact time and the geocentric end of the conjunction exist before the topocentric end, it is possible for the surface-based contact time to occur before the geocentric end of the conjunction. Sometimes, however, it may occur after it.

When, at the time of the topocentric end of the conjunction, the surface-based position of the Sun is to the west of the geocentric position of the Sun, then the surface-based contact time will occur before the geocentric end of the conjunction. This is because, before the geocentric end of the conjunction, the geocentric position of the Moon would be to the west of the geocentric position of the Sun. 

Now, if at the time of contact the geocentric position of the Moon is to the east of the geocentric position of the Sun, then the surface-based contact time would occur after the geocentric end of the conjunction; this is because the geocentric positions of both the Sun and Moon would be in the east only after the geocentric end of the conjunction. 

One might ask: at the time of contact, how is it known whether the geocentric position of the Moon is east or west of the Sun's position? If the geocentric end of the conjunction plus the hours of parallax <term>lambana-ghaṭī: the time difference caused by the observer's position on the surface</term> equals the topocentric end of the conjunction, and if the surface-based half-duration hours <term>sthiryadhā-ghaṭikā: half the total time of the eclipse</term> are less than those hours, then the geocentric position of the Moon is west of the Sun; otherwise, it is to the east.

Now, it is explained when the surface-based contact time occurs before the geocentric end of the conjunction: The minutes of the Moon's parallax are subtracted from the minutes of the surface-based half-duration. Then, the minutes on the ecliptic from the geocentric Moon to the surface-based Sun = <term>Half-dur. 1 min.</term> — <term>Moon par. min.</term> Here, the <term>Sun's parallax minutes</term> are added. Then the surface-based <term>Sun-Moon interval minutes</term> = <term>Half-dur. 1 min.</term> — <term>Moon par. min.</term> + <term>Sun par. min.</term> Since the Sun's parallax minutes are less than the Moon's, the difference between the two is negative. Then the geocentric Sun-Moon interval minutes = <term>Surf. Half-dur. 1 min.</term> — <term>Parallax diff. min.</term>

Then, by proportion:

60 × (Surf. Half-dur. 1 min. — Parallax diff. min.)
------------------------------------------------------------ = <term>Half-dur. 1 hr.</term> — <term>Parallax diff. hr.</term>
Difference in motion <note>the relative speed between Sun and Moon</note>

To calculate the surface-based contact time before the geocentric end of the conjunction, (<term>Half-dur. 1 hr.</term> — <term>Total par. hr.</term>) should be subtracted from the geocentric end of the conjunction. Thus, the surface-based contact time = <term>Geocentric end hr.</term> — <term>Surf. Half-dur. 1 hr.</term> + <term>Parallax diff. hr.</term> Therefore, it is proven that even in the western hemisphere, when the surface-based contact time is before the geocentric end of the conjunction, the half-duration hours must be subtracted from the end of the conjunction and the parallax difference must be added.

It is now explained when the surface-based contact time is after the geocentric end of the conjunction: When the <term>half-duration minutes</term> are subtracted from the Moon's parallax minutes, then the minutes on the ecliptic from the surface-based Sun to the geocentric Moon = <term>Moon par. min.</term> — <term>Half-dur. 1 min.</term> Here, the <term>Sun's parallax minutes</term> must be subtracted. Then the geocentric Sun-Moon interval minutes = <term>Moon par. min.</term> — <term>Half-dur. 1 min.</term> — <term>Sun par. min.</term> = <term>Parallax diff. min.</term> — <term>Half-dur. 1 min.</term>

Then, by proportion: 

60 × (Parallax diff. min. — Half-dur. 1 min.)
-------------------------------------------------------- = <term>Parallax diff. hr.</term> — <term>Half-dur. 1 hr.</term>
Difference in motion

> In the *Siddhanta Shekhara* <note>A major astronomical treatise by Shripati, c. 1039 CE</note>: "From the calculated end of the lunar day, decreased or increased by the half-duration, the parallax should be calculated as before, first for the mean planet and the mean lunar day. Then, from the lunar day, using the half-duration generated from the corrected values, by repeated calculation of the difference in time, the corrected half-durations for contact and separation are found." In this, Shripati has spoken exactly in accordance with the Teacher's <note>Likely referring to Lalla or Aryabhata</note> words, though the second line of this verse is corrupted with erroneous readings.

> In the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>The 12th-century masterpiece by Bhaskara II</note>: "From the mathematically derived end of the lunar day, decreased or increased by the half-duration, calculate the parallax. Apply that to the times of contact and separation, and by repeating this process with the calculated end of conjunction, adding or subtracting, the precise times of contact and release are known in order." This statement by Bhaskara is entirely in agreement with the Teacher's instructions. (Verses 16-17)

It is said here that to know the time of contact, one should first calculate the half-duration based on the corrected latitude at the middle of the eclipse. Subtracting that from the corrected end of the lunar day, one should calculate the parallax and the <term>latitude-parallax</term> <note>Nati: the difference in latitude due to parallax</note>. That is, by calculating the precise time of immersion <note>Sammilana: start of totality</note> and the precise time of emersion <note>Unmilana: end of totality</note> through the aforementioned repeated calculation, the two clear half-durations of totality should be understood as the difference between those times and the middle of the eclipse. Here, the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> has initially accepted the parallax <note>Lambana</note> of the middle of the eclipse as a rough value for both the time of contact and separation; this causes no error in the iterative process. ॥ 16-17 ॥

### ->Rationale<-

First, we consider the eastern hemisphere <note>Purva Kapala: the sky from the horizon to the meridian</note>. Because the surface-view conjunction occurs before the geocentric conjunction, the surface-view contact time naturally occurs before the geocentric conjunction. At the surface-view contact time, the geocentric distance between the Sun and Moon is equal to the sum of the surface-view half-duration arc and the difference in parallax arc. This is because, at the time of contact, the Moon's position is to the west of the Sun's position. The surface-view Sun is to the east of the geocentric Sun; the Moon follows the same principle. The arc-difference between the secondary circles passing through the celestial poles and the centers of the surface-view Sun and Moon is the half-duration arc on the ecliptic. Therefore, by adding the Moon's parallax arc to the half-duration arc, we get the distance from the geocentric Moon to the surface-view Sun on the ecliptic $=$ Half-duration arc $+$ Moon's parallax. By subtracting the Sun's parallax from this, we get the geocentric Sun-Moon distance $=$ Half-duration arc $+$ Moon's parallax $-$ Sun's parallax. When the half-duration arc is less than the Sun's parallax, then by subtracting the half-duration arc from the Sun's parallax, we get the distance from the surface-view Moon to the geocentric Sun; its form is $=$ Sun's parallax $-$ Half-duration arc. Subtracting this from the Moon's parallax gives the geocentric Sun-Moon distance $=$ Moon's parallax $-$ (Sun's parallax $-$ Half-duration arc) $=$ Moon's parallax $-$ Sun's parallax $+$ Half-duration arc $=$ Half-duration arc $+$ Parallax difference. To convert this into time <note>Ghatis</note>, we use the following proportion:

| 60 $\times$ Geocentric Sun-Moon Distance | 60 (Half-duration arc $+$ Parallax difference) | 60 Half-duration arc |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Difference in Sun-Moon motion | Difference in Sun-Moon motion | Difference in Sun-Moon motion |

$+$ $\frac{\text{Parallax difference}}{\text{<unclear>---</unclear>}}$ $=$ Half-duration time $+$ Parallax difference time. It is proven that this much time occurs before the geocentric conjunction. By subtracting this from the geocentric conjunction time, [the contact time] is found.
