### Now, we consider the Western Hemisphere <note>original: "Pashchimakapala" - referring to the western half of the celestial sphere</note>

The surface-based conjunction <term>Darshanta: the end of the lunar month/moment of new moon</term> occurs after the geocentric conjunction. The surface-based first contact occurs before the surface-based conjunction. Therefore, because the surface-based first contact and the geocentric conjunction both occur before the surface-based conjunction, it is possible for the surface-based first contact to occur before the geocentric conjunction, or sometimes after it. When, at the time of the surface-based conjunction, the surface-based solar position is west of the geocentric solar position, then the surface-based first contact occurs before the geocentric conjunction; this is because, before the geocentric conjunction, the geocentric lunar position is indeed to the west of the geocentric solar position. When, at the time of first contact, the geocentric lunar position is to the east of the geocentric solar position, then the surface-based first contact occurs after the geocentric conjunction, because after the geocentric conjunction, both the geocentric solar and lunar positions are in the eastern direction.

We now consider how to determine whether the geocentric lunar position is east or west of the geocentric solar position at the time of first contact. If the surface-based half-duration *ghatis* are less than the parallax *ghatis* added to the geocentric conjunction to find the surface conjunction, then the Moon is west of the geocentric Sun; otherwise, it is to the east. We consider when the surface-based first contact occurs before the geocentric conjunction. By subtracting the Moon's parallax in minutes of arc from the surface-based half-duration minutes, we get the arc on the ecliptic <note>original: "Kranti-vritta"</note> from the geocentric Moon to the surface-based Sun = Sthityardha 1 k - Moon's parallax. By adding the Sun's parallax to this, we get the surface-based Sun-Moon separation = Sthityardha 1 k - Moon's parallax + Sun's parallax. Since the Sun's parallax is less than the Moon's parallax, their difference is negative; thus, the geocentric Sun-Moon separation = Surface Sthityardha 1 k - Parallax difference. Then, by the rule of proportion:

-> 60 × (Surface Sthityardha 1 k - Parallax difference in arc) <-
-> ---------------------------------------------------------- = Sthityardha 1 v - Parallax difference in time <-
-> Difference in daily motion (*Gatyantara*) <-

Assuming the surface-based first contact is before the geocentric conjunction, by subtracting (Sthityardha 1 v - Parallax difference in time) from the geocentric conjunction, we get: Surface-based first contact = Geocentric conjunction - Surface Sthityardha 1 v + Parallax difference in time. From this, it is proven that in the Western Hemisphere, when the surface-based first contact occurs before the geocentric conjunction, one must subtract the half-duration from the conjunction and add the parallax difference. $Cha Cha' - Vi Ra' = \text{Parallax in minutes at the desired time}$ <note>original: "iṣṭakālika-lambana-kalā"</note>. $Cha Vi = \text{The angular distance between the Sun and Moon}$ at the desired time relative to the center of the Earth. > The previously calculated true time of first contact $= D - Sphustha - Lam_1$
> The desired time during the obscuration after the first contact
> $= (D - Mugha - Ilamgha) - (D - Sphustha - Lam_1)$
> $= Sphustha + Lam_1 - Ilamgha - Mugha = I$
> $\therefore Mugha = Sphustha + Lam_1 - Ilamgha - I \dots \dots (1)$
> Now, previously calculated:
> True time of the end of the conjunction $= D - Lam_2$
> True time of first contact $= D - Sphustha - Lam_1$
> The difference between these two is the true half-duration of the first contact phase <note>original: "spāśikaṃ spaṣṭasthitidalam"</note>.

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses
<page-num>441</page-num>

In a solar eclipse, the <term>corrected arm (bhujā)</term> <note>The 'arm' refers to the side of a right-angled triangle used in calculating the distance between the centers of the Sun and Moon</note> is determined. From the <insert>desired</insert> magnitude of the eclipse—just as in the case of a lunar eclipse—the arm is multiplied by the <term>corrected half-duration</term> <note>The time from the start of the eclipse to the maximum obscuration</note> and divided by the half-duration produced by the <term>corrected latitude</term> <note>The angular distance of the Moon north or south of the ecliptic</note> at that specific time. By repeating this calculation several times <note>original: "asakṛtkaraṇena" - a method of successive approximation or iteration common in Indian astronomy</note>, the result is subtracted from the half-duration to find the exact time of the phase. || 18-19 ||

->**The Geometric Derivation**<-

<note>The following abbreviations refer to the accompanying diagram of celestial positions</note>
**G-Ra** = Geocentric Sun. **Ca** = Geocentric Moon.
**Sthā** = Apparent position of the Sun <note>affected by parallax</note>.
**Sthā₁** = Apparent position of the Moon.
**Sthā'** = Geocentric position of the Moon.
**Sthā Sthā₁** = Corrected parallax of the Moon.
**Ga-Sthā** = Corrected parallax of the Sun.
**Ga-Sthā'** = Geocentric distance between the Sun and Moon.
**Sthā' Sthā₁** = Apparent distance between the Sun and Moon.
The diagram illustrates the moment of first contact from a surface-based perspective at the end of the geocentric new moon.

Geocentric Sun-Moon distance + Sun's parallax - Moon's parallax = the distance from the apparent Moon to the apparent Sun = Geocentric Sun-Moon distance - difference in parallax = <term>the upright (koṭi)</term>. Therefore, the Geocentric Sun-Moon distance = difference in parallax + the upright. Now, in the eastern hemisphere from the <term>nonagesimal</term> <note>The point of the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon</note>, the desired time after the moment of contact for a given magnitude = Geocentric end of new moon - Sun-Moon distance <note>in time</note> = Geocentric end of new moon - upright <note>in time</note> - difference in parallax <note>in time</note>. Through iterative calculation of the parallax from the end of the corrected duration, the time of contact is:

Geocentric end of new moon <note>in ghatis</note> — corrected half-duration <note>in ghatis</note> — difference in parallax at contact <note>in ghatis</note> = Geocentric end - corrected half-duration - **La₁**. Here, the difference in parallax at contact in <term>ghatis</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> is **La₁**. The difference between these two, the desired time after contact, is:
**I** = (Geocentric end - upright - difference in parallax) — (Geocentric end - corrected half-duration - **La₁**).
Here, the difference in parallax = **I-La**. Therefore: Geocentric end - upright - **I-La** - Geocentric end + corrected half-duration + **La₁**.

= corrected half-duration - upright - **I-La** + **La₁** = **I**.
Thus: corrected half-duration - **I-La** - **I** + **La₁** = the upright <note>in time</note>.

Now, the corrected end of the new moon = Geocentric end of new moon - **La₁**. Here, **La₁** is the corrected difference in parallax between the Sun and the Moon.

Similarly, from the end of the true lunar day <note>The *tithi*, or lunar day, adjusted for the observer's location.</note>, the parallax is calculated repeatedly. The time of first contact is defined as:
Time of Contact = Geocentric Time — True Half-Duration$_1$ — Parallax$_1$

The difference between these is the Half-Duration of Contact = True Half-Duration$_3$ = Geocentric Time — Parallax$_1$ — (Geocentric Time — True Half-Duration$_1$ — Parallax$_1$) = Geocentric Time — Parallax$_1$ — Geocentric Time + True Half-Duration$_1$ + Parallax$_1$ = True Half-Duration$_1$ + Parallax$_1$ — Parallax$_2$ = Half-Duration of Contact in *ghatis* <note>A *ghati* is a unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note>. Then, by the proportion $\frac{(Parallax_1 — Parallax_2) \times Elapsed}{Half-Duration_3}$, if the result is assumed to be $Parallax_1 — Elapsed\ Parallax$, then:

The measure of the upright time <term>Kotighati</term> <note>The "upright" or vertical component of time used in calculating the eclipse's progress.</note> = $True\ Half-Duration_1 + \frac{(Parallax_1 — Parallax_2) \times Elapsed}{Half-Duration_3} — Elapsed$

= $\frac{True\ Half-Duration_1 \times Half-Duration_3 + (Parallax_1 — Parallax_2) \times Elapsed — Half-Duration_3 \cdot Elapsed}{Half-Duration_3}$

= $\frac{True\ Half-Duration_1 \times Half-Duration_3 + Elapsed \{(Parallax_1 — Parallax_2) — Half-Duration_3 \}}{Half-Duration_3}$

= $\frac{True\ Half-Duration_1 \times Half-Duration_3 — Elapsed \times True\ Half-Duration_1}{Half-Duration_3}$

= $\frac{True\ Half-Duration_1 (True\ Half-Duration_1 — Elapsed)}{Half-Duration_3}$ = Upright Time

Then, $\frac{Difference\ in\ Motion \times Upright\ Time}{60}$ = Upright Arc <term>Kotika</term>. Therefore, by substitution: $\frac{True\ Half-Duration_1 (Half-Duration_3 — Elapsed)}{Half-Duration_3}$

$\times \frac{Difference\ in\ Motion}{60} = \frac{True\ Half-Duration_1}{Half-Duration_3} (Half-Duration_3 — Elapsed) \times \frac{Difference\ in\ Motion}{60} = \frac{True\ Half-Duration_1}{Half-Duration_3}$

$\times$ Minutes of the remaining half-duration = $\frac{True\ Half-Duration_1}{Half-Duration_3} \times$ Upright as in a lunar eclipse = Upright Minutes (1)

= $\frac{True\ Half-Duration_1}{Half-Duration_3} \times$ Base as in a lunar eclipse = Base Minutes <term>Bhujakala</term> <note>The horizontal component of the eclipse triangle.</note>, if Upright Time = Base Time.

Now, $\frac{True\ Half-Duration_1}{Half-Duration_3} \times$ Minutes of the remaining half-duration = Base Minutes. Therefore, the true remaining half-duration$_1$ =

$\frac{Base\ Minutes \times True\ Half-Duration_3}{True\ Half-Duration_1}$. This result should be subtracted from the true half-duration to find the desired time.

Because the calculation of the half-duration and related factors is performed based on the celestial latitude <note>Sanskrit: *shara*</note>, iterative calculation <note>Sanskrit: *asakrit-karma*</note> must be performed; by this, the teachings of the ancient masters are justified. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*: "The 'arm' <note>the side of the eclipse triangle</note> produced at the desired time by the method for lunar eclipses, when multiplied by the half-duration resulting from the corrected latitude and divided by the corrected half-duration, becomes the true 'arm' here. The determination of time is achieved as previously stated; if calculating from the desired magnitude of eclipse <note>istagrasa</note>, it is done iteratively by reversing the multiplier and divisor." By this statement, Shripati <note>an 11th-century astronomer</note> agrees with the *Siddhanta Shiromani*: "The rest of the procedure is as stated for lunar eclipses, but here the 'arm' is multiplied by the half-duration arising from the corrected latitude and divided by that same corrected [half-duration] to find the true 'arm' in a solar eclipse." Regarding the calculation of time from the magnitude of the eclipse, the result multiplied by the corrected half-duration and divided iteratively by the half-duration from the corrected latitude, when subtracted from the half-duration, gives the desired time. By this verse, Bhaskaracharya <note>Bhaskara II, the famous 12th-century mathematician</note> has also spoken in accordance with the ancient masters. (1) Furthermore, the statement in the *Surya Siddhanta*—"In a solar eclipse, the 'upright' <note>kotilipsa</note> multiplied by the mean half-duration and divided by the corrected half-duration is known as the corrected 'upright' minutes"—is also proven correct by this logic. || 18-19 ||

->Now, the specific differences from lunar eclipses regarding the desired magnitude of eclipse and the calculation of time from that magnitude are stated:<-

**Hindi Commentary—** Following the lunar eclipse method, take the "arm" <note>bhuj</note> produced at the desired time, multiply it by the half-duration generated from the instantaneous corrected latitude, and divide by the corrected half-duration (the difference between the time of contact and the middle of the eclipse); this yields the "arm" for a solar eclipse. To find the time from a desired magnitude of eclipse, multiply the "arm" (as calculated in lunar eclipses) by the corrected half-duration and divide by the half-duration generated from the instantaneous corrected latitude. The result obtained by performing this iteratively, when subtracted from the half-duration, results in the determination of the time. || 18-19 ||

### Rationale <note>Upapatti</note>

Look at diagram (A) provided in the Sanskrit rationale. This diagram represents the time of contact from the perspective of the observer on the surface, whereas the true conjunction <note>amavasya</note> is geocentric. **Ga-Ra** = Geocentric Sun; **Cha** = Geocentric Moon; **Sya** = Parallax-shifted position of the Sun; **Sya<gloss>1</gloss>** = Parallax-shifted position of the Moon; **Stha** = Geocentric position of the Moon; **Sya-Sya<gloss>1</gloss>** = Apparent parallax of the Moon; **Ga-Sya** = Apparent parallax of the Sun; **Ga-Stha** = Geocentric distance between Sun and Moon; **Stha-Stha<gloss>1</gloss>** = Distance between the parallax-shifted Sun and Moon. Geocentric distance between Sun and Moon + Solar parallax — Moon's parallax = distance from the shifted Moon to the shifted Sun = Geocentric distance — difference in parallax = the "upright" <note>koti</note>.

Therefore, Geocentric distance = Difference in parallax + Upright. In the eastern hemisphere (before the meridian), the desired time after the moment of contact during the eclipse = Geocentric conjunction — Distance between Sun and Moon = Geocentric conjunction — Upright — Difference in parallax.

From the rule "Parallax is calculated iteratively from the end of the corrected lunar day," the time of contact = 
Geocentric conjunction — Corrected half-duration<gloss>1</gloss> — Difference in parallax at contact = Geocentric conjunction — Corrected half-duration<gloss>1</gloss> — (Moon's parallax<gloss>1</gloss> — Sun's parallax<gloss>1</gloss>).

This calculation is not entirely accurate because the instantaneous latitude <note>the angular distance of the moon from the ecliptic</note> is not known; the half-duration and other factors have been calculated based only on the latitude at the time of the middle of the eclipse. Therefore, an iterative process <term>asakrit-karma</term> <note>repeated calculation to reach a precise value</note> must be performed. This confirms the statements of the ancient teachers. In the *Siddhanta-Shekhara*, Sripati wrote in the Sanskrit verse beginning with **"The base produced from the desired time is like the method for lunar eclipses..."** Similarly, in the *Siddhanta-Shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya also agreed with the teachers' statements in the verses beginning with **"The remainder here is as stated in the lunar eclipse, with the apparent base..."** (1) Through this, the statement in the *Surya Siddhanta* beginning with **"In a solar eclipse, the perpendicular minutes multiplied by the middle half-duration..."** is also proven. ||18-19||

---

### Now he describes the rule regarding which eclipses are observable and which are not:

> The deflection and other factors are like the Moon's; but an eclipse of the Sun less than one-twelfth part is not to be predicted due to its intensity. For the Moon, due to its clarity, an eclipse less than one-sixteenth part is not visible. ||20||

<margin>Sudhakara Bhashya</margin>—"From the sixteenth" means the sixteenth part. The rest is clear. In the chapter on lunar eclipses, the statement by Bhaskara, **"Even if a sixteenth part of the Moon is eclipsed..."** etc., is consistent with this (Lunar Eclipse, Verse 37). ||20||

<margin>Vijnana Bhashya</margin>—Other factors like deflection <term>valana</term> <note>the variation of the direction of the eclipse</note> should be understood as being like the Moon's (as stated in lunar eclipses). Due to the intensity of the Sun (the unbearable sharpness of its light), an eclipse of less than a twelfth part (1/12th) is not to be predicted (because even if eclipsed, a twelfth part is invisible). Because of the clarity of the Moon (due to the extreme whiteness of its rays), an eclipse of less than a sixteenth part (1/16th) is not to be predicted. As stated by Sripati in the *Siddhanta-Shekhara*: **"Due to the intensity of the light of the sun's orb, an eclipsed portion less than a twelfth is not seen. Likewise, a sixteenth part of the cold-rayed moon is not perceived because of the clarity of its rays; therefore, nothing less is noted."** Bhaskaracharya stated this same method of Sripati with slight variation: **"Even a sixteenth part of the Moon, when eclipsed, is not perceived because it is hidden by the mass of light. Due to the intensity of light, a tenth part <note>original: "dashamsha", though the context implies the 12th/16th rule</note> of the sun is not to be predicted by the wise if the eclipse is smaller."** And in the *Surya Siddhanta*:

> **"Due to clarity, even a twelfth part of the Moon is seen when eclipsed. Even three minutes eclipsed..."**

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

## Now, he describes the simplified method for calculating parallax in longitude and latitude.

From the <term>vitribha-lagna</term><note>The point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point (ascendant); the highest point of the ecliptic.</note> (the longitude of the ascendant minus three signs), find the sum or difference of its declination and the local latitude. Subtract this from three signs (90 degrees) and take the sine; this becomes the divisor for the square of half the radius. ||22||

The sine of the difference between the Sun and the <term>vitribha-lagna</term>, divided by that result, gives the parallax in longitude in <term>ghatikas</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note>. From the sum or difference of the <term>vitribha-lagna's</term> declination, latitude, and celestial latitude (polar longitude), ||23||

Take the sine and multiply it by the difference between the mean motions of the Moon and the Sun. Multiply this by fifteen and divide by the radius to find the <term>nati</term><note>Parallax in latitude.</note>. ||24||

**Sudhakara Bhashya (Commentary):** From the ascendant minus three signs (the <term>vitribha</term>), take the degrees of declination and the degrees of latitude. If they are in the same direction, add them; if in different directions, take the difference. Because in a place with low latitude the <term>vitribha</term> is situated near the meridian, these become the zenith distance of the <term>vitribha</term>. Subtracting that from three signs (90 degrees) and taking the sine gives the <term>vitribha-shanku</term><note>The sine of the altitude of the highest point of the ecliptic.</note>. This is the divisor for the square of half the radius. The sine of the distance between the Sun and the <term>vitribha-lagna</term> divided by the result of that division gives the parallax in longitude in <term>ghatikas</term>. The sine of the sum (if same direction) or difference (if different directions) of the <term>vitribha-lagna's</term> declination, its celestial latitude, and the local latitude is the Moon's <term>drikkshepa</term><note>The sine of the zenith distance of the secondary to the ecliptic.</note>. That multiplied by the difference between the mean motions of the Sun and Moon, then multiplied by fifteen and divided by the radius, results in the <term>nati</term> (parallax in latitude).

**The derivation is as follows:** For the sake of simplicity, the <term>vitribha</term> is imagined to be on the meridian, and its zenith distance and altitude are calculated like those at midday. The sine of the altitude is the well-known <term>vitribha-shanku</term>. From the previously established formula, the parallax <term>ghatikas</term> are:
<note>original: $\frac{4 \text{ Sin}(S \sim V)}{\text{R}} \cdot \frac{\text{V-shanku}}{\text{R}} = \frac{\text{Sin}(S \sim V)}{\frac{\text{R}}{\frac{\text{R}}{4 \text{ V-shanku}} }}$</note>
Through this, the calculation of parallax is achieved.

Now, by applying the Moon's celestial latitude to the previously calculated zenith distance of the <term>vitribha</term>, the degrees of the Moon's <term>drikkshepa</term> arc are calculated up to the orbit. For simplicity, the Sun's <term>drikkshepa</term> arc is assumed to be roughly equal to this. Therefore, the two <term>drikkshepas</term> are treated as equal. Then, by the rule "multiplied by the difference of the mean motions of the Sun and Moon," the individual parallaxes are calculated and their difference is taken. This is the clear explanation. ||22-24||

**Vivarana Bhashya (Explanatory Commentary):** From the ascendant minus three signs (the <term>vitribha</term>), the degrees of declination and latitude—their sum if in the same direction, or difference if in different directions—represent the zenith distance of the <term>vitribha</term>, as it sits near the meridian in low-latitude regions. Subtracting this from three signs (90 degrees) and taking the sine gives the <term>vitribha-shanku</term>. This serves as the divisor for the square of half the radius...

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
## Page 448

The sine of the difference between the longitude of the nonagesimal <note>the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note> and the Sun, divided by the result obtained from half the square of the radius, gives the parallax in ghatikas <note>1 ghatika = 24 minutes</note>. The sine of the sum (if in the same direction) or difference (if in different directions) of the declination of the nonagesimal, the latitude of the nonagesimal, and the local latitude is the Moon's sight-motion-force <term>Drkshepa<gloss>the sine of the zenith distance of the highest point of the ecliptic</gloss></term>. That sine, multiplied by the difference between the mean motions of the Sun and Moon and divided by fifteen times the radius, results in the deflection <term>Avanati<gloss>latitudinal parallax</gloss></term>. **[Verses 22-23-24]**

-> **The Rationale** <-

Considering the nonagesimal to be in the meridian circle due to the small difference, the degrees of zenith distance and altitude should be calculated as if at midday. The sine of the altitude is the gnomon of the nonagesimal. From this, the parallax in ghatikas is derived by the previously stated method:

| | | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| = | 4 × Sine(Sun - Nonagesimal) / Radius | × | Nonagesimal Gnomon / Radius | |
| = | Sine(Sun - Nonagesimal) / (Radius² / 4 × Nonagesimal Gnomon) | = | Sine(Sun - Nonagesimal) / ((Radius/2)² / Nonagesimal Gnomon) | = | Sine(Sun - Nonagesimal) / Result |

By this, the calculation of parallax is established.

By adjusting the previously calculated zenith distance of the nonagesimal with the Moon's latitude, the arc of the Moon's sight-motion-force up to the celestial secondary circle is calculated. Due to the small difference, the Sun's sight-motion-force arc is taken as equal to it; thus, their two sight-motion-forces are considered equal. Then, by the rule **"multiplied by the difference in mean motions of the Sun and Moon,"** the individual deflections are calculated, and their difference is termed "Avanati." 

Here, "Vi" refers to the Nonagesimal. "Sine(Sun - Nonagesimal)" is the sine of the distance between the Sun and the nonagesimal. In the *Siddhanta-shekhara* <note>A major 11th-century work by Sripati</note>, it is said: **"The square of half the sine of three signs <note>the radius</note> divided by the result... the sine of the difference between the Sun and the nonagesimal... Or, the parallax is negative as stated... the latitude of the ascendant minus three signs... mixed with the latitude of the nonagesimal... then the multiplier... divided by seventy <note>literally 'sky-mountains'</note> becomes the deflection."** 

This statement by Sripati is consistent with the Teacher's <note>Brahmagupta's</note> teaching, though Sripati adds more detail regarding the division by seventy.

According to the rule **"multiplied by the mean motion of the Sun and Moon,"** etc.:
Sun's Deflection = (Sun's Drkshepa × Sun's Mean Motion) / (15 × Radius)
Moon's Deflection = (Moon's Drkshepa × Moon's Mean Motion) / (15 × Radius)

The difference between these two is:
(Drkshepa × Difference in Motion) / (15 × Radius)

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| = | Drkshepa × (790' 35'' - 59' 8'') / (3438 × 15) | = | Drkshepa × (731' 27'') / 51570 |
| = | Drkshepa / 70 (approximately) | |

This is also stated in the *Surya-siddhanta*: **"The deflection is the result of the Drkshepa divided by seventy."**

# Chapter on the Authority of Solar Eclipses
<page-num>446</page-num>

This alternative method for calculating the latitude-parallax <note>original: "nati"</note> has been stated. Here, the teachers have accepted the zenith distance of the Sun and Moon as being equal. // 22-23-24 //

---

->Now, the calculation of longitude-parallax and latitude-parallax by a simplified method is described<-

**Hindi Commentary —** By taking the declination <note>original: "kranti"</note> of the Nonagesimal <term>Vitribha Lagna: the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</term> and the local latitude, adding them if they are in the same direction or subtracting them if in different directions, one finds the zenith distance of the Nonagesimal. This occurs when the Nonagesimal is near the meridian in regions with low latitude. By subtracting this from 90 degrees <note>original: "three signs"</note>, the sine of the resulting value is the "Sine-Altitude of the Nonagesimal" <note>original: "Vitribhashanku"</note>. The square of half the radius <note>original: "Trijyardha"</note> serves as the divisor. By dividing the square of half the radius by this divisor, a quotient is obtained. Dividing the sine of the difference between the Nonagesimal and the Sun by this quotient results in the longitude-parallax <note>original: "lambana"</note> in ghatikas <note>units of 24 minutes</term>. By combining the declination of the Nonagesimal, the celestial latitude <note>original: "shara"</note> of the Nonagesimal, and the local latitude (adding if same direction, subtracting if different), the sine of the remainder is the "Moon's Ecliptic Zenith Distance" <note>original: "Chandradrikkshepa"</note>. Multiplying that sine by the difference between the mean motions of the Sun and Moon, and dividing by fifteen times the radius, gives the corrected latitude-parallax <note>original: "avanati" or "spashtanati"</note>. // 22-23-24 //

### Mathematical Proof

By assuming the Nonagesimal to be on the meridian (due to small difference), one calculates the zenith distance and altitude of the Nonagesimal as if it were midday. The Sine-Altitude = Vitribhashanku. Then, using the rule "Four times the radius multiplied by the sine-altitude..." etc., the Parallax in Ghatikas = $\frac{4 \times \text{Sine}(Sun \sim Nonagesimal)}{\text{Radius}} \times \frac{\text{Sine-Altitude}}{\text{Radius}}$

$= \frac{\text{Sine}(Sun \sim Nonagesimal)}{\frac{\text{Radius}^2}{4 \times \text{Sine-Altitude}}} = \frac{\text{Sine}(Sun \sim Nonagesimal)}{\frac{(\frac{\text{Radius}}{2})^2}{\text{Sine-Altitude}}} = \frac{\text{Sine}(Sun \sim Nonagesimal)}{\text{Quotient}}$. From this, the calculation of the corrected longitude-parallax is proven.

By applying the correction of the Nonagesimal's celestial latitude to the previously calculated zenith distance of the Nonagesimal, we obtain the arc of the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance up to the secondary circle. For the sake of simplicity <note>original: "svalpantara"</note>, the Sun's ecliptic zenith distance is accepted as being equal to this. Therefore, the ecliptic zenith distances of both (Sun and Moon) are considered equal.

Then, using the rule "Sun-sky-fixed-fifteen-latitude-multiplied" etc., the individual latitude-parallaxes of the Sun and Moon are calculated, and their difference becomes the corrected latitude-parallax <note>original: "avanati"</note>. In that context, Radius = Nonagesimal, Sine (Sun $\sim$ Moon) = 

<note>The vocabulary list below defines the technical Sanskrit terms used in the mathematical proofs above.</note>
<margin>
**Technical Terms:**
- **Solar Eclipse Authority:** The chapter title.
- **Nonagesimal (Vitribha):** The point 90° behind the ascendant.
- **Longitude-Parallax (Lambana):** Shift in position along the ecliptic.
- **Latitude-Parallax (Nati/Avanati):** Shift in position perpendicular to the ecliptic.
- **Latitude (Akshansha):** Terrestrial latitude.
- **Declination (Krantyansha):** Distance north/south of celestial equator.
- **Meridian (Yamyottara Vritta):** The north-south line.
- **Sine-Altitude (Shanku):** The vertical sine of a celestial body.
- **Radius (Trijya):** The standard radius used in Indian trigonometry.
- **Ecliptic Zenith Distance (Drikkshepa):** The sine of the arc between the zenith and the pole of the ecliptic.
- **Proof (Upapatti):** The logical or mathematical derivation.
</margin>

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta
<note>The Corrected Treatise of Brahma, a foundational 7th-century Indian astronomical text.</note>

Regarding the sine of the difference between the zenith distance and three signs <note>90 degrees</note>, Sripati, in the *Siddhanta-shekhara* <note>The Crest-Jewel of Siddhantas, an 11th-century text</note>, has spoken in accordance with the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note> in the Sanskrit verses beginning with "From the difference of the latitudes..." and so on. He only differs from the Teacher's words in saying "the parallax arises from the planet's longitude." From the rule "The mean motion of the Sun and Moon multiplied by..." etc., the Sun's parallax in latitude is:

   Drkshepa · Sun's motion              Drkshepa · Moon's motion                             Drkshepa · Difference in motion
= ----------------------- , Moon's parallax = ------------------------- ; by taking the difference of both = ------------------------------ =
          15 · Radius                          15 · Radius                                          15 · Radius

 Drkshepa · (132945 - 59818)     Drkshepa (73127)     Drkshepa
---------------------------- = ------------------ = ---------- = **True Parallax in Latitude**, with a small difference.
       3415 X 15                    51225              70

By this, the method stated by Sripati—"the parallax arises from the planet's longitude"—and the method for finding the true parallax in latitude stated in the *Surya-siddhanta* <note>The Sun Treatise</note>—"the parallax in latitude is the result of the *drkshepa* <note>sine of the zenith distance of the ecliptic</note> divided by seventy"—are proven correct. ||22-23-24||

### Now he describes the special characteristics:

->**The rest is clear as before; the true nodes of the Sun and Moon are as told by Brahma.**<-
->**Because those told by Aryabhata and others are inaccurate, their results are unclear.**<- ||25||

**Sudhakara Dvivedi's Commentary:** The remaining calculations in the book, such as the duration of the eclipse <note>sthityardha</note>, are as before. Thus, an eclipse calculated using the true nodes of the Sun and Moon as stated by Brahmagupta becomes clear and matches observation. Since the true nodes of the Sun and Moon stated by Aryabhata and others are inaccurate and do not match observation, the eclipses calculated by their solar and lunar nodes are "unclear," meaning they do not match what is seen. ||25||

**Vijnanabhashya Commentary:** The remaining parts of the text (the duration of the eclipse, etc.) are as before (following the methods for lunar eclipses). The eclipse becomes clear (observable) using the true Sun and Moon nodes stated by Brahmagupta (the true nodes of the Sun and Moon told by me). That which was stated by teachers like Aryabhata is not so (not observable) because those (the nodes stated by Aryabhata, etc.) are inaccurate; therefore, the eclipse stated by them is unclear (not fit for observation). In the conclusion of the chapter on eclipses in the *Siddhanta-shekhara*, Sripati says: "Parallax is not accurate when done with the five sines; therefore, what was said by the son of Jishnu <note>Brahmagupta</note> is correct, and has been clearly stated by me as well." This statement by Sripati indicates that his chapter on solar eclipses was written in accordance with Brahmagupta's teachings. In the commentary on the Teacher's statement—"Since there is no agreement between observation and calculation in a solar eclipse using the five sines, I shall explain how that agreement is reached at the end of the lunar day"—the commentator Chaturveda Acharya says:

> "The method of calculating a solar eclipse using the 'five sines' <term>Pancha-jya: the five specific trigonometric values used in Indian astronomy to calculate planetary positions and eclipses</term> as composed by the Teachers is as follows: the sine of the rising point <note>uayajya</note>, the sine of the altitude <note>shankujya</note>, the sine of the zenith distance of the meridian <note>madhyajya</note>, the sine of the motion-parallax <note>drggatijya</note>, and the sine of the zenith distance of the ecliptic <note>drkshepajya</note>. With these, Aryabhata and others, as well as in the *Paulisha-tantra*, calculated the five sines of the Moon using the remaining daylight, the half-day length, and the declination..."

### Now for the Special Explanation

**Hindi Commentary—** The remaining calculations (such as the duration of the eclipse, etc.) are performed as before (similar to the methods described for lunar eclipses). The eclipse becomes clear (observable/accurate) through the corrected Sun, corrected Moon, and corrected Node <note>original: "spashta pata"</note> as stated by Brahma (the Teacher Brahmagupta). It does not become observable through the methods stated by teachers like Aryabhata, because their calculations for the Sun, Moon, and Node are inaccurate <note>original: "asphuta"</note>; therefore, the eclipse calculated by them is indistinct (not matching observation). This is indicated in the *Siddhanta Shekhara* by the verse "It is not accurate using the Five Sines," etc., written in the Sanskrit justification, showing that Sripati spoke in the chapter on solar eclipses according to the ancient teachers. 

Regarding the verse "The unity with observation does not occur," etc., written in the Sanskrit justification, Chaturvedacharya explains it thus: The solar eclipse calculation by the Five-Sine method <note>original: "panchajyavidhana"</note> mentioned by the teachers is this: "The Rising Sine <note>udayajya</note>, Meridian Sine <note>madhyajya</note>, Gnomon Sine <note>shankujya</note>, Sine of the Sine of the Ecliptic <note>driggatijya</note>, and Sine of the Zenith Distance <note>drikkshepajya</note>." By these, teachers like Aryabhata, as well as in the *Paulisha Tantra*, imagined the Five Sines of the Moon through the elapsed/remaining part of the day, the ascensional difference <note>charakhanda</note>, declination <note>kranti</note>, etc. In that way, the solar eclipse calculation described therein by the Ten-Sine method occurs at the end of the new moon; the Teacher will describe the flaws of that in the Chapter on the Examination of Treatises, and I will explain them there as well. 

Having considered the verses such as "Since the solar eclipse calculation is by Five Sines," Sripati said, "It is not accurate using the Five Sines." In the *Surya Siddhanta* and in the *Shishya-dhi-vriddhida*, Lallacharya has stated the solar eclipse calculation using only the aforementioned Five Sines; understanding that to be error-prone, Sripati has relied upon the path stated by the Teacher (Brahmagupta). ||25||

## Chapter on the Rising and Setting of Celestial Bodies

<note>This page serves as a chapter heading for the seventh section of the Corrected Treatise of Brahma <note>original: "Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta"</note>, an influential 7th-century astronomical treatise by the mathematician and astronomer Brahmagupta. The numeral "7" indicates the chapter number. The title "Chapter on the Rising and Setting of Celestial Bodies" <note>original: "Udyāstādhikāra"</note> refers to the mathematical calculations required to determine when planets and stars become visible or disappear near the horizon due to the sun's light.</note>

<term>Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta</term> <note>Literally "The Correctly Established Doctrine of Brahma," this is one of the most significant works in the history of Indian astronomy and mathematics.</note>

<term>Udyāstādhikāra</term> <note>A technical term in Indian astronomy <note>Jyotisha</note> referring to the "visibility" or "heliacal" rising and setting of planets.</note>

# The Corrected Treatise of Brahma (Brahmasphutasiddhanta)

## Chapter on the Rising and Setting of Heavenly Bodies

Now begins the chapter on the rising and setting of planets. First, the author states the purpose for beginning this section:

->Because planets become visible or invisible based on the distance between the planet and the Sun in the east, and the distance between the Sun and the planet in the west, according to their own specific degrees; therefore, I shall describe the calculation of that distance. // 1 //<-

**Sudhakara’s Commentary—** In the east (on the eastern horizon), planets become visible or invisible according to the distance between the planet and the Sun measured in their own <term>degrees of time (kala-amsha)</term> <note>Kala-amshas are units used to determine if a planet is far enough from the Sun's glare to be seen</note>. Similarly, in the west (on the western horizon), they are judged by the distance between the Sun and the planet in their own degrees of time. This means: on whichever day in the eastern horizon the Sun rises a certain number of "time-degree minutes" after the planet has risen, the planet becomes visible at the end of the night. Likewise, on whichever day in the western horizon the planet sets a certain number of "time-degree minutes" after the Sun has set, the planet becomes invisible <insert>or visible</insert> in the evening. Therefore, since the knowledge of rising and setting depends on the minutes of distance between the planet and the Sun, it is necessary to begin this chapter to explain that calculation. // 1 //

**Vishvanatha’s Commentary—** For the reason that in the east (eastern horizon) by the planet-Sun interval and in the west (western horizon) by the Sun-planet interval—measured in their respective degrees of time—the planets respectively become visible or invisible. This is what is being said: on the day in the eastern horizon when the Sun rises after the planet by the required time-degree minutes, the planet is visible in the last part of the night. Similarly, on the day in the western horizon when the planet sets after sunset by the required time-degree minutes, the planet becomes invisible in the evening. For this reason, because the knowledge of rising and setting is dependent on the minutes of the interval between the planet and the Sun, I shall describe that calculation (the means of finding the planet-Sun interval). This is stated in the same manner as the teacher Sripati in the *Siddhanta Shekhara*: "Because in the east by the degrees arising from the planet-Sun interval, and in the west by those situated in the Sun-planet interval, they become invisible or visible due to their proximity to the Sun (the 'sharp-rayed one'), I therefore speak of that calculation for the sake of clear understanding." // 1 //

Header: In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta <note>The Correctly Established Doctrine of Brahma, a seminal 7th-century astronomical treatise by Brahmagupta</note>

Planets are invisible; that is to say, on the day when the Sun rises at a time equal to the "time-parts" <term>kalāṃśa: degrees of time required for a planet to become visible</term> after the planet has risen on the eastern horizon, the planet is visible during the remainder of the night. Similarly, on the day when the planet sets at a time equal to the "time-parts" after sunset on the western horizon, the planet becomes invisible in the evening. For this reason, since the knowledge of rising and setting depends on the time-difference between the planet and the Sun, I shall describe the calculation of that difference (between the planet and the Sun). ||1||

->Now he describes the visibility and invisibility of planets due to their proximity to the Sun:<-

->A planet with slower motion than the Sun, being less in longitude, is visible in the east; otherwise, it is invisible.<-
->A planet with faster motion, being greater in longitude, is visible in the west; a slow-moving one is invisible.<- ||2||

<margin>Sudhakara Dvivedi's Commentary:</margin> A planet that is less than the Sun in longitude and has a slower motion than the Sun <note>original: "ūnabhukti"</note> becomes visible in the east during the remainder of the night when separated from the Sun by the required time-parts. Otherwise, a planet with faster motion than the Sun, even if less in longitude, is invisible in the east during the remainder of the night at that same interval. Likewise, a planet with faster motion that is greater than the Sun in longitude becomes visible in the west when separated by the time-parts. A slow-moving planet that is greater than the Sun in longitude becomes invisible in that same western direction.

The mathematical proof <note>original: "upapatti"</note> here is clear from Bhaskara's rule: "A planet with slower motion than the Sun rises in the east," etc. (Planetary Motion, Rising and Setting, Chapter 4).

<margin>Vijnanabhashya Commentary:</margin> A planet that is less than the Sun and has slower motion is visible in the east; otherwise (if the planet has faster motion and is less than the Sun), it is invisible in the east. Similarly, a planet with faster motion and greater longitude than the Sun is visible in the west, and a planet with slower motion and greater longitude than the Sun is invisible in the west. ||2||

### The Mathematical Proof

Planets with slower motion than the Sun have their disks rendered invisible due to their proximity to the Sun; when they reach the same longitude as the Sun, that is the time of maximum combustion <note>the moment the planet is exactly behind the Sun</note>. After that, because the Sun moves faster, it moves ahead. Following the planet's rising on the eastern horizon, the Sun arrives after an ever-increasing interval. The first appearance of these planets, known as their "rising," occurs during the remainder of the night; thus, their rising is in the east. Then, as the Sun moves to the rear of these planets due to the increasing interval, their appearance occurs in the western direction. When the remaining interval there is exactly equal to the fixed time-parts, they disappear; thus, their "setting" is in the west. 

For planets with faster motion than the Sun, because they move ahead of the Sun after the moment of maximum combustion, their appearance is possible after sunset; therefore, they have a western rising. When they eventually return to a position behind the Sun, they are seen during the remainder of the night; because their disappearance is possible there at an interval equal to the time-parts, they undergo an eastern setting. In the case of Mercury and Venus when they are in retrograde motion, because their motion is less than the Sun's <note>due to their negative velocity</note>, their eastern...

<header>Chapter on Rising and Setting</header>

Rising occurs in the [eastern] direction, and setting occurs in the west. Therefore, the direct-moving <term>Mercury and Venus</term> <note>original: "ऋजुबुधशुक्रौ"</note> rise in the west and reach their setting in that same direction through retrograde motion. Because their motion—resulting from the combination of the <term>Equation of Center</term> <note>manda-phala; the correction for elliptical orbits</note> and the <term>Equation of Anomaly</term> <note>shighra-phala; the correction for the observer's position on Earth</note>—cannot exceed a certain limit ahead of or behind the Sun, these two planets experience both slower and faster motion than the Sun during the interval between their rising and setting due to their <term>retrograde motion</term> <note>vakra-gati</note>. Consequently, their rising and setting can occur in both the eastern and western directions. In the *Siddhanta-Shekhara*, it is stated: "A planet with lesser velocity than the Thousand-Rayed One [the Sun] becomes visible in the east; one with greater velocity becomes visible in the west. Conversely, a planet with greater velocity becomes invisible in the east, and one with lesser velocity becomes invisible in the west, based on the stated <term>degrees of time</term> <note>kalansha; the specific arc of separation required for a planet to be visible</note>." This statement by Shripati <note>an 11th-century astronomer</note> is consistent with what Bhaskara says in the *Siddhanta-Shiromani*: "A planet with lesser motion than the Sun rises in the east, etc." ||2||

->Now, the visibility and invisibility of planets due to their proximity to the Sun are described.<-

**Hindi Commentary:** Planets with lesser velocity than the Sun and those positioned behind it become visible in the eastern direction. Otherwise (planets with greater velocity than the Sun and those positioned ahead), they become invisible in the east. Similarly, planets with greater velocity than the Sun become visible in the western direction, while those with lesser velocity become invisible in the west. ||2||

### Mathematical Proof

When planets with lesser velocity than the Sun have their <term>disks</term> <note>bimba; the visible body of the planet</note> rendered invisible due to their proximity to the Sun, the moment they reach an equal position with the Sun is the "Time of Maximum Combustion" <note>paramasta-kala</note>. After this, because the Sun moves faster, it moves ahead, and the planet gradually appears in the eastern horizon after the Sun has passed. The first appearance (rising) of these planets occurs at the end of the night; therefore, the rising is in the east. Later, as the distance increases and the Sun moves behind these planets, they are seen in the west. There, when the distance becomes equal to the fixed "degrees of time," they disappear; thus, the setting occurs in the west.

For planets with greater velocity than the Sun, as they move ahead of the Sun after the time of maximum combustion, they can be seen after sunset, so their rising occurs in the west. When they return to a position behind the Sun and are seen at the end of the night, they reach their setting in the east when the distance matches the required degrees of time. 

Due to the retrograde motion of Mercury and Venus, they rise in the east and set in the west when their velocity is less than the Sun's. Therefore, direct-moving Mercury and Venus rise in the west and reach their setting there through retrograde motion. Because their movement cannot exceed the limits set by the combination of the Equation of Center and Equation of Anomaly, these two experience both slower and faster motion than the Sun during the interval of rising and setting. Thus, their rising and setting occur in both the east and the west. As stated in the *Siddhanta-Shekhara*: "A planet with lesser motion than the Thousand-Rayed One becomes visible in the east..."

# In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta

The verses written in the Sanskrit commentary follow the same reasoning as stated by the teacher Shripati <note>Shripati (c. 1019–1066) was a prominent Indian astronomer and mathematician</note>. In the *Siddhanta-shiromani*, Bhaskaracharya has also stated these same points in the verse beginning with "The planet rises in the east due to its slower motion..." and so on. ||2||

->Now, he describes the calculation of the ecliptic correction (Ayanadrkkarma) for the purpose of finding the rising and setting times of the planetary disks:<-

**The product of the latitude and the declination of the planet plus three signs, divided by the radius, gives the minutes of arc.**
**These should be subtracted from the planet's position if they are in the same direction, and added if they are in opposite directions. ||3||**

<margin>Sudhakara Dvivedi's Commentary —</margin> The "declination plus three signs" refers to the sine of the declination of the planet's longitude increased by 90 degrees. In the diurnal circle, this represents the ecliptic deflection <term>Ayana-valana: the angle between the circle of latitude and the circle of declination</term>. In the teacher's opinion, by assuming the diurnal circle to be roughly equal to the radius, this itself becomes the ecliptic deflection. The remainder of the logic regarding the latitude and ecliptic deflection is clear.

->The derivation here: "The ecliptic deflection multiplied by the uncorrected latitude and divided by the diurnal sine..."<-

Following the method of Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note>, and assuming the diurnal sine to be equal to the radius and the rising times of the signs to be 1800 minutes, the corrected value should be known. In reality, the ecliptic correction becomes precise when using the diurnal sine of the planetary disk; even Bhaskara, by taking the local diurnal sine, has brought forth a rough calculation, as is clear to those learned in the Siddhantas. ||3||

<margin>Vishnukanta Jha's Commentary —</margin> The product of the latitude and the declination of the planet plus three signs (the product of the celestial latitude and the declination of the planet plus 90 degrees) divided by the radius (divided by the Sine of 90 degrees) results in minutes of arc. These should be subtracted from the planet's longitude if the two (the latitude and the declination plus three signs) are in the same direction (both North or both South). If they are in different directions, they should be added to the planet's longitude. This is the first visibility correction, known as the "Ecliptic Correction" (Ayana). ||3||

->The Derivation Here<-

The point where the secondary to the ecliptic <note>The circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic</note> passing through the center of the planetary disk meets the ecliptic is the "position" of the planet. One must then draw the secondary to the celestial equator <note>The circle passing through the celestial poles</note> passing through that position and through the disk. Then, the diurnal circle of the position and the diurnal circle of the disk must be drawn. The arc of the diurnal circle of the disk between the secondary to the equator and the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the position is the Ecliptic Correction (Ayanadrkkarma). Or, it is the arc of the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator</note> contained between the two secondaries to the equator passing through the position and the disk. The distance from the center of the planetary disk to the planet's position on the ecliptic is the planet's primary latitude. The angle formed between the secondary to the equator and the secondary to the ecliptic at that position is equal to the local ecliptic deflection (the ecliptic deflection at the diurnal circle), which is equivalent to the declination plus three signs. Thus, the planet's primary latitude is one side (base). The perpendicular arc from the center of the disk to the secondary to the equator passing through the position is the second side. The third side lies on the secondary to the equator passing through the position. In this triangle, a ratio of angles is made: if the Sine of the Radius yields the Sine of the mean latitude, then by the Sine of the ecliptic deflection...

# Chapter on Rising and Setting

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Sine of Latitude × Sine of Ecliptic Deflection
By what proportion does the Sine of the Arc of Latitude come? ———————————————— As much as the
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Radius

Sine of Latitude is, so much is the Sine of the Ecliptic Visibility Correction in the diurnal circle of the planetary disk. Therefore:

Sine of Latitude × Sine of Ecliptic Deflection
————————————————————— = Sine of Ecliptic Visibility Correction (in time-degrees),
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Radius

Accepting the non-difference between the sine and the arc <note>A common simplification in ancient trigonometry for small angles</note>:

Latitude × Ecliptic Deflection
———————————— = Ecliptic Visibility Correction (in time-seconds).
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Radius

The Teacher <note>Referring to the author of the primary text being commented upon</note>, due to the slight difference, has accepted the Radius as the local diurnal radius. Based on this, the calculation of the minutes of the Ecliptic Visibility Correction is: <insert>' 1800 x Ecliptic Visibility Correction (in time-seconds) '
——————————————————————
Right Ascension of the sign occupied by the planet</insert>

This is easily understood. This calculation ought to be accurate based on the diurnal radius of the planetary disk, but since the diurnal radius of the disk is unknown, the calculation is stated based on the local diurnal radius; even there, the error generated by accepting the equality of the Radius and the diurnal radius certainly persists. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>The famous 12th-century work by Bhaskara II</note>: "The ecliptic deflection multiplied by the uncorrected sine of latitude and divided by the diurnal radius... divided by 1800 and the right ascension of the occupied sign, gives the ecliptic minutes." Bhaskaracharya also, considering the diurnal radius to be equal to the Radius, stated the calculation of the Ecliptic Visibility Correction. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara* <note>An 11th-century work by Sripati</note>: "The product of the latitude and the versed sine of the planet plus three signs, divided by the Radius... these minutes should be subtracted if the directions are the same and added if different; this is the first visibility method." By this verse, Sripati calculated the Ecliptic Visibility Correction from the Sine of Ecliptic Deflection, which is equal to the Sine of Declination derived from the versed sine of the planet plus three signs as mentioned by Lallacharya. Sripati, while following the Teacher's opinion in many places, occasionally accepted Lalla's view even when it contradicted the Teacher. The Sine of Declination of a planet plus three signs is equal to the Sine of Ecliptic Deflection at the diurnal circle; the Sine of Declination derived from the versed sine of a planet plus three signs is not equal to the Ecliptic Deflection. Therefore, the method of achieving the Ecliptic Visibility Correction mentioned by Lallacharya and Sripati is not proper. In the *Surya Siddhanta*: "The latitude in minutes multiplied by the degrees of declination of the planet plus three signs, etc." This calculation of the Ecliptic Visibility Correction is slightly more precise than those achieved by Lallacharya and Sripati, but the wise should understand that no one's calculation is perfectly accurate. || 3 ||

-> Now, for the purpose of calculating the rising and setting of the planetary disk, the method for Ecliptic Visibility Correction is stated <-

> **Hindi Commentary:** — The product of the Latitude and the Declination of the planet plus three signs should be divided by the Radius. The resulting minutes should be subtracted from the planet's position if the Latitude and the Declination of the planet plus three signs are in the same direction, and added if they are in different directions. || 3 ||

### Mathematical Proof

-> The point where the secondary to the ecliptic passing through the center of the planetary disk meets the ecliptic is the planetary position <-

<meta>This page continues the mathematical derivation of the visibility corrections (Drik-karma) for planetary bodies, specifically focusing on the polar longitudinal correction (Ayana Drik-karma) as discussed in the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta.</meta>

<page-num>462</page-num>
<header>In the Brahmasphuta-siddhanta</header>

The <term>Mean Latitude</term> <note>original: "Madhyama-shara"; the angular distance of a planet from the ecliptic</note> of the planet extends from the ecliptic position to the center of the planetary disk. One must construct the <term>Secondary to the Celestial Equator</term> <note>original: "Dhruvaprota-vritta"; a great circle passing through the celestial poles</note> passing through the ecliptic position and the center of the disk, and then establish the diurnal circles for both positions. Then, the arc of the planetary diurnal circle intercepted between the secondary to the equator and the <term>Secondary to the Ecliptic</term> <note>original: "Kadambaprota-vritta"; a great circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic</note> passing through the ecliptic position constitutes the <term>Ayana Drik-karma</term> <note>the correction for the planet's visibility due to the obliquity of the ecliptic</note>. Alternatively, the arc of the celestial equator intercepted between the two secondaries to the equator is the <term>Ayana Drik-karma</term>. The angle formed by the secondary to the ecliptic and the secondary to the equator at that position is the local <term>Ayana Valana</term> <note>the deflection or angle of orientation</note>. The <term>Ayana Valana at the end of the Radius of the Diurnal Circle</term> is equal to the declination of the <term>Corresponding Point on the Ecliptic</term> <note>original: "Sannibha-graha"; a point on the ecliptic having the same longitude as the planet</note>. 

Thus, in the spherical right-angled triangle formed by these three sides—where the planet's <term>Mean Latitude</term> is the first side, the perpendicular arc from the disk center to the secondary to the equator is the second side, and the third side lies along the secondary to the equator—we apply the ratio of sines: If for the <term>Radius</term> <note>original: "Trijya"; the standard radius of 3438 minutes</note> we obtain the <term>Sine of the Mean Latitude</term>, then what shall we obtain for the Sine of the Ayana Valana? From this, the Sine of the perpendicular arc is derived:

$\frac{\text{Sine of Mean Latitude} \times \text{Sine of Ayana Valana}}{\text{Radius}}$ = Sine of the perpendicular arc.

However, since the Sine of the perpendicular arc and the Sine of the Ayana Drik-karma on the planetary diurnal circle are equal:

$\frac{\text{Sine of Mean Latitude} \times \text{Sine of Ayana Valana}}{\text{Radius}}$ = Sine of Ayana Drik-karma = $\frac{\text{Sine of Mean Latitude} \times \text{Sine of Declination of the Corresponding Point}}{\text{Radius}}$.

By accepting the identity between the sine and the arc (for small angles):

$\frac{\text{Mean Latitude} \times \text{Declination of the Corresponding Point}}{\text{Radius}}$ = Ayana Drik-karma.

Here, the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> has, for the sake of simplicity, accepted the <term>Radius of the Diurnal Circle</term> <note>original: "Dyujya"</note> as being equal to the <term>Radius</term> <note>Trijya</note>. Based on this, the minutes of the Ayana Drik-karma are calculated:

$\frac{1800 \times \text{Ayana Drik-karma}}{\text{Right Ascension of the Sign of the Planet's Declination}}$

The calculation of Ayana Drik-karma would be more accurate if based on the planetary <term>Radius of the Diurnal Circle</term>, but since that is unknown, the Teacher has calculated it based on the local <term>Radius of the Diurnal Circle</term> and assumed it to be equal to the <term>Radius</term> <note>Trijya</note>; therefore, this calculation is not entirely precise. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, the verse beginning with "The Ayana correction is multiplied by the factors..." <note>original: "Ayanam valanasphutegunagana sangunaih"</note> provides the Sanskrit derivation for Ayana Drik-karma, but <term>Bhaskaracharya</term> also accepted the <term>Radius of the Diurnal Circle</term> as equal to the <term>Radius</term>. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, in the verse beginning "When the Versine of the corresponding celestial body..." <note>original: "Kshipte sannibhakhagotkramaja-abhajya"</note>, <term>Shripati</term> calculated the Ayana Drik-karma using the <term>Sine of Ayana Valana</term> (equivalent to the Sine of Declination) derived from the Versine of the corresponding point as stated by <term>Lallacharya</term>. 

<term>Shripati</term>, while following the opinion of the Teacher (<term>Brahmagupta</term>) in many places, has in some instances accepted the views of <term>Lalla</term> against the Teacher's opinion. The Sine of Declination of the <term>Corresponding Point</term> and the Ayana Valana at the end of the diurnal radius are equal. However, the Sine of Declination derived from the <term>Versine of the Corresponding Point</term> is not equal to the Sine of Ayana Valana. Therefore, the Ayana Drik-karma calculations stated by <term>Lallacharya</term> and <term>Shripati</term> are incorrect. In the *Surya Siddhanta*, the calculation of Ayana Drik-karma using "The minutes of the latitude multiplied by the declination of the corresponding point..." <note>original: "Sannibhagraha-jakrantibhaghna kshepalaptika"</note> is slightly more precise than those derived by <term>Lallacharya</term> and <term>Shripati</term>, but the Drik-karma calculation of no single teacher is perfectly accurate. ||13||

<summary>This page critiques various historical methods for calculating Ayana Drik-karma (visibility correction), comparing the approaches of Brahmagupta, Bhaskara, Shripati, and Lalla, while highlighting mathematical inaccuracies regarding the radius of diurnal circles.</summary>

# Chapter on Rising and Setting

## Now, the calculation for the Latitude Visibility Correction is described:

> **Multiply the celestial latitude by the equinoctial shadow and divide by twelve. For a northern latitude, the resulting value is subtracted for the rising sign and added for the setting sign. For a southern latitude, it is added and subtracted respectively to find the rising and setting positions. ||4||**

**Sudhakara Bhashya (Commentary):** From a northern <term>celestial latitude (shara)</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</note>, the resulting correction in minutes of arc is subtracted to calculate the rising sign (<term>udaya-lagna</term>) and added to calculate the setting sign (<term>asta-lagna</term>). Conversely, for a southern latitude, the correction is added and subtracted respectively. These corrections are applied to the planet already adjusted by the previously calculated <term>Ecliptic Visibility Correction (Ayana-drkkarma)</term> to determine the true rising and setting points.

**The Derivation:** On the horizon, the <term>terrestrial latitude deflection (aksha-valana)</term> is considered roughly equal to the <term>equinoctial sine (aksha-jya)</term> directed toward the celestial pole. Taking the calculated latitude as the polar latitude (due to the small difference), and using Bhaskara’s method—"If the latitude deflection arises from the <term>cosine of latitude (lamba-jya)</term>, what would it be for the true latitude?"—and assuming the <term>diurnal circle (dyujya)</term> to be equal to the radius and the rising periods of the signs to be 1800 <note>original: "khakha-ashta-indu" (1800)</note>, the formula for the Latitude Visibility Correction in minutes is:

           Sine of Lat. × Shara     Equinoctial Shadow × Shara
Minutes = ——————————————————————— = ——————————————————————————
             Cosine of Lat.                    12

Following Bhaskara’s rule—"In the case of southern or northern latitude, the application to the longitude is reversed"—the planet, adjusted for the Ecliptic Correction, becomes the "Rising Sign" when subtracted by the Latitude Correction for northern latitudes or added for southern ones. For the "Setting Sign," for a northern latitude, the correction is added (and for southern, subtracted) to the planet plus six signs <note>180 degrees</note>. This represents the point on the eastern horizon when the planet is setting on the western horizon. Here, the Teacher <note>referring to the author of the original verses</note> has subtracted six signs from that value to define the "Setting Sign" as the actual position of the planet on the western horizon at the moment of its setting. ||4||

**Vijnana Bhashya (Scientific Commentary):** Multiply the <term>equinoctial shadow (palabha)</term> <note>The shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note> by the <term>celestial latitude (vakshepa)</term> and divide by twelve. The result in minutes, if the latitude is northern, is subtracted for the rising sign and added for the setting sign. If the latitude is southern, it is added and subtracted respectively. These operations are performed on the planet already adjusted by the Ecliptic Visibility Correction to find the rising and setting longitudes. ||4||

**The Derivation:**

When the planet's position is on the horizon, its physical disk (orb) may be above or below the horizon. One must consider the <term>secondary to the equator (dhruva-prota-vrtta)</term> <note>a great circle passing through the celestial poles</note> passing through the planet's ecliptic position, and another passing through the center of the planet's disk. A <term>diurnal circle (bimbīya-ahorātra-vrtta)</term> is drawn through the center of the disk. The arc of this diurnal circle intercepted between these two polar circles is called the **Latitude Visibility Correction (Aksha-drkkarma)**. Now, from the ecliptic position to the diurnal circle, the true latitude along the polar circle forms one side of a triangle. The second side is on the horizon circle, extending to the intersection of the diurnal circle and the horizon. The third side is a perpendicular circle. The Teacher has treated this as a plane right-angled triangle, where the angle at the ecliptic position is the terrestrial latitude...

<page-num>464</page-num>
<header>In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta</header>

The degrees of the latitude-deflection <note>original: *akshaja-valana*</note> are equal (since it is stated that at the horizon, the latitude-deflection is equal to the sine of the latitude). One angle is a right angle; therefore, the remaining angle is the degrees of the colatitude <note>the complement of the latitude</note>. Then a proportion is made: if the sine of the colatitude <note>original: *lambajya*</note> yields the sine of the true celestial latitude <note>original: *spashta-shara-jya*</note>, then what will the sine of the latitude <note>original: *akshajya*</note> yield? By this, the sine of the arc on the vertical circle or the sine of the arc on the planet's diurnal circle is obtained. Its form is:

<gloss>(1)</gloss> (Sine of True Latitude · Sine of Latitude) / Sine of Colatitude. However,

(Sine of Latitude / Sine of Colatitude) = (Equinoctial Shadow / 12), ∴ (Sine of True Latitude · Equinoctial Shadow) / 12 = Arc-sine of the vertical circle = Arc-sine of the planet's diurnal circle.

Here, due to a small difference, the True Latitude is treated as equal to the Mean Latitude <note>original: *madhya-shara*</note>, and by converting the resulting product into an arc:

(Latitude · Equinoctial Shadow / 12) = the measure of the arc of the planet's diurnal circle. This is not exactly equal to the latitude-based visibility correction <note>term: *Akshaja Drkkarma* — a correction applied to a planet's longitude to find its rising/setting time based on the observer's latitude</note>; therefore, this calculation mentioned by the Teacher <note>referring to Brahmagupta</note> is quite coarse <note>approximate</note>. (1) In this formulation, because the planet's position is at the horizon:

Sine of Latitude = Sine of Latitude-Deflection, and due to the small difference, Sine of True Latitude = True Latitude. Then —

(True Latitude · Latitude-Deflection / Sine of Colatitude) = Latitude-Correction. But (Sine of Latitude / Sine of Colatitude) = (Equinoctial Shadow / 12), ∴ (True Latitude · Equinoctial Shadow) / 12 = Latitude-Correction.

By this, the statement in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* by Bhaskara is justified: "The true celestial latitude multiplied by the latitude-deflection and divided by the sine of the colatitude, or multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by twelve." In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, it is said: "The latitude multiplied by the sine of latitude and divided by the colatitude, or multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by twelve," which is exactly in accordance with what the Teacher said. In the *Surya Siddhanta* as well, this calculation is performed with the phrase "From the equinoctial shadow multiplied by the direction..." and so on. However, the calculation of none of these is perfectly accurate, as is clear from seeing the mathematical proof and the spherical nature of the latitude-based visibility correction. Now, regarding those latitudes, according to Bhaskara's statement "In the celestial latitude, the procedure is direct or inverse in the north and south...":

In the case of **Northern Latitude**, the planet, corrected by the previously calculated precession-correction <note>original: *ayana-phala*</note>, is **decreased** by the minutes of the latitude-correction to find the Rising Sign <note>original: *udaya-lagna*</note>. In the case of **Southern Latitude**, it is **increased**. To calculate the Setting Sign <note>original: *asta-lagna*</note>: in **Northern Latitude**, it is **increased** by the latitude-correction minutes, and in **Southern Latitude**, it is **decreased**. This planet, corrected for precession and increased by six signs <note>180 degrees</note>, represents the point on the eastern horizon when the planet sets on the western horizon, according to Bhaskara's view. Here, the Teacher <note>Brahmagupta</note>, by subtracting six signs from that, considers the resulting point on the western horizon as the planet's Setting Sign. ||4||

---

### Now, the calculation of the Latitude-based Visibility Correction is described:

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiplying the celestial latitude <note>shara</note> by the equinoctial shadow <note>palabha</note> and dividing by twelve (12) gives a result in minutes. If the latitude is **North**, then to find the Rising Sign, one must (1) **subtract** that result, and to find the Setting Sign, one must **add** it. If the latitude is **South**, then one must respectively **add** and **subtract** that result from the planet already corrected by the precession-based visibility correction <note>ayana-drkkarma</note> to obtain the Rising and Setting Signs. (1) Meaning, in the planet already corrected by the previously calculated precession-based visibility correction. ||4||

### Rational Proof <note>Sanskrit: Upapatti; the logical or mathematical derivation of a rule.</note>

When the position of a planet is on the horizon, the center of the planetary disk remains either below or above the horizon. By constructing a <term>declination circle</term> <note>A vertical circle passing through the celestial poles.</note> passing through the planet's position and another through the center of the disk, the arc of the planet's <term>diurnal circle</term> <note>The daily path of a celestial body.</note> contained between them is designated as the **Visibility Correction for Latitude** <note>Sanskrit: Aksha-drik-karma; a correction applied to find the true rising/setting point based on the observer's terrestrial latitude.</note>. In the triangle formed from the planet's position to the diurnal circle, the <term>true celestial latitude</term> <note>Sanskrit: Spashta-shara; the angular distance of a planet from the ecliptic.</note> acts as one side. The second side lies on the horizon from the intersection of the diurnal circle and the horizon to the planet's position. The third side is the perpendicular from the intersection of the diurnal circle and the horizon to the declination circle passing through the planet's position. 

The Teacher <note>Referring to the author of the primary text being commented upon.</note> has treated this triangle as a simple right-angled triangle. In this triangle, the angle at the planet's position is equal to the terrestrial latitude or, more precisely, the <term>latitudinal deflection</term> <note>Sanskrit: Aksha-valana.</note>. Based on the dictum "On the horizon, the latitudinal deflection is equal to the sine of the latitude," one angle is a right angle; therefore, the remaining third angle is equal to the <term>co-latitude</term> <note>Sanskrit: Lambansha; 90 degrees minus the latitude.</note>.

Now, we apply the proportion: If for the <term>cosine of latitude</term> <note>Sanskrit: Lamba-jya.</note> we obtain the sine of the true celestial latitude, then what do we obtain for the <term>sine of latitude</term> <note>Sanskrit: Aksha-jya</note>? From this, the sine of the arc of the perpendicular circle or the sine of the arc of the planetary diurnal circle is derived:

$\frac{\text{Sine of True Latitude} \times \text{Sine of Terrestrial Latitude (A)}}{\text{Cosine of Terrestrial Latitude}}$

However, since $\frac{\text{Sine of Latitude}}{\text{Cosine of Latitude}} = \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{12}$, the formula becomes: $\frac{\text{Sine of True Latitude} \times \text{Shadow}}{12}$

---

$=$ Sine of the arc of the perpendicular circle $=$ Sine of the arc of the planetary diurnal circle. Here, due to a small margin of error, the Sine of the True Latitude $\approx$ True Latitude $\approx$ Mean Latitude. By converting the previous result into an arc, we get $\frac{\text{Latitude} \times \text{Shadow}}{12}$ for the diurnal circle, but this is not exactly equal to the Visibility Correction for Latitude. Therefore, this method described by the Teacher is extremely approximate <note>Literally "gross" or "coarse," meaning it lacks precision.</note>. 

(A) In this form, when the planet's position is on the horizon, the Sine of Latitude $=$ Sine of Latitudinal Deflection $\approx$ Latitudinal Deflection. Thus: $\frac{\text{True Latitude} \times \text{Latitudinal Deflection}}{\text{Cosine of Latitude}} = \frac{\text{True Latitude} \times \text{Shadow}}{12} = \text{Visibility Correction for Latitude}$. 

This validates the statement by **Bhaskara** in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*: "The true latitude multiplied by the latitudinal deflection and divided..." etc. In the *Siddhanta Shekhara*, **Shripati** has spoken in accordance with the Teacher, saying "The latitude multiplied by the sine of latitude and divided by the cosine..." In the *Surya Siddhanta* as well, the Visibility Correction for Latitude is calculated using "The latitude multiplied by the equinoctial shadow..." etc. 

However, it is clear from examining this proof and the region of the latitudinal visibility correction that no one's calculation is perfectly accurate. According to Bhaskara’s statement, "Then, with those latitudes, in the north or south, the rising point is found by the inverse or direct method...": 
1. If the latitude is North, subtract the Visibility Correction minutes from the planet (already corrected for ecliptic longitude).
2. If the latitude is South, add the Visibility Correction minutes to the planet (already corrected for ecliptic longitude).
This gives the **Rising Sign** <note>Udaya-lagna; the point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon.</note>. 

To calculate the **Setting Sign** <note>Asta-lagna; the point of the ecliptic setting on the western horizon.</note>: 
1. If the latitude is North, add six signs <note>180 degrees</note> to the corrected planet and add the Visibility Correction minutes.
2. If the latitude is South, subtract them. 
This gives the longitude of the point on the eastern horizon when the planet is setting on the western horizon, which is the Setting Sign according to Bhaskara. Here, the Teacher has subtracted six signs from that value to accept the actual point on the western horizon where the planet sets as the "Planet's Setting Sign." || 4 ||
